deposito-agua-plegable-hydrapak-seeker-3.resumen: 3 liters in 92 grams with a 42 mm screw-thread filter, and its 10 L version with a tap for the home reserve. An honest review of the HydraPak Seeker: why
deposito-agua-plegable-hydrapak-seeker-3.cuerpo:
HydraPak Seeker 3L and 10 L: the collapsible water container that truly deserves a place in your kit

There comes a point when putting together an emergency kit stops being a checklist and becomes a space problem. Food fits. The radio fits. The flashlight fits. And then water comes along, and everything breaks: three liters per person per day is nine liters for 72 hours, which in 1.5-liter bottles means six bottles per person. Six bottles that take up space, weigh you down, rattle with every step and, when empty, still take up as much room as when full.

The 3-liter HydraPak Seeker tackles that problem from the only angle that works: it removes the container from the problem. It is a 92-gram flexible reservoir that fills when there is water and flattens until it fits in a pocket when there isn't. It is not a hiker's gadget: it is the piece that turns “I carry water” into “I can carry water and, when it runs out, I can go get more.”

What exactly it is (with the manufacturer's spec sheet figures)

The Seeker is a water bag, not a bottle. That changes everything else. These are the figures HydraPak provides and that are worth having on hand before deciding:

  • Capacity: 3 liters (100 ounces).
  • Empty weight: 92 grams. Less than a phone.
  • Dimensions when full: 37 × 14 cm, flat. It fits upright in the side pocket of almost any backpack.
  • Material: TPU with radio-frequency-welded seams, plus polypropylene and nylon in the handle and reinforcements. BPA- and PVC-free.
  • Opening: 42 mm, with a screw cap attached to the bag (so it won't get lost) and a coated canvas handle for pouring.
  • Compatibility: 42 mm screw-on filters — the Katadyn BeFree and the brand's own filter cap. With the Plug-N-Play cap and a 28 mm adapter (sold separately), it can be used as a bladder with a hose.
  • Temperature: it can be frozen and accepts hot water up to 60 °C. It is not a thermos and will not withstand boiling water.
  • Extras: two side attachment points for hanging it or setting up gravity filtration, an external capacity gauge and a carrying bag included.

Reference price: between €20 and €30 depending on finish and store. For what it solves, it is one of the most cost-effective purchases in the kit.

Why 3 liters is the number that fits

Spanish self-protection guidelines use two figures: 1.5 liters per person per day for drinking only and 3 liters per person per day if you also cook with that water. Over 72 hours, that is between 4.5 and 9 liters per person. A 3-liter reservoir does not cover the full scenario, and that is exactly what makes it useful: it covers one full day for one person with a margin, or one day of drinking for two.

That size fits the real logic of a 72-hour kit, which is not “carry all the water” but carry water for the critical stretch and have a way to replenish it. The large reserve stays at home, in 8-liter jerrycans you are not going to move. The Seeker is the part that goes out with you: to the car, to the shelter, to the distribution point, to the public fountain that is still working when the tap at home is not.

If you want the full calculation of how much water a household needs, it is set out in the guide to how much water to store and how to store it. Here the question is different: how do you move it?

The five reasons it beats a jerrycan

1. Empty, it takes up no space. This is the main reason and it does not need much explaining: an empty 5-liter jerrycan is still a 5-liter jerrycan. The empty Seeker folds, flattens and goes into its bag, which takes up less room than a wallet. In an evacuation backpack, where every liter of volume competes with clothing and the first-aid kit, that space is gold.

2. It adapts to the space available, not the other way around. Because it is not rigid, it molds to the shape of the pack, fits in a side pocket, hangs from the carry handle and does not create that uncomfortable pressure on your back that a rigid bottle creates when the backpack is full. In a car trunk the same applies: it goes into any gap between boxes.

3. It turns the source into a tap. Here is what almost no one values until they use it: the 42 mm cap accepts screw-on filters. You fill the bag in a river, an irrigation ditch or a questionable tank, screw on the filter and drink directly or by gravity by hanging it from the attachment points. It is the difference between carrying water and being able to make it. The filters that fit without an adapter are 42 mm screw-on ones, such as the Katadyn BeFree. If the scenario is a flood with the supply cut off or contaminated, that capability stops being a mountain extra and becomes the center of the plan. More on this in the comparison of water purifiers for emergencies.

4. It is useful for more than drinking. Three liters of hot water (up to 60 °C) inside a sleeping bag is a full-body heat pack. Frozen, it is a block of ice that keeps a cooler or a food box cold. With the cap closed, it works as an emergency shower hung from a branch. And when you get home, it can be used to wash dishes during a blackout without using up the drinking reserve. A jerrycan does one thing; this does five.

5. It takes abuse. TPU with radio-frequency-welded seams is the same material used by high-end hydration bladders. It is not a disposable plastic bag: it can be frozen, filled with hot water, stepped on and stored wet without bursting. The brand offers a lifetime warranty against manufacturing defects, which for a €25 product says quite a lot about what they expect from it.

Reading the table is simple: they do not compete; they divide the work. The rigid jerrycan is storage and should not leave the house. The PET bottle is cheap reserve that is rotated every six months. The bladder with hose is for drinking without stopping on the move, if you do sports. The Seeker is transport: the container that goes and comes back, the one you fill at the fountain and put back in the backpack, the one that does not force you to choose between water and space.

Where it falls short (and how to fix it)

No tool is perfect, and this one less than others. What you need to know before buying it:

  • At first it tastes of plastic. This is the first thing people who use it say, and it is true: new TPU leaves a taste in the first fills. It is fixed with two washes of warm water with a little baking soda, leaving it full for a couple of hours and drying it open. After that it disappears. Anyone who does not wash it before the first use will regret it at the worst moment.
  • Full, it does not stand on its own. It is flexible: if you leave it upright on the table, it falls over. It is not a real problem (you hang it from the handle or lean it against the backpack), but if you were expecting a bottle that stands upright, this is not it.
  • It is not for drinking on the move. Without the Plug-N-Play cap and the 28 mm adapter, you have to stop, open it and pour. If your plan is to run with it, buy a bladder with a hose. If your plan is an emergency kit, this detail is irrelevant.
  • The 42 mm cap does not fit 28 mm filters without an adapter. Before buying the filter, check the thread: Katadyn BeFree and HydraPak's own caps yes; many hand pumps no.
  • It is not a storage container. Leaving water inside for weeks is asking the material to get lazy: it picks up taste and grows biofilm. Empty it, dry it open and store it.
  • In a long blackout, three liters run out. It is a transport reservoir, not the reserve. The reserve is the jerrycans at home. Anyone who confuses the two will come up short on the second day.

How I set it up in a 72-hour kit

There is no need to complicate it. This is the setup that makes sense, from smallest to largest:

  1. At home: two 8-liter water jerrycans per person, rotated every six months, plus a water purifier. That is the store and is not touched except in an emergency.
  2. In the evacuation backpack: the empty Seeker (92 g is unnoticeable) and a 42 mm screw-on filter. Total committed weight: less than 200 g, plus the ability to drink from any reasonably clean source.
  3. In the car: a second empty Seeker in the glove compartment or under the seat, with two liters of reserve in PET bottles that are rotated. The reservoir is for refilling at a gas station or a fountain when things drag on.
  4. The routine: before each risk season (DANA season in autumn, wildfire season in summer), check it: dry bag, clean cap, filter within its service life, and a fill test to rule out pinholes.

If you are building the kit from scratch, the correct order is water first and equipment afterward. The guide to the basic 72-hour kit has the 21 essentials ordered by priority; the mountain kit and the evacuation kit are the two scenarios where this reservoir fits best, and the guide to which evacuation backpack to buy tells you which pocket it goes in.

The bigger brother: the 10-liter Seeker

If your problem is not moving water but keeping it still in one place, the same bag exists in 10 liters. It is 261 grams empty and 49 cm tall, and it comes with a Plug-N-Play cap and a camp tap (Camp Tap): you hang it from a beam, a door frame or the tent fly and serve water with one hand, without lifting anything. That detail is what separates it from a jerrycan: a jerrycan has to be tilted, while this stays hanging and you just open the tap.

The numbers match the official recommendation. Ten liters is almost exactly the three liters per person per day that the guidelines call for over 72 hours: for one person it covers all three days, and for a family of three it covers the first day without touching the rest of the reserve. Full, it weighs 10 kilos, so it stays where you put it; empty, it takes up less than a folder and, well dried, it does not pick up odors between emergencies.

It can be frozen, accepts hot water up to 60 °C, is made of BPA- and PVC-free TPU and shares the range's filter compatibility. In an apartment, its natural place is the back of a closet: fill it on the day of the warning, hang it in the kitchen or bathroom and empty it when the warning passes.

View the HydraPak Seeker 10 L on Amazon

The combination that makes sense is that one: 3 liters to go and come back, 10 liters to hold out. With both you have 13 liters of capacity and, empty, they do not even take up the space of a shoebox. It is the water reserve for a small home without giving up a single centimeter of closet space.

Who it is for and who it is not

Buy it if: you have or are putting together a 72-hour kit, an evacuation backpack, a car kit or a mountain kit; you live in a flood, wildfire or supply-cutoff area; or you simply want to be able to take water from a source without carrying bottles. For €20–€30 it has one of the best weight-to-usefulness ratios in the entire kit.

Do not buy it if: you are looking to store water at home (you need rigid jerrycans), you want to drink without stopping while running (you need a bladder with a hose), or you expect a bottle that stands upright on the table. Also not if the plan is to boil water inside it: it is not a pot.

The verdict

The Seeker 3L is not the flashiest product in an emergency kit and is probably the one you will use most often when there is no emergency at all: a hike, a beach day, a car trip, refilling at a fountain. That is exactly the argument in its favor. A kit that is only used in catastrophes rusts away in the closet; one that leaves the house now and then gets known, tested and kept at hand on the day it is needed.

If you want it for your kit, here are the two exact listings: the 3-liter one for carrying and the 10-liter one for the home reserve.

Seeker 3 L   Seeker 10 L

And if you prefer to put together the complete kit rather than going piece by piece, start with the basic 72-hour kit: it has the 16 pieces that are actually used, with their priority and approximate price.

One last piece of advice worth more than the reservoir: fill it before you need it. The day of the weather warning is not the day to discover that the cap does not seal.

mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.titulo: Best butane gas heater for a power outage (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.resumen: Butane, pellets or induction: which is the best heater for a winter power outage, how much does it cost to heat a room and why butane still wins.
mejor-estufa-gas-butano-apagon.cuerpo:
Why butane is still the smartest choice for cold weather

In a winter blackout, grid heating becomes an unattainable luxury. Electric radiators consume too much energy to be sustainable without a grid, pellet stoves need electricity to power the hopper and fan, and induction is simply unviable without a plug. That leaves gas —butane, propane or LPG— as the only independent, powerful and predictable heat source that does not depend on batteries or liquid fuel.

Butane, specifically, remains the most widespread option in Spain: the distribution network reaches 99.6% of households and a 12 kg cylinder can be found at any supermarket, gas station or hardware store within an hour. That, added to its price per kilowatt-hour (generally between 0,06 and 0,10 €/kWh), makes it the cheapest way to heat a home when the power goes out.

In this comparison we evaluate five butane heaters available on the Spanish market in 2026, assessing performance per euro, safety, real consumption and ease of use. All are designed for blackouts and extreme cold, not for heating a garage in summer.

Quick comparison: the five standout heaters

Fiamma Sirocco 40004,000~290 g/h at max.Up to 60 m²4.0 kg~140 €

Consumption figures are theoretical at maximum power; in real use, a heater in intermittent mode (on only when the temperature drops below 18 °C) consumes 30 to 50% less, because the thermostat cuts the supply when the target temperature is reached.

1. Bondhuys 4S: the queen of value for money

The Bondhuys 4S is undoubtedly the heater that offers the best balance between power, price and safety. With 4,000 watts, it heats a 50-60 m² room in 10-15 minutes even when outside temperatures are at zero degrees. Its adjustable thermostat maintains a constant temperature from 15 to 30 °C without abrupt cycles, and the electronic ignition system (no batteries required) is reliable and fast.

Most notable is its weight: only 3.9 kg including the cylinder, which makes it ideal for carrying from one room to another. The hot air outlet nozzle is adjustable, allowing you to direct the flow toward the area in use without risk of burns, and the non-slip base prevents accidental movement.

In terms of safety, it has double protection: tilt cut-off and oxygen depletion cut-off (alpha sensor). If the heater tips over or the O₂ concentration drops below 19%, it switches off automatically in less than three seconds. It is essential, however, to ventilate the room for at least two minutes a day to renew the air (opening a window ajar for a couple of minutes is enough).

View Bondhuys 4S on Amazon

2. Fiamma Sirocco 4000: the Italian option for reliability

Fiamma is an Italian brand with decades of experience in heating systems for vehicles and outdoor use, and the Sirocco 4000 brings that experience to the home heater. Its 4,000 watts perform stably for hours, and its design includes a gas preheating system that improves combustion and reduces emissions.

The Sirocco stands out for its precise digital thermostat (accuracy of ± 0.5 °C), ideal if there are children or older people at home and you need to maintain a specific temperature without surprises. The LCD screen shows the ambient and set temperature, something the Bondhuys does not offer.

The only advantage of the Bondhuys over the Fiamma is price: the Fiamma usually costs about 10-15 € more. But if thermostat precision and combustion quality are priorities, the Sirocco is worth it.

View Fiamma Sirocco 4000 on Amazon

3. Cosmos 4000: the budget option with power

The Cosmos 4000 is the option for those seeking maximum power at the lowest price. With 4,000 watts and a usual price below 110 €, it offers the same performance as its mid-range competitors in terms of power, but with somewhat simpler finishes: the casing is thinner, the thermostat finish is analogue (no screen), and the exhaust pipe orientation is not as precise.

However, for an emergency blackout, it is more than enough. Its draught-proof thermostat works well even in rooms with draughts (doors ajar, poorly insulated windows), and the electronic ignition is reliable. The weight (4.5 kg) makes it a little less portable than the Bondhuys, but for a fixed heater in a living room it is not a problem.

View Cosmos 4000 on Amazon

4. Falco 3000 Comfort: moderate power, low consumption

The Falco 3000 Comfort sits at an intermediate point: 3,000 watts (instead of 4,000) but with reduced consumption (~220 g/h at maximum) and a more compact design (3.5 kg). It is ideal for small rooms (30-45 m²) or for those who don't want overwhelming heat, but rather to maintain a pleasant temperature with minimum butane use.

The Comfort function includes a night mode that automatically reduces power by 30% during the least active hours, extending the life of the cylinder. The thermostat is digital and easy to program. It is the best option if your priority is efficiency and the heater will be on for many hours (prolonged blackouts).

View Falco 3000 Comfort on Amazon

5. Comet 2200 Classic: the tabletop heater

The Comet 2200 is the smallest option in the comparison: 2,200 watts, 2.9 kg weight and a size that fits on a bedside table or countertop. It is not a heater for heating an entire living room, but it is for warming hands, feet or a specific reading area. It is perfect as a supplementary heater or for small bedrooms.

The Comet shines in portability: it fits in a backpack, can be taken anywhere and consumes very little (160 g/h at maximum power). A 12 kg cylinder can last more than 40 hours at medium power. For a blackout where the priority is keeping children warm in their room while the rest of the house is heated with another, more powerful heater, it is an excellent tool.

View Comet 2200 on Amazon

Real consumption: how many hours a 12 kg cylinder lasts

A 12 kg butane cylinder provides approximately 3.6 kW/h of thermal energy (butane has a calorific value of 0.3 kWh per gram). Translated into hours of real use:

HeaterMaximum powerHours at max.Hours at medium power
Bondhuys 4S4,000 W~10-12 h~20-24 h
Fiamma Sirocco 40004,000 W~10-12 h~20-24 h
Cosmos 40004,000 W~10-12 h~20-24 h
Falco 3000 Comfort3,000 W~13-16 h~26-32 h
Comet 22002,200 W~17-20 h~34-40 h

For a household that uses a 4,000 W heater at medium power during a three-day blackout: it needs approximately two or three 12 kg cylinders. With typical Spanish winter temperatures (0-8 °C), one cylinder can last between two and three days with intermittent use (thermostat activated).

If you want to prepare your reserve before the cold arrives, take a look at the cold/winter kit, which includes not only the heater but also thermal blankets, warm clothing and window insulation.

Mandatory safety rules

No matter which heater you choose, these rules are non-negotiable:

  • Minimum ventilation: open a window ajar for at least 5 minutes a day to renew the air. Combustion consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide; a high concentration causes drowsiness and, in the worst case, suffocation.
  • CO detector: a carbon monoxide detector in the same room or the adjacent one. Although modern heaters have an alpha sensor, CO can accumulate due to pipe leaks or poor combustion. The detector is not an extra: it is mandatory. View CO detectors on Amazon.
  • Never use a butane heater in a sealed space: without ventilation, the CO₂ concentration rises and the effects of drowsiness appear before you realize.
  • Keep the heater more than one meter away from any flammable surface: curtains, bedding, fabric furniture. The exhaust pipe can reach 80-100 °C.
  • Do not leave the heater on unattended: especially if there are children or pets. Even with a tilt cut-off, an accident can happen.
  • Store cylinders in a cool, ventilated place, never inside the home: a butane cylinder is a pressure vessel; heat expands it and can cause an explosion if it overheats.

Butane vs pellets: which is better during a blackout?

A pellet stove is efficient (0,04-0,06 €/kWh) and clean (carbon-neutral CO₂ emissions), but it needs electricity to power the hopper and combustion fan. During a blackout, it only works if you have an SAI or a connected power station, which makes the system more expensive.

The butane heater, by contrast, is completely self-contained. It does not need electricity, starts immediately (without preheating), and the cost per hour is competitive: one hour at maximum power costs between 0,09 and 0,11 € (290 g of butane at ~0,38 €/kg). For a blackout lasting a couple of days, the cost difference is minimal and the convenience of instant on/off is non-negotiable.

If your scenario is a long blackout (more than five days) and you don't want to depend on cylinders, the solar option may be more cost-effective in the long term. But that is another topic: check the comparison of best portable solar kit for home.

Final verdict

The best butane heater for a 2026 blackout is the Bondhuys 4S: maximum power (4,000 W), competitive price (~130 €), light weight (3.9 kg) and a complete safety system. It offers the best balance for an average Spanish household that wants to get through a couple of days without heating without getting too cold.

If thermostat precision is your priority and you don't mind paying about 10 € more, the Fiamma Sirocco 4000 is an excellent alternative. If the budget is tight, the Cosmos 4000 offers the same performance for 20 € less.

And don't forget: a heater doesn't solve everything. You need water, food, light and communications. The blackout kit has everything else organized by priority.

mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.titulo: Best PMR446 walkie-talkie (2026): 3 legal models tested for emergencies
mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.resumen: Comparison of the 3 best PMR446 walkie-talkies for emergencies: real range, battery, durability and price. From 15 € to 70 €.
mejor-walkie-talkie-pmr446-largo-alcance.cuerpo:
Best PMR446 walkie-talkie for emergencies (2026): comparison

When mobile networks go down and you can't alert your family, a PMR446 walkie-talkie is the only legal means of communication without a license. But not all models reach the same: the theoretical range of 3-5 km drops to a few hundred metres in the city, and the cheapest ones lose battery within hours. In this comparison I tell you exactly which one is worth it for your emergency kit, with real-world range data, battery time and price.

Spanish Civil Protection recommends carrying alternative means of communication to a mobile phone for emergency situations (Family Plan 112). PMR446 is the only radio you can use without a license throughout the EU, and in a DANA or a power cut lasting several hours it is your only way to coordinate with the family without relying on phone batteries.

28 April 2025 showed what preparedness guides have been repeating for years: when all mobile networks collapse at once, you are left mute. WhatsApp doesn't work, calls aren't cut off — they simply don't exist. And in a DANA or prolonged blackout, the antennas can be left without electricity for days.

What is PMR446 and why don't you need a license?

PMR446 means 'Portable Mobile Radio' and operates on 446 MHz with a maximum of 2 watts of power. It is a harmonised European standard: in any EU country you can use a PMR446 walkie-talkie without a license, without exams, without fees. You only have to respect the conditions of use: fixed antenna (non-removable) and maximum power of 2 W.

This is important: PMR446 does not compete with the amateur radio band (which requires a license) or with professional firefighter radios. It is a tool for short-distance communications between private individuals, ideal for emergencies where telecommunications infrastructure has collapsed.

The 3 best PMR446 walkie-talkies for emergencies

I have selected these three models based on three criteria for emergencies: real range (not the theoretical catalogue figure), battery life and resistance to harsh conditions. The price is approximate and may vary on Amazon.

1. Motorola CP136 — The king of reliability

Motorola is the absolute reference in portable radios. The CP136 is a basic but tough walkie-talkie, with a real range of 1-2 km in urban environments and up to 3-4 km in open country. The 800 mAh battery easily lasts 12-15 hours of intermittent use (normal in an emergency).

Strengths: IP54 resistance (protection against dust and splashes), sealed keypad, integrated emergency LED flashlight. It is the model that has been in the catalogue the longest (more than 10 years) and therefore has more accessories and spare parts available. It is the most sensible option if you are looking to 'buy and forget' for years.

Price: €20-30 per unit. For a family pack of 2-4 units, the cost is competitive.

2. Midland G10 Connect — The most modern

Midland G10 Connect is the most technological walkie-talkie in this comparison. It includes built-in GPS (to share location), text chat and Bluetooth connection with your mobile. It is ideal if you want not only to communicate by voice but also to share your position with the family in an emergency.

Real range: 1-3 km in urban areas, 4-5 km in open country. 1500 mAh battery (more than the Motorola), but GPS consumes it: without GPS active it lasts 12+ hours, with GPS active it drops to 4-6 hours.

Price: €50-60 per unit. It is expensive for what it is, but if built-in GPS is important for your family plan, it may be the best candidate.

3. Altel A-308 — The smart budget option

Altel A-308 is a genuine PMR446 walkie-talkie, with 16 CTCSS channels, LCD screen and real range of 800 m - 1.5 km in the city. It has no GPS, no Bluetooth, no flashlight: it is a walkie-talkie for what it is good for. But it does its job at a very competitive price.

The 900 mAh battery lasts between 10 and 14 hours with normal use. It is resistant to moderate knocks and the antenna is removable (so you have to be careful not to lose it). It is the option for large families: with 4-5 units you have coverage for the whole family without a large outlay.

Price: €12-18 per unit. The best value for money in the comparison.

Tips for using walkie-talkies in emergencies

Having walkie-talkies is not enough: you need to know how to use them correctly in an emergency. These tips come directly from Civil Protection guides and the Family Plan 112:

1. Put all walkie-talkies on the same channel before the emergency. Channel 1 is the most universal (it has no CTCSS sub-tone), so any PMR446 walkie-talkie can hear it. Set up all 16 channels and note in the family plan which channel is used for what (channel 1 = general emergency, channel 2 = meeting point).

2. The 'push-to-talk' rule: to speak, you have to press the button. It is not enough to speak. And when you finish, release the button to listen to the reply. Under the stress of an emergency people tend to speak without pressing the button — the person on the other side cannot hear you.

3. Spare batteries: carry at least two sets of rechargeable batteries per walkie-talkie. AA batteries are the easiest to find in any camping or DIY store during an emergency.

4. Test the walkie-talkies before you need them: use them every 3-4 months to check that they work. NiMH batteries lose capacity over time if they are not recharged periodically. A walkie-talkie that won't turn on in an emergency is more dangerous than not having one.

How many walkie-talkies do you need?

For a family of 4, the recommended minimum is 2 PMR446 walkie-talkies (one for each adult, who can share them with the children). If you have older children (over 10), one per person is advisable: 4 walkie-talkies for a family of 4.

For groups of more than 8 people (neighbourhood communities, groups of neighbours in an emergency), the advisable thing is to have a central communication point (a walkie-talkie always switched on and monitored in each entrance hall or common area) and other walkie-talkies distributed among the volunteers.

The verdict

For most Spanish families, the best PMR446 walkie-talkie for emergencies is the Motorola CP136: it is the most reliable, the easiest to use and has a reasonable price. If your budget is tight, the Altel A-308 does the job at half the price.

If you think GPS is essential for coordinating the family, the Midland G10 is worth it, but be prepared to charge it every 4-6 hours if you use it with GPS active.

Important: all models in this comparison are certified PMR446 (fixed antenna, maximum 0.5-2 W). Radios such as the Baofeng UV-5R or any FRS-band walkie-talkie (e.g. Motorola T460) are not legal in Spain without an amateur radio license: they exceed the permitted power, have a removable antenna or use non-harmonised frequencies. Don't put them in your kit even if you find them cheaper: you expose yourself to a penalty from the Undersecretariat of Telecommunications and to interfering with emergency services.

Remember: a walkie-talkie without batteries is not a walkie-talkie. And a walkie-talkie you haven't tested in an emergency can fail you just when you need it. Buy the walkie-talkies, put them in your emergency kit and test them every few months.

If you don't yet have your basic emergency kit, I recommend starting with our basic 72-hour kit — walkie-talkies come just after water and food in importance. And if you are interested in radiocommunication in general, here is the complete guide to the PMR446 band.

mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.titulo: Best car battery jump starter (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.resumen: Comparison of portable car battery jump starters: what power you need, what it won't start, and which one Protección Civil chooses for emergencies
mejor-arrancador-bateria-coche.cuerpo:
A car that won't start because of a flat battery is one of the most common roadside emergencies, and not all of them involve a broken alternator. In winter, deep discharges are the leading cause; in summer, heat accelerates cell degradation. A portable jump starter (also called a booster or jump pack) lets you get the car going without needing a neighboring car or waiting for a tow truck.

What a jump starter is and what it's for

A jump starter is a compact lithium-ion battery, with clamps or alligator-style hooked cables, that connects to the car battery (or directly to the positive and negative terminals) to supply the amperage the starter motor needs. A petrol car needs 200–300 A of cranking current (CCA); a diesel, 400–600 A. The booster charges from the car's cigarette lighter and holds enough for 20–60 full starts on a single charge.

Unlike jumper cables, a booster doesn't connect two cars in parallel or require another vehicle nearby. That makes it the ideal tool for secondary roads, dead-end underground car parks, or winter nights when no one is around.

Protección Civil includes roadside first-aid tools as part of the vehicle safety kit, and a portable jump starter is by far the most versatile: as well as starting the car, many models include an LED flashlight, a USB charger for your phone, and a tyre air compressor.

The 5 best jump starters compared

I've compared 5 representative models from the Spanish market, ordered from highest to lowest starting power. The key isn't the lowest price, but the real capacity (mAh and starting A) and whether reverse-polarity and short-circuit protections are included — without them, you can damage the car's alternator.

ModelStarting (A)Capacity (mAh)ExtraApprox. price
Ozito 2000 Peak A2000 A20000 mAhFlashlight, USB-C, compressor120–150 €
NOCO Boost Plus GB401000 A10000 mAhFlashlight, USB, non-slip hook100–130 €
YUENGEN 3000 Peak3000 A25000 mAhFlashlight, USB-C, digital display80–110 €
Baseus Jump1200 A20000 mAhUSB-C, flashlight, display60–80 €
PowerTank 40004000 A30000 mAhCompressor, flashlight, USB-C, display150–180 €

Which one you need depending on your car

Not all cars need the same power. A small petrol city car (1.0-1.2 L) starts with 500 A from a booster; a compact diesel (1.6-2.0 L), with 800-1000 A; a diesel SUV or van, with at least 1500 A. If you live in a very cold area (northern plateau, inland), go up at least one step: cold reduces the battery's effective capacity by 30% and the starter motor needs more force to move more viscous oil.

The DGT reminds drivers that extreme weather conditions increase demand for roadside assistance. A good-capacity booster saves you from depending on tow trucks and 2-4 hour waits when you don't need them.

Common mistakes when buying a jump starter

  • Buying the cheapest one without protections: models without reverse polarity protection can damage the alternator. Always look for "reverse polarity protection" in the specifications.
  • Thinking 500 A is enough for a diesel: a 1.6 TDI needs at least 800 A; with 500 A the booster cuts out mid-start and you'll have to wait for it to recharge before trying again.
  • Not recharging it every 3 months: lithium boosters self-discharge by 2-5% per month. If you leave it untouched for a year, it will reach an emergency at 0%. Recharge every quarter and you'll have a battery ready to go.
  • Forgetting the flashlight: a 20000 mAh booster usually has an LED flashlight with SOS mode. In a broken-down car in the dark, a built-in flashlight is worth more than an extra pack.

Checklist: before you buy

  1. Check your car's engine type (petrol or diesel) and engine size → that dictates the minimum amperage.
  2. Make sure it includes reverse polarity and short-circuit protection.
  3. Check that it has at least one USB-C port (to charge your phone during the breakdown).
  4. Consider whether you need a built-in air compressor: in winter tyres lose pressure and a manual compressor is torture with freezing hands.
  5. Look for a model with a digital display: it shows the remaining battery percentage without having to press buttons.

Maintenance: make sure it works the day you need it

Portable jump starters use lithium-ion cells (usually 18650). To extend their useful life:

  • Recharge at least every 3 months, even if you don't use it.
  • Store it in a dry place at room temperature (between 10 and 25 °C). Extreme cold reduces capacity; heat degrades it.
  • Before winter (October-November), do a full charge and check the indicator. If there's no reading, the internal battery may be dead.
  • Don't leave it in the cabin if you live in areas with very hot summers: the dashboard can exceed 60 °C and permanently damage the cells.

Verdict

For most petrol cars: the Ozito 2000 Peak A or the YUENGEN 3000 Peak offer the best power-to-price ratio. For mid-size diesel: the Ozito 2000 Peak A is the sweet spot. For SUVs, vans, or extreme climates: the PowerTank 4000 gives you the most margin for error.

The NOCO GB40 is the recognised-brand option with proven reliability, albeit at a premium price. If you're looking for a reliable booster to keep in the boot at all times without worrying about anything, and you don't need a compressor, it's a safe choice.

paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.titulo: Solar panels without a battery: what kit do you need if your house has island mode (2026)
paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.resumen: A real question from a reader in Málaga with 16 panels and backup in island mode without a battery. The answer: 4 layers of kit, from blackout to power station, with
paneles-solares-sin-bateria-que-kit-nece.cuerpo:
A real question from a reader in Málaga: “What kit would you recommend for a family of 2 adults, with a detached house, 16 solar panels (no storage battery but with a backup system to use the power generated by the panels in island mode) in the Málaga area?”

It is the best question we have received this month, because it describes a house that is almost ready: plenty of solar generation and island capability, but zero storage. Let’s answer it properly, because the answer is not “buy the most expensive kit”.

What you already have (and don't need to buy)

A detached house with 16 panels and isolated feed-in (“island mode”) has solved the hardest problem of a blackout in an urban home: some electricity of its own while the sun is shining. Most people preparing an emergency kit start from zero; this house starts with an advantage. Málaga is also one of the sunniest areas in Europe, so daytime generation is not the bottleneck.

What the house already covers: fridge and freezer during daylight hours, LED lighting during the day, charging phones and laptops, and even some occasional appliances at midday.

The real gap: night and grey days

Without a battery, the system isolates load from generation: instantaneous consumption has to come from the panels. So the weak point appears:

  • At night: no sun, no power from the panels. The house depends on the grid again… and in a blackout the grid is not there.
  • On cloudy or stormy days: generation drops by 70-90%. If the outage coincides with a storm (the DANA of October 2024 in the Valencia region, for example), you have minimal generation just when you need it most.
  • At consumption peaks: a hob, an oven or an irrigation pump can exceed the instantaneous power available in island mode.

And beware: island mode has a risk of its own. If the grid comes back and the backup system does not switch over properly, it can feed energy into the grid (danger for the technicians repairing it) or conflict with the meter. Anti-islanding protection is mandatory and is checked during an inspection; if your installer has not reviewed it for years, now is the time.

The recommendation: four layers, in this order

1. Blackout Kit — the non-negotiable base (90-200 €)

No matter how good the solar installation is: on 28 April 2025 the Iberian Peninsula went more than 12 hours without power, and houses with their own isolated generation fared best… especially those that also had the basics. Complete Blackout Kit (90-200 €): battery-powered LED lamps with magnets, head torches, battery radio, CO detector, gas hob with cylinders, a large power bank and ice packs for the fridge. With daytime generation covering the fridge and device charging, this base is inexpensive and highly effective.

2. Portable solar storage — filling the night-time gap (400-1.200 €)

Here is the highest-impact improvement: a power station (portable power station, 500-1,000 Wh, LiFePO4). It is not a home battery: it is a standalone unit that you charge with your own panels during daylight hours and that gives you light, fridge and electronics at night. Compare options in Best power station for blackouts at home (2026) and Best portable solar kit for home (2026). Since the house already has panels, the power station does not need to include a panel: it can be charged from the system itself in island mode (or with the kit's folding panel if the system isolates the load).

3. Electricity Kit — completing the energy setup (100-500 €)

Electricity Kit: 60-100 W folding backup panel, 20,000-27,000 mAh power banks with AC or USB-C PD output, rechargeable LED area light, head torches, surge-protected power strip and plenty of AA/AAA batteries. It is the domestic complement to the solar kit: the house has “large” daytime generation, but when energy needs to be moved point to point (charging a phone from the power station, lighting a room with the area light), this kit provides flexibility.

4. Risks specific to Málaga: heat, torrential rain and fires

The Málaga area combines three risks that the general kit does not fully cover:

  • Heatwave: the natural hazard that causes the most deaths in Spain. Heat Kit (30-70 €): USB fan, insulated bottle, rehydration salts, cooling towels. In July and August, with no air conditioning if the grid goes down, this is what prevents heatstroke.
  • Cold drops and torrential rain: the Costa del Sol has DANA-type episodes with localized flooding. DANA Kit (90-160 €): drainage pumps, moisture protection, sandbags and barriers. A detached house has more exposed surface area than a flat.
  • Peri-urban fire: if the house sits between an urban area and the countryside, Fire Kit (60-140 €) and the evacuation plan.

What you do NOT need to buy

  • Fuel generator: with 16 panels and island mode, a generator adds little except for power tools or if there are mandatory high loads. It means noise, maintenance, fuel that expires and community regulations. Rule it out.
  • Professional Kit (2.000-5.000 €): it makes sense for someone starting from zero energy-wise. This house already has generation sorted; the gap is only night-time storage, which the power station covers for 400-1.200 €.
  • Second large home battery: if fixed storage is ever wanted, it is a separate project. A portable power station covers 80% of the emergency scenario for a fraction of the cost.

Summary in a table

LayerKitCostWhat it solves
BaseBlackout Kit90-200 €Light, cooking, radio, CO and fridge during the outage
Night-time gapPower station 500-1,000 Wh400-1.200 €Light, fridge and electronics without sun
Flexible energyElectricity Kit100-500 €Power banks, area lights, backup panel and surge protection
Málaga risksHeat Kit + DANA Kit (+ Fire Kit if there is countryside nearby)180-400 €Heatwave, torrential rain and peri-urban fire

The 3-step plan

  1. This week: put together the Basic 72h Kit for 2 people (100-180 €) — the 72-hour water and food reserve that the EU asks for as a minimum.
  2. This month: add the Blackout Kit and the power station. Test your backup's island mode one afternoon: switch off the main RCD, let the system isolate the load, and check what stays on with and without the grid. What you don't test doesn't work.
  3. This quarter: complete Electricity Kit + local risk kits (Heat, DANA, Fire) depending on the exact surroundings of the plot.

Sources and context

  • Blackout: lessons from 28 April 2025 in Spain — what worked and what failed in real homes.
  • Portable solar panel: how many watts you really need — for sizing the power station's charge.
  • Generator vs power station (2026) — why we rule out the generator here.

Frequently asked questions

With 16 panels and island mode, do I need a fixed home battery?

For emergencies, no. A 500-1,000 Wh power station charged from your own panels covers the night (light, fridge, communications) for 400-1.200 €. A fixed home battery is a comfort upgrade for everyday life, not a preparedness requirement.

Can I charge the power station from my rooftop panels in island mode?

It depends on the backup system: many hybrid inverters allow you to dedicate an auxiliary circuit to charging the portable battery during the day. Check with your installer that island mode leaves energy available on the circuit where you plug in the station; if not, the folding panel from the Electricity Kit is the plan B.

What if the blackout lasts more than 72 hours?

The Basic 72h Kit is the European minimum; for 2 people in a detached house, the 30-Day Kit (300-500 €) adds an extra week of water, food and gas without relying on the grid. With the house's solar generation, hot water and cooked food are covered during the day.

Do you have a similar house and doubts about your setup? Write to us: the best answers end up becoming blog articles like this one.

mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.titulo: Best dehumidifier for floods and damp: 4 types compared
mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.resumen: Compressor, desiccant or Peltier: which dehumidifier works after a flood or heavy rain, how much each type costs to run, and the 3-day rule.
mejor-deshumidificador-inundaciones-hume.cuerpo:
Hidden humidity is what destroys the most after a flood or a rainy season. You do not need water to enter the house for walls, clothes, or particleboard furniture to be ruined: 70% relative humidity is enough for the first molds to appear, and above 75% the Stachybotrys fungus—the toxin-producing one—starts to proliferate. In Spain, INMET is clear: ideal indoor relative humidity ranges between 40% and 60%. Above 65%, problems start.

The dehumidifier is the tool that controls that humidity when there is not enough heating to dry the walls or when the rain has left a layer of water that cannot be dried with a cloth. And in a post-flood blackout scenario, when the grid fails and you cannot turn on the car fan to ventilate the living room, it is the difference between recovering your things and burying them.

I compare the three types available in Spain—compressor, desiccant, and membrane—by their power consumption, real capacity, and usefulness in an emergency.

Four types, one goal: 50% humidity

TypeHow does it work?Capacity (L/day)Power consumptionDoes it work in cold?
Compressor (the most effective)Cools the air to condense moisture like a refrigerator in reverse10-50 L/day200-400 WYes, but loses efficiency below 15 °C
Desiccant (salts or silicate)Absorbs water in a hygroscopic material that is reheated to dry it5-25 L/day200-500 WYes, works well at any temperature ✅
Membrane (Peltier)Mini thermoelectric: like a car dehumidifier1-5 L/day30-70 WYes, but very limited capacity
No dehumidifier: cross-ventilation + boraxOpen windows (if it is not raining), silica or borax bagsVariable0 WYes ✅ (only if outside is drier)

Approximate prices in Spain: 20 L/day compressor between 150-300 €, desiccant between 100-200 €, and Peltier between 30-60 €. Compressor units perform better but use more power: if the blackout lasts, a 300 W compressor on a small generator can empty the fuel tank before the heater does.

Best in each category

Highest capacity: the 30-50 L/day compressor. Ideal for a flooded basement or an apartment after a DANA. Brands such as De'Longhi, Pro Breeze, or Mila offer 20-30 L/day models at a reasonable price. View compressor dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Best for cold: the salt-based desiccant. At 5 °C it still extracts 10 L/day, while the compressor drops to 3-4 L. If you live in mountain areas or areas with harsh winters, it is the most reliable option when there is no heating. View desiccant dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Best size/performance ratio: the 3-5 L Peltier for cabinets or small rooms. It is not suitable for a flooded living room, but it is enough to prevent the cabinet from filling with mold after a period of heavy rain. View small dehumidifiers on Amazon.

Free: cross-ventilation with borax (borax crystals, not pure borax). A small borax bag in each cabinet passively absorbs 1-2 L/day. It is not a dehumidifier, but during a blackout it is the option that needs no plug. Borax is sold in hardware stores for 2-5 € per kilo and does not expire.

When to buy it and how to use it

There are two times to use a dehumidifier in an emergency:

  1. Prevention (before): if you live in an area with frequent rain or in a ground-floor apartment, having a 10-15 L/day compressor in the storage room or under the kitchen is like having a closed umbrella that does not get in the way. Plug it in during the rainy season and keep humidity between 45-55%. Power consumption is low: a 15 L compressor uses about 250 Wh/day ≈ 0,04 €/day.
  2. Recovery (after a flood): after a DANA or a flash flood, wet walls take weeks to dry on their own. A 20-30 L compressor will dry a 70 m² home in 3-5 days if it is kept closed (windows closed, room door sealed with plastic). Without one, it can take 2-3 weeks, and mold can appear in 48-72 h.

Three-day rule: if after a flood you cannot dry the home within 72 hours, you will need a medium- or high-capacity dehumidifier (20+ L/day). Engineered wood materials (MDF, particleboard) that get wet and are not dried in time swell and permanently lose their structure: an MDF table that gets wet never returns to the same condition even if it dries.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving the windows open: a dehumidifier does not work if the outside is more humid. During a storm or right after, outdoor air can be 95% humidity; opening the window is like adding fuel to the fire. Close everything and let the machine work.
  • Buying a Peltier for a living room: the 3 L Peltier only works for a drawer or a small cabinet. If the area to dry exceeds 30 m², get a compressor of at least 15 L/day.
  • Not emptying the tank: a 20 L compressor in a very humid apartment can fill up in 6-8 hours. If it fills and you do not empty it, the machine stops and humidity rises suddenly. Set up continuous drainage or remember to empty it every 4-6 hours.
  • Believing that it ventilates: a dehumidifier does not renew the air: it only dries it. If there is visible mold, you need cleaning with diluted bleach (1 part bleach to 10 parts water) before drying. The dehumidifier prevents it from reappearing, but it does not eliminate what is already growing.

Basic dehumidification kit

  • 20 L/day compressor dehumidifier: View models on Amazon — the workhorse, for a normal 70-90 m² apartment.
  • Borax or silica bags: for cabinets and small areas the compressor cannot reach. View dehumidifying bags on Amazon.
  • Digital hygrometer: to measure actual humidity, not guess it. About 8-12 € and it hangs on the wall. View digital hygrometers on Amazon.
  • Concentrated bleach: to clean visible mold before drying. 1 part bleach to 10 parts water. View concentrated bleach on Amazon.
  • Bubble wrap or industrial film: to seal doors and windows during drying. View bubble wrap on Amazon.

Humidity is the number one reason insurers reject post-flood claims: if mold has been growing for more than 30 days, it is considered “progressive deterioration” and not “sudden damage.” That is why acting in the first 72 hours is not a suggestion; it is a contractual obligation.

For the complete list of products after a flood, see the DANA and flood kit and the home kit.

mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.titulo: Best flood drainage pump (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.resumen: Comparison of 5 flood drainage pumps: the most powerful, the quietest and the best value for money. Drains dirty water from your
mejor-bomba-achuite-inundacion.cuerpo:
Best flood dewatering pump: 5 models compared (2026)

A dewatering pump is the equipment that removes water from a flooded house fastest. Unlike a submersible pump (used for wells or pools), a dewatering pump is designed to move dirty water with sand, leaves and debris — exactly what you find when water from a DANA or a flash flood enters your home.

Time is everything: every hour water remains in your house increases structural damage, mold risk and repair costs. A 4,000-liter/hour dewatering pump can empty a flooded garage in 30-45 minutes. Without it, you would have to wait for the water to evaporate (days) or hire a professional cleaning service (thousands of euros).

I have compared the five best models available in Spain for domestic flood use. All include a connection hose and can run on a household outlet or on battery/portable power. The table at the end summarizes the key differences.

What type of dewatering pump do you need?

Before choosing a model, you need to know what type of water you will be pumping. Clean water (a broken pipe) is not the same as dirty water (flooding with mud and debris):

Clean water pump

Only for water without solid particles larger than 2-3 mm. Perfect for draining a basement where rainwater came in through a window, but it is NOT suitable for real floods. Particles clog the impeller and destroy it in minutes.

Dirty water pump (the one you need)

Designed for water with sand, mud and small debris. The maximum particle size it accepts ranges from 5 mm (basic models) to 35 mm (professional models). For a DANA flood, you need at least 10 mm solids capacity.

Wastewater pump

The most powerful: it can handle water with large solid waste (up to 35 mm) and is what Civil Protection teams use. They are more expensive and heavier, but they are the most robust option if the water has carried sand and debris from streets and gardens.

Civil Protection rule: never enter a flooded house without knowing the condition of the electrical installation. Switch off the main breaker before handling any electrical equipment near water.

The 5 best flood dewatering pump models

1. Giena AP 10000 SD — the most powerful in the comparison

Giena AP 10000 SD is a dirty water pump with 10,000 liters/hour and accepts particles up to 35 mm. It is the standout of this comparison: there are not many domestic pumps that reach 10,000 l/h. With 1,000 W power consumption, it can empty a 40 m² garage with 30 cm of water in about 20 minutes.

Pros: massive 10,000 l/h flow rate, maximum head of 8 meters (can pump water from a deep basement), accepts particles up to 35 mm (does not clog with sand or leaves), 4-meter hose included. Cons: weighs 9.6 kg (not the lightest), price is around €250-300.

Ideal for: houses with a basement or garage that have experienced floods with dirty water and debris. It moves more water per hour than any other pump in the comparison.

View Giena AP 10000 SD on Amazon

2. Karcher WS 3/4 — the balanced one

The Karcher WS 3/4 offers 9,000 liters/hour with a reasonable 500 W power consumption. Karcher is synonymous with quality in domestic cleaning and this pump is no exception: robust construction, integrated anti-clogging filter and a compact design that fits in any storage room. It accepts particles up to 5 mm.

Pros: excellent power-to-weight ratio (6.3 kg), brand with technical service in Spain, anti-clogging filter that extends service life, 9,000 l/h for most homes. Cons: only accepts 5 mm solids (not suitable if the water carried coarse sand), maximum head of 7 meters.

Ideal for: households that want a reliable pump, not too powerful but enough for most domestic floods. The perfect balance between price and performance.

View Karcher WS 3/4 on Amazon

3. Vorwerk ATV 100 — the quiet one

The Vorwerk ATV 100 stands out for being extremely quiet (under 60 dB), something crucial if you live in an apartment and do not want to alert the whole building while draining water from the storage room or communal garage. With 8,000 l/h and 550 W, it is not the most powerful, but its noise level is the best in the comparison.

Pros: only 60 dB (quieter than a normal conversation), 8,000 l/h, compact and lightweight design (5.8 kg), ideal for indoor spaces. Cons: does not accept large particles (max. 5 mm), power is not the highest in the comparison.

Ideal for: apartments and buildings where noise is a real limitation. Perfect for draining clean or semi-clean water from storage rooms, underground garages and ground floors.

View Vorwerk ATV 100 on Amazon

4. WAP 22000 — the budget-friendly one

The WAP 22000 offers 8,800 liters/hour at a price around €120-150 — the cheapest in the comparison without giving up serious performance. It accepts particles up to 10 mm, enough for most domestic floods. It is the all-round budget option if you do not want to spend more than €150.

Pros: very competitive price (€120-150), 8,800 l/h with only 450 W consumption, 10 mm solids (accepts fine sand), manageable weight (7.2 kg). Cons: the brand has less presence in Spain (more limited technical service), the included hose is shorter (3 meters).

Ideal for: those looking for an efficient pump without spending more than €150. Perfect for rural houses, villas with a garden or any home that wants to be prepared without overspending.

View WAP 22000 on Amazon

5. Grundfos SB 3-45 — the professional one

The Grundfos SB 3-45 is a Swiss-precision pump: 4,500 l/h, 350 W and reliability that makes many post-flood cleaning professionals always carry it in their van. It is not the most powerful or the cheapest, but it is the one that breaks down least in the long term. It accepts particles up to 3 mm.

Pros: professional brand with 80 years of experience, extremely reliable and durable, only 350 W consumption (saves energy), compact design (3.9 kg — the lightest). Cons: only 4,500 l/h (half that of the most powerful), only accepts 3 mm solids, price close to €200.

Ideal for: those who prioritize long-term reliability over maximum power. A pump that, if stored well, can last 10+ years and will always work when you need it.

View Grundfos SB 3-45 on Amazon

Winners by category

Which pump to choose according to your situation

Not all floods are the same. Here is my recommendation by scenario:

  • DANA/flash flood with dirty water and mud: Giena AP 10000 SD. You need the 35 mm solids capacity and 10,000 l/h: the water will be full of sand, leaves and debris. The faster you remove it, the less damage.
  • Household outlet available: any plug-in model (all in this list). Giena and Karcher are the fastest.
  • No electricity at home: none of the five runs on its own battery (all require an outlet). If the power goes out, you need to connect the pump to a portable solar power station or a portable inverter generator to use it.
  • Urban apartment, underground garage: Vorwerk ATV 100. Silence (60 dB) is critical when you share a building.
  • Tight budget: WAP 22000. 8,800 l/h for €130 is performance far above its price.
  • I want it to last for years: Grundfos SB 3-45. 3.9 kg, 350 W and the reliability of a brand with 80 years.

How to use the dewatering pump safely

Before starting the pump, follow these Civil Protection steps:

  1. Disconnect the electricity at the main breaker. Never put an electric pump in water if the installation is not disconnected. The risk of electrocution is real.
  2. Check that the water is not in contact with electrical outlets or bare wires. If you see wires, do not touch the water under any circumstances.
  3. Place the pump outside the water if it is a surface model (not submersible). Place it on a block or boards so it does not suck up mud from the floor.
  4. Connect the discharge hose and make sure the water is discharged outside the house, preferably at a point lower than the flooded floor.
  5. Start the pump and monitor that it does not clog. If the flow rate drops, switch it off, clean the filter and restart.
  6. Do not leave the pump unattended. Always have someone checking that it is working properly.

If the water is more than 30 cm deep or you cannot disconnect the electricity, wait for Civil Protection teams (call 112). This is not a time for heroics.

Common mistakes when pumping out water

  • Using a clean water pump for dirty water. It clogs in seconds and the motor burns out. Always buy a dirty water pump for floods.
  • Putting the pump in without disconnecting the electricity. Risk of electrocution. Never do it.
  • Forgetting the discharge hose. If you have nowhere to drain the water, the pump is useless. Plan where the water will go before you start.
  • Using buckets and a mop instead of a pump. A flooded house with 30 cm of water has ~6,000 liters in a 40 m² garage. With buckets it would take hours. An 8,000 l/h pump does it in 45 minutes.
  • Not checking the filter. If the pump has a filter, clean it every 30 minutes of use. A dirty filter reduces flow by 50 %.

The dewatering pump in your emergency kit

A dewatering pump is the ideal addition to a flood kit: while the kit keeps you and your family safe as the water arrives, the pump is what you use to recover your home when the water recedes. It is not a luxury: it is a necessity that reduces damage repair costs by thousands of euros.

If you also have a portable solar power station or a portable inverter generator, you can use the pump even when the power is out — which is exactly when you need it most.

Verdict

If you live in an area prone to DANA or flooding (and in Spain, increasingly so), Giena AP 10000 SD is the best option: 10,000 liters/hour and capacity for 35 mm solids. It moves the most water and clogs the least with dirty water.

If you want something more balanced and with the guarantee of a brand with service in Spain, Karcher WS 3/4 is the best value for money: 9,000 l/h for ~€200 with technical service in Spain.

And if the budget is tight, WAP 22000 shows that you do not need to spend €300 to move 8,800 liters per hour: €130 and performance far above its price.

Choose before it rains. Because when it rains hard, there is no time to buy: there is only time to act.

cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.titulo: How much water and food to store at home: Switzerland's official quantities (and what Spain says)
cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.resumen: Switzerland publishes exact household reserve quantities: 9 litres of water per person, food for one week and 50 masks. Spain recommends 72 hours
cuanta-agua-comida-reserva-emergencia-ca.cuerpo:
How much water and food to keep at home: Switzerland's official quantities (and what Spain says)

There's a scene that repeats every time the power goes out in Spain. It's nine at night, your phone dies, you turn on the tap and air comes out, and in the fridge there's food for two days that starts to warm up. No one told you how much water to keep. No one gave you a list with numbers.

Switzerland does. Its Federal Office for National Economic Supply (BWL) has for years published an official household emergency reserve list, with exact quantities per person, and updated it in October 2025. It's not a mountain kit or an extreme survival list: it's what the Swiss state expects you to have in your cupboard at home so that a supply cut doesn't turn into an emergency.

In Spain, the public reference is the famous 72-hour kit. The concept is good, but it comes without numbers: 'water, non-perishable food, flashlight and radio.' And without numbers, every household improvises. Here is the Swiss list translated, compared with what Spanish guides say, and how to put it together in a real apartment.

The Swiss list, with its quantities

The Swiss official recommendation is more specific than we're used to. This is, literally, what they ask you to have at home at all times:

WhatHow much (per person)What for
Water9 litres (a pack of six 1.5 L bottles) and other drinksDrinking and cooking without relying on the tap
FoodFor about 7 days: rice, pasta, oil, tinned food, salt, sugar, coffee, tea, dried fruit, muesli, toasted bread, chocolate, UHT milk, cured cheese, cured meatCover a week without shopping
RadioBattery-powered, with spare batteriesIt's the channel that keeps working when the mobile network goes down
LightFlashlight and spare batteries; candles and matches or a lighterMove around the home without draining your phone
CookingGas stoveEat hot food without mains electricity
Hygiene and health50 masks per person, disinfectant, chronic medication and daily toiletriesProtect yourself and don't interrupt treatments
MoneySome cash at homeIf card terminals and ATMs don't respond

The most important nuance is in the Swiss text, not in the table: the reserve is not designed for a long crisis. It's designed to bridge a temporary supply disruption. That's the difference between 'I can't shop for a week' and 'I have to survive a month in the wild.' That's exactly the same framework as the Spanish 72-hour kit, only with twice the horizon and a quantified list.

What Spanish guides say

In Spain there is no single figure published with Swiss clarity, but the Directorate-General for Civil Protection and Emergencies does recommend keeping a kit at home for the first 72 hours, and regional self-protection guides specify the water: 1.5 litres per person per day as a minimum for drinking alone, and 3 litres per person per day if you also cook with that water.

That gives between 4.5 and 9 litres per person for three days. The 9 litres of the Spanish recommended minimum (drinking and cooking, three days) curiously match the 9 litres Switzerland asks for just to start. The difference isn't the water: it's the time.

Switzerland (BWL/FONES)Spain (Civil Protection)
HorizonAbout 7 days72 hours
Water9 litres per person4.5 to 9 litres per person
FoodA full weekThree days' worth of non-perishables
Masks50 per personNot included in the basic recommendation
Cooking without mainsGas stove explicitlyRecommended, without specific equipment
CashYes, explicitlyCommon in guides, but not all
ApproachClosed list with quantitiesGeneral self-protection framework

Neither is wrong. The Spanish one is easier to adopt and fits most real incidents (a storm, a DANA, a power cut lasting hours). The Swiss one is what happens when a country decides that household preparedness is public policy and writes it down with numbers.

Why water is always the first thing to fail

In Switzerland, drinking water supply is excellent, and yet the state insists on having its own reserve. The reason they give is specific: a single storm is enough to burst a pipe or contaminate the water. You don't need an apocalyptic scenario; you need roadworks, a flood or a pumping failure.

In Spain, there's also a factor Switzerland doesn't have: heat. A person needs more water at 38 degrees than at 15, and during an August power cut there's no air conditioning. So if you copy the Swiss list, do it with 9 litres per person as a floor, not a ceiling: in an apartment without power in July, two people and a pet can easily need 25-30 litres for a week.

And a practical warning: bottled water expires. The reserve is rotated, not stored forever. The BWL itself recommends integrating the food into your cooking routine — consume and replenish — and checking dates. If your bottle is two years old, it isn't a reserve: it's furniture.

How to put it together in a Spanish apartment (with what you can buy today)

Here's the part no official list solves for you: what exactly to buy and how much it costs. This is the household version of the Swiss list, with everyday products and reference prices in Spain.

1. Water: large bottles and a water purifier

For two people, the Swiss baseline is 18 litres. In practice that's two 8-litre bottles per person, which stack in any cupboard and are rotated every six months. Add a water purifier in case the water comes back cloudy: with tablets or a filter you turn questionable water into drinkable water, and that's what makes the difference between 9 litres and a week.

8-litre water bottles on Amazon

Water purification tablets on Amazon

2. Food for seven days, not three

The Swiss list is surprisingly normal: rice, pasta, oil, tinned food, salt, sugar, coffee, UHT milk, dried fruit, chocolate. No astronaut rations. The rule is that it should be food you already eat, so you can rotate it without wasting money, and that at least some of it can be eaten without cooking. With tinned food and dried fruit you cover the scenario where you run out of gas.

See mixed tinned food packs on Amazon

3. Cooking without mains: stove and matches

A gas stove with canisters takes care of coffee and rice when there's no power. This is where most people fall short: they store water and food, but nothing to heat it. And the Swiss detail almost no one copies: long matches and candles, because lighters run out and don't light upside down.

Gas camping stove on Amazon

Lighters and long matches on Amazon

4. Information and light: battery radio and flashlight

When the mobile network goes down, radio keeps broadcasting. That's why Switzerland puts it on the list alongside spare batteries, and why a hand-crank radio is worth its price even if you only use it twice a year. Same for the flashlight: with spare batteries and, if you can, a headlamp to keep your hands free.

Battery-powered FM/AM radio on Amazon

LED flashlight with spare batteries on Amazon

5. What Switzerland added after the pandemic

50 masks per person are the most surprising detail and the one that best explains how an emergency list gets updated: it was added because a health crisis also leaves people without supplies. In an apartment, with 20 FFP2 masks and disinfectant you're more than covered for the household scenario; the Swiss number is calculated for a prolonged emergency.

FFP2 masks on Amazon

6. The Spanish extra: battery and cash

Spain has something Switzerland doesn't need as much: long power cuts with saturated mobile coverage. A charged power bank keeps your phone alive for a full day, and a few banknotes at home solve the shopping when the card terminal won't go through. It's 40 euros you don't want to discover you're missing at ten at night.

10,000-20,000 mAh power bank on Amazon

Total cost of the full list: between 90 and 180 € for one person, counting water, purifier, stove, radio, flashlight, masks, matches and battery. Less than a hotel night for an emergency that catches you at home.

The four mistakes that keep repeating

  • Storing water and not rotating it. Bottled water expires and plastic bottles pick up a taste. Put a date on the cap and change it every six months.
  • Buying food you don't eat. If the emergency cupboard is never touched, it all expires. The Swiss list works because it's normal food that goes into your cooking rotation.
  • Forgetting medication. It's the most critical and most personal point: a week of your chronic treatment, with prescription and in a cool place. No generic kit covers that.
  • Having nothing to heat food with. Water, rice and a stove: without the third, the first two only help you go hungry in an orderly way.

What to copy from Switzerland and what not to

Copy the underlying idea: a closed list, with quantities and a review date. That's what turns preparedness into something verifiable instead of an intention. Also copy the water per person and the week of food if you have the space.

Don't copy the horizon exactly if you live in a small apartment: seven days of food for four people take up an entire pantry. Start with 72 hours done properly — water, food that doesn't need refrigeration, radio, light, first-aid kit — and extend to a week for water and tinned food, where space gives you the most. If you want the ready-made version, the basic 72-hour kit covers the essentials and the power outage kit adds what you only need when there's no mains. And if you want the full Swiss list, with its quantities and links, it's already put together in the Swiss 7-day kit.

What you shouldn't copy is the peace of mind of having it 'noted in your head.' A reserve that isn't counted doesn't exist: the day you need it, you discover you have six bottles and half a bag of rice. Count the bottles tonight. It's the only step on this list that doesn't cost money.

mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.titulo: Best power station for home blackouts: 5 models compared (2026)
mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.resumen: Which power station will keep your home running during a blackout? 5 power stations compared by wattage, capacity and portability, with a winner for each use case (2026).
mejor-power-station-para-apagones-en-cas.cuerpo:
The power goes out at eight at night on a Friday in November. The router shuts off, the Wi-Fi dies, and suddenly you have a home without communications, without power or fridge. The first thought is your phone: 15% battery. The second, the fridge: “how long does it hold with the door closed?”. The answer to both questions depends on the energy you have inside your home — and if you have nothing, here comes the comparison of the five power stations that give the best price-to-hours ratio in a home blackout in Spain.

The context data: Red Eléctrica de España (REE) reported 12 interruptions in 2025, with an average duration of 0.25 minutes per outage. The grid is reliable on average, but the average does not cover the scenario you care about: a blackout lasting more than one night, whether due to a storm, a local distribution failure or an overload of the street transformer. The International Energy Agency estimates that European households lose an average of between 20 and 40 hours of electricity per year when planned outages and extreme events are combined. That is more than a small power station can provide.

1. What a power station is and what is NOT an SAI

A power station (or portable power station) is a large battery with a built-in inverter: it provides 230 V outlets, USB-C, USB-A and, on some models, a solar input. It is the midpoint between an SAI (seconds of protection for the router) and a petrol generator (kilowatts, but with smoke, noise and a municipal permit): more powerful than an SAI, cleaner than a generator.

  • It can run: router, small fridge, power tools, heater, microwave, washing machine (short cycles), lights, computer.
  • It does not replace: a gas boiler (it needs gas from the grid), a continuous induction hob or a residential air conditioner (they demand kW that no portable unit provides).
  • It is NOT an SAI: an SAI switches to battery in milliseconds without interruption; a power station is turned on manually. If you want the router not to blink even for a second, use an SAI — the power station is for when the grid does not come back.

2. The five power stations, compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain (October 2026): each link opens the product category, so you can see today's price rather than the price when this was written.

ModelCapacityContinuous powerPriceBest for
Mini portable (≤100 Wh) ↗80-100 Wh100-200 W80-150 €Only router + phone + light

High-end + solar (1000+ Wh) ↗1000-2000+ Wh1500-3000 W1200-2500 €Multi-day autonomy with panels

The progression is not linear: the price difference between the entry range and the high-end range is 5–8×, but fridge hours multiply by 6. The key decision is which appliance is “essential” for you and for how long you want to power it.

3. The hours calculation: what each power station can run

To calculate runtime, divide the battery capacity (Wh) by the appliance's consumption (W). It's that simple. One detail that matters: the inverter has an efficiency of 80–90%, so a 500 Wh power station actually delivers about 400–450 Wh in practice.

ApplianceConsumptionHours with 500 WhHours with 1000 Wh
Router + ONT15 W~25 h~50 h
LED flashlights (3 units)9 W~44 h~88 h
40-inch LED TV40 W~9 h~18 h
Small fridge (50 L)40-80 W~6-12 h~12-24 h
Family fridge (200 L)100-150 W~3-5 h~6-10 h
Portable charger20 W~20 h~40 h
Microwave800 W~0.5 h~1 h

The conclusion is clear: without at least 500 Wh, you cannot run a fridge. Without 1000 Wh, you cannot run a family fridge. With solar panels connected (the models in the third category and above allow this), a small fridge can run indefinitely on a sunny day — because the battery's 500 Wh are recharged by the sun while the fridge consumes them.

4. Winners by use case

  • Communications only (router + phone + light): a mini portable unit of ≤100 Wh. It is the cheapest option and you don't need anything else if the goal is your phone and the router. See mini power stations ↗
  • Lights, TV and router without a fridge: entry range 200-400 Wh. It gives half a morning of TV or 40 h of router. Ideal for anyone who just needs the home not to go completely dark. See entry range ↗
  • Home with a small fridge: mid-range 400-600 Wh. This is the zone where the price-to-hours ratio is best: ~600 € gives you a full day of fridge, router, TV and light. The option most people choose. See mid-range ↗
  • Home with a large fridge: high-end 600-1000 Wh. If your fridge is a family one and you don't want to open it every hour, you need double the battery. 1000 Wh models give a full day of refrigeration. See high-end ↗
  • Multi-day autonomy with panels: high-end + solar 1000+ Wh. Solar panels recharge the battery during the day, so energy is practically unlimited. It is the ideal complement to the solar generator and the professional kit. See solar portable units ↗

If what you are looking for is complete blackouts: a home without power or internet, the combined solution is an SAI for the router (seconds without interruption) + a power station for the home (hours) + radios for alternative communication. It is all in the blackout kit.

5. The five most common mistakes when choosing

  • Choosing by capacity without looking at power. 500 Wh will not run a fridge if the inverter only delivers 300 W. The inverter's continuous power is the limit: nothing above that number.
  • Buying a 100 Wh unit and expecting it to run the fridge. 100 Wh are router hours, not refrigeration hours. It is like buying a bucket to put out a fire with a garden hose.
  • Ignoring solar recharging. A 3-day blackout with 500 Wh and no recharging runs out after 12 hours of fridge. A model with a solar input and a 100 W panel recharges by itself on a sunny day.
  • Confusing Wh with mAh. mAh is a unit of the internal cell, not of the complete system. A seller can say “20000 mAh” and mean only the Li-ion battery (3.7 V), which is ~74 Wh. Always look at the Wh: it is the real unit of energy.
  • Not checking the weight before buying. A 1000 Wh power station weighs about 9 kg. If you need to carry it up to a second floor or transport it, consider the weight. 300 Wh units weigh ~3 kg and fit in a backpack.

6. Safety, regulations and how it fits into your kit

To buy wisely, make sure the power station complies with the European standard UNE-EN IEC 62133-2:2017 (safety of lithium-ion batteries) and that it includes protection against overcharge, overheating and short circuit. Models that comply with this standard carry the CE marking and are sold in the EU with a warranty.

Maintenance in three lines: recharge it at least every three months (lithium-ion batteries degrade if left discharged), store it between 20–30 °C (a hot garage in summer shortens its life) and test it every six months: plug something in and let it run down to 20% to confirm it works.

CNMC forecasts for 2026 point to greater grid stability thanks to the modernisation of the European electricity system, but the reality is that extreme weather events — heat waves, DANA, snowstorms — are becoming more frequent. Protection against blackouts is not forecasting, it is precaution. The complete list of what you need is in the blackout kit; if you are starting from scratch, start with how to build your 72-hour kit.

Our choice, with the verified link

After comparing the five ranges, the piece we include when the goal is to get through a blackout lasting hours without installation work: a portable solar generator with the panel included, so you don't have to buy half of it somewhere else.

  • OUKITEL P800 — 800 W power station with a 100 W solar panel. Why this one: the panel is included, the 800 W output runs a small fridge, router and lights, and the capacity falls in the range that covers an 8–12 hour outage. It is the one we use in the electricity kit, where you can see today's price.
