mejor-kit-solar-portatil-para-casa.titulo: Best portable solar kit for home (2026): 5 models compared
mejor-kit-solar-portatil-para-casa.resumen: Comparison of 5 portable solar power stations for the home: the one that can handle a fridge, the most balanced one and the one that's enough for phones. Power
mejor-kit-solar-portatil-para-casa.cuerpo:
Best portable solar kit for home: 5 models compared (2026)

A portable solar kit for home is a power station —a stationary battery with an inverter and AC/USB ports— to which one or more flexible solar panels can be connected. The result is a system that charges your battery with the sun and delivers clean electricity, with no noise and no fumes. Unlike a gasoline generator, you don't need to store fuel and you can leave it plugged in for days without supervision.

What is it for in your home? Keeping the fridge, fiber router, mobile phone and lights on during an outage lasting hours or a couple of days. It won't power an entire home (heating, kitchen appliances or the pool pump), but it will power what you really need when the power goes out.

I have tested and compared the five best-selling models in Spain in the 500-1000 Wh category (the one that fits in a suitcase, not in a truck). The table at the end summarizes everything at a glance.

How to choose your solar power station: what really matters

Before looking at brands, there are three numbers that make the difference between a kit that gets you through a blackout and one that doesn't even last until midday.

Real capacity (Wh): how many charges it gives you

Wh (watt-hours) measure how much 'fuel' the battery has. A 500 Wh power station can charge a 60 Wh laptop about 6-7 times (including conversion losses), or keep a 15 W router running for 25-30 hours. With 1000 Wh, you double that.

The practical formula: kit Wh ÷ device consumption in W = hours of runtime. For a home that wants to keep a fridge (100-200 W) + router (15 W) + lights (30 W), the combined load is around 150-250 W. A 500 Wh power station would give about 2-3 hours of fridge use (the fridge opens and closes from time to time, so in practice a little more), while a 1000 Wh one would give 4-6 hours.

For 72 hours of off-grid runtime, you need something more: either a 1500-2000 Wh power station with panels that charge during the day, or a gasoline generator as backup for nights without sun.

Output power (W): what you can plug in at the same time

The output watts indicate how many devices you can have running at the same time. A 300-500 W model is enough for a mobile phone, tablet, router and lights; an 800-1000 W one is also enough for a small fridge, a tool charger or a small TV. If you want to keep a large combi fridge running (300-400 W at startup), you need at least 1000 W continuous and 2000 W peak.

Included panels: how many W and how they fold

The panel is what recharges the battery during the day. A 100 W panel produces about 60-80 Wh real (losses due to temperature, angle and cloud cover) in Spain on a spring-summer day; in winter, half. The ideal is a kit that includes at least one 60-100 W panel and allows you to add another one in series.

The 5 best portable solar kits for home in 2026

1. EcoFlow Delta 2 — the one that handles everything

The EcoFlow Delta 2 (1024 Wh, 1800 W output) is by far the most powerful in this comparison. It charges from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes from a wall outlet and in about 4-5 hours with a 160 W panel. It has an expansion port to reach 2048 Wh if you need it.

Pros: the output power (1800 W) allows a combi fridge, small microwave and tools; ultra-fast charging from a wall outlet; the mobile app to monitor charge and consumption. Cons: it weighs 12 kg and its price (close to €1000) is the highest in this comparison.

Ideal for: homes that want a complete solution for 1-3 days off-grid, with the option to expand to 2000 Wh.

View EcoFlow Delta 2 on Amazon

2. BLUETTI AC200MAX — the robust one

The BLUETTI AC200MAX offers 2048 Wh (expandable to 4096 Wh) and 2200 W output. It is the largest in this comparison: 26.3 kg, but it fits in a garage. It charges from 0 to 80% in 90 minutes from a wall outlet and with solar panels up to 500 W.

Pros: massive capacity for 72 h, expandable with modules, USB-C PD 140 W ports. Cons: the weight (26 kg) limits its real portability and the price exceeds €1500 without panels.

Ideal for: homes with space in a garage or storage room that want maximum runtime without a gasoline generator.

View BLUETTI AC200MAX on Amazon

3. Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro — the perfect balance

The Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro (1002 Wh, 2000 W) is in the sweet spot: more than enough power for almost any household use, 12 kg (not too light but manageable), and a competitive price with included panels (1-2× 100 W). Full charge in 2 h from a wall outlet or about 6-7 h with panels.

Pros: balance between power, weight and price; the monitoring app is simple and reliable; the included panels make it easy to start without complications. Cons: no capacity expansion like the Delta 2.

Ideal for: the average user who wants something powerful but doesn't want a 25 kg station in the garage.

View Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro on Amazon

4. Anker Solix F3800 — the new one with LFP lithium

The Anker Solix F3800 is a newer model with a lithium iron phosphate battery (LFP, which lasts 3000+ cycles instead of the 500-1000 of LFP) and 3840 Wh capacity. With 3600 W output, it is the beast of this comparison. It charges with panels up to 3000 W of solar input.

Pros: LFP technology (much greater durability), enormous capacity, 3600 W output. Cons: price (€2000+), weight (40+ kg) and the fact that it only makes sense if you have the space and budget for a semi-permanent installation.

Ideal for: homes that want a long-term solution, without handling gasoline, that can permanently replace the generator.

View Anker Solix F3800 on Amazon

5. VTOMAN Flash 1500 — the value-for-money option

The VTOMAN Flash 1500 offers 1548 Wh and 2000 W at a price around €700-900 (without panel). LFP battery, touchscreen and USB-C PD ports. It has the best capacity-to-price ratio in this comparison.

Pros: the best Wh per euro ratio (≈€0.98/Wh), LFP technology, 2000 W power. Cons: the brand has less presence in Spain than EcoFlow or Jackery, with more limited technical support.

Ideal for: anyone who wants the maximum capacity for their money and doesn't mind finding technical support on their own.

View VTOMAN Flash 1500 on Amazon

Solar panels: how much they produce in Spain

A 100 W panel in Spain produces, on annual average, between 150 and 200 Wh per day (1.5-2 kWh), depending on orientation and time of year. In winter (December-January), irradiance drops by 40-50%: the same panel delivers 80-120 Wh. In summer, it can exceed 250 Wh.

This means that with a 100 W panel you are not going to recharge a 1000 Wh power station on a cloudy winter day. The key is to have panels that add up to at least twice what you consume per day, and to point them south without shade.

Yes, you can also use the panels with the blackout kit as a complement, but for main use you need something more than a panel hanging in the balcony window.

Portable solar or gasoline generator?

They are not mutually exclusive, and in fact the combination is what most people use. Portable solar charges when there is sun (zero noise, no fumes); the gasoline generator comes in when night approaches and solar charging is over. The generator vs power station comparison details when each one makes more sense.

If your priority is silence, not having to store gasoline and not carrying it up stairs, portable solar is the right path. If you need to power a large fridge for three days without sun, combine solar + generator.

Checklist before buying

  • Capacity ≥ 500 Wh for minimum use (mobile phone, router, lights). ≥ 1000 Wh for fridge included.
  • Output power ≥ 800 W if you want to connect a small fridge. ≥ 1500 W if you also want a microwave or tools.
  • LFP battery (iron phosphate) if you are going to use it long term: 3000+ cycles vs 500-1000 of old LFP.
  • Included panels or at least compatible ones (MC4 or XT60 connectors).
  • Minimum 2-year warranty with technical service in Spain.
  • Weight and dimensions: make sure you can carry it up the stairs if you live in a high-rise flat.
  • Monitoring app: knowing how much battery is left and how many W you are consuming at each moment is essential.

Common mistakes

  • Buying only the power station without panels. The battery drains in a couple of days off-grid and, if you don't have panels, it won't recharge until the power comes back. Always buy the kit with at least one panel.
  • Pointing the panel north or into the shade. A panel in partial shade loses up to 80% of its production. Always point it south, with no obstacles.
  • Underestimating fridge consumption. A fridge consumes 100-200 W on average but draws 300-900 W peak at startup. If the output power is not enough, the fridge won't start and will cut out.
  • Forgetting the connection cables. Panels have MC4 connectors that sometimes don't fit directly into the power station. Check beforehand or bring adapters.
  • Thinking it will power everything. A portable power station is not a construction generator. Turn off heating, air conditioning and induction hobs; keep the essentials running and the sun will keep it on.

Verdict

For most Spanish homes, the Jackery Explorer 1000 Pro is the ideal point: 1000 Wh to keep the fridge and router running, 2000 W output for whatever you plug in, included panels to start without complications and 12 kg that anyone can move. If your budget is tighter, the VTOMAN Flash 1500 gives you more Wh per euro.

If your priority is absolute runtime (72 h+ without sun), the BLUETTI AC200MAX is the most capable, although it weighs 26 kg. And if you want the most advanced model with the highest power, the Anker Solix F3800 is the ultimate beast: 3840 Wh, 3600 W and an LFP battery for years of use.

And remember: a portable solar kit is the energy piece of a blackout kit. Without water, without a first-aid kit and without a radio there is no plan. Start with the basics and add clean energy.

If energy and total autonomy are your thing, the professional energy and autonomy kit includes everything you need (SAI, 800 W of solar panels, LFP batteries, Starlink) to keep your home running off-grid.

mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.titulo: Best portable inverter generator (2026): power, noise and what kills
mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.resumen: How to choose an inverter generator without getting the power rating wrong: start-up surges, real fuel consumption per tank, carbon monoxide and noise with neighbours.
mejor-generador-electrico-portatil-inver.cuerpo:
What an inverter generator is and why it is not the same as a cheap one

An inverter generator starts a petrol engine, produces alternating current, converts it to direct current, stabilises it electronically and converts it back into clean alternating current. The result is a sine wave with distortion below 5%, stable even as the load rises and falls. A conventional generator with AVR delivers a dirtier wave, with the frequency fluctuating according to what you plug in.

What does that change at home? An inverter can safely power the router, laptop, TV, boiler or the SAI of a blackout kit, while a cheap conventional one makes electronics restart, buzz or simply fail to start. During a blackout, almost everything you want to keep running is electronics: that is where the buying decision is made.

The price of that difference is real: an inverter costs more per kilowatt than a conventional generator of the same output. For home use it is worth it; for construction sites and power tools, not always.

How much power you really need (and why peak power changes everything)

Every generator advertises two figures that are not the same: continuous power (what it can sustain indefinitely) and starting or peak power (what it can sustain for a few seconds). The motor of a fridge, freezer or pump does not draw its rated power when it starts: it draws 2 to 5 times more during the first second. If the peak is not enough, the generator stalls or the appliance does not start.

ApplianceContinuous consumptionStarting peak
Class A fridge-freezer100-200 W400-900 W
Freezer100-250 W500-1,000 W
Router + fibre ONT10-20 W—
Laptop60-90 W—
55" LED TV80-120 W—
Six LED bulbs50-70 W—
Boiler circulation pump60-100 W200-300 W
Microwave800-1,200 W—
Drill or power tool500-1,000 W1,500-2,500 W

The correct calculation: add up the continuous consumption of everything you want to have on at the same time and add the peak of the most demanding appliance, not the sum of all peaks. For a flat with a fridge, router, laptop and lights, an inverter with 2,000 W continuous and 2,200-2,400 W peak is more than enough. If you also want to cover the boiler, microwave or power tools, the reasonable jump is to 3,000-3,500 W.

How long it lasts on a tank (the calculation almost nobody does)

A small inverter uses between 0.6 and 1 litre per kilowatt-hour generated, depending on how heavily loaded it is. Translated into tanks: a 4-litre one lasts 3-4 hours at half load; a 10-litre one, 8-10 hours; a 15-20-litre one, a day and a half with intermittent use.

For a 72-hour blackout, that is between 25 and 40 litres of petrol. And that is where the part nobody plans for comes in: storing fuel. Ethanol-free, in approved jerrycans, outside the home, and rotated every three months (with stabiliser it lasts considerably longer). If your scenario is a week or more without the grid, the generator is not the complete answer: first compare generator and power station with solar panels, because you do not have to go and buy solar kWh.

What really kills: carbon monoxide

A generator emits carbon monoxide, which is odourless, colourless and kills without warning. Never indoors. Never in the garage, not even with the door open: the gas builds up inside and rises. Never on an enclosed balcony or an interior drying area. The unit goes outdoors, on a firm surface, with the exhaust pointing away from doors and windows and several metres from them.

And at home, a carbon monoxide detector on the floor where you sleep. It is not an extra: it is the difference between a scare and a tragedy. We cover this in more detail in the comparison of CO detectors.

Noise and neighbours: what the rules say

A 2 kW inverter stays at around 58-65 dB at seven metres; a conventional one goes above 70. There is no specific state law for domestic generators: the municipal noise ordinance applies (typical limits of 55-65 dB by day and 45-55 dB at night in residential areas) and, if you live in a community of owners, the building rules. A generator at full load on a terrace at eleven at night is an almost guaranteed complaint, and in many buildings it is directly prohibited. We explain this in generator and building regulations.

Petrol inverter generator or power station with solar panels?

 Inverter generatorPower station + solar panels
Sustained powerHigh (2-3.5 kW and more)Medium (0.5-2 kWh battery)
DurationAs long as there is fuelUntil the battery and sunshine run out
Noise58-65 dBNone
Fumes and COYes: outdoors onlyNo
MaintenanceOil, spark plug, fuelAlmost none
Cost per kWhLow3-5 times higher
When it winsLong blackouts, fridge, boilerFlat, zero noise, daily use

The combination that works in a genuinely prepared home is mixed: power station and solar panels for the small and permanent loads, generator for what demands a burst of power. If you do not want any kind of combustion, the complete route is the professional energy and self-sufficiency kit, with solar panels and lithium batteries.

Checklist before buying

  • Real continuous power (not the brochure figure) and starting peak.
  • Pure sine wave with declared distortion (below 5%).
  • Tank: from 8-10 litres to last a night without refuelling.
  • Electric start and, if possible, remote control: at three in the morning you do not want to be pulling a cord.
  • Weight and wheels: a 40 kg unit does not get carried up to a third floor on its own.
  • Protection against overload, low oil and automatic shutdown when out of fuel.
  • Technical service with a presence in Spain and a warranty of at least two years.
  • Noise declared at 7 metres, not at one metre.

2 kW inverter options with electric start: see models and prices on Amazon. To cover a boiler or power tools as well, 3 kW models.

Maintenance: make sure it starts on the day you need it

  • Oil change after the first 5 hours and then according to the manual (every 50 hours or once a year).
  • Fresh petrol: no six-month-old fuel. Stabiliser if it is going to sit unused.
  • Start it for 15 minutes once a month, with some load plugged in.
  • Spark plug and air filter checked once a year.
  • Never store it with a full tank for months without stabiliser.

Mistakes that cost you dearly

  • Male-to-male cable to the house consumer unit. It is the fastest way to electrocute a worker repairing the grid in your street. Connect to the consumer unit with a transfer switch; if you do not have one, run extension leads to the appliances.
  • Buying 5 kW just in case. It uses more fuel, is noisier and always runs below its optimum load: it gets dirty and wears out sooner.
  • Not calculating the peak. The generator stalls just as the fridge starts.
  • Using old petrol. The engine will not start and you blame the equipment.
  • Skipping the first oil change. The first five hours are what decide the engine's life.
  • Putting it in the garage. See above: it is the number one cause of CO deaths during blackouts.

Verdict

For a household that wants to get through a one- to three-day blackout without losing the fridge, router or communications, the target is a 2,000 W continuous inverter with electric start and an 8-10 litre tank. If you also want a boiler, microwave or power tools, 3,000-3,500 W. Below 1,500 W you will come up short as soon as a fridge comes on; above 5 kW you will be paying for noise and fuel you do not use.

And remember what a generator does not solve: without water, without a first-aid kit, without portable light and without a radio there is no plan. The full list, with the buying order and what you already have at home, is in the blackout kit and in the basic 72-hour kit.

mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.titulo: Best snow chains 2026: 5 options and when the DGT requires them
mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.resumen: Metal chains, snow socks or winter tyres: 5 options compared by price and use, with what the DGT requires and the most common mistakes.
mejores-cadenas-para-la-nieve.cuerpo:
Every winter it's the same: the snow warning arrives, the mountains fill up, and drivers who are only heading to the fuel station discover they don't have chains, don't know how to fit them, or the ones they bought three years ago no longer fit their current car. Choosing well keeps you from being stranded on a mountain pass with poor visibility—and from arriving late where you were going—and it isn't expensive: the difference between one set of chains and another is twenty or thirty euros.

The Spanish rule is simple, and it bears repeating: there are no fixed dates. The obligation to carry chains (or winter tyres that replace them) is set by the signs on each stretch and by the road conditions reported by the DGT, not by a calendar. Before setting off, the official thing to do is check traffic conditions at dgt.es or mapamovilidad.dgt.es, call 011, or listen to radio bulletins; and if there is an AEMET warning for the area, it is better to postpone the plan. The rest—what to buy, how to fit them and how to store them—is in this comparison.

1. What the DGT requires, in four points

  • The sign rules, not the calendar. Where the chains-required sign is displayed, you cannot continue without chains (or another authorised device). The official sign catalogue was updated by Royal Decree 465/2025, so some maps and manuals show different codes for the same sign: look at the sign on the stretch, not the wording of the regulation.
  • Winter tyres only replace chains if they are marked. The DGT allows driving without chains—when the sign requires them—on tyres marked with the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol (3PMSF); the M+S marking alone is not enough as a substitute. They are designed for temperatures below about 7 °C.
  • Speeds and fitting position: maximum 30 km/h with metal chains and 50 km/h with textile ones; always on the driving axle (both wheels on that axle) and, if the car is four-wheel drive, at the front.
  • Driving with chains is not the same as driving normally: no sudden acceleration or braking, and on road without snow braking distances are longer—remove them as soon as the stretch ends.

2. The five types compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain. Each link opens a search for that type, so you see the price of the day, not the price when this was written. And before you pay, check your tyre size (something like 205/55 R16, on the tyre sidewall or on the driver's door): a chain that is not your size is not a chain, it is extra weight in the boot.

TypeWhen it is worth itLimitIndicative price
Metal link chains ↗The benchmark: valid on any stretch with a sign, lasts for years30 km/h30-80 €
Quick-fit chains (tensioner) ↗Fit in half the time and with cold hands: same rules, more convenient fitting30 km/h50-130 €
Textile snow socks ↗Fit in a minute without getting dirty; valid where the road allows textile devices50 km/h20-55 €
Winter tyres 3PMSF ↗Snowy area or weekend trips every week: they replace chains where the sign requires themAccording to tyre60-120 € per wheel
All-season tyres ↗No seasonal change; in repeated snow they perform less well than a proper winter tyreAccording to tyre70-140 € per wheel

3. Winners by case

  • Most drivers (an occasional trip to the mountains): metal chains in your size, basic ones properly adjusted. They are accepted on all roads and are the cheapest thing that really works.
  • You live in a snowy area or go up several weekends in a row: 3PMSF winter tyres. With them you comply where the sign requires chains, and you don't spend the rest of the year with a set of chains taking up space in the boot.
  • Cold hands, in a hurry, or have never fitted them: textile snow socks on stretches that allow fabric (they are the quickest to fit)—and if you don't know whether your route allows them, metal chains.
  • Off-road and unpaved tracks: metal chains with a tensioner, always; gloves and a headtorch in the same bag as the chains.
  • Tight budget: better a basic chain in your size than a “cheap” one in another size. The following year add the gloves and the torch.

4. How to fit them, according to the DGT itself

  • Stop in a safe place, off the carriageway and without a slope: better to drive the car into a wide car park than to stop on a hard shoulder with poor visibility.
  • Driving axle: front if the car is four-wheel drive; rear if it is rear-wheel drive. Both wheels on that axle, never “one on each side”.
  • Fitting: rigid ring behind the wheel, centred, outer ring, tensioner, and hook up the excess so it does not hit the wheel arch.
  • Drive gently, without sudden acceleration or braking, and remove them when the snowy stretch ends: on clean asphalt they get in the way and wear down.
  • When storing: wash and dry them. Road salt corrodes them from the inside, and a rusty chain breaks just when you need it most.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Not trying them beforehand. The first fitting in a car park with warm hands takes two minutes; on a snowy mountain pass without gloves, twenty. Do it once at home.
  • Buying by price without checking the size. The cheapest chain that won't fasten around your wheels is not a bargain: it's a trip to the fuel station just to get out of the car park.
  • Taking snow socks to a stretch that only allows metal chains. If the sign specifies it or your usual route requires it, metal chains: they are the ones that work in every case.
  • Storing them wet or with broken elastic straps. A two-minute check at the end of the season: clean, dry and in a bag without holes.
  • Relying only on the GPS. Road conditions are checked at dgt.es and mapamovilidad.dgt.es, by calling 011 and in radio bulletins; if there is a restriction or an AEMET warning, postpone the trip, do not force it.

6. The boot kit, in six items

In addition to chains in your size: work gloves (winter gloves get soaked), a torch with spare batteries, an old towel for your hands and mud, water and something to eat in case you are stranded for a couple of hours, and the blanket or extra coat for passengers. All of that lives in the car kit alongside the V-16 beacon, the high-vis vest and the first-aid kit; the full breakdown is in what to carry in an emergency car kit. And if the warning comes with the house unprepared, the basics for getting through a snowstorm without power are in snowstorm at home: what you need; dressing in layers, step by step, in dressing in layers.

mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.titulo: Best emergency backpack 2026: 6 evacuation backpacks compared
mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.resumen: Which backpack do you grab if you have to leave home in ten minutes? 6 types compared by liters, weight and price, winners by use case and what goes inside (2026).
mejor-mochila-emergencia-evacuacion.cuerpo:
At 23:40 the order comes: water is coming in along the lower street or smoke can be seen from the neighboring village. You have minutes, not hours. That is the only reason for the evacuation backpack: prepared in advance, in the same place for weeks, ready to grab in one go while the rest of the house gets up.

The official framework is European: the European Union Preparedness Strategy calls for guidelines so that the population can be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours while help arrives, and the Spanish Red Cross brings it down to practical terms: an easy-to-carry backpack, of reasonable weight and accessible, whose contents are checked regularly. What to fill it with is covered in the evacuation kit; here is the question most often left half-answered —which backpack to buy— with six types compared by liters, price and real use.

1. Four decisions before looking at prices

  • Capacity by hours, not by wishful thinking. 18-25 liters for 24 hours or for the office; 30-40 liters for two or three days with a coat, water and food; 45-60 liters only if you have to leave with several people's belongings. The 72-hour benchmark pushes an adult who is going to walk toward 35-45 liters.
  • Loaded weight: between 10% and 15% of your body weight. It is the same rule applied to school backpacks: 70 kg → 7-10 kg on your back. More than that, after twenty minutes you are slower than someone carrying less, and in an evacuation time is exactly what you do not have to spare.
  • A back system that distributes the load. Wide, padded straps, a breathable panel and, above all, a hip belt: a backpack without a hip belt loaded with more than 10 kg turns the lower back into the weak point. Heavy items close to the back and at shoulder height; soft and bulky items at the bottom; what you need along the way (water, flashlight, documents) within reach.
  • Water and light outside, not inside. An exterior pocket or mesh for the bottle and an attachment point for the flashlight: stopping to open the backpack in the middle of a crowded hallway is not the same as drinking while walking.

2. The six types compared

Approximate prices on Amazon Spain. Each link opens the search for the type, so you see the price of the day, not the one from when this was written.

TypeLitersWhen it is worth itApproximate price
40-50 L trekking backpack ↗40-50The adult who is going to walk: the best capacity per kilo, hip belt included as standard35-90 €
35-45 L MOLLE tactical backpack ↗35-45Fixed, organized kit: external anchors for pouches, first-aid kit or headlamps30-75 €
Pre-assembled evacuation backpack ↗30-40It arrives assembled, but you have less control over the contents: it still has to be checked50-120 €
18-25 L daypack ↗18-2524 hours, office, car and short route: the cheapest and the one you will also use most day to day18-45 €
15-20 L children's backpack ↗15-20Each child gets their own, with their clothes and their toy: making the adults carry only their own things is already enough15-35 €
Backpack with wheels or trolley ↗40-80Older adults, reduced mobility or heavy loads (water, large bottles): you roll it, you do not carry it40-110 €

3. Winners by case

  • Evacuation on foot (DANA, fire, order to leave): 40-50 L trekking pack with hip belt. It is the one that handles the weight without punishing you: 45 L trekking backpacks ↗.
  • Kit ready to grab and go: 35-45 L tactical pack with external anchors, if you organize by pockets: MOLLE tactical backpacks ↗. Especially useful if you keep it already packed in the entryway closet.
  • Home with older adults or back problems: the wheeled one, no debate. Better to push than to drag someone along with a 12 kg backpack.
  • Family with children: one large adult backpack plus a small one per child. Babies and children in an emergency sets out what each age carries.
  • Office, car and one-day route: the 18-25 L one, the only one you will really use for the rest of the year: waterproof daypacks ↗.
  • If you have pets: the family one plus a separate bag with water, leash, veterinary documents and food: emergency plan with dogs and cats.

4. What goes inside: the split across five compartments

The backpack is the wrapper; the contents are half the kit list. What cannot be missing from any of the six types:

CompartmentWhat it carriesReference
DocumentationCopies in a waterproof bag: ID, health card, policies, paper contactsemergency folder
Water and food1.5-3 L per person and bars, nuts or canned food that do not need cookinghow much water you need
Light and batteryHeadlamp, spare batteries and a charged powerbankbest flashlight · best powerbank
Health and warmthFirst-aid kit, 5-7 days of chronic medication and layered clothingdressing in layers
The deciding itemsCharged phone, battery-powered radio and the written family plan (meeting point and who to call)family emergency plan

If you still do not have the base assembled, the order is the usual one: first assemble your 72-hour kit, then choose the backpack that carries it. The other way around costs more.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Overloading it "just in case". Going over 15% of your body weight turns a walking evacuation into a trip to the emergency room: the backpack you cannot carry with you is not your backpack.
  • Buying the cheapest one without trying it on. Without a hip belt and with thin straps, the difference shows at minute five, not in the product photo.
  • Making the backpack one person's business. If only one person stores and checks it, when that person is not home the backpack stops existing: everyone has to know the place and the contents.
  • Never checking it. Dead batteries, expired documents, summer clothes in the middle of winter. The Red Cross insists on regular checks: every six months, ten minutes, on the calendar.
  • Forgetting what does not fit in the backpack. The car, the exit route, the water at home and the original documents are prepared separately; the backpack only carries the essentials for moving.

6. The ten-minute test

The only test that counts: set a timer, grab the backpack and walk out the door closing it behind you. Ten minutes with the house asleep is a good target. If you were missing something, write it down and buy it; if you had five minutes to spare, remove weight. Then leave it in the same place —visible, labeled and within everyone's reach— and practice with the family: who grabs it, who collects the documents, who alerts the grandparents. What is practiced beforehand is done afterward with a cool head, and that is where the emergency is won.

Our choice, with the verified link

Of the six types compared, the one that solves the most common case (leaving home with the essentials and your hands free for the children or the dog): a 40-liter waterproof backpack.

  • A AM SeaBlue 40 L — large-capacity waterproof hiking backpack. Why this one: 40 L fits the five-block split without falling short, the back and waist take the load off —which matters from 8 kg upward— and the waterproof fabric protects what cannot get wet. It is in the evacuation kit and in the fire kit, with today's price.

mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.titulo: Best SAI (UPS) for home and router: 6 types by VA and watts (2026)
mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.resumen: How long does your router and PC last in a blackout? 6 SAI compared by VA and watts, winners by use case and the 5 most common mistakes (2026).
mejor-sai-ups-casa-apagon.cuerpo:
It's 12:33 on a Tuesday and the router's power goes out. Eight seconds, the power comes back and that's it — until by the third week the laptop restarts on its own or the modem drops every time a breaker trips. That's the job of a UPS (uninterruptible power supply): ride out the seconds when the grid doesn't supply power and protect the home when the power returns.

The figure that anchors this article comes from Red Eléctrica: in 2025 the peninsular system recorded 12 supply interruptions, 29% fewer than in 2024, with an Average Interruption Time of 0.25 minutes, far from the 15 minutes in Article 26.2 of Royal Decree 1955/2000. The Spanish grid is excellent on average, but averages don't comfort you when the outage hits you: here's what UPS you need and how many VA you need.

1. What a UPS does (and the three things it doesn't do)

A UPS is a battery with an inverter and a switch: when the grid voltage drops, disappears or spikes, it switches to battery in milliseconds and keeps supplying power — the router doesn't even notice. It also filters the surges that arrive just as power returns.

  • It does power: router, ONT, laptop, TV, chargers, LED lights, carbon monoxide detector: 15 to 300 W.
  • It doesn't power: fridge, oven, hob, washing machine or heating: more than 1,000 W with even higher startup draw, which a 1,000 VA UPS won't run for even a second. For that, you need a generator or power station.
  • It is not a voltage stabilizer: it corrects voltage but doesn't provide a single second of battery backup. If the power goes out, it goes down with you.
  • It is not a generator: it doesn't create energy, it stores it. Its runtime is measured in minutes.

2. The six types, compared

Approximate prices on Amazon Spain: each link opens a search for that type, so you see today's price, not the price when this was written.

TypeWhen it's worth itApproximate price
DC mini-UPS for router and ONT ↗Communication only: the cheapest and the one that gives the most hours30-60 €
Offline UPS, 400-650 VA ↗First desktop PC or TV + router45-80 €
Line-interactive 1,000-1,500 VA with AVR ↗Work computer with monitor and peripherals70-140 €
Online double-conversion ↗Equipment that can't afford even a micro-interruption200-500 €
UPS with expandable external batteries ↗You want hours, not minutes: runtime expandable by hand150-400 €
2,000-3,000 VA UPS ↗Several devices at once and a small electrical panel180-350 €

The difference between the first and the last isn't the brand: it's how much battery you have inside. One detail that decides the purchase: the output waveform — for a router and TV, any model works, but for power supplies (laptops, audio) the ideal is pure sine wave, because some cheap UPS units have a flattened sine wave that chargers reject with a beep.

3. The VA calculation: how much you really need

UPS units are sold in VA (volt-amperes), not watts, and that's where most buying confusion comes from. Since the relationship between the two is the power factor — between 0.6 and 0.7 on a home UPS — count on W ≈ VA × 0.6: a 1,000 VA UPS handles around 600 W. The model's datasheet is what counts.

What you want to powerApproximate consumptionRecommended UPSApproximate runtime
Router + ONT15-30 WDC mini-UPS or 400-650 VA UPS2-4 h
Router, TV and chargers80-150 W650-1,000 VA UPS45-90 min
Laptop + monitor60-120 W1,000-1,500 VA UPS1-2 h
Desktop PC with monitor300-500 W1,500-2,000 VA UPS (pure sine wave)8-15 min
Fridge, oven or heating1,000-3,000 WNone: power station or generator—

The runtimes are ranges calculated on the stock battery (12 V and 7 Ah is around 84 Wh) and the inverter's real efficiency: they're useful for comparing models, not for signing on the dotted line, and they collapse if you leave it discharged or in the heat. Translation: what a UPS buys you isn't hours of a powered home, it's that your communications don't go down while you decide what to do — and that decision is in the blackout kit.

4. Winners by use case

  • Router and ONT, first and foremost: a DC mini-UPS, the one that gives the most hours for the price. If you prefer a conventional UPS, the 600-900 VA for router and ONT ↗ is the sweet spot: it lasts the time you need and also protects against the surge when power returns.
  • Remote work with a laptop: a 1,000-1,500 VA line-interactive unit with AVR: see line-interactive UPS units ↗. AVR maintains voltage without draining the battery during afternoon brownouts.
  • Desktop PC that can't reboot: an online double-conversion unit, which always powers from the batteries: the one in the electricity kit.
  • A home where the lights have already gone out several times: a UPS with expandable external batteries: see expandable models ↗. The only way to go from minutes to hours.
  • If the goal is the whole home: it isn't a UPS, it's a portable power station ↗ with a solar panel: compare first in generator vs. power station.

5. The five most common mistakes

  • Buying by VA without looking at actual watts. Calculate what you'll plug in using the table above, and only then look at the price.
  • Loading it with the fridge. Not only will it not run it: it will leave the battery dead right when you need it for the router.
  • Forgetting the battery. Lead-acid batteries last 3-5 years; an expired one is a UPS that shuts down with you. Set a calendar reminder every two years.
  • Buying it and not testing it. Unplug from the grid for a second: if the equipment reboots, either it's connected wrong or the model isn't suitable for that load.
  • Confusing it with a voltage stabilizer or a generator. If you need hours of fridge or heating, you're in the wrong article: see power banks and power stations.

6. Standards, maintenance and how it fits into your kit

To buy sensibly, just make sure the model complies with the harmonized European standard UNE-EN IEC 62040-1:2019 (safety requirements for UPS units, in force in Spain with amendments from 2021, 2023 and 2025): it guarantees that the device is safe to touch, not that it will last for hours.

Maintenance in three lines: load test every six months (disconnect from the grid for a minute), ventilation (let the UPS breathe, never in a closed cabinet) and battery replacement before the unit starts complaining. Golden rule: test it on a normal day, not during the blackout.

In March 2026, the CNMC published its recommendations report on the April 28, 2025 incident: it mitigates sudden voltage changes and strengthens inspection of protection systems. The grid will improve, but protecting your home is still up to you. The list is in the blackout kit and in the lessons from April 28; if you don't have the base set up yet, start with how to build your 72-hour kit.

mejor-extintor-domestico.titulo: Best home fire extinguisher 2026: 6 types and where to place it
mejor-extintor-domestico.resumen: Which fire extinguisher for home: powder, CO₂, foam or Class F. Six types compared with price, where to place it and the one-minute monthly check.
mejor-extintor-domestico.cuerpo:
The pan catches fire, the power strip trips, or a candle falls on the curtain: there is very little margin between a plate catching fire and having to run out, and in Spain that margin is lost every day. In 2024, 234 people died in fires and explosions in Spain, 172 of them inside homes, and among the probable causes electrical ones lead, with 41.9%. These are the figures from the Fire Victim Study by Fundación MAPFRE and APTB (Professional Association of Fire Technicians), which has been collecting data from fire services and forensic medicine institutes since 2010.

The extinguisher is the cheap answer: between 25 and 60 € for a fire that starts while you are at home. The regulations require them to be installed and maintained in buildings and premises —RIPCI, Royal Decree 513/2017, is the reference regulation—, but inside a private home there is no legal obligation. Here you decide which type puts out what, with six compared and where to hang it.

1. First decide this: what class of fire you have

On the label of any extinguisher there is a letter: it is the only thing that matters when buying. Standard UNE-EN 3-7 sets out the classes and the “typical homes” the device must put out:

ClassWhat burnsWhere you find it at home
ASolids: wood, paper, fabric, cardboardSofa, curtain, wardrobe, waste-paper bin
BLiquids: petrol, solvents, oilWorkshop, garage, gas cylinders
CCombustible gasesButane, kitchen gas
DMetals (industrial use)Almost never in a home
FHot cooking fats and oilsFrying pan and deep fryer: the most common at home

The practical translation: ABC powder covers A, B and C, almost everything that burns in an apartment. What it does not cover well is the frying pan (Class F): the oil goes out on the surface and reignites as soon as you move it. For cooking, a Class F extinguisher (foam or water with additive) or, better and faster, cover the pan with its lid or a fire blanket. Throwing water on it is the classic way to get burned: it vaporizes and carries burning oil all over the kitchen.

2. The six types, compared

Indicative prices on Amazon Spain for CE-marked extinguishers; each link opens the search for that type, so you see today's price, not the price when this was written.

TypeWhen it is worth itIndicative price
ABC powder, 1–2 kg ↗First purchase: backpack, hallway, pantry20-35 €
ABC powder, 6 kg ↗Whole house, garage or communal area40-70 €
CO₂, 2 kg ↗Electrical panel or workshop: leaves no residue40-65 €
Class F foam (6 L) ↗Kitchen: the only one for hot oil35-60 €
Water with additive / aqueous ↗Kitchen and living room: effective and not very messy30-55 €
Fire blanket or aerosol ↗On the hob and in the car: stops fire early10-25 €

3. Best choice by situation

  • A single unit for an apartment: 6 kg ABC powder, the same one mounted in stairwells; if the budget is tight, the 2 kg one already covers an incipient fire: see ABC powder extinguishers ↗.
  • Kitchen used often: Class F foam next to the door, never above the hob, plus a fire blanket in the drawer below: see Class F extinguishers ↗.
  • Electrical panel or storage room: 2 kg CO₂, which leaves the equipment and cables usable afterwards: see CO₂ extinguishers ↗.
  • Garage or workshop with fuel: 6 kg ABC powder on its wall bracket and visible from the entrance: see 6 kg extinguishers ↗.
  • Car boot and caravan: fire blanket or small extinguisher, because in a van what catches fire first is the fridge and clothing — the rest goes in the car kit: see fire blankets ↗.

Honest warning: a 2 kg extinguisher empties in about 10–15 seconds of spray. It is for a fire that has just started, not for a room in flames. If you haven't put it out after two passes, it's time to get out.

4. Where to put it (and the one-minute monthly check)

  • Near the exit, never on the other side of the fire. Firefighter rule: you don't cross the room that is on fire to get it. Visible, with no furniture in front and with signage above.
  • Height and mounting. On its bracket, at hand height and away from heat, damp and knocks. On the floor or behind a door that opens towards it: the classic mistake.
  • Monthly check (60 seconds): pressure gauge needle in the green zone, tamper seal and pin intact, hose free of cracks, body free of rust. And turn it upside down a couple of times a year so the powder doesn't cake.
  • Formal inspection: if it is mounted in an installation subject to the RIPCI, maintenance is carried out by an authorised company: annual inspection and pressure test every five years. In a private home it is not mandatory, but the same is advisable: the service life is around 20 years from manufacture (Tecnifuego) and it must be replaced earlier if the needle does not return to green.
  • During a power outage, double-check. Candles and generators raise the risk just when no one is looking: check the gauge and the candle before nightfall. The detail is in the power outage kit.

5. Five mistakes that make the extinguisher useless

  • Water on an electrical fire. First cut the power if you can, then use CO₂ or powder with a dielectric test.
  • Buying by colour. Red says nothing: look at the label with the A/B/C/F letters and the rating. An aerosol is not a 6 kg extinguisher.
  • Covering it with the washing machine or boxes. The one that has been in the storage room for years doesn't exist.
  • Overconfidence. The extinguisher is for a fire on a plate. If the flame reaches the ceiling or there is dense smoke, close the door and get out.
  • Forgetting the rest of the system. The extinguisher does not warn you: that's what the smoke detector is for, and to avoid lighting unnecessary fire, the flashlight. All of that is in the fire kit and in passive fire safety and electrical fires.

6. If a fire breaks out: four steps, in this order

  1. Alert: call 112 before touching the extinguisher, with the address and what is burning. Wrong information is worse than late information.
  2. Protect the exit: extinguisher in hand, upright, hose at the base of the fire and one step from the door.
  3. One attempt only: two short passes. If it doesn't go down, drop the extinguisher, close the door behind you and get out without grabbing anything else.
  4. Never go back until the fire service authorises it, even if “only ashes are left”: smoke is what kills.

That completes the fire kit. The rest of the house —light, water, warmth and documents— is put together in the same afternoon with the first-aid kit guide and with how to build your 72-hour kit; if you only prepare one corner, make it the home or shelter-in-place kit.

mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.titulo: Best carbon monoxide detector: 6 types compared (2026)
mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.resumen: How to choose a CO detector: the thresholds of the UNE-EN 50291 standard, 6 types compared with prices, where to place it and what to do if the alarm sounds.
mejor-detector-monoxido-carbono.cuerpo:
It gets cold, you turn on the heater, close the room so the heat doesn't escape, and fall asleep. That scenario — domestic, everyday, typical of any winter in Spain — is the one that most often ends up in the emergency room: carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless and tasteless; it doesn't warn you, and neither does your body. The CO detector is the cheapest device in the whole house that decides whether you wake up in time. It costs less than dinner and needs no installation, no electricity and no app.

The numbers are in the official reports: according to the Toxicovigilance Programme of the Ministry of Health, carbon monoxide is the most common toxic substance in Spanish emergency departments, with between 5,000 and 10,000 poisonings a year and an average of 125 deaths annually. And the National Plan of Preventive Actions for Low Temperatures 2025-2026 reminds us every winter that cold brings heating, braziers and generators: the risk rises just when you shut yourself in most.

1. What the standard requires: the table that determines whether it alarms in time

In Spain you can buy everything from 15 € detectors to 80 € devices, and the difference is not the brand: it is whether they comply with the European standard UNE-EN 50291-1:2018 (ratified by AENOR in February 2021), which sets out the test methods and performance requirements for domestic CO detectors. A compliant device must alarm within these times:

CO concentrationWhen the alarm must sound
30 ppmNot before 120 minutes (and it must sound within that period)
50 ppmBetween 60 and 90 minutes
100 ppmBetween 10 and 40 minutes
300 ppmIn under 3 minutes

Two readings. First: the standard does not monitor low background levels; it warns before the damage is significant — that is why it won't go off with the chimney open one afternoon, but it will if the generator has been in the garage for half an hour. Second: once it triggers, the alarm will not quieten until it drops below 50 ppm: the fact that it 'turns itself off' does not mean the air is clean. For placement, EN 50292 (selection and installation) applies: every room with a possible combustion source and every bedroom. The electrical side of the same risk is covered in passive fire safety and electrical fires.

2. The six types, compared

Approximate prices on Amazon Spain for detectors with an electrochemical sensor compliant with EN 50291. Each link opens the search for that type: you see the price of the day, not the one from when this was written.

TypeWhen it is worth itApproximate price
Basic battery-powered with audible alarm ↗First purchase, rented home, bedroom20-30 €
With concentration display (ppm) ↗Home with a heater, wood, fireplace or butane30-45 €
Sealed 10-year battery ↗Bedroom and hallway: fit and forget30-50 €
Combined smoke + CO ↗One device for both blackout risks40-70 €
With phone alert or interconnected ↗Large home, several floors, absences50-90 €
For motorhome, caravan or sailboat ↗Use on the move, batteries and wide temperature range30-60 €

3. Winners by category

  • Best value for money: the basic battery-powered model with an electrochemical sensor. If you only buy one, it's this one: see battery-powered CO detectors ↗.
  • Best for the bedroom: sealed 10-year battery, no battery changes and with an end-of-life indicator: see long-life battery models ↗.
  • Best with a heater or firewood: with ppm display, to see whether the concentration rises before it sounds: see detectors with a display ↗.
  • Best for a home with an expected blackout: combined smoke + CO: in a blackout, candles, heaters and a generator coexist, and smoke and CO arrive together: see combined detectors ↗. Beware the usual confusion: a smoke detector does not detect carbon monoxide, nor vice versa.
  • Best for a motorhome or van: vehicle-specific model, battery-powered: see caravan detectors ↗.

If the budget is very tight, the priority is not the detector: it is to ventilate and not heat with combustion inside the home. With that and a well-chosen flashlight, you are covered — the selection is in best heater during a blackout and in keeping warm without electricity.

4. Where to put it (and where never to)

  • Yes: in every bedroom, in the hallway that serves them and in the room where you burn anything (open-plan kitchen, fireplace, workshop). Follow the manufacturer: almost all specify 1-3 meters from the source, on the ceiling or high on a wall and away from drafts.
  • No: inside a cupboard, behind a curtain, above the extractor hood or next to a window: there the air arrives late or is renewed too quickly, and it measures badly.
  • Garage: a domestic detector is no good for a running car: you need higher-range models there and, better still, never leave the engine running in an enclosed space.
  • Maintenance: monthly test with the button, dust it every six months (recommended by the Community of Madrid) and replace it at the end of its service life, 5 to 10 years depending on the model: the device itself will warn you.

5. Five mistakes that defeat the detector

  • Relying on smell. CO has no smell: by the time you notice it, you have already been breathing it for a while.
  • Heating with the gas oven. The Ministry of Health says it literally: never use the stove or oven to heat a home.
  • Generator, chainsaw or boiler inside the home or in the garage. Combustion engines in an enclosed space are the classic source of mass poisoning.
  • A heater left on at night with the room closed. Ventilating is the cheapest measure: better to lose some heat than to have no air.
  • One detector for the whole house. Air does not travel between floors or through closed doors: at least one per floor and one in every bedroom.

6. If the alarm sounds: four steps

  1. Get out of the room with everyone — without 'checking what it is', without turning anything off and without going back in to look for anyone.
  2. Ventilate from outside and do not go back until the emergency services authorize it.
  3. Call 112 from outside: people affected, symptoms and which combustion source was running.
  4. Have the source checked by a professional before turning it back on: a badly sealed boiler or chimney will repeat the episode.

And the warning most often ignored: headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion that ease when you leave the house are the typical picture. If you wake in the early hours with your head pounding and the heating on, get out.

The detector is the first euro of the winter kit: alongside it go radio, light and warm clothing in home or lockdown kit, electrical safety in electricity kit and cold in cold and snow kit. If you haven't put anything together yet, start with how to build your 72-hour kit: it takes half an afternoon.

mejor-starlink-espana-precio.titulo: Best Starlink in Spain: price, plans and which to choose (2026)
mejor-starlink-espana-precio.resumen: Starlink in Spain 2026: the three residential plans with official pricing, kit rental at 10 €/month, Roam, and which one suits you.
mejor-starlink-espana-precio.cuerpo:
Almost every Starlink question that reaches this blog starts the same way: how much does it really cost, and which plan do I need? In 2026 it changed twice: in March Starlink went from two plans to three, and in June it added 10 €/month for kit rental for new sign-ups. Here are the official prices as of today, the comparison, and the verdict for each case.

This is not a niche product: based on network traffic, Starlink would already be the sixth-largest operator in Spain, with more than half a million users, and during the April 28, 2025 blackout, satellite was one of the few services that kept working. That is the argument of this site: that the connection should not disappear exactly when you need it. The lessons from that day are in the April 28 blackout; the equipment, in the Starlink kit.

1. The five Starlink plans in Spain, compared

Starlink sells two families of plans in Spain: Residential (fixed home) and Itinerant (motorhomes, sailboats, use while moving). All include unlimited data and a 30-day trial with a full refund. The prices are those on Starlink's official website for Spain:

PlanPrice/monthDownloadPriorityWho it's for
Residential 10035 €up to 100 Mb/s (limited)NoSmall apartment, second home, basic use
Residential 20045 €up to 200 Mb/sNoFamily with remote work and several devices
Residential Max65 €more than 400 Mb/sYes, the highestLarge house, mesh network, many screens
Itinerant 100 GB45 €100 GB at high speed, then at low speedNoMotorhome or sailboat with occasional use
Itinerant unlimited95 €unlimited while movingNoNomadic life, working from anywhere

Winners by category: the Residential 200 (45 €) is the sweet spot: it doubles the basic speed without paying for Max priority. For a small apartment or second home, the Residential 100 (35 €) is more than enough. The Max (65 €) only pays off with several connected devices at once or real priority during peak hours. For the van, the Itinerant 100 GB (45 €) with Standby Mode.

One warning: Starlink adjusts rates frequently (twice in 2026). Check the price at checkout on the official plans website, not the one in an article from six months ago.

2. The equipment: since June 2026 it is rented, not bought

What most people miss: since June 2026, new sign-ups also pay 10 €/month for the kit (antenna and router):

  • Residential 100: 45 €/month actual (35 for the plan + 10 for the kit).
  • Residential 200: 55 €/month actual (45 + 10).
  • Residential Max: 75 €/month actual (65 + 10).
  • The 10 € is 120 € a year, and the equipment is not yours: if you cancel, it must be returned.

Two nuances: a “rental adjustment” often appears that brings those 10 € down to 0, so go by the checkout price, not the table price; and professional installation is optional, from about 172 €, only for complicated roofs (the app tells you where to point it; anyone can set up the basic one).

If you choose just one thing, the Starlink Mini: it fits in a backpack, has an integrated router, runs directly on DC power, and goes over 200 Mb/s. It is the one that makes sense in an emergency kit; here you can see accessories and mounts for Starlink Mini ↗.

3. Is it worth it in your case? Yes if…, no if…

It is worth it when: fiber is not available or actually reaches only 20 Mb/s; fixed 5G drops at night; you live in a village or an isolated mountain house; or it is a second home used for weeks at a time (with Standby Mode at about 10 €/month instead of paying the full rate all year).

It is not worth it when: you have stable, cheap fiber; when you need internet anywhere in the country rather than at one address (that is what mobile data is for); or if you do not want a monthly fee, because the large part of the cost is the monthly charge.

And the point almost no one calculates beforehand: power. A terminal uses 60-75 W active and 20-40 W idle, so without mains power you have to supply it: with a portable power station ↗, with a folding solar panel that recharges during the day, or, if it is a fixed installation, with the SAI for the router. A 20,000 mAh power bank is not enough for the antenna. How many watts you really need: portable solar panel for 72 hours and generator vs. power station.

You also need clear sky: a tree or a badly oriented roof ruins the connection just like a blackout. If the antenna cannot see the sky, Starlink is not your solution: first look at the best emergency 4G router.

4. Cheaper alternatives before paying 45 € a month

OptionWhen it winsTypical cost
4G/5G router with a data SIM ↗There is mobile coverage on your street and you need no more than 100 GBEquipment 0-100 € + 15-40 €/month
eSIM / second data SIMFor leaving the village or the family's second device0-20 € + data allowance
Starlink Residential 100There is no reliable mobile coverage and you need real bandwidth35 €/month (+ kit)
Satellite messaging and GPSOnly alerts and location without coverage: little traffic, long battery lifeEquipment + annual fee
PMR446 walkie-talkies ↗Internal group communication with no network available40-80 € per pair

The full comparison: emergency connectivity, best data SIM, and communicating without a mobile network. The rule: layers — mobile for everyday use, router or Starlink for the home, satellite or radio when everything else goes down.

5. The five most common mistakes when signing up

  • Signing up for Max out of habit. Priority is only noticeable at peak times; for a normal house, Residential 200 performs the same and is 30 €/month cheaper.
  • Looking only at the plan rate. The real price is plan + rental: 45, 55, or 75 € a month. Always check the total on the first bill.
  • Installing it without checking the sky. The app has an obstruction map: use it BEFORE paying and drilling into the roof.
  • Leaving the trial for the blackout. You have 30 days to return it: test it on a normal day, with rain, and with the TV on.
  • Forgetting where the power will come from. Without a socket, Starlink is a metal dish: first the power source and the battery that sustains it.

6. Where to start today

If the decision is “yes, I want it,” go to the official sign-up website, check your address on the coverage map, and choose between 100 and 200. Step-by-step installation is in Starlink during a blackout.

For the complete plan, the Starlink kit collects the selection, the blackout checklist covers the rest of the house, and the method is in how to put together your 72-hour kit. Test it one afternoon: on the day you need it, it will matter that you had already tested it.

generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.titulo: Generator and noise in the community: how many dB will they tolerate (2026)
generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.resumen: dB limits under Law 37/2003, Royal Decree 1367/2007 and your local by-law: how to use the generator without a fine and without annoyed neighbours.
generador-ruido-normativa-comunidad.cuerpo:
A two-day blackout, the generator you bought “just in case” and, at 23:40, a knock at the door: the neighbour can’t sleep. The answer to “is this even legal?” isn’t in any forum: it’s in Law 37/2003 on Noise, in your local council’s ordinance and in the Horizontal Property Act.

1. National law: where domestic activity begins and where it stops being domestic

The Law 37/2003 of 17 November on Noise is the main rule, and its article 2.2.a) gives the key: outside its scope are “domestic activities or the behaviour of neighbours, when the noise pollution produced by them remains within tolerable limits in accordance with municipal ordinances and local customs”.

Translation: switching on your generator is a domestic activity… until it stops being one. As soon as you exceed what your local council considers tolerable, you enter the penalty regime: article 28.5 allows local ordinances to classify as an infringement “noise produced by domestic activities or by neighbours”.

SeverityFineWhen it applies (summary)
MinorUp to €600Breaching the law without falling under the serious categories
Serious€601 – €12,000Exceeding the applicable limit values, without serious harm
Very serious€12,001 – €300,000Exceeding them with serious harm or risk to health

2. The figures in Royal Decree 1367/2007: how many dB are tolerated at night

The Royal Decree 1367/2007 sets the quality objectives in Annex II. For a residential land-use sector in existing built-up areas (Table A): 65 dB during the day, 65 in the evening and 55 at night. Inside the home (Table B), which is what is measured in the neighbour’s bedroom: 45/45/35 in living rooms and 40/40/30 in bedrooms.

Each city sets the periods; the Community of Madrid Ordinance divides the day into daytime (7:00–19:00), evening (19:00–23:00) and night-time (23:00–7:00). Between 65 in the day and 55 at night there are 10 decibels, which the ear perceives as twice the noise: what at eleven is a nuisance, at one is grounds for a complaint.

3. Your generator already shows the dB on the label

Generators are no exception: the Directive 2000/14/EC, transposed in Spain by the Royal Decree 212/2002 (BOE-A-2002-4099), requires declaring the guaranteed sound power level of generators under 400 kW. That figure appears on the label and in the technical data sheet. Typical values, measured at 7 metres — the standard distance in data sheets:

Type of equipmentNoise at 7 mWhat it is useful for at home
Soundproof inverter (briefcase type)48 – 60 dB(A)The quiet option: lights, fridge, router
Portable open-frame (cheap)70 – 80 dB(A)The noisiest: it sounds like a vacuum cleaner
Installed generator (standby)60 – 75 dB(A)Detached house with space away from the neighbour
Power station (battery)~30 dB(A)Fan only: zero noise and zero fumes

Two rules of physics explain almost all conflicts: every +10 dB is perceived as twice the noise and sound drops by about 6 dB each time you double the distance. A 72 dB open-frame at 7 metres sounds like 66 at 14 and 60 at 28: moving the equipment away from the neighbour’s patio is worth more than any barrier.

4. The municipal ordinance: the text that actually fines you

National law provides the framework, but your local council draws up the fine. Search for “noise pollution ordinance” plus your municipality: there you’ll find the decibels per zone, the time restrictions and the penalties. As an example, the Seville Ordinance: “Generators and transformers must be installed in such a way that they are properly insulated against noise and vibration.”

Note the word insulated: it doesn’t say “silent”, it says insulated against noise and vibration. Vibration travels through the building structure and wakes the neighbour even when the air is quiet.

5. The residents’ community: the fast route isn’t the fine

If the noise comes from a neighbour — or you cause it — the shortest route is the Horizontal Property Act. Its article 7 prohibits carrying out in the home any activities that contravene the general provisions on nuisance, unhealthy, harmful, dangerous or unlawful activities:

  • Request from the chairperson, on their own initiative or at any owner’s request, with a warning of legal action.
  • Action to cease if it persists and the general meeting authorises it: the judge may order immediate cessation as a precautionary measure, “under warning of incurring the offence of disobedience”.
  • Judgment that, in addition to cessation and compensation, may deprive you of the use of the home for a period of no more than three years.

A badly placed generator can cost you the fine, the compensation and, in the worst case, the use of your own home.

6. How to use it without sleeping with the penalty hanging over you

  • Never inside, not in the garage, not in the building’s storage room. Carbon monoxide kills before the fine does; a battery-powered CO detector on each floor is the cheapest measure in the kit.
  • Move it away and aim it. The 6 dB per doubled distance works in your favour; point the exhaust outwards and never against a wall that reflects the sound.
  • Anti-vibration base. A rubber mat cuts the path of vibration into the structure — the Seville ordinance requires it: anti-vibration mats.
  • Timing. From 23:00 to 7:00 the target drops from 65 to 55 dB: that’s when the same nuisance becomes a formal complaint file.
  • Eco mode and actual load. Data sheets state noise at a quarter load; with the equipment at full wattage it goes up. For lights and chargers, a quiet inverter generator delivers the same with half the noise.
  • If you live in a flat, don’t buy an engine. A power station provides power with no noise, no fumes and no argument with the residents’ community.

7. The most costly mistakes

  • Believing that domestic activity is always allowed: the law excludes you only “within tolerable limits” according to your ordinance.
  • Looking only at the watts in the shop: if the data sheet doesn’t give dB(A) at 7 m, it’s equipment you don’t want in a building.
  • Installing it right against the party wall: noise and vibration for the same neighbour, and the ordinance expressly mentions it.
  • Forgetting CO and fuel: safety is covered in the blackout kit guide and the first decisions in what a blackout taught us.

8. Where to start today

If you don’t have a generator, first decide whether you really need one: for a flat, the comparison between generator and power station is conclusive. If you already have one, take out the data sheet, note the dB at 7 m, count the metres to the neighbour’s patio and look up your municipal ordinance. To calculate watts before buying: portable solar panel and emergency solar generator.

Noise isn’t solved with good intentions: it’s solved with decibels, metres and timing. And what your home must withstand without power is in the electricity and backup kit.

nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.titulo: Snowed in at home: 8 key points to get through days without power (2026)
nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.resumen: What you need when snow is forecast: safe heating, water, food, power, a car with chains, and the mistakes Filomena taught us, with official sources.
nevada-en-casa-que-necesito.cuerpo:
When AEMET turns the warning map orange, the problem is not postcard-perfect snow: it is the days that follow. Roads cut off, power that does not come back, heating down and the supermarket with empty shelves. Storm Filomena (January 2021) is still the benchmark in Spain: AEMET itself describes it as an episode of an exceptional nature, with accumulated snow of up to 50 cm in Madrid city and minimum temperatures of -26.5 °C. In many homes what failed was not that it snowed: it was that no one had prepared for three days without being able to shop.

This is the list of what I need at home when a snowfall is forecast, in order and with the reason why. If you do only one thing, do the first.

1. Check the official warning, not the WhatsApp group

Everything starts with the AEMET warning map: yellow (be careful), orange (significant risk) and red (extreme risk, with implications for your safety). Complement it with the Civil Protection recommendations and with 112 if there is a real emergency.

And before you move the car, DGT repeats it in every winter warning: check the weather forecast and road conditions before setting out, and keep chains or winter tires at hand. Traffic authorities can restrict traffic for vehicles that do not carry that equipment and may even close roads preventively. The practical rule: if the trip is not essential, do not make it.

2. Heating: what warms and what kills

When the power goes out, what kills in winter is not the cold but carbon monoxide: odorless, invisible and produced by any poorly ventilated combustion. It is the first rule on the list:

  • Never a generator inside the home, not in the garage, not in the entrance hall, not right next to a window. The reason is in the generator vs power station comparison: in an apartment, a power station is the only option.
  • Gas or combustion heater: only with the room ventilated and never while you sleep. A butane gas heater handles a living room, not a house closed up all night.
  • Battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on every floor and near the bedrooms. It costs less than a dinner and is the only thing that warns you before it is too late: battery-powered CO detector.
  • Keep the house warm, not just the people: cover the window at night with a curtain or blanket, close rooms that are not in use and dress in layers at home. The details are in maintaining body temperature without electricity and in dressing in layers.

The cold-specific items are in the cold and snowfall kit.

3. Water and food: three days without being able to shop

A snowfall cuts roads and delays deliveries, so calculate at least 3 liters of water per person per day (drinking, hygiene and cooking): the figure and how to store it are in how much water to store per person. Buy food that can be eaten without gas and without cooking: canned goods, canned legumes, nuts, sliced bread, coffee and a can opener (if you forget the manual one, a knife and a pot are not enough).

And as soon as the power goes out, the order is: use fresh food first (meat, fish, dairy), then frozen food. The fridge lasts hours, not days; the full schedule is in keeping food without a fridge, and if you live alone or want extra margin, in portable cooler for emergencies.

4. Light, information and batteries

Snowfall scares happen at dawn, in a dark hallway. Equipment that solves them, with indicative prices:

ItemWhat it is really forIndicative price
Battery-powered headlampHands-free for going up to the attic, down to the storage room or helping a neighbor8-15 €
Assortment of AA/AAA batteriesFlashlights, radios and detectors; with the expiration date noted10-20 €
Battery or hand-crank radioOfficial information without grid power or a phone battery: radio is the first source when the power goes out15-35 €
20,000 mAh power bankThree or four phone charges: to send and receive alerts25-50 €
Foldable solar panelExtends battery life for several days; under overcast skies it produces little, so do not count on it as your main source40-80 €
Candles with a stable holderOccasional backup, always on a sturdy surface and away from curtains5-12 €

Full comparisons are in best emergency flashlight, best power bank and best hand-crank and solar radio; how many watts you really need, in portable solar panel.

5. The car: chains, tires and common sense

DGT repeats it every winter: carry chains or winter or all-season tires if you are going to drive through areas with a snowfall warning, check road conditions before setting out and leave the left lane free for snowplows. If the snow catches you on the road: do not abandon the vehicle, slow down and call 112.

The kit goes in the trunk before the storm is announced: snow chains, a pair of waterproof gloves (fitting chains with freezing hands is impossible) and a thermal blanket. The full vehicle list is in the car kit.

6. Neighbors, older people and anyone living alone

In a building, logistics are worked out among everyone: who shops if someone cannot go out and who has the key to the elderly person's apartment. A call at the same time every day to someone who lives alone is not courtesy, it is a status check: the script is in living alone and being prepared, the equipment in the elderly person's kit and the phone numbers you cannot do without in official emergency resources. If there is daily medication, check the week's dose and keep the prescription up to date: chronic medication without a pharmacy.

7. The five mistakes repeated in every snowfall

  • Going out 'to have a look' while snow is falling. The road that 'is fine' at ten may be closed at twelve.
  • Turning on the generator or heater in a closed space. It is the mistake that causes the most hospitalizations in winter.
  • Buying only food that has to be cooked and discovering at 21:00 that there is no gas, water or can opener.
  • Keeping phone numbers and documents only on your phone. With no power and 8% battery, the contact list does not exist: print it. The full folder is in emergency folder and documents.
  • Waiting for the neighbor to warn you. When the supermarket is overflowing, it is already too late to buy the important things: batteries, spare batteries, first-aid kit and medication.

8. Where to start today

If you are starting from zero, the basic 72-hour kit gives you the common base and on top of that goes the cold-weather and car equipment. The method for not forgetting anything is in how to build your 72-hour kit and the first-moment decisions, in what a blackout taught us.

Snowfall gives days of warning: use them, and when it arrives all you will have to do is look out the window.
