generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.titulo: Generator vs power station: 2026 comparison for a blackout
generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.resumen: Generator or power station? We compare power, runtime, noise, cost per hour and regulations for riding out a blackout in Spain.
generador-vs-power-station-comparativa.cuerpo:
On 28 April 2025, at 12:33:30, the peninsular electricity system dropped to zero. The Committee for the Analysis of the Circumstances Surrounding the Electricity Crisis of 28 April —created by the National Security Council and whose report was approved by the Council of Ministers on 17 June 2025— concluded that the origin was multifactorial, ruled out a cyberattack and put the full restoration of supply on 29 April at 14:36. In many homes the power came back much earlier; the problem was everything that went without power in the meantime: the fridge, the boiler, the entryphone, the water pump.

That is why the buying question is no longer “what am I missing from the kit?” but how much power you need and, above all, where you are going to put it. That is where two very different answers meet: a fuel generator or a power station (a stationary battery with an inverter and, optionally, a solar panel). We compare them using Spanish data —power, runtime, cost per hour, noise and regulations— so that you decide before the next outage, not during it.

What you need to power (do this before looking at prices)

Power is measured in watts and it gets used up very quickly. A practical guide for the first 72 hours:

  • 100-200 W: router and ONT, phone chargers, three or four LED lights, carbon monoxide detector. Anything in this article can run these.
  • 300-700 W: laptop, television, kettle, microwave occasionally, vacuum cleaner.
  • 1,000-2,000 W: domestic fridge at startup, oil boiler (circulation pump only), well pump.
  • Above 2,500 W: ceramic hob, oven, washing machine, air conditioning. There a small generator falls short, and a 500 Wh power station will not even complete one oven cycle.

With that list in front of you, the comparison makes itself clear.

Generator vs power station: the table

CriterionGasoline generator (inverter)Power station + solar panel
Continuous power1,000-3,000 W, with peaks up to double at startup600-2,000 W output and 500-2,000 Wh capacity
Runtime4-8 h per 4-5 L tank, and for as long as there is gasoline500 Wh ≈ 6-10 h for a small fridge or about 10 h for router, lights and chargers
Cost per hour1-1,80 €/h of gasoline (approximate)0 € in use; 150-400 € one-off cost for the panel
Noise58-75 dB(A) at 7 m depending on modelSilent: just the fan
Use in an apartmentImpossible ❌ (carbon monoxide, noise and regulations)Yes ✅ inside the home
RechargingGasoline, with stock that expiresSun, grid or car engine: free and no management
Weight15-30 kg8-25 kg
Approximate price350-900 € + 50-100 € for the fuel can400-1.200 € + 100-300 € for the panel

Figures are approximate for Spain, intended for comparison, not for placing an order: they assume gasoline at around 1,5 €/L and usual shop ranges. A conventional generator without an inverter is cheaper, but it delivers a waveform that damages sensitive electronics: if you are going to plug in the computer or router, insist on pure sine wave output.

Winner by category

  • City apartment → power station. It does not burn fuel, does not make noise and does not emit carbon monoxide. A 1,000-1,500 Wh station and a folding panel cover a small fridge, lights and phones: view portable power stations and 20-40 W folding solar panel, the minimum to keep phones and flashlights charged.
  • House with a storage room, ventilated garage or garden → inverter generator. It is the only way to boil, heat or run a large fridge for days: view inverter generators.
  • Router and computer (the first thing to save) → SAI/UPS. Cheap, silent and instantaneous: 600-900 VA SAI/UPS. It does not replace the previous two: it buys you the first minutes while you decide.
  • Long scenario (several days) → both: station for day-to-day and generator for high-consumption loads, with the panel as a safety net.

Noise: why a generator does not belong in a building entrance

Here the comparison is won on points, and it is the figure almost nobody checks before buying. A “silenced” inverter generator is around 58-65 dB(A) at seven meters according to its datasheet; a conventional one exceeds 70. A building entryphone is around 50-55 dB. On a quiet street at three in the morning, a generator on the balcony can be heard from the apartment next door.

And the legal framework leaves no room: Article 7.2 of the Horizontal Property Act prohibits carrying out in the home activities that “contravene the general provisions on nuisance, unhealthy, harmful, dangerous or illegal activities”, while the noise limit values in residential areas are set by Spain's Noise Law 37/2003 and its implementing royal decrees (Noise Code, BOE) together with each municipality's local ordinance. In practice: plugging in a generator on the balcony or in the garage of a residential building is both a neighbor dispute and an infringement. If you want the regulatory detail, it is in the BOE's Community of Owners Code.

Carbon monoxide: the argument that settles the debate

The rule is short and admits no exceptions: never use a generator inside the home, in the garage, in the communal hallway or right next to a window. The engine emits odorless carbon monoxide, and serious poisonings during blackouts often happen exactly like that, with someone trying to spend a warmer night or charge their phone in the storage room. Protección Civil and the European Commission's preparedness plan agree on the same thing: distance, ventilation and a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on the wall, one meter from the bed and away from the ceiling.

If the home is an apartment, that option is off the table: the generator is out of the equation and the power station wins by default.

Shopping in 10 minutes

  • First the small stuff: basic 72-hour kit and 20,000 mAh power bank. They cost less than an hour of generator use and solve 80% of nights.
  • If you live in an apartment: 1,000 Wh power station plus a folding panel. The wattage calculation is in portable solar panel: how many watts you really need.
  • If you have a storage room or garden: 2,000 W inverter generator with pure sine wave output, and the solar generator alternative so you do not live off gasoline.
  • What you do not buy twice: before plugging in heating, check the comparison of heaters without power; the fridge and the rest of the list are in blackout kit and electricity kit.

With 28-A on the table —the official conclusions are in the non-confidential report of the analysis committee— the question is no longer whether there will be another outage, but whether that afternoon you will have the fridge running or you will be calling the neighbor. Choosing between a generator and a power station is not choosing technology: it is choosing whether your home has somewhere to store twenty kilos of noisy iron… or not.

baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.titulo: V16 beacon mandatory in 2026: rule, €80 fine and how to choose it
baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.resumen: Since 1 January 2026, the connected V16 beacon is the only legal means of signalling a stopped car: what the DGT requires and how to choose an approved one.
baliza-v16-obligatoria-2026.cuerpo:
1 January 2026 has already passed, and with it a twenty-six-year-old habit: warning triangles are no longer a valid way to signal a stopped car on the road. Since that date, the only legal device is the connected V-16 luminous beacon, and anyone still relying on the triangles in the boot is breaking the rules — the offence is minor and carries an 80 € fine.

This is not a technological whim: the DGT estimates that around 25 people are killed each year after being struck by traffic on the road after getting out of their vehicle, many while they were placing precisely the warning triangles. With the V-16 you do not get out of the car: it is switched on from inside and, in addition to the light, it sends the vehicle's position to other drivers. Here you can see what the regulation requires, how it works, where it is placed, the fine, the myths and what to check before buying.

What the regulation requires from 1 January 2026

The obligation is set out in Annex XII of the General Vehicle Regulations and came into force on 1 January 2026: from that date the connected V-16 is “the only legal means of signalling immobilised vehicles,” according to the DGT.

  • Mandatory for passenger cars, vans, buses, dual-purpose vehicles, trucks and non-special vehicle combinations. It is not mandatory on motorcycles, but the DGT considers its use “highly advisable.”
  • Warning triangles may remain in the vehicle's equipment, but they no longer serve to signal a breakdown on the road.
  • Abroad, it is valid in the countries that signed the Vienna Convention (Portugal, France, Germany, Italy…), which accept the device from the country of registration.
  • And a current note: from 1 October 2026, motorcycles must also carry a high-visibility reflective vest as part of their mandatory equipment (RD 518/2026). The beacon does not replace the vest.

Why it changed: the calculation nobody wanted to make

Signalling with a triangle forces you to walk at least 100 metres along the carriageway with traffic passing beside you; the United Kingdom even banned them on high-speed roads for that reason. The V-16 tackles both fronts: it is activated without leaving the passenger compartment and adds virtual visibility to the physical light — the location of the stopped vehicle appears in navigation devices, mobility apps and variable message signs, so that drivers brake before they see you.

How it works: no mobile phone, no app and no subscription fee

  • Self-contained: built-in, non-removable GPS chip and SIM card. No phone, no apps, no pairing: you switch it on and that's it.
  • Connectivity included in the price, with a minimum of 12 years guaranteed by regulation and no surcharge from the network operators.
  • When activated, it sends the exact location to the DGT 3.0 platform, which distributes it to navigation devices, apps and signs. Without a data network, the light still works.
  • It does not call 112 or your insurer: it only signals and sends a position. You make the call.
  • After activation, Article 130.3 of the General Traffic Regulations applies: if the vehicle cannot continue and there is a safe place outside, you get out on the side facing away from traffic; if it is not safe, you stay in the passenger compartment with your seat belt fastened.
Connected V-16 beaconWarning triangle
Status since 1/1/2026Only legal meansNot valid for signalling
PlacementFrom inside, on the highest partOn foot, 100 m along the carriageway
Warning to othersLight + position on DGT 3.0Reflected light only
Risk for the person signallingYou get out of the car only if it is safeExposed to traffic
Approximate price8-25 €—

Where to store it and how to place it

Three DGT rules that are always forgotten: store it charged in the glove compartment or in another accessible place in the vehicle — not in a closed boot or at home —; switch it on and place it from inside, on the highest part of the vehicle; and in buses or trucks, where the roof is out of reach, on the driver's door. Activate it once at home to check that it works and to know where it goes on the day you need it.

Before buying: certification is a must

There are more than two hundred models on the market and the DGT is blunt: only the one that appears on its official list of certified devices is valid, all certified by IDIADA or LCOE, with the laboratory and certificate number engraved on the lens.

  • Check the DGT list before paying, not the photos in the listing: it is the only check that saves you from a surprise.
  • Be wary of subscriptions: if they ask you for a monthly fee “so that it connects,” it is not the model required by the regulation.
  • No registration with your data: no app and no sign-up in your name; when you buy it, the beacon is not linked to any person or registration plate.
  • Where to buy it: approved connected V-16 beacon (the one in the car kit), compare approved V-16 beacon models or, if you do not have one yet, reflective vest.

The fine: a minor offence and 80 €

Not carrying the V-16 beacon is a minor offence punishable by an 80 € fine, the same amount that previously applied to anyone driving without warning triangles. That is the easy part: the real cost of going without it is standing on the hard shoulder at night waiting for someone to see you. That is why the car kit marks it as essential: it costs about two dinners and is bought once.

Three myths circulating on social media

  1. “It tracks your movements.” It only transmits when activated, and what it sends is the location plus a technical identifier of the device itself: the AEPD confirms that there is no record linking the beacon to the identity of the person using it, or to the registration plate, and the regulation prohibits additional functionalities.
  2. “You have to register it with your ID card or install an app.” False: it does not need an application, a phone or personal data when you buy it.
  3. “It calls 112 by itself.” Also false. If there are injuries or the situation is serious, you call 112 and, if appropriate, your insurer's assistance service.

A ten-minute checklist for this week

  1. Check that your beacon appears on the official DGT list and that the certificate number is engraved on the lens.
  2. Charge it and leave it in the glove compartment; test it once and put it back charged.
  3. Keep the vest within reach — not under the luggage in the boot — and your phone charged.
  4. Agree at home who gets out and on which side, or whether you simply stay inside with your seat belts fastened.
  5. Check the rest of the car kit: first-aid kit, torch, water and power bank, the things that keep that call to 112 alive.

The beacon solves signalling, not the rest of the scenario. The context is in the lessons from the 28 April blackout and the full list of what is mandatory and what is advisable in the car kit for 2026. The foundation — water, light and food for 72 hours — is still in the 72-hour basic kit.

mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.titulo: Best long-lasting canned foods for emergencies (2026)
mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.resumen: Best long-lasting canned foods for emergencies: 9 products compared, which date to check on the packaging and the 5 common pantry mistakes.
mejores-conservas-larga-duracion.cuerpo:
At 21:40 the power goes out and the first thing you do is open the fridge to see how much is left. After twelve hours the freezer is already warm and, after thirty-six, the question is no longer what you fancy but what can still be eaten. At that point a well-chosen preserved food is worth more than any gadget: food that lasts months or years without refrigeration, without power and without you doing anything.

That is the official criterion: the European Union Preparedness Strategy calls for 72 hours of self-sufficiency per household and Protección Civil recommends non-perishable food and water for three days. In Spain there is no shortage of food, what is missing is a plan: the Food Waste in Spain Report 2024 (MAPA) puts at 1.125 billion kilos or litres what we throw away each year, with 97.5% in households and about 24 kilos per person. We buy food that ends up in the bin while the emergency reserve does not exist.

I compare nine long-life preserved foods available in any supermarket or on Amazon Spain: how long they last unopened, what each one is really good for and its weak point.

Best before is not use-by: the date that decides whether you throw it away or not

AESAN devotes an entire campaign to separating the two concepts, and Regulation (EU) 1169/2011 regulates them. Confusing them is the main cause of throwing away a reserve that is still good:

  • Best-before date — canned foods, pulses, rice, pasta, flour, oil, honey. It indicates how long the food retains its quality. After that date it is still safe: it may lose texture or flavour, but you don't throw it out just because of the date.
  • Use-by date — fresh meat and fish, certain dairy products, ready meals. That one cannot be stretched: do not consume after the date.
  • In a blackout the fridge is the first thing you lose. Fresh food and items with a use-by date go within 24–48 hours; preserved food is the last thing to leave the plan.

Tip: write the date on each jar or tin when you store it, keep the can opener in the same drawer and apply the FIFO rule —what comes in goes in front; what is already there gets eaten first—. That way the reserve is renewed with your normal shopping instead of expiring in a cupboard.

The nine best long-life preserved foods, compared

Approximate shelf lives for unopened packages in a dry, cool, dark place: the date printed on the package sets the actual shelf life.

ProductApproximate shelf lifeIdeal for
MRE-9 emergency ration, 24 × 500 g20 years unopened (expiry stated in the listing)The drawer you only touch in a real emergency: a complete meal without cooking
TREK'N EAT macaroni and cheese, freeze-dried 140 g3 to 4 years (manufacturer's shelf life)Hot food without a fridge and with minimum weight: prepared with hot water
Luengo cooked lentils in a jar, 570 g2 to 3 years unopenedA proper meal without fire: already cooked, eaten cold with bread
Calvo light tuna in olive oil, 8 × 65 g2 to 4 years unopenedDaily protein that also gets rotated in your usual shopping
Calvo sardines in olive oil, 120 g2 to 4 years unopenedDinner without opening anything else: just a can opener, no water and no fire
Peach halves in extra syrup, 480 g1 to 2 years unopenedFast sugar and a morale boost, especially for children with little appetite
Natural mixed nuts, 1 kg6 to 12 months unopened (the fat goes rancid with heat)Light calories: no water, no fire and nothing else
Raw multifloral honey, 1 kgYears: it does not spoil (crystallising does not ruin it)Energy, sweetening coffee and cracked lips and throat
Whole UHT milk in cartons, 6 × 1 LMonths unopened (date on the carton)The most used and the one that expires fastest: buy it to rotate

Direct links to each product listing with our affiliate identifier. No prices on the page: they change daily, and here we give criteria, not a price tag.

Winner by category

  • For the 20-year drawer: the MRE-9 ration. The only one on the list with a declared two-decade shelf life: buy it once and don't touch it until you need it.
  • For the pantry you use every day: tuna and sardines. They deliver in an emergency and deliver in March: the best reserve is the one eaten before it expires.
  • To eat without fire or water: sardines with nuts. If the plan depends on lighting something, it is not a plan.
  • For space and weight: the freeze-dried ration. 140 g per meal: it fits in the evacuation backpack and doesn't weigh down the cupboard.
  • For cooking without a fridge: the jar of pulses. Already cooked, no gas or soaking, cold or warm.

Six storage rules decided before the blackout

  1. Dry, cool and dark. Never on the garage floor or next to the boiler: dampness dents cans and heat turns the fat in fish and nuts rancid.
  2. Out of the sun. A can in the light all summer tastes of cardboard.
  3. Damaged packaging, out. Dented, swollen, rusty or with the lid popped, throw it out without argument, even if the date is good.
  4. Once opened, fridge and eat. In a warm room, hours; never leave an opened jar 'for tomorrow' on the counter.
  5. Manual can opener in the same drawer. Without power there is no socket, and without a can opener there is no dinner: it is the cheapest item in the kit.
  6. Test it beforehand. A night without power using what you already have stored teaches you more than any list: you'll discover that the can opener is missing, not the tuna.

Five mistakes that leave the pantry the same as the first day

  1. Buying special 'emergency food'. What you don't eat in normal life you won't eat in an emergency either, and it also expires sooner: build the reserve from what you already eat.
  2. Storing it in the storage room or garage. A Spanish summer in a storage room is the worst enemy of preserved food.
  3. Not checking dates when shopping. Two identical cans, two different dates: take the one that lasts longest and note it in the drawer.
  4. Cooking only if there is power. If the whole plan needs the ceramic hob, in a blackout there is no plan: mix ready-to-eat products with products that only need hot water.
  5. Not knowing how much there is. An inventory on the fridge door, with dates, prevents emptying the whole cupboard 'just in case'.

With this you cover the flank that no flashlight fixes. The full setup is in how to store water and food at home and in rotating food by date; menus without power, in eating without power: menus for 3 days; and what to do with what spoils when refrigeration is cut, in preserving food without a fridge. The whole set fits into the basic 72-hour kit and the home or confinement kit.

kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.titulo: Baby emergency kit: what to keep at home by sections (2026)
kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.resumen: What to keep at home for a baby when the power goes out or you have to evacuate: safe water, formula, waterless hygiene, documents and cold. Checklist by sections.
kit-emergencia-bebe-familia.cuerpo:
The power goes out at three in the morning, and the heaviest thing isn't the flashlight: it's the baby waking up. In a household with small children, the 72 hours of self-sufficiency recommended by the EU Preparedness Strategy aren't measured in cans or batteries, but in bottles, diapers and safe water: things that, without power and running water, suddenly stop being automatic. This is the list for assembling a baby's emergency kit without duplicating anything and without overspending, because a good part of it is already at home.

The good news is that a baby doesn't need a separate giant kit: they need the family kit to have a drawer (or bag) with their name on it. The Baby Kit page brings together 32 essentials at an estimated cost of around 90-170 €, and you already use several of those products daily — what you need to do is rotate them, not buy twice.

1. Eating and drinking without power

It's priority number one and has three parts:

  • Water for preparing formula. A baby counts as one more person: to the 3 liters per person per day add whatever you need for hygiene. Store water in closed bottles and have a purification method — purification tablets approved for use with infants, dosed exactly according to the instructions. With safe water, formula is prepared just as always.
  • Backup milk. If the baby takes formula, keep an unopened container of the same type they take now, with the best-before date clearly visible and an expiry check every three months. If breastfeeding, the item is a manual breast pump (it doesn't depend on power) and storage bags. Any guidelines for storing expressed milk are set by your midwife or pediatrician: write them in the kit folder, don't rely on memory.
  • Heating without electricity. A chemical bottle warmer works without gas or a plug and in just a few minutes. A more homemade alternative: fill a wide-mouth thermos with hot water before the power goes out.

A public health detail worth remembering in any scenario: AESAN advises against raw milk unless it has been boiled first because of the risk of pathogenic microorganisms. If an emergency puts you in front of a neighbor with cows and no power, that doesn't change.

2. Hygiene without running water

When tap water doesn't come, the diaper-changing routine gets complicated — but not so much if the supplies are together:

  • Backup diapers (a pack of 20-25 in the current size) and cleaning wipes as a plan B for washing.
  • Watertight bags for dirty clothes and used diapers: without water, smell is the first problem, and the bags contain it.
  • Washing bottles and nipples: if there's no mains water, wash with purified or boiled water and mild soap, and sterilize with cold-water tablets. You don't need electricity, you need a plan.
  • Barrier cream and mild bar soap — a bar lasts months and doesn't melt like gel.

3. Health, temperature and documents

This is where an emergency gets expensive if you're not prepared:

  • Digital thermometer, oral rehydration solution with dosing syringe (for vomiting or diarrhea, the dosage is set by the leaflet or your pediatrician) and nasal aspirator with saline solution: a cold that at home is a nuisance weighs more in a blackout without heating.
  • The waterproof pouch with health record, vaccination card and the baby's DNI or passport, inside the kit — not in a drawer in another room. Add a child identification card with name, date of birth, allergies, medication and two contact phone numbers that don't depend on your mobile phone.
  • Favorite small toys and backup pacifiers in a waterproof bag. It's not a luxury: it's what separates an acceptable night from an impossible one.

4. Warm clothing and evacuation

Cold and leaving are the other two fronts:

  • Spare warm clothing: a sleep sack or one-piece pajamas in the current size plus one for growth, hat, mittens and a children's emergency thermal blanket (or a small fleece blanket if you prefer). Babies lose heat before adults.
  • Ergonomic baby carrier: if you have to leave in a hurry, the baby carrier leaves your hands free for the backpack and for the other child. It's best to have tested it in daylight, not for the first time at three in the morning.
  • The rest of the scenario is covered by the household plan: meeting point and who picks up each child, and the evacuation bag ready by the entrance.

Checklist in a table

AreaEssentialAlready at home
Eating and drinkingUnopened container of formula, stored water, purification tablets, chemical warmerThermos, clean bottles, spoon
HygienePack of diapers, wipes, waterproof bags, cold sterilizing tabletsMild soap, changing bag
HealthThermometer, oral rehydration solution, nasal aspirator, waterproof pouch with documentsCream, gels, regular medication
Warm clothing and leavingSpare sleep sack, thermal blanket, tested baby carrierHat, mittens, fleece blanket

The four common mistakes

  1. Buying a different type of formula “just in case” than the one the baby takes now: they may reject it exactly when there is no alternative. Keep exactly the same one.
  2. Spreading it around the house: if you have to leave in two minutes, something gets left behind. One drawer or one bag, all together and labeled.
  3. Not writing anything down: allergies, feeding schedule, pediatrician's phone number, where the backup is. In the panic, no one remembers anything.
  4. Depending only on your mobile phone: your sole flashlight and source of information. A separate flashlight and a battery-powered radio solve what the phone cannot.

The baby kit isn't put together in one shopping Sunday: it is reviewed every three months to change diaper sizes and check expiry dates, just as you go over the age-by-age checklist for babies and children and the basic 72-hour kit that supports the rest of the household. If you only do one thing today, make it this: put three days of diapers, an unopened can of formula and the pouch with the documents in a bag. The rest will come.

mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.titulo: Best water purifier for emergencies (2026): 7 filters compared
mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.resumen: Best water purifier for emergencies: 7 filters compared by price and use, what each method removes, and the 5 mistakes that leave the water unchanged.
mejor-purificador-agua-emergencia.cuerpo:
After the DANA, several municipalities went days without drinking water while large water bottles sold out in shops. And in a winter blackout the problem isn't just electricity: within three days a household reaches the 72 hours of self-sufficiency recommended by the European Union Preparedness Strategy, and you decide whether you drink from the tap, the river or a bottle. That's where the emergency water purifier comes in: it's not about surviving in the jungle, it's about making any cloudy water drinkable without ending up in the emergency room.

I compare seven real options from Amazon Spain —personal filters, gravity filters for the home, a bottle with a filter and tablets— with their price, ideal use and, above all, with what each one does not do. With emergency water the mistake doesn't show today: it shows at 36 hours.

What Spanish regulations require and what a filter does not solve

In Spain, tap water is regulated by Royal Decree 3/2023, which sets the technical and health criteria and quality control: if it comes out of the tap, it is fit to drink. The problem appears when supply is cut or when turbidity rises after a storm. That's where Civil Protection takes over: water for three days and, if there are doubts about quality, boil or disinfect. Its Family Emergency Plan guide expressly includes “water purification tablets” and “water (for 3 days)”.

And here comes the part almost no one explains when buying:

  • Membrane filters (0.1–0.2 microns, depending on the manufacturer) remove bacteria, parasites and most microplastics. They do not remove viruses, which are much smaller, or solvents, pesticides or hydrocarbons.
  • Chlorine or chlorine dioxide tablets do cover viruses, but they leave a taste and need contact time (minutes) before drinking, and they don't remove turbidity or chemicals either.
  • Boiling is the safest and crudest method: it kills everything alive, but it doesn't remove dirt, doesn't remove heavy metals and uses gas or batteries just when you don't have them.
  • No method fixes water with chemicals (a leak, a spill, diesel in the estuary). That water is not made drinkable: it is discarded.

The conclusion: a filter alone is never enough. The real combo is filter + tablets + the option to boil. And don't forget the reserve —three litres per person per day—, put together step by step in how much water you need and how to store it.

Comparison: the seven emergency water purifiers

ProductTypeApproximate priceIdeal for
LifeStraw personal filterStraw / personal filter26,95 €Backpack, trails and “the one who has nothing”
LifeStraw Peak Series SoloCompact personal filter33,34 €Regular use, more flow than a basic straw
Membrane Solutions 0,1 µmPump/straw filter18,99 €Tight budget (the cheapest)
Waterflow 3-stageCarbon filter24,97 €Best value for money
Waterdrop with gravity bagGravity filter27,00 €Home: fill, hang and serve several people
Membrane Solutions WS02Removable higher-flow filter52,99 €Motorhome, country house, family kit
LifeStraw Go with bottleBottle with integrated filter67,48 €A single object that already goes full in your backpack
Purification tabletsChemical disinfection9-25 €Cover viruses, which no filter on this list catches

Prices checked today on the Amazon.es product page: they change daily, take them as an order of magnitude. The links go directly to the product page with our affiliate ID.

Winner by category (depending on the scenario you face)

  • Best for the evacuation backpack: the LifeStraw. It fits in a pocket, needs no replacement parts and works without learning anything: it's the one you buy if you only buy one.
  • Best for the home: the gravity filter with bag. Fill it, hang it and let it drip into a container: it gives several people drinking water without bending down to a puddle. The most convenient with children and older people.
  • Best budget: the Membrane Solutions at 18,99 €. It does the job without costing more than a box of canned food.
  • Best value for money: the 3-stage Waterflow. With activated carbon it improves smell and taste: river or cistern water without carbon tastes bad and ends up being thrown away.
  • Best mandatory add-on: purification tablets. Cheap, light and long-dated: the only thing on this list that covers viruses. Without them, the filter alone leaves you with a false “safe water”.

Three real uses in a Spanish household

  • After a DANA or a flood. It comes out cloudy or with a boil notice: filter for drinking and chlorine for surfaces. The cleaning order is in returning home after a flood.
  • A blackout lasting several days. The toilet cistern and the water heater are still full, but the pump doesn't work. Filling containers from the bathtub and filtering them is faster than carrying bottles upstairs. The full script is in the blackout kit.
  • Field or trail water. River, spring or motorhome tank: the same filter works at the weekend. Which is exactly what most kits lack: equipment that never gets its first use.

The five mistakes that leave the water just as it was

  1. Filtering very cloudy water directly. Dirt clogs the membrane and leaves you with no flow in minutes. First let it settle or prefilter it with a clean cloth, then filter.
  2. Using the filter for water with chemicals (diesel, solvent, a cistern treated with garden products). Nothing on this list removes them: discard the water.
  3. Buying tablets and not checking the expiry date. Tablets lose strength; keep them dry, in their closed jar, and write the date on the jar with a marker. Just like with pantry food: what's expired isn't a reserve.
  4. Filtering and drinking without allowing contact time if you also use tablets: with cold water it takes several minutes. Write it on the container label, so it isn't decided by whoever is thirstiest.
  5. Not testing it beforehand. Equipment that has never been used gets used badly. Filter a glass of water at home and see how long it takes: in a blackout you'll already know what it does.

What to buy today (and what to leave ready)

Minimum, cheap list: a three-stage filter for the home, a personal filter for each person leaving the house, a strip of purification tablets and a pot with a lid for boiling. With that you cover bacteria, viruses and the emergency route without electricity. The set fits into the basic 72-hour kit and, if you live in a flood-prone area, into the DANA and flood kit.

And an idea that saves money: the water reserve still comes first. A purifier doesn't replace containers, it extends them. The three-litres-per-person-per-day rule, containers and rotation in how to store water and food at home.

mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.titulo: Best heater without electricity: 5 types to get through a blackout (2026)
mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.resumen: Butane, pellets or electric: which heater works when the power goes out, how much it costs per hour and why an electric one is no use in a blackout.
mejor-estufa-sin-luz-apagon.cuerpo:
In April the blackout lasted a few hours at eighteen degrees. In January, the same outage at three in the morning is another matter: without heating, a home loses degrees in a few hours, and the National Plan for Preventive Actions against Low Temperatures from the Ministry of Health says it bluntly: cold not only causes hypothermia, it also “increases traffic accidents and falls from ice patches, as well as fires and carbon monoxide poisoning from gas heaters, braziers, etc.” That sentence sums up this article: choosing the best heater for when the power goes out is about not turning the living room into a medical problem.

I compare the five types bought in Spain —butane, pellets, electric, catalytic, and the no-heater option— by their cost per hour and what they need to work when the grid is down.

How much heat you need (and why heating the whole house is a trap)

A 4,000 W heater does not heat a flat: it heats its room. The strategy for a blackout is to reduce the volume —small room, closed door, people together—. A rough rule for a closed room of 15-20 m²:

  • Well insulated (thick walls, double-glazed window): 700-1,000 W is enough.
  • Poorly insulated or with high ceilings: it needs 1,500-2,000 W.
  • Above 2,500-3,000 W in 15 m² is wasted money and more risk.

And an idea that matters more than wattage: heating does not replace clothing. Layered clothing + hot food + a low heater works; the breakdown is in dressing in layers in an emergency and the night plan in how to maintain body temperature without electricity.

Comparison: the five types of heater without power

TypePower / consumptionApproximate cost per hourWorks without grid?
Butane heater with oxygen depletion cut-off4,200 W · 12.5 kg cylinder ≈ 30-40 h0,40-0,50 €Yes ✅
Pellet heater6-8 kW · 1.2-1.6 kg of pellets/h0,70-0,95 €Yes, but it needs a plug for the auger and fan
Electric heater (convector or split)2,000 W · 0,15-0,18 €/kWh0,30-0,36 €No ❌ (only with power or a generator)
Catalytic butane heater (flameless)2,400-3,000 W · smaller cylinder0,30-0,45 €Yes ✅
No heater: layers + electric body warmer + survival blanket0 W consumption0 €Always ✅

Approximate prices for Spain: 12.5 kg cylinder at 15-18 €, pallet pellets at 0,45-0,60 €/kg, and electricity at 0,15-0,18 €/kWh. They are for comparison, not for signing a contract.

Winner by category

  • Best for a real blackout: the butane heater with oxygen depletion cut-off. It does not depend on anyone, heats in minutes, and one cylinder lasts several nights: 4,200 W with automatic oxygen depletion cut-off (about 84 €). The cut-off prevents the heater from continuing to burn in a closed room.
  • Best for a whole house: pellets, if you already have the heater and the pallet. It heats an entire floor and works out cheap per hour, but almost all need a plug for the auger, fan, and ignition: without power, they do not start.
  • Best combo cooking + heat: the portable butane stove (20-45 €). It is not a heater, but it heats water and food without turning on the home kitchen: in three days of outage it pays for itself with the first pot.
  • Best budget: the no-heater option. A thermal survival blanket (3-8 €), a reusable electric body warmer for when the power comes back, and a warm sleeping bag get you through the night: less than a gas cylinder, and it cannot fail.

What about the catalytic heater? It is the cleanest version of butane: it burns with no visible flame and gives softer heat, more pleasant in a small room. It is worth it if an older person or a child spends the day there; for a budget kit, the money is better spent on butane and a CO detector.

The serious mistake: buying an electric heater for the blackout

It is the most common mistake: a 2,000 W convector is cheap, silent, and does not generate carbon monoxide, which is why it sells so well. The problem is that during a blackout there is no voltage and the electric heater becomes furniture. To make it work you would need a 1,500-2,000 W generator; what batteries can really handle is in best power bank for a blackout and in emergency solar generator.

Data point from the Spanish context: according to the CNMC Household Panel, 43.2% of households have a contracted capacity of between 4 and 6 kW and spent an average of 47,8 € per month on electricity. With two 2,000 W convectors plugged in you are already at the limit of that capacity; in an outage that is not a bill problem: it is that there is no current to consume.

Carbon monoxide: the four rules that save the night

CO has no smell, no sting, and no warning: the initial symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea) are confused with a cold, and cases are concentrated from October to March, just when heaters are turned on. Official recommendations are identical across all administrations:

  • Ventilate twice a day, 15 minutes each time, even if it is cold. It is the literal instruction of the Ministry of Health's Cold Weather Plan.
  • Turn off electric and gas heaters during the night. Also from the Cold Weather Plan: sleeping with the heater on is the decision people regret most.
  • Do not use camping stoves, barbecues, braziers, or the kitchen oven inside the home, and do not block the ventilation grilles. This is the recommendation of the 112 services and Civil Protection.
  • Battery-powered carbon monoxide detector on the wall, one metre from the bed and away from the ceiling. It costs between 15 and 35 €: see CO detectors. No heater in this article is complete without one.

Checklist before the first cold snap

  • Butane heater with oxygen depletion cut-off and two spare cylinders: the second one always runs out on the first night.
  • CO detector with new batteries and the replacement date noted.
  • Tape and plastic to seal windows: a poorly sealed room demands twice the power.
  • Blankets, warm sleeping bag, and thermal clothing; lighters and long matches out of the reach of children.
  • Food and water that do not need fire: three-day menus without cooking.

If the outage drags on, the heater is only one piece: the full list is in the cold and winter kit and in the blackout kit.

mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.titulo: Best power bank for emergency kit 2026: 4 models and real mAh
mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.resumen: How much capacity you really need during a blackout: 4 charges per 20,000 real mAh, 4 models compared, and the mistakes that drain the kit's battery.
mejor-powerbank-emergencia-capacidad.cuerpo:
The blackout of 28 April 2025 left half the country without power and with phones at 2%. Most people solved it with the power bank they had charged in a drawer. But if the power is out for several days, that drawer runs out: within 24-48 hours your phone becomes a glass weight, and with it radio streaming, the map, family WhatsApp and the phone flashlight. This is the guide to choosing the emergency power bank that truly sustains you for 72 hours — with the real capacity you need, the honest figure brands hide (mAh) and four compared models.

How much capacity you really need for 72 hours

A modern smartphone has a 4,000-5,000 mAh battery. On a normal day, one full charge lasts; in an emergency you'll use the phone much more (calls, WhatsApp, flashlight, map), so the realistic estimate is 2 charges per day. On that basis:

  • 72 hours, 1 phone: 10,000-20,000 mAh.
  • 72 hours, 2 phones (partner or family): 20,000-30,000 mAh.
  • 7 days or more: 30,000 mAh + portable solar panel to recharge during the day.

There's a nuance that no product spec sheet tells you and that changes the purchase: the advertised mAh are not the mAh that reach your phone. A 20,000 mAh battery at 3.7 V stores about 74 Wh; when converted to USB output (5-9 V) and with electronics losses, what actually arrives is between 13,000 and 14,500 mAh — that is, 65% to 72% efficiency, the range independent labs measure with units from known brands. Translated: a 20,000 mAh power bank gives 4 full phone charges, not the 8-10 the brochure suggests. With 10,000 real mAh (about 2 charges) you just about get through 72 hours; with 4 charges, comfortably. That's why 20,000 mAh is the recommended minimum and not a whim.

Comparison: the 4 emergency power banks I recommend

Ordered by use case, not by price. All are verified Amazon.es listings with the same criteria: published real capacity, USB-C input and output, and a price consistent with what they offer.

ModelCapacityOutputsApprox. priceBest for
High-capacity power bank ≥20,000 mAh with cables included20,000 mAh (74 Wh)USB-C + USB-A, dual output25-50 €The 72h kit standard: 4 phone charges and two devices at once.
External battery 10,000-20,000 mAh, two outputs10,000-20,000 mAhDual USB output20-40 €Second battery for your partner or child: redundancy for under 30 €.
Compact power bank 10,000-20,000 mAh10,000-20,000 mAhUSB-C + USB-A15-35 €The one that stays in your bag every day: if it's always with you, you never forget it.
Lightweight power bank + USB cable10,000 mAhUSB-C25-50 €Mountain and evacuation kit: light and keeps your phone going for the weekend.

The winner for most people: the first one, 20,000 mAh with cables. It's the one used in the basic 72-hour kit, the blackout kit, the earthquake kit and the connectivity kit: four different scenarios have ended up choosing the same one, and that consensus says more than any brochure.

What to require from an emergency power bank (the checklist)

  1. Capacity: 20,000 mAh minimum — 4 full phone charges, the number that gets you through 72 hours without anxiety.
  2. Dual output — charge two people's phones at once, or phone + radio, without taking turns.
  3. USB-C input and output — recharging the power bank itself takes 3-4 hours and it's the connector you already have at home. If it also supports Power Delivery (PD), it can charge tablets and some lightweight laptops too.
  4. Real percentage indicator — the usual four LEDs lie halfway through a charge; a numeric display (or percentage) tells you how much is really left when you decide whether to turn on the light.
  5. Built-in LED flashlight — costs nothing extra and in the kit acts as backup if your main flashlight runs out.
  6. Shock-resistant — it falls off the table at 3 a.m. in the dark; it has to keep working.

Typical mistakes with the kit's power bank

  • Buying it discharged. The power bank is checked like the rest of the kit: 100% charged and rotated every 3-6 months. A battery that has been sitting in a drawer at 10% for a year won't save you the night you need it.
  • Trusting the mAh on the label. 20,000 real mAh means 4 phone charges; if the price is suspiciously low, be wary of the real capacity (unknown brands often deliver half).
  • Using it as a permanent tap. Full discharge and recharge cycles extend cell life; keeping it plugged into the wall at 100% all year does it no favors.
  • Forgetting the cable. A power bank without a cable is an elegant brick. Keep it with the battery, not in another drawer, and have a spare if you rely on USB-C.
  • Dismissing air travel. If you're evacuating by car it doesn't apply, but if you have to fly: IATA (and European EASA) allows up to 100 Wh without authorization (≈27,000 mAh), always in carry-on baggage and never in the hold; between 100 and 160 Wh you need airline permission, and above 160 Wh it cannot fly. A 20,000 mAh (74 Wh) travels without problems.

And if the blackout lasts more than three days

The power bank is the reserve, not the power station: it runs out, full stop. To go beyond 72 hours, the combination that works is power bank + 30-50 W portable solar panel. With summer sun, a 30-50 W panel recharges a 20,000 mAh battery every 2-3 days (in winter, multiply by two or three); that way the phone and radio don't depend on the power coming back. You'll find the real watt calculations in portable solar panel for emergencies and the full combo in 72-hour solar generator. And don't forget the radio: official information comes via hand-crank radio, which doesn't drain your battery reserve.

The verdict

A 20,000 mAh power bank with USB-C and dual output is the standard for the 72h kit: 4 phone charges, 74 Wh (flies without paperwork) and 25-50 € well spent. If you have a partner or children, add a second 10,000-20,000 mAh one — cheap redundancy that turns a scare into a minor detail. And remember the only rule that matters: it comes out of the drawer 100% charged and is rotated every 3-6 months. The full kit list, with the power already sorted, is in the basic 72-hour kit.

mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.titulo: The best emergency radio with hand crank and solar panel (2026)
mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.resumen: Emergency radios with hand crank and solar panel compared: runtime without batteries, range, mobile charger and which one to choose for 72 hours.
mejor-radio-emergencia-manivela-solar.cuerpo:
When the power grid goes down, phones lose signal and the WiFi dies. A radio is the ONLY device that can keep receiving official information for your area during a prolonged blackout. Don't underestimate it: it's your link to the outside world when everything else fails.

Why a hand-crank radio?

A phone with a power bank lasts for hours (maybe a day). A hand-crank radio lasts FOREVER: crank it for 3 minutes and you get 15-30 minutes of broadcasting. The solar panel is the perfect complement: leave it in the sun and it charges itself.

Non-negotiable features

  • FM + AM + SW: Official stations use different bands. You don't get to choose. An emergency radio must receive ALL of them.
  • Portable and light (<400g): If you have to carry it during an evacuation, it can't weigh like a brick.
  • USB charging: Besides the crank and solar, it must be able to charge via USB cable. That's the main charging method.
  • LED flashlight: A radio without a built-in flashlight is an incomplete radio.
  • USB to charge your phone: It works as a power bank. Your phone is your main communication tool; the radio keeps it going.

The best options for a 72h kit

The hand-crank, solar-powered emergency radios that meet ALL the requirements above are:

2-IN-1 HAND-CRANK RADIO WITH SOLAR PANEL

Receives FM, AM, SW and NOAA (if you have it at hand). Includes LED flashlight, SOS emergency light and power bank for your phone. IPX4 water-resistant (handles light rain). Weight: ~380g. Runtime: 30 min with a full crank, 4h in low mode on battery.

HAND-CRANK EMERGENCY RADIO

Simpler but lighter (~300g). Runs on hand crank, solar or AA batteries. Perfect if you only need the basics without the fuss. Includes flashlight and SOS mode.

The verdict

The emergency radio is the most underrated item in a 72h kit. Spend ~25-35€ on one that receives FM+AM and has a crank + solar panel. When the blackout comes, you'll be grateful for every euro.

mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.titulo: The 7 best flashlights for a 72-hour emergency kit (2026)
mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.resumen: 7 emergency flashlights compared by real runtime (lumens and hours), price and durability: which one deserves a place in your 72-hour kit.
mejor-linterna-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
A 72-hour kit without light is like a backpack with no bottom: nice but useless. The flashlight is one of the first five items that appear in ALL civil preparedness guides in Spain, Europe and the US. It is not negotiable.

Why a flashlight (and not candles)?

Candles pose a fire risk that you don't need during an emergency. A quality LED flashlight offers:

  • Instant on (no need to wait for it to light)
  • Zero fire risk
  • Up to 100,000 hours of LED life
  • Adjustable brightness (full light to search for something, dim light so as not to dazzle)

What you should demand from an emergency flashlight

  1. Water resistance (IPX7 or higher): A DANA won't give you any warning. If it rains inside the backpack, the flashlight must keep working.
  2. Minimum runtime of 8 hours: In low mode. If it only lasts 30 minutes in high mode, check the low mode.
  3. Rechargeable batteries or USB: Batteries run out and get forgotten. A USB model is recharged with a power bank.
  4. SOS mode: A button that flashes in Morse. It can be the difference between being found and not.
  5. Hook or magnet: To leave it on the ceiling and keep your hands free.

The 7 flashlights we recommend for your kit

I have tested them or researched them in depth. These are the ones that best balance quality and response for a 72-hour kit:

1. Waterproof LED flashlight with built-in power bank

The most practical option: it is the flashlight AND the external battery. You charge one cable and you already have two kit items. Runtime: ~8h in low mode, ~1.5h in high. Water resistance: IPX7. Weight: ~200g.

2. Hand-crank flashlight with solar radio

If you're looking for an all-in-one solution: crank for 2 minutes and you get 15 minutes of light. The radio lets you listen to official broadcasts if the network goes down. Ideal as a secondary flashlight.

3. USB-rechargeable LED headlamp

If you need to keep your hands free (change a bulb, search in a backpack, attend to someone), a headlamp is the best. It goes on your head and doesn't fall off.

4. Magnetic emergency flashlight with dusk sensor

It sticks to any metal surface and turns on by itself when the house lights go out. Perfect for the storage room, the fuse box or the fridge.

5. "Fireball"-type flashlight (EMERGENCY GLOBE)

No, it's not some strange Chinese invention. Spherical flashlights with a solar panel and pull switch have been in civil protection guides in Canada and Finland for years. 360° light (not directional). Ideal for lighting an entire room.

6. Headlamp with basic night vision

For the more adventurous: it lets you see in total darkness with infrared light invisible to the human eye. It is a gadget you probably don't need... but if you ever need to move around your home at 3 in the morning without turning anything on, it is pure gold.

7. Kit of 3 small flashlights (redundancy strategy)

Three flashlights at ~5€ each, stored in different places in the backpack. If one is lost, another works, and the third is for when a neighbor asks you for one. Redundancy is the basis of preparedness.

The verdict

For a basic 72-hour kit: a USB-rechargeable LED flashlight + a pack of 2 small flashlights as backup. Total investment: ~25€. It gets you through the first 72 hours of darkness.

botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.titulo: Complete emergency first aid kit: 15 items you can't do without (2026)
botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.resumen: What an emergency first aid kit should contain and what you don't need: a block-by-block list for every household, checking expiry dates and 8 mistakes that make it useless.
botiquin-emergencia-lista-completa.cuerpo:
Health is the second section of the 72h kit (after water) and the one with the most variations depending on your family. Here is the universal base list and the adaptations for special cases.

The core first aid kit: 15 non-negotiable items

  1. Sterile gauze (pack of 4): To cover wounds without fibers getting in.
  2. Elastic bandages (3 units, 8cm): To immobilize or hold gauze in place.
  3. Adhesive bandages (assorted sizes, 20 units): For small wounds and scratches.
  4. Single-dose antiseptic (10 units): Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine. Alcohol-free.
  5. Blunt-tip scissors: To cut bandages or clothing if necessary.
  6. Tweezers: To remove splinters or debris from a wound.
  7. Paracetamol (500mg and 1g): Pain and fever. Always follow the patient information leaflet and do not combine it with other medicines without checking their product information.
  8. Anti-inflammatory (ibuprofen 400mg): Inflammation and pain. It is not suitable for everyone: allergies, stomach, kidney or heart problems are contraindications. Check its product information (AEMPS) and confirm with a healthcare professional.
  9. Antihistamine (loratadine or cetirizine): Allergic reactions. Important if you live in an area with many plants or bees.
  10. Anti-diarrheal (oralit + loperamide): Diarrhea in an emergency is much more dangerous than at home (dehydration).
  11. Antipyretics (children's paracetamol): If there are children at home.
  12. Nitrile gloves (pair): To protect yourself when treating someone.
  13. Emergency thermal blanket: Prevents hypothermia. It weighs 20g and can save your life.
  14. Burn cream: Aloe vera gel or a specific cream. Burns are common in emergencies involving improvised cooking.
  15. Family medical list: Names of regular medications, allergies, blood group, emergency phone numbers.

Important: this list is a guide, not medical advice. Before taking any medicine, read the patient information leaflet and its product information (available on the AEMPS website) and, if you have doubts—pregnancy, children, chronic illnesses or other medicines—consult a healthcare professional or pharmacist.

Adaptations by situation

With babies: add pediatric oral rehydration solution, digital thermometer, extra pacifiers (if they are used to them), spare diapers.

With older adults: Chronic medication for 5 extra days (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid, heart). Include a manual blood pressure monitor.

With pets: External antiparasitic, veterinary collar (to stop them licking wounds), medications if they are for chronic conditions.

The verdict

A basic emergency first aid kit costs between 30-50€ if you buy everything new. But the most valuable part is not the kit itself: it is your family's chronic medication. If someone at home takes daily medication, those 5-7 days of reserve ARE the emergency kit.

alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.titulo: Emergency food: what to eat, how much to store, and how to rotate it without throwing anything away
alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.resumen: Which foods last for years and which expire soon: rotate by date, consumption order, and how to set up a pantry that doesn't go to waste.
alimentos-emergencia-caducidad-rotacion.cuerpo:
Why food expires before the emergency

Water is the top priority, and you shouldn't wait until you're very thirsty to look for it. Food is the second thing people forget when preparing a kit, and also the thing that spoils most often: people buy special 'emergency' cans or jars that end up in the bin because they expire. The solution is simpler: the best emergency food is the food you already eat.

Many European and Spanish guides recommend a reserve of at least 72 hours; it is not a legal obligation. The key is not to buy 'emergency food' but to rotate what you already eat: that way the reserve gets used, restocked, and doesn't turn into a museum of cans.

The golden rule: buy to eat, not to store

The most effective method is FIFO (First In, First Out). It works like this:

  1. Buy an extra of what you already eat regularly: one more packet of pasta, two more cans of tuna, one extra packet of biscuits.
  2. When you use the extra in your normal life, replace it directly in the reserve.
  3. Your emergency stock rotates itself, without you having to think about dates or expiry.

This turns an 'emergency reserve' into something that requires no management: it is simply your regular pantry with an extra 20–30%. If you already shop every week, you don't need a special shopping trip: add one unit of what you already eat and let rotation do the rest.

Non-perishable foods: the list that actually works

Not all foods last the same amount of time. The dates in the table are indicative and refer to quality in a dry, cool pantry; the manufacturer's label takes precedence. They are not a safety guarantee if the packaging is damaged or has been stored poorly.

FoodApproximate shelf lifeHow to store itSafety note
White rice (sealed)2 yearsAirtight container, dry, cool placeCooked rice: refrigerate and keep no more than 3–4 days
Honey2 years or more if well sealedClosed jar, not refrigeratedDo not give honey to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism
SaltPractically no expiryClosed container, away from moistureIt does not replace drinking water or medical care
Dry pasta2 yearsSealed packet, away from lightOnce cooked, refrigerate and keep 3–4 days
Low-acid canned goods (tuna, pulses, meat)2–5 yearsUnopened, cool, dry placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep 3–4 days
High-acid canned goods (tomato, fruit)12–18 monthsUnopened, cool, dry placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep 3–4 days
Salted biscuits or crackers6–9 monthsWell-closed packetIf they get damp or smell bad, discard them
Nuts6–12 monthsAirtight container, coolRancid ones are noticeable by smell and taste; do not use them
Dark chocolate6–12 monthsAway from heatHeat-related blooming is not dangerous, but it loses quality
Powdered milk3–5 years unopened, depending on packagingDry place; once opened, follow the labelDo not use expired milk for a baby
Energy bars6–12 monthsIndividually wrapped, unopenedCheck allergens before storing them
Stock in a cartonThe date on the packaging; usually around 1 yearUnopened, cool placeOnce opened, refrigerate and keep 3–4 days

What people forget: salt keeps practically indefinitely and honey lasts a long time if well sealed, but neither replaces a varied diet or hydration. Salt does not 'prevent fainting': if someone feels dizzy or is dehydrated, assess the situation and seek help; do not give spoonfuls of salt.

How much food for 72 hours: a practical reference

There is no single figure: it depends on whether you have a kitchen available. If the power outage leaves the fridge not working but you can heat canned goods over a fire, you need fewer ready meals. If you have no safe way to cook, you need everything ready to eat.

Scenario1 person (72 h)2 people (72 h)Family of 4 (72 h)
With safe cooking3–4 main servings + 2–3 snacks + 100 g nuts6–8 servings + 4–6 snacks + 200 g nuts12–16 servings + 8–12 snacks + 400 g nuts
No cooking (ready to eat)5–6 ready servings + 4 snacks + 150 g nuts10–12 servings + 8 snacks + 300 g nuts20–24 servings + 16 snacks + 600 g nuts

A family of 4 needs approximately 20–24 ready servings, snacks, and nuts for 72 hours without cooking. It is a reference, not a prescription: adjust according to ages, appetite, medication, and special needs. Cost depends on the supermarket and brands; you don't need to buy 'survival' products to cover it.

The 'double packet' rule in practice

The simplest method that works requires no inventories or dates. Every time you go to the supermarket, apply these rules:

  • Canned goods: if you buy a pack of 4 cans of tuna, add 2 more. The extra ones are your reserve; don't separate them from the pantry.
  • Pasta or rice: if you use a 500 g packet a week, keep another one closed. One gets used, the other restocks.
  • Biscuits or crackers: one extra packet. They are the snack for the first day, when you don't yet want to open a can.
  • Nuts: one extra bag. They expire before canned goods, so they go first in the rotation.

With normal shopping and a little foresight, a family can have the full reserve without a huge outlay. You don't need to fill a cupboard all at once: rotation does the work.

When to check the reserve: a practical schedule

You don't need a calendar or alarms. Do the check every time the clocks change (March and October), just as you do with remote-control batteries:

  • Check dates: 2 minutes. Look at the dates on nuts, biscuits, powdered milk, and canned goods.
  • Complete what is missing: if something expired, replace it with a new one and put it at the front.
  • Restock what was used: if the reserve went down (because of a trip or journey), top it up with the next shop.
  • Check special needs: if there are babies, allergens, or restricted diets, check that the stock is still valid and sufficient.

Preparedness is a habit, not a one-off act. Checking twice a year takes less than 10 minutes and prevents throwing food away or discovering a problem when the supermarket is no longer available.

Common mistakes with emergency food

1. Buying special 'emergency food'. Freeze-dried meals can last for years, but they also cost more and don't always match what you eat. With canned goods and dry foods you already eat, you have a reserve that rotates and isn't wasted.

2. Not having anything ready to eat. If the power goes out and you don't have a safe way to cook, unopened cans won't solve dinner. Keep bars, biscuits, and nuts for the first day.

3. Storing food in a hot or humid place. Heat and humidity degrade packaging and food. Choose a cool, dry, dark place; if the pantry gets very hot in summer, find another spot.

4. Forgetting salt and hydration. Salt is useful for cooking, but it is not a medicine and does not by itself prevent fainting. In an emergency, water and medical care come first.

5. Not thinking about dependents. Babies (formula or infant milk), older people (soft or specific diets), pets, and people with allergies have their own needs. Each one needs its own reserve and check.

How much does the setup cost?

The cost depends on the shop, the brands, and what you already have at home. There is no fixed figure: 12–24 main servings, snacks, nuts, pasta, biscuits, and stock can cost from a normal shop to considerably more if you choose prepared products. Start with what you consume and add one extra unit; you don't need to set up a restaurant pantry.

Buying canned goods: Search for assorted canned goods on Amazon →

Buying energy bars: Search for energy bars on Amazon →

Buying nuts in bulk: Search for mixed nuts on Amazon →

Food within the 72h kit

Food is only one part of the puzzle. If you want a complete pack with water, light, power, and food, the Basic 72-Hour Kit has everything verified. For specific scenarios, the power outage kit includes emergency cooking, and the DANA kit adds supply protection.

And if you only want the food without the rest, apply the double packet rule on your next supermarket shop. In two weeks you'll have the 72 h reserve, without spending on 'emergency food' and without throwing anything away.

Do canned foods really expire?

For canned goods, the date usually indicates quality more than safety: an intact can, with no dents at the seams, no rust, no swelling, and no leaks, may keep its quality beyond the 'best before' date, but that does not authorize adding years to the date. If in doubt, discard it. But don't use it as a general rule: if the can is dented, swollen, smells bad, or gas comes out when you open it, discard it. When in doubt, don't take the risk.

Can you cook without electricity or gas?

Yes, but you need a safe heat source and ventilation. A camping stove should only be used outdoors or in a well-ventilated space; never inside a home, tent, or car, due to the risk of carbon monoxide. Without safe cooking, eat ready-to-eat foods and don't improvise with fuels.

What should you do if there are babies or allergens?

For babies, always follow the label on formula or infant milk and the preparation instructions; do not use expired products and discard any leftovers after a feed. If there are allergies, store foods labeled as free from the allergen and check the labels every time: formulations change. For medical diets, consult a professional before building the reserve.

If you found this article useful, share it with someone who lives alone. A person without a reserve is the one who suffers most in the first 24 hours of any emergency.

starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.titulo: Starlink in a blackout: setting it up, powering it and whether it's worth it (2026)
starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.resumen: A practical guide to Starlink in emergencies: real power draw, how to power it off-grid, cost, installation and which alternatives to line up before buying.
starlink-emergencia-72h-conectividad.cuerpo:
When the power goes out across a whole area, the first thing that fails isn't the fridge: it's information. The router dies, the phone loses data and local networks get saturated. That's the moment many people think of Starlink, SpaceX's satellite constellation that promises internet from any spot with a clear sky. This article is the practical guide: what Starlink solves in a 72-hour emergency, what it doesn't solve, how much it consumes and how to power it when there's no grid, so you can decide sensibly whether it deserves a place in your preparedness plan — or whether something simpler and cheaper is enough.

The official recommendation is the usual one: the European Union Preparedness Strategy asks households to keep 72 hours' worth of supplies, and the Directorate General for Civil Protection and Emergencies insists on keeping a reliable source of information during any incident. Starlink can be that source, but only if you're clear about how it stays powered without a socket. Let's take it step by step.

What Starlink is (and why it comes up in every emergency)

Starlink is a constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites offering broadband internet without relying on ground infrastructure: there's no fibre to lay and no mobile towers in between. You only need three things: a terminal with a clear view of the sky, an active data connection through its network and electric power to run it. That last condition is the one to hold on to, because it's usually what's missing just when you need it most.

In an emergency scenario, that architecture has one concrete advantage: even if the power plants, substations or mobile towers in your area are out of service, the satellites are still up there. If the local grid is down but the satellite operator's infrastructure works, you can get connectivity back in minutes. It's the exact opposite of what happens with the mobile network, which depends on towers with limited battery backup and generators.

What Starlink is NOT: three wrong expectations

Before spending money, it's worth taking apart three common ideas:

  • It's not a cheap emergency plan B. The terminal is a serious purchase and the monthly fee is recurring. If you're not going to use it day to day, there's no point buying it «just in case»: you'll have spent money on a piece of kit that loses value in a drawer while your 72-hour plan is still missing the basics (water, light, first-aid kit, radio).
  • It doesn't work blind or indoors. It needs line of sight to the sky: narrow balconies, inner courtyards with high walls or dense forest degrade the signal noticeably.
  • It doesn't replace official radio or 112. For official alerts and Civil Protection warnings, the route is still the emergency radio and the national emergency channels; for real emergencies, 112. Starlink gives you additional routes (messaging, checking sources, calls over data), not a replacement.

That said, there are scenarios where it changes the picture completely: evacuations to rural areas with no coverage, work in the mountains, houses on industrial estates or in villages with poor mobile coverage, and of course long blackouts where the mobile network gets saturated with people trying to call.

The key point: how much it consumes and how to power it off-grid

Here's the question that really matters. A typical residential Starlink terminal draws around 60-75 W in active use and somewhat more than 20-40 W at rest, depending on the model and whether it's in sleep mode. Translated into a three-day blackout, with reasonable use of about 10-12 hours a day, you're talking about between 0.7 and 1.2 kWh per day… and that's where most plans fall apart, because that comfortably exceeds the capacity of almost any handheld power bank.

The realistic options, in order of practicality:

  • Power station. This is the serious option: a 1,000-2,000 Wh battery with a 220 V output gives you one or two days of Starlink plus the router, lights and phone charging. Switch it on only when you need it and put the terminal in standby to stretch the margin. The Electricity Kit gathers the selection and the article on portable solar panels explains how many watts you really need to recharge it in the sun.
  • Portable solar panel. With a well-oriented 100-200 W panel, a morning of decent sun returns a good part of a full day's consumption. It's the combination that lasts the most days, but it depends on the sky: on a storm day or with heavy overcast, generation drops — and that's where the battery cushion comes in.
  • Large power bank as a short reserve. A 20,000 mAh power bank or more with 65 W output (the 20,000 mAh model in the kit is one example) powers the terminal for a few hours: enough for a quick look at maps and alerts, not for working or leaving it on all night.
  • Car alternative (carefully). Some terminals work with 12 V vehicle adapters. Use it with the engine running or with a monitored auxiliary battery: leaving the vehicle draining the starter battery is a sure way to end up without a car and without internet at the same time.

Golden practical rule: Starlink is the last link in the power chain, not the first. First you secure water, power and heat or cooling; then communications; Starlink goes in that third layer, together with the phone and the radio.

What it really costs, no surprises

There are two separate line items, and it's best not to mix them:

  • Equipment (one-off). The terminal is around 500-700 € for the standard residential model and goes above that figure for mobile or higher-performance versions. Add accessories depending on the setup: roof or mast mount, a long extension cable if the good window is far away, and a case or transport bag if you're going to move it.
  • Subscription (monthly). In Spain the residential plan is around 45-60 € a month, with portable plans somewhat more expensive because of use on the move. Cancelling and reactivating is possible, but with a re-provisioning cost in some cases: read it before, not after.

The total for the Starlink Kit (terminal + accessories + a year of subscription) is easily a family holiday budget or more. The useful question isn't «can I afford it?», but «what other gap in my preparedness plan does this money leave uncovered?». If your first-aid kit is empty and your basic kit doesn't exist, prioritise that first; it's all in the basic 72-hour kit.

Setting it up in 30 minutes: commissioning

Home installation is simple, and the time to test it is NOW, on a good day, not with the power out:

  1. Choose a location with a clear sky. Mount the terminal on a roof, a high balcony or a large window facing a wide angle of sky. The right mounting bracket keeps the first gust of wind from bringing it down.
  2. Connect it and let it calibrate. The terminal aligns itself and searches for satellites; the app tells you whether the position is good. If the app reports poor signal at the first location, raise or move the terminal before accepting it.
  3. Power it from your backup system. Check that it starts from the power station and note how many Wh it uses in one real hour of use. That figure, measured by you, is worth more than any table on the internet for planning your days of autonomy.
  4. Test the use cases that matter to you: a family video call, checking the alerts map, messages. Check whether your home router also starts from the battery — if not, you'll have WiFi with nothing behind it.
  5. Leave EVERYTHING labelled and accessible: cables, adapters and manual in a waterproof bag with the terminal. During a night-time blackout nobody improvises well.

One safety detail: if there's a thunderstorm or a severe weather warning, disconnect the outdoor terminal. You can check the official AEMET warnings report… using Starlink itself while there's power, of course.

Redundancy: Starlink shouldn't go alone

No single system gets you through an emergency, and satellite is no exception: a tree fallen on the antenna, a sandstorm or a constellation failure leaves you with no route. Sensible preparedness stacks independent routes, in this order of increasing cost:

  1. Emergency radio — battery, crank or solar: official information without internet, at almost zero cost. The basis of the Communication Kit.
  2. Mobile phone with coverage and a data SIM — if the local tower holds up. The analysis of which data SIM survives a blackout best and the one on emergency 4G routers cover this layer.
  3. Light satellite messaging — devices such as a satellite messenger that send position and short messages with no mobile coverage: the most reliable way to say «I'm fine» when nothing else works.
  4. Starlink — full bandwidth, the last step and the most power-hungry.

The full philosophy — when to combine each route and in what order — is developed in the companion guide Emergency connectivity: Starlink, radio and satellite and in how to communicate without a mobile network. This article focuses on making sure that, if you decide to carry Starlink, you carry it actually working.

Coverage and legality in Spain

Two clarifications that save you grief:

  • Coverage. Availability of the residential service in Spain isn't uniform: there are areas with a quota or waiting list and others where the portable service has restrictions on use while moving. Check coverage with your exact address BEFORE buying the terminal; the official check is done on the operator's website and saves you paying for equipment you can't activate.
  • Installation. Mounting an antenna on the roof or façade of a shared building subjects the work to the building's rules and, in heritage areas or on accessible rooftops, to additional procedures. On isolated roofs and detached houses it's much more straightforward, but check the municipal by-law again if you're unsure.
  • Responsible use. Even though the terminal depends on a private network, in an emergency your consumption still counts: if the network is congested, prioritise short messages and voice calls over streaming. The same logic as with 112: not congesting is part of being prepared.

Checklist: don't buy it until you can answer this

QuestionIf the answer is «no»…
Do I already have water, power, first-aid kit and food for 72 h?…finish the basic kit first. Starlink is a luxury for a complete plan.
Do I have enough power for 1 kWh a day off-grid?…you need a power station or solar panel before a terminal.
Have I checked coverage with my address?…don't buy the equipment yet.
Do I have a secondary communication route (radio, SIM, messenger)?…set up the basic redundancy of the communication kit.
Have I tested everything on a good day, not during the emergency?…book a weekend afternoon for the full test.

The four common mistakes

  1. Buying the terminal and not the power. It's the number one mistake: the blackout comes, the terminal starts up and the battery runs flat in a few hours. Work out your Wh first, then buy.
  2. Installing it on the day of the blackout. Calibration, location and cables are tested with sun and time. On the day of the emergency you only switch on what has already been tested.
  3. Forgetting the router. Starlink gives you a connection, but if your router doesn't start from the battery, the home WiFi stays dead. Check that the whole chain (terminal + router + mobile phone) is powered.
  4. Getting complacent and dropping the radio. Satellite connectivity is one more layer, not the base. The battery radio and 112 remain the backbone of official information.

In short: Starlink in an emergency is an excellent tool for anyone who already has the basic layers covered and can power it off-grid. Start there — lessons from real blackouts and the first 30 minutes of a blackout show that information rules — and decide with the full plan in front of you: Starlink Kit if power is already sorted, or better still stay in the blog guide comparing alternatives if it isn't yet.
