panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.titulo: Portable solar panel for emergencies: 3 types and 5 mistakes (2026)
panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.resumen: Portable solar panel for emergencies: types, actual wattage and scenario comparison, with 5 mistakes that make it useless. Official sources.
panel-solar-portatil-72h-emergencia.cuerpo:
When the power goes out on your street —or across half the neighborhood—, the bottleneck is usually not food or water: it is energy. The phone dies, the router goes down and the fridge stops getting cold. A portable solar panel is the cleanest way to replenish that energy for as long as the outage lasts: no gasoline, no noise, no fumes and no depending on fuel being restocked. That said, buying “a panel” blindly is the best way to end up with a useless object just when you need it. Here we explain which type you need, how much energy it really provides and what mistakes to avoid.

What a portable solar panel is (and what it is not)

A portable solar panel is a surface of photovoltaic cells, usually foldable, that converts sunlight into DC electricity. You cannot use that electricity directly at home: it has to be stored in a battery (a power station or a battery bank with a charge controller) and from there draw the 220 V or USB ports that power your devices.

  • It is not a generator: on its own it will not power the washing machine or a countertop fridge. It needs a battery in between.
  • It only produces during the day: energy is generated in between and consumed at night, so system design is half the job.
  • It does not depend on the grid or fuel: as long as there is sunlight, there is charging. That is its advantage over a fuel generator.

How much energy you really need

Before looking at watts, ask yourself the right question: which devices do I want to keep running, and for how long? The following table gives approximate consumption and runtime values on a 500 Wh battery (half a usable kilowatt-hour), which is a common size for home power stations:

DeviceApproximate consumptionRuntime with 500 Wh
Mobile phone (full charge)10–15 Wh per chargeDozens of charges
Laptop50–70 Wh per chargeAbout 6–8 charges
Router or 4G modem10–15 W continuousSeveral days in cycles
10 W LED bulb10 W continuousDozens of hours
12 V portable fridge40–70 W in cycleHalf a day without recharging
Hand-crank radio charger0 W (generated by hand)Endless reserve

Notice the pattern: lighting and connectivity are cheap to maintain; the fridge is expensive. If your priority is staying informed and reachable, a small panel is enough. If you want to keep food from spoiling, you need a significantly larger system. For the full calculation by scenario, take a look at how many watts a portable solar panel really needs.

The three types of panel (and which one you need)

  • Rigid monocrystalline: more watts per euro and more efficient, but it takes up space and does not fold. It is worth it if you are going to install it permanently on a balcony or in a van.
  • Foldable travel panel (PET or ETFE): it folds like a wallet, weighs only a few kilos and fits in a car trunk or a cupboard. It is the star format for an emergency kit, because what matters is not having a panel, but having it where you are when the power goes out.
  • All-in-one (panel + integrated battery): total simplicity and a good companion for the sofa or a camp table, although the battery is usually smaller.

When comparing, look beyond watts: cell type (monocrystalline versus polycrystalline), water resistance (IP rating), the connectors it comes with (MC4, XT60 or a universal DC cable) and, above all, whether it is compatible with the battery you already have. An excellent panel that is disconnected from your battery is worthless.

Comparison by scenario: what power rating to choose

ScenarioRecommended panelRecommended batteryWhere it fits
Mobile phone, radio and lights only20–60 W foldable200–300 WhBlackout kit
Light remote work for 72 h (phone + laptop + router)100–200 W foldable500–1000 WhElectricity kit
House with a fridge and real light bulbs300–600 W (two panels)2000 Wh or moreProfessional kit
Balcony or static caravanRigid 100–200 WDepends on useHome kit

How much a panel produces per day (the figure nobody advertises)

The watts in the catalog are instantaneous power under laboratory conditions, not daily energy. In practice, in Spain a well-oriented 100 W panel usually delivers around 300–500 Wh per day in summer, and considerably less in winter, under overcast skies or with partial shade. The useful rule: assume real performance well below the figure on the box and design with a margin. A cloudy day is not a panel outage, but it does cut output a lot.

How to get the most out of it on the day of the outage

  • If there is advance warning, charge the battery beforehand: starting with the battery at 100 % buys you half a day of leeway.
  • Orientation and angle: facing the sun, at an angle of about 30–45°. A panel in the shade performs close to zero, not “a little less”.
  • Timing: it produces mainly from 10:00 to 17:00; that is the window to use for charging.
  • Priority order: first information and communication (phone, router, radio), then lighting and, if there is any left over, the fridge.
  • Ventilate and disconnect: devices on standby also consume power; turning off what is not needed extends runtime by several hours.

The five mistakes that make your panel useless

  • Buying a panel without a battery and discovering that it will not power anything at 220 V.
  • Focusing only on watts and forgetting the battery's Wh: the system is panel plus battery.
  • Leaving the panel behind a window pane: glass cuts a large part of the output.
  • Storing the battery discharged for months; the cells will suffer when you need it most.
  • Not checking connectors and compatibility until the day of the outage.

What to buy: three entry points

  • Budget entry point: a small 20–40 W foldable panel, designed to keep phones, flashlights and the radio charged. It is the one recommended by the blackout kit and falls in the 40–80 € range: see portable solar panel on Amazon.
  • Recommended option for 72 h: a 100–200 W foldable panel with high-efficiency cells, which can already run a laptop and a portable fridge without drama: search for 200 W foldable solar panels.
  • Complete solution: a solar generator with an included panel (300–500 Wh battery), all in one backpack. In the 250–450 € range and ready to connect: search for portable solar generators.

If you already have the battery and only want to expand, search directly for 100 W foldable solar panels. And if the foreseeable emergency is a long outage lasting several days, the panel is only one piece: check it as part of the solar generator for emergencies and the guide to power banks for the emergency kit.

Where it fits into your preparedness

A portable panel does not live alone: it lives inside a kit. In the basic 72-hour kit, electrical power is one of the essential categories alongside water, light and communication. In the electricity kit you will find the complete combination of panel, battery and accessories, and if the outage coincides with a DANA or a weather warning, it is worth reviewing the first 30 minutes of a DANA outage before connecting anything. For when it is time to preserve food, here is what lasts without a fridge and what to throw away, and if the night becomes long, the best heater to get through the night without power.

Official sources

  • IDAE (Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving) — official information on self-consumption and energy efficiency.
  • European Commission — EU Preparedness Strategy — the European recommendation to be self-sufficient for 72 hours.
  • Red Eléctrica de España — official data on supply and grid operation.

With a panel, a battery and a little discipline, three days without power stop being an energy problem and become an organizational one. And that can always be prepared for.

nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.titulo: Portable cooler for emergencies: how long it holds without power (2026)
nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.resumen: Portable cooler for emergencies: types, real power consumption, off-grid power, and AESAN's 4-hour rule so you don't have to throw food away.
nevera-portatil-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
Three days without power at home and the first thing that spoils is the fridge: meat, fish, milk, leftovers. Keeping food under control is one of the most reassuring things when a long blackout hits, a DANA leaves a neighbourhood without power, or a storm brings down the line. A portable emergency fridge does not replace your refrigerator, but it buys you time: it keeps food below the recommended temperature while the grid comes back.

In this article we explain which type suits you depending on the scenario, how much energy it really uses, how to power it when there is no socket, and what AESAN says about when to throw food away. At the end you will find a checklist to have everything ready before the power goes out, because once there is no electricity you can no longer freeze anything.

What is a portable fridge and what is it not?

A portable fridge is an insulated box with a compressor, heating element or absorption pump that lowers the temperature inside. It runs on 220 V (the household socket), 12 V (the car cigarette lighter) or, with the right adapter, a portable battery or a solar panel. It is used in the car, in the garage, in a country house or on the balcony of the emergency kit.

What it is not: a replacement for the domestic freezer. Nor is it a quiet-compressor camper van fridge that cools to −20 °C all week without power: every model has a limit, and that limit depends on the outside temperature, how many times you open the lid and the power it receives.

The three types, in a table

TypeHow it coolsBestWorst
CompressionSame principle as your home fridge, with gas and motorActually cools, withstands outside heat and lowers the temperature considerablyThe most expensive and the heaviest
ThermoelectricPeltier effect: a plate that cools one side and heats the otherCheap, lightweight, no moving parts, almost no maintenanceCools little: about 15–20 °C below ambient, not suitable for freezing
AbsorptionHeat applied to an ammonia solutionAlmost silent and runs on gas or the car's heating elementVery sensitive to tilt, uses a fair amount of power and is uncommon

The practical rule: if what you need is to keep things cold for several days with little energy, compression. If it is a weekend add-on with ice and cold packs, a thermoelectric one may be enough. And if what you are carrying is medication that cannot exceed a certain temperature, the criteria change: reliability matters there, not price.

How much energy it uses and how long it lasts off-grid

Consumption depends on size, insulation and climate, but as an order of magnitude, a medium-sized compression fridge does not consume continuously: the compressor runs in cycles, with peaks of tens of watts and rest periods. Thermoelectric models do tend to consume more constantly while they are switched on. Before buying, check the model's energy label and multiply it by the hours you want to cover; that will tell you what battery you need.

In terms of portable batteries: a portable solar panel with a medium-capacity power station can keep a compression fridge running for much of the day if it gets sun, while a normal power bank is only good for short bursts or for very efficient models. Something similar happens with the car: the 12 V socket is convenient, but do not drain the starter battery, because that is what will start the vehicle when you need to leave.

The four-hour rule (what AESAN says)

The Spanish Agency for Food Safety and Nutrition makes it clear in its recommendation after blackouts: as long as the home refrigerator stays below 5 °C for less than four hours without opening the door, in principle no food has to be discarded; after those four hours, perishables must be thrown away (meat, fish, chicken, eggs, milk, fresh cheese and leftovers). The freezer holds freezing temperature for at least 24–48 hours without being opened, and food that still has ice crystals can be refrozen.

That is where the portable fridge comes in: it bridges the gap for the most delicate foods just when the refrigerator stops being reliable. And a detail that AESAN repeats and that is hard to believe: never taste food to see if it is still good; neither appearance nor smell is a guarantee. To find out how to keep eating without refrigeration, see our guide to keeping food without a fridge or refrigeration and the three days without power menu.

What to put inside (and what not to)

  • Goes in: milk and dairy products you are going to consume soon, eggs, meat and fish already portioned, leftovers from the previous meal, fresh cheese, cut fruit and refrigerated medication if there is any.
  • Stays out: canned goods, soft drinks, alcoholic drinks, chocolate and condiments: AESAN reminds us that many foods we keep in the fridge do not need it and keep perfectly well at room temperature.
  • Useful at the bottom: pre-frozen cold packs or ice packs. They give the initial boost and extend runtime when energy is scarce.
  • For measuring: a fridge thermometer with min/max recording. Without it you are guessing, and if you have medication or baby food, guessing is not good enough.

If a long outage is forecast, the sensible thing is to prioritise: first what spoils soonest, then the rest. That priority order is the same one we use in expiry date control and rotation.

How to use it properly during the emergency

Performance is decided in the details. Pre-cool the interior with ice or frozen bottles before loading it, so you do not spend the first hour of battery power bringing down the temperature of an empty space. Close the lid right away and resist the temptation to look every few minutes: every opening lets heat in. If it is in the car, keep it away from direct sunlight and the dashboard; the outside temperature sets its ceiling. And if you are going to power it with a portable battery, leave some margin: that same battery also provides lighting, charges the phone and powers the radio in the communication kit.

Five common mistakes

  • Buying a thermoelectric model expecting compression performance: if you really need to lower the temperature, the Peltier plate falls short when the ambient temperature rises.
  • Relying on opening it to check: opening the fridge or portable fridge to “look” shortens runtime and raises the temperature of all the contents.
  • Leaving the 12 V socket on all night with the car stopped: you can end up with a flat starter battery just when you need it most.
  • Storing food that is already expired or half-eaten: nothing gets fixed inside the fridge; it only gets cold.
  • Not having a thermometer: without a temperature reading there is no possible decision about what to keep and what to throw away.

Checklist to have it ready before the blackout

  • Freeze cold packs or water bottles in advance; if severe weather is forecast, that is the moment.
  • Set the fridge to the minimum necessary setting and do not open it while the outage lasts: you gain hours of margin.
  • Check that the portable fridge and its cables are accessible, not buried in the storage room.
  • Keep the portable battery charged and know where the 12 V cable is.
  • Place the fridge thermometer and note the starting temperature.
  • Decide in advance what to consume first: perishables first, always.
  • Review the rest of your inventory with the blackout kit and the home kit.

Official sources

  • AESAN — What to do with food in the fridge and freezer after a power outage.
  • Directorate General for Civil Protection and Emergencies (MITECO) — information and self-protection plans.
  • AEMET — weather warnings to know in advance when an outage may occur.

Where it fits into your preparation

The portable fridge is one more piece of the whole, not the heart of the kit. It fits into the basic 72-hour kit and complements the flashlights and the emergency solar power. If the scenario is a DANA-type storm, also review the sequence for the first 30 minutes; and if you are going to buy one, compare models with honest searches: 12 V / 220 V compression portable fridge, reusable cold packs, min/max fridge thermometer and small portable fridge with cold packs.

mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.titulo: Best emergency data SIM (2026): which carrier has you covered
mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.resumen: Emergency data SIM: how to choose a carrier, set up two different networks and check coverage before a power outage in Spain.
mejor-sim-datos-emergencia-cobertura.cuerpo:
When the power goes out, the first thing many people check is not the fridge: it is whether they have a phone line. A long blackout, a DANA or a severe storm can leave cell towers without power, and then each network shows its true colors. This article does not aim to declare a universal “best operator” —that does not exist— but to give you criteria for choosing the best emergency data SIM in Spain and, above all, for not depending on a single network.

What fails first when the power goes out?

Mobile base stations do not run by magic: they need electricity. When the outage hits, each tower stays alive as long as its battery or generator holds out —in practice, a few hours— and then it goes down. Towers physically damaged by wind, trees or floods take much longer to come back, because they require repair, not just recharging. That is why in a wide-area blackout coverage degrades in waves: first 4G disappears in outlying neighborhoods, then only some areas keep a signal.

There are two additional effects worth anticipating. The first: the network becomes congested. Everyone wants to notify their loved ones at the same time, and calls take up a lot of bandwidth; messaging and SMS weigh much less and often get through first. The second: other services also depend on the power grid. Red Eléctrica de España (REE), the system operator, publishes status and incident notices, and 112 emergency centers run on their own backup power: call 112 only in a real emergency, never to “find out what is going on.”

What “best SIM” really means

The honest answer depends on three things: where you live, where you work and where you travel. An operator that is best on your street may be the worst in your family's town. That is why this article will not sell you a winner: it will give you the method.

SIM typeHow it worksWhen it fits
Operator with its own networkDeploys and maintains its own tower infrastructure.You want priority and proven coverage without depending on third parties.
Virtual operator (MVNO)Rents a large operator's network; they tend to invest less in their own rural coverage.You are looking for price and only need data where coverage is already good.
Secondary backup SIMCheap, ready and active only for the bad day.The golden rule: two SIMs on different networks, not from different brands.

Note a nuance that is always overlooked: two different brands sharing a network means both go down at the same time. Before buying, review the virtual operator's terms: during congestion, the host's own network may get priority, and that difference shows up on the very day you need it most.

The golden rule: two different networks, always

Redundancy is the cheapest lever in all of preparedness. With a dual-SIM phone —or with two phones, one on each network— you protect yourself against the most common scenario: one network becomes saturated or goes down and the other keeps working. The second SIM does not have to be expensive or have a lot of data: its job is to get through a short message and a call when the main one fails.

  • If you live with more people, ideally you have SIMs on different networks at home, not all from the same operator.
  • Test the secondary one from time to time: a SIM forgotten in a drawer often ends up disconnected for inactivity.
  • If the network goes down completely, use other routes: communicating without a mobile network covers the alternatives (WiFi messaging, radio, paper) and the backup 4G router keeps the whole house connected with a single SIM.

Coverage: check it, do not assume it

The bars on your phone measure signal strength, not actual service quality, and even less so under stress. The reliable reference is the coverage maps published by the operators themselves and information from the regulator: the Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) is the body that supervises the telecommunications sector in Spain and publishes reports on coverage and service quality.

Check three locations before deciding: your home (including the bedroom and the landing), your workplace or business, and your usual route —including secondary roads—. If you live or travel in mountain areas, consider an external phone antenna: with a marginal signal, a couple of decibels of gain make the difference between sending a message and not sending it.

How much data do you really need in an emergency?

Far less than you think. In a blackout scenario, the essentials are messaging, the occasional call, offline maps and checking official alerts: a small monthly data allowance is more than enough, as long as you are not streaming. Three habits help more than any unlimited plan:

  1. Download maps of your area for offline use before the network fails.
  2. Prioritize SMS and lightweight messaging while the network is congested; calls only if essential.
  3. Turn off sync and background data: during a blackout, every percentage of battery counts.

If you are going to prepare the SIM calmly, a well-chosen prepaid data SIM and a periodic top-up prevent you from finding yourself without credit on the very day of the outage. Never memorize exact prices: compare current offers yourself, because they change with every campaign.

Checklist: what to check before the next alert

  • Activate and test the SIM — test call, mobile data and an SMS, on the phone where you will use it.
  • Keep the account up to date — with no credit or an unpaid bill, the line can be cut just when you need it.
  • Write down the PIN and PUK — on paper, outside the phone: if you get the PIN wrong, the device asks for the PUK, and without it the card is blocked.
  • Coverage verified — home, work and route, with the operator's map in front of you.
  • Second network ready — activated, tested and at hand (not in a drawer untested for years).
  • Power for the phone — charged power bank and, if possible, solar charging: without battery, the best SIM in the world is useless. See the blackout kit and the guide to the best emergency power bank.
  • Phone numbers on paper — those of your closest contacts and 112, written down: if the phone dies, memory helps too.

The rest of the communication kit

The SIM is the main piece, but it does not work alone. With one or two well-chosen SIMs you can build a redundancy chain that goes from the simplest to the most powerful:

  • Portable router or mifi — shares the connection with several devices: portable mifi with battery or the full comparison in best emergency 4G router.
  • External antenna — for weak areas: outdoor 4G antenna.
  • Satellite backup — when not a single tower is left standing, Starlink in emergencies is the Plan B that saves the day, with its page at Starlink kit.
  • Radio and short messages — PMR446 radios need no tower at all.

All of this fits into the central communications page: communication kit, with the essentials ordered by priority.

Five mistakes that repeat in every emergency

  1. Relying only on the bars: they measure strength, not whether the network will accept your call at nine at night on a chaotic day.
  2. Two SIMs on the same network (even if they are different brands): they go down together and the “redundancy” was an illusion.
  3. Forgetting the secondary SIM: a prepaid SIM with no top-ups may be disconnected for inactivity under each operator's terms.
  4. Using up data the day before: streaming and downloads the previous day leave the allowance empty just when it is time to check in.
  5. Confusing home WiFi with coverage: the home router does not work without power; the SIM and the phone are what you have left.

Official sources so you do not improvise

Before believing any campaign, check the sources directly: the telecommunications regulator (CNMC) for coverage and quality data, Red Eléctrica de España (REE) for the status of the power grid, and the official channels of Protección Civil and 112 for recommendations during incidents. During a blackout, updated official information is worth more than any rumor in a messaging group.

Where it fits into your preparedness

A well-chosen data SIM is cheap insurance against isolation: it costs little, takes up no space and only requires that you test it from time to time. It fits any scenario, from a DANA or blackout in the first 30 minutes to a long-duration outage. Build your preparedness in layers: basic 72-hour kit for the essentials, communication kit to stay connected, and if you live in an isolated area, mountain kit. The best SIM is not the cheapest or the most advertised: it is the one you still have active, tested and with a second network waiting alongside it.

mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.titulo: Best emergency 4G router: internet when everything fails (2026)
mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.resumen: Emergency 4G or 5G router: types, how to choose it, where to place it and what to check before the next blackout or DANA in Spain.
mejor-router-4g-emergencia-sin-internet.cuerpo:
When a DANA cuts the fiber, a blackout takes out the local telephone exchange or the mobile network gets saturated because everyone wants to call at the same time, the internet stops being a luxury and becomes a safety tool: knowing what is happening in your area, receiving the AEMET or Protección Civil alert, letting your people know and, if it comes to it, asking for help on WhatsApp instead of waiting for the line to come back.

The temptation is to use your phone as an emergency router. It works for a few hours and then nothing works: a phone battery doesn't last long when tethering, the screen turns off and the thing heats up. The real alternative is a 4G or 5G router with a battery, designed to stay on for days, share WiFi with several people and leave your phone free for calls.

Why a router and not your phone?

The differences are not about convenience, they are about battery life:

What you measurePhone tethering4G/5G router with battery
Real battery lifeTwo to four hours of active useEight to twelve hours depending on model and load
Connected devicesOne or two before it strugglesTen or more without breaking a sweat
SignalInside your pocket or backpackPlace it by a window or with an external antenna
Battery of the device itselfYou drain it and are left without a phoneIndependent: your phone stays available
Continuous useIt heats up and slows downDesigned to stay on

And there is a detail that weighs heavily in an emergency: if the router is by the window and the phone is in your pocket, the network is received by whoever has the better antenna, not whoever is in more of a hurry.

What you need for it to work on the bad day

A router alone doesn't work miracles. To be ready when you need it, you need three things, and all three are bought or prepared weeks in advance:

  • A SIM with active data. If you haven't topped up for months, the line may well be cut off for lack of balance. Check your card's validity today, not on the day of the alert. The comparison of data SIMs for emergencies explains what to look at (validity, coverage and enough gigabytes).
  • Power to recharge it. A router like this uses little power, but if the blackout drags on you need to charge it: a power bank with enough capacity or a portable solar panel will keep you from being left in the dark. In the blackout kit and the electricity kit, backup power is already covered.
  • Coverage where you will be. The network goes down sooner in an empty industrial park than in a city center. Check your operator's coverage map before buying, and if you live or shelter in a weak-signal area, consider external LTE antennas: in the mountains or at a country house, they change the conversation.

The three types of emergency router

There is no single “best router”: there are three formats, and each solves a different scenario.

FormatWho it's forBestWhat to watch
4G mobile hotspot with battery (mifi)Evacuation backpack, car, people on the moveSmall, charges from a power bank, fits in a pocketLower antenna power and fewer devices at once
Home 4G/5G router with backup powerHouse, apartment, fixed shelterCoverage throughout the home and genuinely stableNeeds mains power: think about the UPS or generator
Router with external antennasWeak-signal area, countryside, mountains, garagePlug-in RP-SMA antennas and much better receptionMore installation and more cables to carry

If your priority is the backpack, aim for the small format. If your priority is keeping the whole house connected during a blackout that lasts days, aim for the home router with backup power. Take your time looking at portable 4G routers with battery, 4G routers for home or portable mifis.

How to choose it: six points that really matter

  • Battery, not “portable”. It should clearly state how many hours it lasts when on and whether it can run while charging. Eight hours or more is a good baseline to get through the night.
  • 4G bands and, if you can, 5G. In congested areas 5G relieves pressure; in rural areas 4G with good low-band support rules, because it reaches farther.
  • SIM without ties. An unlocked router lets you switch operator when yours gets congested. Before buying, confirm it does not come carrier-locked.
  • External antenna connector. Even if you won't use it today, having RP-SMA antennas available saves you from changing router later.
  • WiFi for several devices. The kid's tablet, the work laptop, the TV and the family phones: if the router supports few clients, it falls over as soon as half the neighborhood shows up.
  • Simple administration. It should be configurable from your phone and have a one-button restart: at three in the morning nobody wants to touch IPs.

Signal is decided by where you put it

The golden rule is dead boring and it works: near the window, high up and with no metal around it. A router hidden behind the television or in the hallway cupboard loses decibels you need. Put it on a balcony, a shelf or the top table; if you have an external antenna, point it toward the window with the best view of the horizon.

Before trusting coverage, check it where you will be: operators publish their maps and the CNMC, as the telecommunications regulator, keeps information on coverage and service quality. We explain it in detail in how to check coverage before buying the SIM.

Security: a router is a door into your home

A router with the factory password and outdated firmware is the fastest way for someone to slip into your network while you are distracted. Three steps, five minutes:

  • Change the admin password and the WiFi password to ones that are not the label on the bottom.
  • Update the firmware from the app or the panel; if your device no longer receives updates, consider replacing it.
  • Keep guests separate from important devices (the work laptop and the home tablet don't have to be on the same network).

INCIBE, the Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad, reminds the public in its guides that the home network is the first line of defense: its home security recommendations are the natural complement to any emergency router.

The day of the alert: five-minute checklist

  1. Charge the router to 100% and place it by the window or at the highest point in the house.
  2. Check that the SIM has balance and that you are getting some signal (the bar in the router app counts).
  3. Connect only the essentials: phones, radio and laptop. Keep the console and TV off the 4G network if you're short on data.
  4. Share the network with your people all at once, so nobody keeps asking for the password.
  5. Follow official alerts: AEMET publishes forecasts and weather warnings (aemet.es) and Protección Civil coordinates self-protection recommendations (proteccioncivil.es). If there is immediate risk, 112 always comes first.

The mistakes that leave the router useless

  • Buying the router and not the SIM. The device works, the line doesn't: it happens more than you'd think.
  • Leaving it uncharged for months. Batteries drain; a quarterly check (and a full charge) avoids the surprise.
  • Believing there is coverage because your phone has bars. Phones and routers don't see alike; check with the map and with a real test at the point where you will use it.
  • Spending data on downloads. In an emergency gigabytes run out fast: prioritize messaging and alerts, leave the series for later.
  • Thinking it is the complete plan. If the network goes down completely, the router doesn't conjure a signal out of nowhere. That is the next layer.

When there is no coverage: plan B

A 4G router depends on the mobile network. If you live in an area where that network is weak, you need redundancy, and there are three paths we already cover in the blog: real connectivity redundancy (satellite, radio and mobile), Starlink as an emergency connection for those who can afford it, and PMR446 radios for short-range talking without depending on anyone. Communication without a mobile network sets out the whole scheme.

The idea is not to have everything: it is to decide in advance what your first route is, what your second is, and who you will meet if both fail. That simple agreement is worth more than any gadget.

Where it fits into your preparedness

The emergency router is the communications piece of the kit. If you are building yours from scratch, the communication kit brings together the essentials and the DANA and flood kit covers the scenario that most often leaves entire neighborhoods without a line. And if you prefer to start with the basics, the 72-hour kit guide gives you the foundation on which everything else rests.

Official sources

  • INCIBE — Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad: security guides for the home network and the public.
  • AEMET — Agencia Estatal de Meteorología: official forecasts and storm warnings.
  • Protección Civil — Secretaría General de Protección Civil y Emergencias: self-protection recommendations for emergencies.

generador-solar-emergencia-72h.titulo: Emergency solar generator: how much runtime it gives and 5 mistakes (2026)
generador-solar-emergencia-72h.resumen: How much battery do you really need? Real runtime in watt-hours, what it charges and what it doesn't, how many panels, and 5 mistakes when choosing (2026).
generador-solar-emergencia-72h.cuerpo:
Three days without power is not an exotic scenario in Spain: it is what happens when a storm leaves an entire neighbourhood without supply, when the grid becomes unstable in the middle of a cold snap, or when roadworks cut a cable. Protección Civil maintained the alert for showers and storms on the peninsular Mediterranean coast and the Balearic Islands on 16 October 2026, and autumn storms are, year after year, the most frequent cause of local electricity cuts. What decides whether that night is uncomfortable or unpleasant is not the blackout: it is whether you had somewhere to plug in the hallway light, the mobile phone and the fridge.

An emergency solar generator solves exactly that: it converts sunlight into electricity stored in a battery, with no noise, no fumes and no fuel to store. Below is the full calculation —how much energy you really need, how much battery and how many panels are required— and the mistakes that leave many people with a device that cannot even run a fridge.

1. What a solar generator is (and what it is not)

It is worth getting the names right, because in shops they are used as if they were synonyms, and they are not:

  • Folding solar panel: it only generates electricity while the sun is shining on it. Without a battery it stores nothing.
  • External battery or power station: it stores energy and delivers it through a mains socket, USB or 12 V. It does not charge itself: it needs someone to feed it.
  • Solar generator: the two together —panel + battery— in a kit that works from the first minute. This is what we are talking about here.
  • Petrol or diesel generator: it burns fuel to produce light. It works at night and under clouds, but it makes noise and smoke, and it needs refuelling.

The practical difference is simple: solar does not depend on an external supply that runs out; as long as there is sun it keeps charging, and it can stay set up on the balcony for weeks. In exchange, its output depends on the sky. If you want to compare solar with fuel face to face, the comparison between generator and power station breaks down scenarios, noise and cost of use; and if the solar route already suits you, the post on portable solar panels covers the three types and the buying mistakes.

2. The calculation that matters: watt-hours

The whole decision comes down to a single figure: the watt-hours (Wh) each device consumes each time you use it, and how many Wh fit in the battery. Nothing more. Power (W) tells you how much it uses while running; capacity (Wh) tells you how long it lasts.

DeviceTypical useApproximate consumption
Mobile phoneOne full chargeAround 10–15 Wh
LaptopWorking for 4 hoursBetween 40 and 60 Wh per charge
4G/Wi-Fi routerOne hour switched onAround 10 Wh
LED bulbOne night of useBetween 5 and 10 Wh
Emergency radioSeveral hoursA few Wh per hour
Portable car fridgeOne hour of cyclingAround 30–50 Wh
Battery charger4 AA batteriesLess than 20 Wh

These are textbook estimates, not laboratory measurements: your laptop may use considerably more if it has a graphics card. The idea to hold on to is the order of magnitude —charging a mobile phone costs a tiny fraction of what heating water costs— because that is where the battery size comes from.

3. How much battery you need by scenario

With the table above, setting yourself up for the night is arithmetic. Three real scenarios, with no extra gear:

72-hour scenarioWhat it supportsRecommended capacity
Basic survivalMobile phones, torches, radio, router for short periodsBetween 300 and 600 Wh
Home in remote modeThe above plus laptop, LED lighting and portable fridgeBetween 1,000 and 1,500 Wh
High autonomyThe above plus tools, a small pump and continuous loadsAbove 2,000 Wh

The temptation is to buy the biggest battery “just in case” and end up with no panels, which is the mistake in point 5. It is worth remembering that the battery produces nothing: it only stores. A 12 Wh mobile phone charged four times a day is about 50 Wh per day; a portable fridge that runs in cycles can consume in one day what three mobile phones use in a week. If your priority is the fridge —for medication or for food from the home fridge— prioritise capacity over extras.

If you are looking for the minimum, inexpensive version, the highest-capacity power bank handles level 1 without installing anything; and the plan for the first 30 minutes in a DANA or blackout tells you what order to act in when the power goes out just as you are having dinner.

4. How many panels and how long they take to charge

Panels are sized with a rough but reliable rule: in good conditions, a 100 W panel delivers around 300–400 Wh on a full day of sun (direct light from morning to afternoon, with reasonable tilt). That is, three effective hours of sun are the usual reference point for the calculation. From there:

PanelApproximate daily outputWhat it is for
20–40 WAbout 60–140 WhMobile phone, torches, radio. Small, steady charge
100 WBetween 300 and 400 WhHome in remote mode: mobile phones, LED, router, some fridge
200 WBetween 600 and 800 WhDaily laptop and fridge with margin
400 W (or two 200 W)More than 1,000 WhLarge batteries and fast recharges between storms

The sky is in charge, and in autumn and winter it is even more so: with drizzle or overcast sky, output falls to a fraction of the nominal figure —often to half or less— and the days are shorter. AEMET is the official source for knowing what sky to expect this week; Red Eléctrica de España (REE) publishes how the electricity system is behaving. The practical rule: size for the worst day of the year, not for the best day in August. If you live in the north or in a foggy area, add 50% more panel to whatever the calculation gave you.

5. What it powers and what it does not, no illusions

This is the part that many product sheets keep quiet about. The short list:

  • Yes, with room to spare: mobile phones, tablets, laptops, torches and LED bulbs, radio, router, security cameras, battery chargers, hand tools, fans.
  • Yes, with a tight margin: portable fridge (in cycles), capsule coffee machine, iron, small microwave —anything that heats water uses a lot, a great deal.
  • No, forget it: ceramic hob and oven, electric water heater, air conditioning, resistance heating, heat pump, hairdryer. A water heater can consume in half an hour what the entire battery stores for three days.
  • With a separate calculator: well water pump, soldering iron, workshop compressor. They can be started with large batteries, but you have to calculate it device by device and check the start-up surges.

If your priority is heating in winter, electricity is not the way: see the post on heaters without power and the blackout kit, which organises priorities, light and heat in the same place. To keep the home safe while the grid comes back, the electricity kit gathers everything that plugs in.

6. The five most common mistakes

  1. Buying only a battery, without panels. A power station without a panel is an expensive brick: you charge it at home and when the power goes out you use it once. If you cannot pay for both, start with the panel.
  2. Counting on August sun to solve a November blackout. Sizing is done for the worst day, not the best.
  3. Measuring in watts instead of watt-hours. “It has 1,000 W” does not say how long it lasts; “it has 1,000 Wh” does.
  4. Leaving the battery discharged in the storage room. Lithium batteries lose charge on their own: recharge it every three months and leave it at half charge if you are not going to touch it for a long time.
  5. Buying by the number of sockets and not by power. Eight sockets that only accept light loads are no use for anything that heats.

And a sixth that is pure foresight: not buying anything. The difference between an afternoon blackout and a three-day one is almost never about money; it is about having looked into it in advance.

7. Setup in five steps

  1. Place the panel in the sun, facing south and at the tilt specified by the manufacturer; on a window or balcony it works, but with lower output.
  2. Connect the panel to the battery with the appropriate cable (panels have MC4 connectors; the battery comes with its own or you buy one separately).
  3. Wait for the battery to accept charge: with good light it starts filling within minutes.
  4. Connect your devices to the battery —mains sockets for 220 V items, USB for small ones— and switch off anything you are not using.
  5. Close the cycle every day: take the panel out into the sun in the morning, leave the battery upstairs and note down how much you consumed. After three nights of records you will know whether you have too much or too little.

So that the night has light without burning through the battery, switch off what you do not need and turn on only two or three LEDs: a hallway LED bulb uses in one hour what a mobile phone uses in minutes.

8. Safety: what you need to know before plugging in

The good thing about the solar route is that it burns nothing inside the home: there is no carbon monoxide, no smoke and no risk of fire from combustion. Fuel generators, by contrast, must never run in an enclosed space or near ventilation grilles —which is why the carbon monoxide detector is part of the same conversation.

The points you do need to watch with solar equipment:

  • Water and outdoor connections: take the panel in when it really rains and protect the sockets. Wet connectors corrode and stop delivering a good charge.
  • Heat and ventilation: the battery copes better at a cool room temperature with airflow; do not put it under the bed or in a closed cupboard while charging.
  • Supervised charging while there are people at home, as with any device containing lithium.
  • Zero noise, zero regulations: because it makes no noise, you do not impose noise on the community. If you end up using a fuel generator as backup, check the noise regulations of the residents' association before starting it.

9. What to look at before paying anything

Buying checklist, in order of importance:

  • Capacity in real Wh, not mAh (mAh at 5 V are not the same as at 12 V, and shops play with that).
  • Output power in W —enough for what you want to plug in— and if the manufacturer states start-up surges, check them.
  • Battery type: lithium with LFP chemistry lasts many more cycles than others; for occasional emergency use, whichever you have at hand and well preserved.
  • Solar charging input on the same connectors as your panels, without improvised adapters.
  • Warranty and spare parts availability in Spain, not just an online shop.
  • Real weight: if it weighs more than you are willing to carry up to the balcony, you will not use it.

If you prefer to buy separate parts, here are direct searches for the most common items: portable power stations, folding solar panels and a 20–40 W folding solar panel that is already verified in our catalogue for charging small devices. Affiliate links: if you buy through them, kit72h receives a commission at no extra cost to you.

10. How this fits into a 72-hour plan

Light is only one piece. The recommendation in official guides —three days of autonomy without basic services— is the axis around which the whole site is built, and there electricity sits alongside water, food, documentation and communication. The Secretaría General de Protección Civil y Emergencias publishes preventive recommendations by scenario, and the European Commission's Directorate-General for Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO) sets out the European approach to citizen preparedness; on the official sources page you will find them all linked in detail.

The sensible order, if you start from scratch: cover communication and information first (mobile phone with battery and radio), then light, then cold and food. With the plan in the basic 72-hour kit and the list in the blackout kit you have the base; the solar generator is what gives that plan electrical autonomy. If you also want to stay connected when broadband goes down, communication without a mobile network explains what works and what does not when the network goes down.

Summary in three lines

The calculation: aim for 500 Wh if you only want mobile phones and light, and 1,500 Wh if you want a fridge and laptop. Recharging: a 100 W panel gives around 300–400 Wh per day in good sun, and half or less on a cloudy day. Discipline: battery charged and panel tested before you need it, not during. With that, a three-day blackout becomes a day of work in the shade of the balcony.

conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.titulo: Emergency connectivity: Starlink, radio and satellite (2026)
conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.resumen: Emergency connectivity: what to do when all networks go down. Starlink, amateur radio, PMR446 walkie-talkies and satellite messenger, with a plan B.
conectividad-emergencia-starlink-radios-.cuerpo:
When the power grid goes down, the first thing to go is the internet. Then mobile coverage. In a DANA, a prolonged blackout or an earthquake, the three most-used systems —WiFi, mobile and fiber— can fail simultaneously. And without communication, there is no coordination, no information, no help.

This is where serious preparation separates from improvisation. It is not about buying the most expensive gear: it is about having three independent systems that work autonomously. If one fails, the other two stay alive. If two fail, the third holds up.

This guide covers the three layers of emergency connectivity, from the easiest (Starlink) to the most robust (HF radio), with products, costs and when to use each one.

Layer 1: Satellite internet — Starlink

Starlink is the closest thing to terrestrial broadband internet that exists. It works from any point on the planet with a clear view of the sky, without fiber infrastructure or cell towers.

How does it work?

A flat terminal (the “Dishy”) is placed on a roof, balcony or garden and points to SpaceX’s satellite constellation orbiting at 550 km altitude. The terminal draws between 50 and 100W in normal operation (5-10W in standby), so a lithium battery or a 200W solar panel keeps it running indefinitely.

Emergency specifications

  • Speed: 50-200 Mbps download, 10-20 Mbps upload (Gen 3)
  • Latency: 30-80 ms (identical to fiber in practical use)
  • Coverage: Global in areas with a clear view of the sky — Spain is covered across most of its territory
  • Installation: 5 minutes, no tools
  • Power draw: 50-100W (running) · 5-10W (standby)
  • Resistance: Withstands winds up to 120 km/h, rain, snow and hail

Costs

Plan Terminal price Monthly price Use
Residential ~500-600 EUR ~50 EUR/month Fixed, same location
Mobile in transit ~1200 EUR ~45 EUR/month Mobile (car, boat, camping)
Temporary ~500-600 EUR ~100 EUR/month One-off emergency, cancellable

When to use Starlink in an emergency?

Starlink is ideal when you need real internet — video calls, downloading documents, access to emergency systems — and no terrestrial infrastructure is available. It is especially useful for:

  • Emergency shelters or coordination points that need connectivity
  • Command centers where information needs to be transmitted
  • Homes in rural areas without fiber or 4G coverage
  • Evacuation to an area where the network is down

Limitation: The terminal is large (57 x 57 x 3 cm, 4.5 kg). It is not portable in an emergency backpack. It requires a fixed location with a clear view of the sky.

View Starlink on Amazon ↗

Layer 2: Cellular connectivity — redundancy

Mobile is the most-used communication system. And that is why it is also the most vulnerable: a single carrier going down leaves everyone disconnected. The key is to have two different carriers and a router that manages them.

Industrial 4G/5G router with dual SIM

An industrial router such as the Peplink MAX BR, Gargoyle or similar accepts two SIMs from different carriers (e.g., Movistar + Orange). If one tower goes down, the router switches to the other automatically. They also offer:

  • WAN/LAN: Ethernet ports to connect WiFi routers or a switch
  • VPN: you can connect your home router to a remote point
  • PoE: powered over network cable, ideal for roof installation
  • External antennas: SMA connectors for high-gain antennas
  • Web monitoring: dashboard to view network status, battery and signal

High-gain panel antenna

In rural areas, the 4G signal may be weak but usable if the antenna is pointed correctly toward the nearest tower. An 18-23 dBi panel antenna improves the signal by 10 to 20 dB.

Procedure:

  1. Install the antenna on a 3-5 metre mast on a roof or façade
  2. Point it toward the nearest tower (apps such as CellMapper show towers on a map)
  3. Connect the coaxial cable (LMR-400, low loss) to the 4G/5G router
  4. Configure the router with the two SIMs

Search 4G/5G panel antennas ↗ · Search industrial routers ↗

Layer 3: Satellite messaging — the last resort

When everything goes down — Starlink off due to lack of power, router with no signal, and no radio — the satellite messenger is the last system that works. It does not require terrestrial infrastructure or a clear view of the sky to send text messages.

Garmin inReach Mini 2

The best-known satellite communication device for emergencies. It works on the Iridium network (global coverage, including the poles). It offers:

  • Two-way messages by SMS or to predefined contacts
  • Global SOS (connects to rescue coordination centers)
  • Built-in GPS with real-time location
  • Battery life of 2-3 days in normal mode (weeks in power-saving mode)
  • Water-resistant (IPX7), drop-resistant
  • Smartphone app: send messages from your phone without the device

Cost: ~350-450 EUR device + 30-50 EUR/month data plan

Zoleo

Alternative with a web dashboard: you can see your family’s location in real time from any browser. It works on Iridium and Globalstar networks (dual network for a higher chance of connection).

Cost: ~300-400 EUR device + 30-50 EUR/month plan

When to use the satellite messenger?

It is the device that should never be the only one, but it should always be in the evacuation backpack. It is used to:

  • Send an SOS signal when there is no other means
  • Communicate your location to family when you are lost
  • Confirm to family that you are okay when connectivity returns
  • Receive emergency alerts (on some models)

View Garmin inReach Mini 2 ↗

Layer 4: Radio — the system that does not fail

Radio is the oldest, cheapest and most reliable communication system. It does not depend on satellites, does not need infrastructure, and does not get saturated by volume. When everything else fails, radio keeps working.

Professional PMR446 walkie-talkies

PMR446 walkie-talkies are the most basic and accessible communication system. They do not require a license, operate on 16 predefined channels and have a range of 2 to 5 km in open terrain (less in the city).

A set of 4 professional walkie-talkies (Motorola Talkabout or similar) costs ~100-200 EUR and is shared among family members. They are useful for:

  • Coordinating intra-family evacuation (who goes where, when)
  • Communication at home during an emergency (between floors)
  • Coordination with neighbors or nearby rescue teams
  • Communication in areas where mobile does not reach (even if only 2 km)

Specifications: 16 channels, 0.5-2W power, IP67 (water-resistant), LCD, VOX (hands-free), LED lights.

Search PMR446 walkie-talkies ↗

Amateur HF radio (CETIC license)

Amateur radio is the deepest layer of emergency connectivity. With a shortwave antenna and an HF radio, you can communicate with any point on the planet through ionospheric propagation. It does not need any infrastructure.

To get started:

  • License: free exam at CETIC (Centro de Ensayos de la Industria de las Telecomunicaciones). You can prepare with free online material.
  • Radio: Icom IC-7100 or Yaesu FT-710 as a starting point (~600-1200 EUR)
  • Antenna: shortwave antenna or dipole (100-300 EUR)
  • Range: local (VHF) → regional (HF day) → international (HF night)

Amateur radio operators actively collaborate with Civil Protection in Spain through REDVOL (Red de Voluntarios en Emergencias de Telecomunicaciones). If you have a license and want to collaborate, there are local groups in every region.

Search HF radios ↗

Triple redundancy strategy

Professional preparation is not based on a single system, but on triple redundancy: three independent systems that work autonomously. If one fails, the other two stay alive. If two fail, the third holds up.

Layer System Total cost Independence When it fails
1 Starlink (satellite) ~500 EUR + 50 EUR/month No terrestrial infrastructure No power / no clear sky view
2 Industrial 4G/5G router (2 SIMs) ~400-800 EUR + 80 EUR/month Alternative carrier Towers down + no power
3 Satellite messenger ~350 EUR + 30 EUR/month Independent satellite network No battery
4 PMR446 walkie-talkies ~100-200 EUR Zero infrastructure No battery / limited range
5 Amateur HF radio ~600-1200 EUR No infrastructure at all Requires license + skill

The minimum functional budget

The essentials for decent connectivity when networks go down:

  • PMR446 walkie-talkies (4 units): ~150 EUR
  • Industrial 4G/5G router + 1 panel antenna: ~600 EUR
  • Satellite messenger (Garmin inReach): ~350 EUR
  • Minimum total: ~1.100 EUR (without subscriptions)

With Starlink it rises to ~1.600 EUR upfront + ~80 EUR/month in subscriptions, but you get real broadband internet.

What you do not need to buy (yet)

Amateur HF radio is the most powerful layer but requires training and a license. It is not essential for most households. If you are interested, start with PMR446 walkie-talkies and the satellite messenger; HF radio is a learning path you can begin studying once you have the basic systems covered.

Summary: what to buy, when and why

The rule of three layers

Each layer is an independent system. If one fails, the other two keep working.

antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.titulo: External mobile antenna: real coverage in mountains and valleys (2026)
antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.resumen: Practical guide to external mobile antennas: how to diagnose signal, which type is worth it depending on the case, how to install it and what mistakes to avoid in the mountains.
antena-externa-movil-cobertura-montana.cuerpo:
If you live or spend seasons in a mountain area, a deep valley or the countryside, you already know the symptom: one signal bar, calls that cut off and data that won't load just when you need it most. An external mobile antenna is not a tech toy: it is the cheapest way to turn poor coverage into a stable connection at home, in the refuge or in the second home. This guide explains what fails, how to diagnose it in ten minutes, what type of solution suits you and how to install it without making the mistakes that make the improvement worthless.

Why the signal fails right there

Mobile coverage is not uniform on the map: operators' antennas are designed to serve population centres and communication routes, and the terrain does the rest. A hill between you and the tower, a narrow valley or a building with thick walls reduces the strength of the signal reaching your device. The result is that two houses a hundred metres apart can experience different realities.

Official data confirms it. The Ministry of Economic Affairs, Trade and Enterprise gives national coverage of fifth-generation mobile networks (5G NSA+SA) of 99.27% as of 30 June 2025, with 98.10% in standalone mode. That percentage is a national average: it doesn't tell you what happens in your back yard or on the north slope. That's why the first thing is not to buy, but to look at the official map and then measure at your own point.

And an important nuance: an external antenna does not create signal where there is none. What it does is capture the signal that already exists, weaker, and bring it inside with fewer losses. If at your location no operator reaches even with an antenna on the roof, the way is not the antenna but another technology: satellite or radio. Hence it is worth reading first what works when the mobile goes down and Starlink in an emergency so as not to spend on the wrong solution.

10-minute diagnosis before spending money

  • Check the official coverage maps from the CNMC and the Ministry for your specific address: you'll see 4G and 5G coverage by block and by operator, and there you start ruling things out.
  • Try several points and several windows: go up to the top floor, go out into the garden, move to the opposite side of the building. Note where the mobile behaves best; that point tells you where the cable should enter.
  • Change operator before blaming the device: with a second prepaid SIM (or with a neighbour's mobile) you check whether the problem is your network or the location.
  • Try another device: an old mobile with a deteriorated antenna or a case that blocks signal simulates poor coverage. If two devices behave the same in the same place, the problem is the network.
  • Measure before and after: note the bars or, better, the signal level shown by the phone itself in service mode information. Without a baseline measurement you won't know whether the antenna has done anything.
  • Check whether the failure is data or voice: sometimes calls work and browsing doesn't (or vice versa). The solution and the right equipment are not the same.

What type of solution you need

There is no universal antenna: it depends on the distance to the tower, the number of users and whether the problem is outside or inside the house. This is the quick decision map.

SolutionWhen it fitsWhere it is installedIndicative cost
Omnidirectional external antennaSeveral towers around or tower not visible; simple domestic useMast or wall, as high as possibleAbout €30 to €80
Directional antenna (Yagi / panel)Specific known tower at some distance; high gainPointing at the tower, on roof or balconyAbout €40 to €120
Repeater / signal amplifierWeak but existing signal outside and dead inside the buildingExternal antenna + indoor unit + cableAbout €100 to €300
4G/5G router with external antennasYou want internet at home, not just calls: several devices at onceOn the router, antennas outsideAbout €60 to €200
Indoor WiFi extenderThe signal arrives well but dies between floors or wallsIn the hallway, between the router and the dead spotAbout €25 to €70

Omnidirectional antenna: the simple option

It captures signal from any direction, so you don't need to point it at anything. It is the best option if you don't know where the nearest tower is or if your area changes operator frequently. It usually comes with a window mast and pre-terminated coaxial cable. Look for a high-gain 4G/5G external antenna.

Directional antenna: the one that performs best in remote areas

It points at a specific tower and concentrates all the gain in that direction. It performs much better than the omnidirectional one when the tower is far away, but it requires aiming: a few degrees of error eat up the improvement. It is worth it if you can see the tower from home or locate it on the official map.

Repeater or amplifier: when the problem is the building

If there is signal outside and none inside (concrete walls, windows with metal mesh, basements), the antenna alone is not enough: you need a unit that receives outside, amplifies and re-transmits inside. It is the typical solution for stone houses and old buildings. Use CE-marked equipment designed for domestic use: a badly adjusted repeater saturates the tower cell and can worsen the network for all neighbours.

Router with external antennas: if what you want is internet

If your goal is to bring stable WiFi to several rooms, the shed or the workshop, the way is a 4G/5G router that accepts external antennas (with standard connectors) and, if you travel or change location, with dual SIM slots so you can switch operator. On the market there are industrial 4G/5G routers with dual SIM and external antennas designed precisely for this; if the problem is only WiFi inside the house, a long-range WiFi extender with directional antenna is usually enough. Also compare the best 4G emergency routers and review which data SIM saves you before signing anything.

How to install it: six steps

  1. Choose the outside point: as high and as clear as possible, ideally with line of sight to the tower and no metal nearby (gutters, metal shutters, awnings).
  2. Aim it (if directional): locate the tower on the official map, align the antenna and fix the mast loosely so you can correct it.
  3. Run the cable at the shortest possible length: every metre of thin coaxial cable loses gain; if you need a long run, use lower-loss coaxial cable and avoid unnecessary bends.
  4. Seal the penetration: the hole in the wall must be sealed against water and damp — in the mountains, a costly leak costs more than the antenna itself.
  5. Connect to the indoor unit and power it (if it is a repeater or router): keep the indoor antenna away from the outdoor one to avoid feedback and a noise loop.
  6. Measure again and compare with your diagnosis note. If the improvement is marginal, check orientation, connections and cable length before considering the installation good.

Four mistakes that cancel out the improvement

  • Antenna behind glass with metal mesh or a metal roller shutter: the shielding cuts the signal almost completely. If you can't take it outside, don't expect miracles.
  • Cheap and overly long cable: it is the number one cause of installations “that don't work”. Buy suitable coaxial cable and cut off what is left over.
  • Amplifying noise instead of signal: if there is nothing outside to amplify, the repeater multiplies interference. Diagnosis first, gain afterwards.
  • Not measuring before and after: without measurement, subjective impression rules and you end up throwing away a solution that perhaps only needed two degrees of orientation.

What to check before a warning or a blackout

The antenna is part of the same circuit as the rest of your connectivity, and in an emergency several links fail at once. Before a storm, a DANA or a scheduled outage arrives, go over the first 30 minutes checklist: check that the router and repeater are protected by a surge protector, keep a charged power bank for the mobile and a crank radio with solar panel as a warning channel when the data network goes down completely. And if the scenario is spending days without service, set up the rest of the circuit: communication kit, Starlink kit and mountain kit.

Also remember that the antenna needs electricity: in a prolonged blackout, the mobile network goes down sooner than people think because the backup batteries of the towers are not infinite. That is why coverage should not be your only channel — PMR446 radio and connectivity redundancy exist for that.

Verdict

A well-chosen external antenna is one of the improvements with the best cost-benefit ratio you can make in a country or mountain house: no building work, no monthly fee and an immediate effect on calls and data. The rule is always the same — measure first, choose the type according to where the problem is (outside, inside or in the device itself), install with a short cable and correct orientation, and measure again. And if the budget doesn't stretch, start with what is free: official map, moving the phone to another window and a second SIM to find out whether you are missing an antenna or missing coverage.

  • CNMC — Fibre and mobile coverage map in Spain
  • Ministry — Broadband service maps (includes 4G and 5G mobile coverage)
  • Civil Protection and Emergencies (MITECO)
  • AEMET — weather warnings

terremoto-espana-que-hacer.titulo: Earthquake in Spain: what to do before, during and after (2026)
terremoto-espana-que-hacer.resumen: What to do before, during and after an earthquake in Spain: official recommendations, IGN data and the lessons from the Granada earthquake series.
terremoto-espana-que-hacer.cuerpo:
On Tuesday, 18 August 2026, at 10:37, a magnitude 4.8 earthquake at a depth of 5 kilometers struck the province of Granada, with its epicenter northwest of Gójar. That same day there were four earthquakes of magnitude 4 or higher, with aftershocks of 4.3 and 4.2 in Alhendín, and the Junta de Andalucía ordered the preventive evacuation of six blocks in Las Gabias: 371 homes and around 600 people out of their homes while technicians inspected pillars and cracks. Three people sustained minor injuries.

The important thing is not the magnitude: it is that hundreds of families were left not knowing when they could return. Earthquakes do not announce themselves, so the only part of the script you control is you, and only if you work on it before the shaking starts. This is the sequence recommended by Civil Protection, with data from the Instituto Geográfico Nacional (IGN).

Spain has more earthquakes than you think

The IGN's National Seismic Network located 5,729 earthquakes on the Peninsula during 2025, of which 182 were felt by the population. The total varies greatly from one year to another —when a seismic series such as the one in Granada begins, it shoots up— but the pattern is always the same: thousands of tiny movements, a handful that are perceptible and, from time to time, one that is really felt.

Year (Peninsula)Earthquakes locatedFelt by the populationMagnitude above 4
202111,32980625
20228,84330823
20235,0991986
20244,9162033
20255,7291827

In 2025 there were 7 earthquakes above magnitude 4 and none reached 6: almost all go unnoticed. The problem is the one that does not.

Why the ground shakes and why no one can predict it

Spain lies on the edge of the Eurasian plate where it collides with the African plate, over the Azores-Gibraltar-Tunisia fracture; this is explained in the Civil Protection seismic risk guide, which is equally blunt about what we cannot do: “There is currently no method capable of predicting the time, place and magnitude of an earthquake.” There is no app or advance warning. The only thing that works is being prepared when it arrives without warning.

What is calculated is the building. The Spanish seismic-resistant construction standard, NCSE-02 (Royal Decree 997/2002), sets as its purpose avoiding loss of human life and reducing economic damage. Not all buildings are in the same situation: that is why, in Las Gabias, technicians inspected each block before authorizing return, and why the Patronato de la Alhambra preventively closed the Nasrid palaces that afternoon. No house is “safe” or “dangerous” in the abstract: it is inspected and decided with the report in hand.

Before: five things to do this week (they cost 0 €)

  • Secure the shelving, the TV and the tall wardrobes to the wall. In an earthquake, injuries almost never come from the ground: they come from what falls.
  • Locate the gas shut-off valve and check that it turns. After the shaking you will have seconds, and your hands will be trembling. If you smell gas, do not turn anything on: no switches, no matches.
  • Closed-toe shoes and a flashlight next to the bed, tied on or under the mattress: broken glass is not visible in the dark.
  • Written family agreement: meeting point and a contact outside the province, because local lines become saturated first. It is in family emergency plan.
  • Documents, first-aid kit and backpack near the door: the emergency folder with DNI, deeds and policy, the medication from the emergency first-aid kit and the backpack already packed.

During: you have between five and thirty seconds

The official recommendation fits into three verbs: drop, cover and hold on. Get on all fours, get under a sturdy table and hold on to the furniture: it will move with you and protect you from what falls. Three prohibitions prevent the rest of the injuries:

  • Do not run out to the stairs or use the elevator: stay where you are until the shaking stops.
  • Do not run out into the street from upper floors. Stay away from windows, mirrors, shelves and façades. If you are already in the street, go to an open space away from cornices and cables.
  • If you are driving, stop in an open place: not under bridges, not next to streetlights, not under cables.

After: the part almost everyone forgets

  • Before stepping on the floor, put on shoes. Just after getting up and in the dark, glass is on the floor and cannot be seen.
  • Do not go back inside until it has been inspected. In Granada the evacuations were preventive because of cracks that grew between one inspection and the next; if you see new cracks or a door that no longer closes, do not go in and report it.
  • Expect aftershocks in the following hours: no one can tell you which ones or when, so the rule is the same as at the beginning.
  • Reliable information, not rumors. ES-Alert is the “reverse 112” issued by Civil Protection via Cell Broadcast, and its Civil Protection Alert level cannot be disabled on your mobile phone; the battery-powered radio does the rest, as covered in communicating without a mobile network and official resources on your mobile.
  • Document before moving anything: photos of cracks and fallen objects for the insurer and the city council: without evidence there is no case file.

Three myths that come back with every seismic series

“Nothing really happens here.” On 11 May 2011 Lorca shook with magnitude 5.1 and intensity VII: nine dead and more than 300 injured. On 25 December 1884 the Arenas del Rey earthquake (Granada) destroyed some 4,400 houses and left damage in another 13,000, with around 800 fatalities according to the geophysics institute of the University of Granada. What kills is not the magnitude: it is the distance, the ground and the condition of the building.

“You can know when the next one will come.” No: that is the literal wording from Civil Protection. Be wary of anyone announcing dates.

“Magnitude explains everything.” Magnitude measures the energy released and does not change as you move away from the epicenter; intensity —the European EMS scale, from I to XII— measures how it was felt at a specific place and decreases with distance. A 4.8 at 5 kilometers below the outskirts of a capital city is felt across the entire metropolitan area; the same 4.8 far away is barely perceived.

Your list for this week

  1. Screws and fixing key: TV and shelving secured to the wall.
  2. Locate the gas shut-off valve and test it.
  3. Closed-toe shoes and a flashlight next to the bed.
  4. Write the family agreement: meeting point and contact outside the province.
  5. Update the document folder, the medication and the date on the backpack.
  6. Keep the battery-powered radio charged and locate the official warning channels.

The item-by-item detail is in the earthquake kit and in the evacuation backpack; if you are only going to assemble one, let it be the basic 72-hour kit, the one that supports you when the building holds but there is no power, water or gas.

kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.titulo: Emergency kit at work: what to keep and what to do (2026)
kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.resumen: A kit for the nine hours away from home: what to keep in your office drawer and how to get out of a building in a real evacuation. INSST regulation cited.
kit-emergencia-trabajo-oficina.cuerpo:
It's 9:12 on a Tuesday. You're on the third floor of a building with forty people, your backpack on the back of the chair, your car in the basement and your phone at 30%. If the fire alarm went off right now: do you know which door you exit through from your desk, where the assembly point is, and what you have in your drawer to get through the next two hours without depending on anyone?

Almost all the emergency kits we prepare are for home. And that's fine, because home is where you sleep. But add up the rest of the day: nine hours at work, two commuting and only eight sleeping. Your backpack in the closet covers exactly the part of the day when almost nothing happens. This guide is for the other part: the kit that goes with you, the one kept in a drawer, and the two questions you can ask at your office today to find out whether you'd get out of the building in three minutes or fifteen.

1. Work is where you're caught most off guard (and it's not your fault)

At home you know the noises, you know which door squeaks and you go out in the dark without thinking. In an office building you decide almost nothing: you depend on someone else's alarm, someone else's staircase, whether the stairwell door is locked, whether the work on the floor below has left boxes in the corridor. And above all, you depend on habit: almost every evacuation alert you've experienced in your life was a drill, so your brain decides, without being asked, that “it'll be another test alert.” People who leave a building late almost never leave late for lack of information: they leave late because they thought it wasn't serious.

That bias has a cheap antidote called knowing your route. And your company has a legal obligation to have everything else sorted out. Article 20 of Law 31/1995 on Prevention of Occupational Risks obliges the employer to analyse possible emergency situations and adopt the necessary measures for first aid, firefighting and worker evacuation, designating the staff responsible for putting them into practice. And when the building's activity falls within its scope, the Basic Self-Protection Standard (Royal Decree 393/2007) also requires a self-protection plan with regulated structure and content, including drills, maintenance and periodic reviews.

Translated into real life: that document exists, it's in a management or prevention drawer, and you haven't read it. It isn't a company secret: it's information you can ask for. The INSST (National Institute for Safety and Health at Work) has published the reference guide on emergency plans and self-protection plans, and it highlights the detail that fails most in practice: the plan is written once and forgotten, when what keeps it alive is drills and reviews.

2. The kit that goes with you: nine things that fit in a drawer

You don't need to turn your desk into a bunker. The idea is to cover the two hours after an incident without depending on anyone: so you're not short of water, light, battery, your medicines or footwear for walking if you have to walk back. All of this fits in a 40 cm drawer or in a cloth bag hanging from your chair.

What to keepWhat it's really forApprox. price
1 L water bottle and food that won't melt (bars, nuts, a can and a can opener)If you have to wait at the assembly point or walk back, the first thing you notice isn't hunger: it's thirst and a foggy head. Replace it every six months.3-8 €
10,000-20,000 mAh power bank with a short USB-C or Lightning cableWith no signal and no light, your phone is your map, your flashlight and your contact with home. A phone at 30% is two hours of anxiety; with a power bank, two days. Charge it on the first Monday of every month.20-40 €
Your personal medication for 24-48 h and a photo of the prescriptionNobody builds a work kit thinking about their own pill. If you take something for a chronic condition (thyroid, blood pressure, asthma, anxiety medication), carry an extra dose; ask your doctor or pharmacist how to store it and whether it tolerates office temperatures.varies by prescription
Small flashlight or headlamp and a whistleIn a blackout, emergency stairwells have their own lighting until the building's battery runs out. A whistle uses no power and carries farther than your voice.10-20 €
Two or three FFP2 masksSmoke, construction dust, mud or simply a corridor full of people coughing. They're also useful on the way if there's ash or poor air quality.5-10 €
