The criterion for choosing each item is the same one we use in the basic 72-hour kit: things that solve what will really happen, not what looks good in a photo. If you work at a computer all day and want the home version, the reasonable starting point is to know how to build your 72h kit without spending too much.

3. The self-protection plan: it exists, it's mandatory and nobody has read it

Here's the biggest shortcut in this guide. You don't have to design anything: someone in your building has already done it, and all you need is four questions and a three-minute walk.

  • Where is the plan, and when was the last drill? The INSST reminds us that evacuation drills must be carried out at least once a year, and that taking part in them is how you detect mistakes before they become serious. If your company hasn't held one since before the pandemic, you already know something useful.
  • Who is the emergency officer for my floor, and who is my evacuation officer? When the alarm sounds, someone has to count heads. If you don't know who that is, you're one of the people nobody is going to count.
  • Where exactly is the assembly point? Ask for the address, not “across the street.” And check that it isn't somewhere the wind leaves you breathing the building's smoke.
  • Which two evacuation routes apply to me from my desk? Always two: if the main one fills with smoke, the second has to be in your head, not just on the green sign.
  • How do you alert a deaf colleague or someone with reduced mobility? A deaf person doesn't hear the alarm (you need visual alerts or someone to tell them), and a stopped elevator leaves a wheelchair user with no way out. There is a solution — refuge points, visual alarms, designated assistance — but it only works if someone knows their name in advance. In many buildings that person is a visitor or a colleague who is just passing through.

The walk is the rest of it: today, leave your desk and go down to the street following the evacuation route, counting doors and looking at where the exits you never use are. It takes three minutes. The same route, with smoke, in a hurry and with forty people going down, isn't the same. And while you're at it, check something you can actually fix yourself: that your backpack, boxes or scooter aren't blocking an evacuation route, because routes must always be signposted and clear.

At home the logic is the same and you prepare in the same way: if you haven't done it yet, start with the family emergency plan, not with buying things. And if someone in your household depends on medical equipment, the fine detail is in monitoring chronic conditions without power.

4. The alarm sounds: how to get out of a building without leaving anyone behind

Self-protection plans and INSST guides agree on the essentials, and almost all the mistakes seen in a real evacuation are on this list:

  • Never the elevator. In an emergency it stops exactly where you don't want it to. If you're already inside and it stops, press the alarm or door-open button, call 112 from the elevator itself and say which floor you're on: 112 answers even if you don't have your operator's signal and even if your phone has no credit.
  • Leave the work, but take your key and phone. Not the laptop: it's heavy, gets in the way and is useless at the assembly point.
  • Go down on the correct side and don't cut across against the flow: a good share of the jams on an emergency stairway are people going up to look for someone.
  • If there's smoke, crouch low. Hot smoke collects above. A damp handkerchief over your mouth doesn't protect you from carbon monoxide, but it traps some particles and gives you seconds of visibility.
  • Close doors as you leave. A closed door delays the fire by minutes that are worth a lot; leaving them open gives the corridor to the smoke.
  • At the assembly point, count your people. And here's the advice that prevents the most problems and almost nobody practises: agree in advance who is responsible for whom. You, with the new colleague, the intern or the visitor who doesn't know the building; someone else, with whoever is slower. If nobody is responsible for anybody, everyone assumes.
  • Don't go back in. Not for your backpack, not for your phone, not for your car, not for “a second.” It's the classic mistake in every real evacuation, and in fires with casualties there's almost always someone who went back.

If you can't get out: make yourself visible and make sure you're counted

There's a case almost nobody practises and that happens more often than it seems: the exit is worse than your location. The corridor full of smoke, the stairway impassable, an emergency door that hasn't been opened in two years. Then the right decision is to stop trying to get out.

  • Close the door and seal the gap with a wet towel or a piece of clothing. You gain time and keep smoke out of the room.
  • Call 112 and say three things: street and number, floor, and which façade you're on (“fourth floor, window facing the square”). That sentence is what gets you found sooner.
  • Make yourself seen: a light-coloured garment hanging out of the window, your phone flashlight if it's dark, and your whistle if you have one. And shout to let people at the assembly point know: from outside they can tell the firefighters which floors are occupied.
  • Don't jump from the window as a general rule. On upper floors it's an almost certain injury, and smoke moves faster than it seems.

That same pattern — close, seal, alert and make yourself seen — is the one used when the danger is outside rather than inside: smoke from a nearby fire, chemical smoke from an industrial estate, a leak. The difference is that then the instruction comes from Protección Civil, via ES-Alert or radio: if they tell you not to go out, you don't go out, even if your car is in the basement and you have a meeting at ten.

5. When the emergency is outside the building: blackout, red alert and basements

Not everything that happens to you at work starts inside. A long power cut, a DANA with a red alert or an alert to your phone from Protección Civil can reach you with the building intact and the problem outside: no train, no bus, no elevator and the car park turned into a trap.

  • The ES-Alert alert is the National Civil Protection Alert Network: it sounds on your phone even if it's on silent, it's aimed at phones in a specific area and it can't be turned off. That low, loud beep isn't a hoax or a test: it's the official instruction. Read it in full before you move and do what it says (stay put, don't go out, don't drive).
  • Never go down to the basement for the car with an orange or red alert, or when water is already running down the ramp. Garage ramps are among the first places to flood and where most people are rescued from. If water rises up the ramp, you go up to the highest floor.
  • Blackout in the office: phone or drawer flashlight, never candles or lighters (and no combustion appliance in an enclosed space). If the building has no generator, the elevators stop: don't use them even for a second after a cut. And if there's a SAI or UPS, what really deserves continuity is the router and the phone: switch off sensitive equipment so it doesn't suffer the surge when power returns, just as you would at home.
  • Communicating when the network is overloaded: send a text with the essentials instead of calling. On a congested network a short message usually gets through before a call, and it lets you say where you are and that you're okay. The details are in communicating without a mobile network.
  • Walk back? It can be the best decision and also the worst. With a red alert, don't move: fifteen centimetres of moving water can sweep a person away, and underpasses and dry riverbeds fill in minutes. Once the alert is over, go via known places, in closed shoes, and tell someone your route and expected arrival time.
  • The journey is part of the kit too. If you go by car, don't depend on the office: water, a blanket, a flashlight and a power bank live in the car all year. The detail is in the car kit, and the lessons from 28A — signal down, card terminals dead, people trapped in tunnels — in what we learned from the 28 April blackout.

And if it drags on and you have to get home without transport, the reference is the evacuation kit: what to take if you have to leave on foot and spend the night away. If you live alone, add another layer: the plan for living alone starts with deciding who will call you if something happens.

6. What you can do today, in fifteen minutes

  1. Put five things in the drawer: water, bars, a headlamp, a power bank with cable and your medication. With that you're no longer naked before a four-hour outage.
  2. Ask about the plan and the assembly point. One email to risk prevention is enough: it's information your company has and that you can ask for.
  3. Walk the route from your desk to the street and count doors. Notice where the second exit is.
  4. Write down five phone numbers on paper and keep them in your wallet; and turn on AEMET alerts on your phone if you haven't already.
  5. Set a calendar reminder every six months to check expiry dates and recharge the power bank. A kit that isn't checked is a box of old things.

And the mistakes that keep happening, so they don't happen to you:

  • Confusing “I've thought about it” with “I've done it.” Thinking about where you'd get out is not the same as having walked it once.
  • The power bank always dead. It's useless if it had gone six months without charging on the very day the power goes out.
  • Deciding on the spot who helps whom. Decide beforehand, without rush, and in writing if necessary.
  • Going out into the street with a red alert “to get home sooner.” That's exactly the moment to stay put and on high ground.
  • Going down to the basement for the car. We repeat the advice because it's the mistake that puts the most people in hospital in every DANA.

A work kit isn't bought all at once and you don't need to spend 200 euros: it's nine objects, four questions and three minutes of walking slowly and looking at doors. Today, on your coffee break, you can do the five things on the list. Tomorrow, if the alarm sounds, you'll already know it isn't just another alarm.

salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.titulo: Mental health and sleep in an emergency: how to keep going (2026)
salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.resumen: Sleeping, eating and calming down are not the soft part of the plan: they are the decisions made after two nights without sleep. WHO framework, shifts and rest.
salud-mental-y-sueno-en-una-emergencia.cuerpo:
It's 21:40 and the power goes out. Twenty minutes later you've sorted the fridge: you know what to throw away and what not to. What no one has taught you to sort out is the other part. The child asking whether the power will come back before bedtime, your mother calling you at two in the morning frightened because she can't see anything, or your own brain at three still going over the list of things that could still go wrong. Emergencies aren't won with flashlights and water bottles alone: they're won by sleeping, eating and keeping your head in the right place. This is the part of the kit that doesn't go in a box.

And this is not a soft or secondary issue. Sustained stress takes away your appetite and your sleep, and when you've had two nights with almost no sleep you make worse decisions: you leave the door open, you drive at night to 'get there sooner', you don't see the puddle across the road. WHO has studied this for years in its emergency guidance, and the conclusion is very practical: what helps in the first 72 hours is not a speech, it's four concrete things —safety, information, human contact and rest— and all of them can be prepared today.

1. What official manuals say: look, listen, connect

The reference guide in Spanish is “Psychological first aid: Guide for field workers”, by WHO with War Trauma Foundation and World Vision International. It is intended for people helping others in a disaster, but the framework is so simple that it works just as well for a neighbour, for your father or for yourself. It comes down to three actions.

  • Look: check that you are in a safe place, who needs help first and what basics are missing: water, warmth, a dry place, real information. Before talking about feelings, you deal with thirst, cold and noise.
  • Listen: approach, introduce yourself, ask what they need at that moment and don't force them to tell their story. The guide itself recalls a conclusion from the WHO mhGAP working group: a very distressed person should be offered psychological first aid, not forced to go over what happened. Let those who want to talk talk, yes; interrogate those who don't, no.
  • Connect: help them reach family, services that are working and practical information. One good piece of information given in time (when the power will come back, where there is drinking water, which road is closed) calms more than any nice phrase.

What you can do in the next 10 minutes: drink a glass of water and eat something even if you're not hungry. Sit down and do two minutes of slow breathing (four seconds in, six seconds out). Use the 5-4-3-2-1 technique —name in a low voice five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch, two you can smell, one you can taste— when you notice your head going in loops. And tidy one single room to turn it into your 'command post': a table with the radio or charged phone, the flashlight, water, paper and pen. Visible order translates into calm.

What seems like a good idea but isn't: using alcohol to sleep (it leaves you asleep for the first part of the night and awake and more anxious for the second), having the TV or radio with news on a loop at all hours (it feeds the sense of catastrophe and doesn't give you a single useful fact), borrowing a sleeping pill from a neighbour (if you use something to sleep, do it through your doctor or pharmacist) and saying 'we'll sleep when this is over', because sleep debt is also paid in the next day's decisions.

2. Sleeping when there is no light, no silence and no calm

The second or third night of an emergency is the most critical moment: you have used up the adrenaline of the first day and you arrive shattered, but your head won't slow down. Four measures solve much of the problem, and none costs money if you already have the kit put together.

  • Fixed times. Go to bed and get up at the same time, even if you are not working and sleep in fits and starts. The internal clock doesn't understand blackouts: it understands routine.
  • The bed is for sleeping only. If you haven't fallen asleep after 20-30 minutes, get out of bed and do something calm in dim light —read, write, tidy— until sleep returns. It is the classic recommendation of sleep guides and works better than tossing and turning for rebound insomnia.
  • Less caffeine in the afternoon and no stimulants in the middle of the night. Coffee, tea and cola drinks stay in your system for hours; if you're on watch, ration them.
  • Cover screens and use a battery-powered clock. The phone informs you and steals your sleep: set two times a day to check the news —in the morning and late in the afternoon— and leave the phone charging in another room at night. A battery-powered alarm clock for €8-12 saves you from looking at the time at 3:40 in the morning.

For the environment, three common-sense things almost nobody prepares: darkness (a sleep mask, or an improvised curtain, because a streetlight or an LED can leave your face lit all night), silence (foam earplugs; if the noise is outside, a radio station talking softly or a constant radio sound masks it better than nothing) and coolness or warmth depending on the season —if the problem is cold or heat, you have the full rules in how to maintain body temperature without electricity. And a golden rule: never sleep on bare floor; mat, cardboard and blanket in layers, as explained in dressing in layers.

If something at home needs watching —a sick person, the water level, the downstairs neighbour— don't let the same person always do it. Divide the night into blocks and write it on paper, not from memory:

BlockWho is on watchWho sleeps
22:00 - 01:00Person APerson B
01:00 - 04:00Person BPerson A
04:00 - 07:00Person APerson B (or a 30-min nap)

The watch shift is deliberately short: three hours can be sustained, six cannot. And one last tool that almost always works: the notebook by the bed. Before you go to bed, write down the three or four worries that are going to wake you and what you can do about each one tomorrow. Getting them out of the mental loop and leaving them on paper is the cheapest way for the brain to accept letting them go.

3. Children: routine calms more than any explanation

A child doesn't need to know the full truth of a disaster: they need to know what is going to happen in their day. The presence of an adult who doesn't shout and routine —water, teeth, story, light— do more than any conversation. Three rules for tonight:

  • Tell them the truth, but keep it short and give them a plan. “There's no power because there's a very big outage. We're at home, there's water and food, and Mum and Dad are here. Tomorrow we'll look at it with the flashlight.” No details that will scare them and no promises you can't keep (“tomorrow the power will definitely come back” is a promise; “tomorrow I'll tell you as soon as they know” is not).
  • Give them a job. What most reduces children's fear is having a role: carrying the flashlight, noting the times, checking the water containers, handing out the blankets. It is their way of feeling they control something.
  • Sleep next to them if they ask. This is not the night to teach them to sleep alone. The comfort object (blanket, soft toy, pacifier, story) comes out of the cupboard and goes into the evacuation bag from now on.

Also: no news on a loop in front of them, and a dim light in the hallway all night so they don't wake up in total darkness they don't recognise. If after several days the child doesn't eat, doesn't sleep or is very irritable, talk to your paediatrician. You have the detail by age in babies and children in an emergency and the materials in the baby and breastfeeding kit.

4. Older people, people with chronic illness and those who live alone

Here preparation happens before the disaster, not during it. Darkness disorients older people faster than hunger: they lose their sense of the hallway, get up at night and fall. Concrete solutions:

  • Beacon lights in the hallway and bathroom. Four LED battery lights that come on by themselves cost less than €15 and prevent the most common fall during a blackout. Everything an older person's kit needs is detailed on its page.
  • Towel at the edge of the bed and a clear path. No chairs or boxes between the bed and the door: at night and without light, they become an obstacle.
  • A call at the same time every day. It's not a chat: it's a welfare check. And always with a designated backup person, because the person making the call can get sick too. It is the basis of what I covered in living alone and being prepared.
  • Check in in person, not by WhatsApp. If there is hearing loss, a message is no use: you have to knock on the door, speaking loudly and facing them. The same applies to mobile alerts, which should be explained beforehand.

With chronic medication, the order of the day is to keep to the schedule and not improvise doses: pill organiser and a written list, with the days marked. If there are insulins or medicines that need to be kept cold, check how to ensure 2-4 weeks without a pharmacy and always consult your doctor or pharmacist for any decision about doses or storage. And if the person has cognitive impairment, don't argue with their reality: redirect —water, blanket, hand, song, photo—.

5. The person holding things together can also fall apart

In every home there is someone who acts as the switchboard: they call, organise, don't sleep, and after three days they burn out. If you are that person, this is for you.

  • No one stays on watch two nights in a row. Write it on the fridge door in large letters, because it's the first thing everyone skips.
  • Eat and drink even if you're not hungry. Five minutes of salty food and a glass of water every three hours do more than a coffee on the run.
  • Name a backup out loud. “If I can't, call Marta and she knows where everything is.” Above all, write the important phone numbers down on paper: the full list is in the official resources you should have saved.
  • Get outside for five minutes a day. Fresh air, the street, walking. WHO has documented it: physical activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression and improves sleep, and that counts double when everything is upside down.

And set an honest limit on your role: you don't have to fix anyone. Accompanying, sorting out the practical things and handing over the baton is already all that can be done on the first day. If you or someone in your home has gone several days without sleeping or eating, if sadness settles in or ideas of not wanting to live appear, that is not managed with willpower: call 024, the suicidal behaviour helpline of the Ministry of Health, free and available 24 hours a day, or 112 if the emergency is immediate. With any clinical doubt, consult your doctor or pharmacist.

6. Your rest and head kit: ten items and a seven-day plan

None of these items is expensive, and all of them get used at home on any bad night, not only in a disaster. Put the small items in a cloth bag inside the basic 72-hour kit and leave the large ones in the bedroom.

ItemWhat it's really forApproximate price
Foam earplugs (5 pairs)Sleep with a radio station, a generator or a street on alert€3-6
Cloth sleep maskReal darkness when there are streetlights, candles or an LED on€5-8
Headlamp with red modeMove around at night without waking anyone and without wrecking your sleep€10-15
Battery-powered alarm clockKnow the time without turning on your phone at 4 in the morning€8-12
Battery or hand-crank radioOfficial information without a network or phone battery, and constant sound for sleeping€15-25
Small notebook and penEmpty the worry loop before bed and write down phone numbers€2-4
Deck of cards or paperback bookTwo hours of quiet activity without screens, children included€5-10
Extra light blanketSleep warm without sweating: layers, not a heavy blanket€10-15
1.5-litre water bottleHaving water next to you keeps you from getting up in the dark and drinking less€1
Minimal toiletry bag and wipesWashing your face and teeth restores a sense of normality€4-6

And this is the seven-day plan to have all this sorted before you need it, at fifteen minutes a day:

  • Day 1. Write on a sheet of paper the key phone numbers (112, 024, doctor, school, two neighbours, two family members) and the family meeting point. One paper copy in your wallet and another taped inside the hall cupboard.
  • Day 2. Set up the command table: radio, flashlight, charger, water, paper, pen. One table, always the same one.
  • Day 3. Buy earplugs, sleep mask and battery-powered clock. They go in the bedside drawer, not the storage room.
  • Day 4. Prepare the 'dinner without power': cans, nuts, fruit and water accessible, and a tray with what you need (can opener, spoon, napkins) so you don't open cupboards in the dark.
  • Day 5. Try a two-hour night without mains power at home: flashlights, safely placed candles, no screens. You'll discover what's missing before you need it.
  • Day 6. Explain the plan to the children and give them a specific task (flashlight, water list). Ten minutes is enough.
  • Day 7. Call the family member who lives alone and agree the time of the daily call. And tell a neighbour who to contact if they don't see you.

With this you have covered what no flashlight can fix: sleeping, eating, keeping your head together and knowing who to call. If you want to divide the work by scenario, start by putting together your 72-hour kit and the first decisions of a blackout; and if tonight you are already in the middle of the mess, the urgent stuff is in the home or shelter-in-place kit.

conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.titulo: Storing food without a fridge: what keeps and what to throw away (2026)
conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.resumen: What to throw out and what can be saved when the power goes out: AESAN's official times and temperatures for fridge, freezer and pantry, plus reliable homemade methods.
conservar-comida-sin-nevera-ni-frio.cuerpo:
The power goes out at 21:40. By 21:55 you've already opened the fridge “to see what's in there”, by 22:10 the freezer, and the next day you're faced with a warm fridge containing meat, fresh cheese and leftovers you don't know whether to throw away. That moment — deciding what's saved and what goes in the bin — is exactly what this guide solves: hours and temperatures measured by the Spanish Agency for Food Safety and Nutrition (AESAN) during the 28 April 2025 blackout, plus a pantry you can set up today so you don't depend on refrigeration.

And it's not a whim: the EU Preparedness Union Strategy (March 2025) asks households to have enough supplies for 72 hours. Almost all kit lists include water, a flashlight and a radio, but very few say which food really keeps without refrigeration or cooking. That's what you'll see here, along with what you can do in 20 minutes after you finish reading.

1. The hours that decide everything: your fridge without power

The first thing to understand is that the enemy isn't “the blackout”, it's the temperature each food has reached. The fridge doesn't heat up all at once when the breaker trips: it holds the cold like a cooler box, which is why what matters most isn't how long the outage lasts, but how many times you've opened the door. With the door closed, a well-stocked fridge keeps food below 5 °C for about 4 hours; a full or half-full freezer keeps things frozen for between 24 and 48 hours. With the door opened every so often, those figures fall apart on their own.

The official AESAN rules, published after the 28A blackout and included by the Ministry of Social Rights, Consumer Affairs and Agenda 2030, are these:

  • Outages of less than 4 hours (without opening the door): nothing needs to be discarded because of the blackout.
  • Outages of more than 4 hours: temperatures have probably gone above 5 °C, so throw out perishables: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, fresh cheese and leftovers. Throw them out even if you cook them well: the risk isn't eliminated by the heat of a frying pan, and those foods can also contaminate others through contact.
  • Whole fruit and vegetables: they keep without refrigeration if they still look good. Cut up or already made into prepared salad: in the bin.
  • Freezer: if the food still has ice crystals, is hard and cold, it can be refrozen. If it has completely thawed but is still cold, eat it that day. If you're not sure how long it has been thawed, discard it.
  • Canned goods, soft drinks, chocolate and drinks you kept in the fridge out of habit: they don't need refrigeration and are perfectly fine.

And the rule that sums them all up: never taste a food to decide whether it's safe, and don't trust smell or appearance. If in doubt, out. Throwing away 12 euros of food is infinitely cheaper than food poisoning in the middle of an emergency, with emergency departments overwhelmed and no way to get there by car.

SituationWhat to do
Outage < 4 h, door closedEverything is still fine. Don't throw anything away.
Outage > 4 hThrow out perishables: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, fresh cheese, leftovers.
Whole fruit/vegetablesIt keeps. If cut or prepared, throw it out.
Freezer, 24-48 h without openingIf ice crystals remain: it can be refrozen. Thawed and cold: eat within the day. Doubts: out.
Canned goods and closed packaged foodsPerfect outside the cold. Once opened, put in the fridge and eat within 2-3 days.

2. What really keeps outside the cold

Here's the heart of the matter: a prepared home isn't one with a full fridge, it's one with a pantry that doesn't depend on the fridge. These shelf lives are approximate — they depend on temperature, humidity and how you store things — but they're enough to decide what to buy extra next time you go to the supermarket:

FoodWithout refrigeration, closedKey to making it last
Canned goods (tuna, sardines, cooked pulses, tomato)2-5 yearsDry place, no knocks or dented cans. Once opened: fridge and eat within 2-3 days.
Dried pulses, rice, pastaYearsAirtight container and dark. Moisture is the only thing that kills them.
UHT / powdered / condensed milkMonths unopenedOnce opened, fridge and 2-3 days. Powdered is the most heat-resistant.
Olive oil12-18 monthsDark and cool. Light and heat turn it rancid before the date does.
Honey, salt, sugarPractically indefiniteClosed jar. If honey crystallises, it isn't bad: that's normal.
Nuts and dried fruit6-12 monthsAirtight container; heat makes them rancid even if they don't look bad.
Whole cured sausage (chorizo, salchichón, jamón)WeeksWhole, hung in a dry, ventilated place. Sliced and packaged, it does need refrigeration.
Potato, onion, garlic, sweet potato, whole pumpkinWeeksDark, dry and ventilated, separated from each other. Potato and onion never together.
Unwashed eggsWeeks in a cool placeIf it's hot, move them to the coolest spot in the house and eat them soon.

Notice the pattern: everything that keeps without refrigeration has three things in common — it's dry, it's acidic or it's factory vacuum-packed. And everything that spoils quickly is moist and only mildly acidic: fresh meat, fish, fresh dairy, leftovers. With that criterion you can already set up half your pantry without memorising any table.

3. What you should never do (and some popular advice that's bad)

There are habits that circulate in every emergency and that are directly dangerous. These four, specifically:

  • Tasting food to see if it's still good. It's the first thing AESAN says not to do. The pathogens that grow with heat don't reliably change taste or smell.
  • Trusting the appearance of home-canned food. Botulinum toxin doesn't change colour, smell, taste or texture: a contaminated jar can taste perfectly fine. And botulism is mainly associated with home preserves of low-acid vegetables — chillies in oil, asparagus, green beans, beetroot, corn — according to AESAN documents. If a home-made jar has a bulging lid, releases gas when opened or smells odd: into the bin, without tasting it.
  • Freezing “so as not to throw it away” food that has already been out of the cold for hours. The freezer slows things down, it doesn't fix them. An open container, a lifted lid or a lunchbox that has been on the counter all afternoon doesn't become safe by putting it in the freezer: what has already multiplied is still there. Freeze what was cold; throw out what was lukewarm.
  • Leaving cooked food at room temperature “for a while”. AESAN is clear: cooked food should be eaten straight away, or kept above 60 °C, or below 5 °C. The lukewarm range is exactly where germs thrive.

And one that does work, even if it sounds like grandma's advice: heating a home-made preserve well before eating it. Public health documents recommend boiling or heating food for at least 10 minutes at 80 °C or above: botulinum toxin is destroyed by heat, so a well-boiled stew is much safer than that same jar eaten cold on toast. Even so, the best measure is not to make preserves of low-acid vegetables without a tested recipe and without acidifying with citric acid.

4. How to set up a pantry that doesn't depend on the fridge

Buying isn't the same as storing. I've seen 200-euro pantries ruined by a damp corner. What matters:

  • Where: cool (ideally below 20 °C), dry, dark and ventilated. The three worst places in a Spanish home: on top of the fridge or next to the oven, a sun-facing balcony, and a damp garage or storage room. Check AEMET warnings and, if weeks above 35 °C are coming, move delicate foods to the coolest part of the house.
  • In what: airtight glass jars with a seal or plastic containers with a rubber lid. Open plastic bags and cardboard boxes are an invitation for moths and weevils.
  • The trick almost nobody uses against bugs: if you have free freezer space, leave the packet of pulses, rice or flour inside for 48-72 hours before transferring it to the jar. It kills the eggs and larvae that came in the packaging and stops an infestation appearing three months later.
  • Cans: don't stack them in unstable towers, don't let them get wet (a rusty can eventually perforates), and don't use dented ones. Large cans always at the bottom. And a bulging can is not opened: it's thrown away.
  • Humidity: use the silica gel sachets that come in shoeboxes and mix them into jars of pasta and biscuits.
  • Date and order: marker pen on the lid with the month of purchase and the FIFO rule: new at the back, old at the front. A 10-minute review twice a year stops you discovering the problem just when you need it.

How much should you buy? Start with what's realistic: 72 hours of food that needs neither refrigeration nor cooking (the basic 72-hour kit gives you the list), then a week and, only when that rotates well, the jump to a 30-day kit. If you're unsure where to start, I explain it in detail here: 72-hour kit or 30-day kit.

5. Preserving without cold when the fridge never comes back

If the outage stretches beyond a day or two, you have three resources and plenty of traps. The real resources, in order of reliability:

  • Vinegar and acid: vinegar lowers the pH below 4.6, and Clostridium botulinum doesn't develop there. Vegetable pickles with vinegar are the safest and quickest home method: cut, blanch, cover with vinegar and brine, close and store in the dark. Pickled garlic and onion last for months.
  • Salt: salting and strong brines dry food out by osmosis and slow bacteria. It works with fish, pork belly and vegetables. It isn't suitable for everything: salted meat has to be cooked afterwards.
  • Drying: sun and air for tomatoes, peppers, figs, grapes or mushrooms, or an oven at minimum temperature if you have gas. It needs dry air; in humid northern areas it goes mouldy before it dries.
  • Fermentation: sauerkraut, kimchi or fermented pickles with 2 % salt acidify on their own and last for months. They need a clean jar, vegetables kept under their own liquid and a cool place.
  • Sugar: jams and preserves with plenty of fruit and plenty of sugar keep without refrigeration once opened if you cover them well and don't put dirty spoons in them.

And the traps, which are worth being clear about because they cause the most home poisonings: covering vegetables in oil (chili peppers, garlic, dried tomatoes) creates exactly the oxygen-free environment botulism needs, if you haven't acidified them first; home vacuum-sealing leftovers without sterilising isn't preservation, it's a culture; smoking by eye at home isn't a safe long-term preservation method. And if you make preserves in a water bath, bear in mind that boiling at 100 °C doesn't destroy spores: it's only reliable with acidic foods (tomato, sweetened fruit, pickles) or with a pressure cooker and tested recipes. For everything else, better to freeze, dry or not do it. And when in doubt, ask your doctor or pharmacist: they can advise you on citric acid, doses and preserves.

If you're in the middle of an emergency and the food is already warm or thawed, the important thing is to eat it in order: first the perishables that were in the freezer and have thawed, then the fridge and, finally, the pantry. You have complete menus without cooking or a fridge in what to eat if the power goes out: three-day menus and the details of how to store everything in storing water and food at home.

6. What you can do today in 20 minutes

None of this is any use if it stays theoretical. You can do these six things this afternoon, with what you already have or with a small purchase:

  • Put a thermometer in the fridge (a few euros) and check that it's at 4 °C or below. If it isn't, you've been paying for electricity for nothing.
  • Set aside the last shelf for things that survive without cold: canned goods, nuts, chocolate, oil. That way, when the power goes out, you know what not to touch.
  • Freeze half-full water bottles or jugs in the free spaces in the freezer: they act as a cold reservoir and, when they thaw, they're drinking water. And tell everyone at home: the fridge does not get opened.
  • Write on the fridge door the time of the last outage and a note with the 4-hour rule. In an emergency nobody remembers the figures.
  • Put an airtight jar of pulses and another of rice in the pantry, and add them to the shopping list when you use them.
  • Review your actual kit: blackout kit, home kit and, if you cook with gas or want to eat hot food, a gas stove with cartridges and ventilation. With that and a well-stocked pantry, a three-day outage stops being a food problem.

What happened on 28 April 2025 left a very specific lesson in Spanish homes: the fridge held out, water came out of the tap as soon as pressure returned, and what failed was not knowing what to do with the food. It's solved in an afternoon, and that afternoon is today. You have the full review of the day after the blackout in lessons from 28A and water — the other pillar — in water: how much you need and how to make it safe to drink.

panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.titulo: Portable solar panel: how many watts you really need (2026)
panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.resumen: Most emergency kit solar panels overpromise: how many real watts to expect, what wattage to buy, and how to pair it with a power bank.
panel-solar-portatil-realista-quantos-wa.cuerpo:
The blackout on 28 April 2025 left half the country without power and with a phone at 2%. Most people solved it with the power bank they already had charged. But if the power goes out for several days and there is no sun (or it rains for weeks), the power bank drops to zero and doesn't recharge. This is where the portable solar panel comes in, and why almost everything sold on Amazon doesn't do what it promises.

I'm not going to sell you a 300-watt panel for your balcony. I'm going to tell you what a real panel can do — or not do — when you're left without power, and which panel + battery combo makes sense to get through a week without grid power.

The trap of advertised watts

A portable solar panel advertised as 100 watts rarely delivers 100 real watts. The reason isn't a scam — it's physics: panels are measured under standard test conditions (STC), which are 1000 W/m² irradiance, cell temperature at 25 °C and AM 1.5 spectrum. In real life:

  • Irradiance in Spain never reaches 1000 W/m² on a sustained basis (even in summer, the ceiling is usually between 800 and 950 W/m²; official AEMET and IAE data confirm this).
  • Cell temperature easily rises to 45-65 °C in direct sun: each degree above 25 °C reduces power by 0.3% to 0.5%. At 55 °C, a panel loses 9% to 15% of its power.
  • The sun's angle of incidence changes constantly; if the panel isn't perpendicular to the sun, you lose 20-40% of performance.

A 100 W panel correctly oriented on a clear June day in Spain delivers 60 to 80 real watts, and only for about 5-6 hours of the day. A 50 W panel correctly oriented delivers 30 to 40 real watts. That's the figure you need to use for your calculations.

How much energy do you need in an emergency?

Before buying, you need to know what you're going to charge. Here is the minimum most people need to keep running:

  • Phone (full charge): 10 to 15 Wh (a modern 4000 mAh phone at 3.7 V is ~15 Wh; with charger efficiency and losses, you need ~12-15 Wh net).
  • Battery-powered FM radio: 0-2 Wh (if it uses AA batteries, the panel won't charge them; if it has a USB port, 1 to 2 W).
  • LED headlamp: 2 to 5 Wh per charge.
  • Power bank you recharge: a 20,000 mAh power bank at 3.7 V is 74 Wh; with boost losses, you need to put about 90 Wh net into it.

This gives an idea of how much a panel generates on a real sunny day:

Advertised panelActual watts (good day)Equivalent sun hoursWh/dayPhone charges
30 W18-22 W5 h90-110 Wh6-8
50 W30-40 W5 h150-200 Wh10-15
100 W60-80 W5 h300-400 Wh20-30

Don't be fooled: with a 30 W panel you can already recharge a 20,000 mAh power bank every two or three days in summer. In winter, multiply the time by two or three (fewer sun hours, low angle). On a cloudy day: multiply by three or four.

The combo that really works: panel + power bank

A solar panel on its own isn't much use in an emergency: it generates energy when the sun is out, not when you need it. What you need is generate + store. The minimum useful combo is a 30-50 W panel plus a power bank of at least 20,000 mAh. Here's how it works:

  • You generate with the panel when there is sun (between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., preferably with the panel facing south and perpendicular to the sun).
  • You store it in the power bank, which is already part of your basic 72h kit.
  • You use it when you want: at night, in the rain, with the phone in your pocket.

The key is that the power bank has a USB input that supports the voltage and amperage coming from the panel. A 50 W panel generates 5 to 6 V at 8-10 A: you need a power bank that accepts that input (most modern ones do). If not, you'll have to use a solar controller (PWM or MPPT), which adds cost and complexity.

What panel size is enough?

For household use in a crisis:

  • 30-50 W (the minimum): charges a phone 6 to 10 times a day in summer. Recharges a 20,000 mAh power bank every 2-3 days. Fits in a backpack. This is what I recommend for most households if you're only going to charge a phone and radio.
  • 50-100 W (the reasonable option): recharges the power bank every day in summer, every two days in winter. Enough to keep phone, radio and headlamp running without worry. Takes up a bit more space but fits in a car trunk or on a terrace.
  • 100-200 W (the portable maximum): recharges the power bank several times a day. Useful if you need to power something else (a room LED light, a USB fan), but you start to need structure and a fixed surface. It's not a backpack item: it's a terrace setup.

What to look for (and what not to) when buying a panel

The current market has everything. The important thing is to tell what works from what is decoration:

  • Monocrystalline panels are more efficient (higher conversion percentage) than polycrystalline ones: a 100 W monocrystalline panel weighs less and takes up less space than a polycrystalline one of the same wattage. The price difference is minimal.
  • Folding or rigid panel: folding ones are practical to carry in a backpack; rigid ones are more durable and are installed permanently on a terrace or balcony. There isn't a big difference in performance if the monocrystalline cell is the same.
  • Built-in controller: many panels already include a PWM regulator or a direct USB connector. If they don't, you need a separate controller (5 to 20 €). Always check that it's compatible with your power bank.
  • Avoid panels with a built-in battery: the battery heats up in the sun, degrades and is also much heavier. The right approach is a separate panel + power bank.
  • Water resistance matters: look for panels rated IP65 at minimum if you're going to use them outdoors. During a DANA it rains, and you're not going to keep the panel under a roof.

Typical mistakes

  • Buying a large panel without thinking about where to set it up: a 100 W panel needs about 6-7 m² of surface to deploy (double-panel folding models measure ~1.5 x 1 m; four-panel models ~2 x 1 m). If you don't have a south-facing terrace or balcony, it ends up in the shade of a tree and is useless.
  • Not having a power bank charged beforehand: the panel generates energy when the sun is out; if you don't store it, you lose the hours without sun. The power bank is the bridge between generation and consumption.
  • Pointing the panel at the sky: the sun isn't always overhead. In winter, at 10 a.m. or 4 p.m., the angle is very low and performance drops 30-50%. Adjust the panel angle according to the time of day.
  • Covering the panel without noticing: a leaf, a coaster, a patch of thick fog. If the panel gets dirty, output drops 10-30%. Clean it from time to time.
  • Confusing watts (W) with watt-hours (Wh): the panel says 100 W: that's 100 watts when the sun is perfect at that instant. Wh are what you generate in a day (W × h). To know how many phone charges you can expect, multiply the real W by the equivalent sun hours.

What if there's no sun for weeks?

That's the real limitation of a portable solar panel: it doesn't generate when there's no sun. And in Spain, the months with the highest risk of crisis (autumn and winter) are precisely the ones with the least sun. That's why the panel is a complement, not the base of the kit. The base is the charged power bank (which you already cover in the blackout kit) and the battery-powered radio. The solar panel is what ensures that, when the sun comes back, you don't have to depend on anyone to recharge.

The EU recommends 72 hours of autonomy; the solar panel helps you go beyond those three days if the crisis drags on and the sky clears. But if all you have is a panel and not a power bank, you have nothing.

Practical summary

  • Reasonable minimum: 30-50 W monocrystalline panel + 20,000 mAh power bank.
  • Ideal: 50-100 W panel + large power bank (20,000-30,000 mAh) with a wide USB input.
  • Fixed installation: if you have a south-facing terrace, a fixed 100 W rigid panel is best: no need to orient it, it doesn't move, it generates all day.
  • Remember: the panel is not the base of the kit. The charged power bank, battery-powered radio and non-perishable food are. The solar panel takes you from 3 days to a week if the sky clears.

The blackout kit includes a power bank and solar panel as recommended items; the guide to eating without power details the order of consumption; the basic kit is the base to which you add any other item.

seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.titulo: Passive home safety: saves lives without doing anything (2026)
seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.resumen: Smoke detectors, fire extinguishers and electrical codes are not decoration: they are your home's first defenses: what to install, where, and how to maintain them.
seguridad-pasiva-hogar-incendios-electri.cuerpo:
A home fire is the most likely emergency and the one that gives you the least time to react: a fire can sweep through an entire apartment in less than five minutes, and toxic smoke kills more people than flames. Passive fire safety in the home is all the elements that work without you doing anything: detectors, fire-resistant materials, extinguishers and electrical installation rules that act before you have to run. They are not unnecessary expenses: they are your family's first line of defense.

What is passive fire safety

In safety engineering, a distinction is made between active protection (extinguishers you press, sprinklers you trigger, calls to 112) and passive protection (detectors that sound on their own, fire doors that block the spread of smoke, cables that do not catch fire, materials that do not spread flame). Passive protection is what warns you or protects you while you sleep, without you having to decide anything. And it is also the most undervalued in Spanish homes.

The Technical Building Code (CTE), Basic Document DB-SI, already requires fire-resistance levels for construction elements and the installation of detection systems in new buildings. But in private homes, responsibility for detectors and extinguishers is yours. And it should not cost you more than 60 euros a year.

1. Smoke detectors: the first warning

Smoke detectors are the single item that saves the most lives in a home fire. They warn you in the first minutes, when you can still get out or call for help, and they do so at night, when you are not aware. The Community of Madrid has standardized this in all its guides:

  • Optical: recommended for bedrooms, living rooms and rest areas — they detect smoke from slow-burning and smoldering fires, the most dangerous because it is invisible at first but already kills.
  • Heat detectors: for kitchens or storage rooms, where normal cooking smoke would not trigger false alarms. They activate at a fixed temperature (usually 57 °C).
  • Location: on the ceiling, at least 3 meters from bedrooms. Each floor of the home needs at least one. In single-story homes under 60 m², one may be enough, although two are recommended: living room and hallway.
  • Monthly test: press the test button every month. Batteries are changed when clocks change, like watch batteries.
  • Every 10 years: replace the whole detector. It does not last forever: the sensor gets dirty and degrades.

Price: 8-15 € per new optical detector. A pack of 4 detectors with batteries included costs around 30-50 €. It is not a luxury: it is what separates a scare from a tragedy. And in many buildings they are already installed under new-build regulations, but check that they work.

2. Electrical safety: preventing short circuits and overloads

Faulty electrical installations are the leading cause of home fires. Not because of a mysterious wiring failure, but because of overloads you can control:

  • Do not daisy-chain power strips: plugging one power strip into another multiplies the risk of a short circuit. A power strip has limited capacity, and a heater or hairdryer can overload it.
  • Multi-socket strip with switch and thermal protection: buy power strips with an internal fuse that cuts out if there is an overload. They cost 3-5 € more than a standard one and are the difference between a power cut and a fire.
  • RCD and circuit breaker in the electrical panel: they are required by regulations and must react in milliseconds if they detect a leak or a short circuit. If your panel does not have them or you are unsure, an electrician can check them in an hour.
  • Old wiring: if your home is more than 25-30 years old and an electrician has never checked it, do it. Aluminum cables or installations with deteriorated insulation are a latent risk.

Price: a safe multi-socket strip, 10-20 €. A professional electrical inspection, 60-120 €.

3. Kitchen: the highest-risk area

The kitchen is the room where most home fires start: grease catching fire, oil on fire, gas left on without a flame. The recommendations are simple, but you do not apply them until it happens to you:

  • Never leave the kitchen unattended when there is an open flame. If you have to leave, turn it off. Fire spreads in seconds.
  • Extinguisher near the kitchen: class F (flammable liquids and grease), specific for kitchen fires. A water extinguisher on a pan of burning oil can be counterproductive — class F is the right one.
  • Lids or a kitchen spray extinguisher: if a pan catches fire, put the lid on and cut off the fire. The oxygen runs out and the flame goes out on its own. Never pour water on burning grease.
  • Keep flammable items away from flames: towels, kitchen cloths, plastic bags and scourers away from the burner.

Price: class F extinguisher, 15-25 €. The pan lid, free if you already have one.

4. Extinguishers and how to choose them

One extinguisher does not suit everything. In a Spanish home, what you need is:

  • ABC powder (6 kg): the most versatile for the home. It works for wood, gas, flammable liquids and electricity up to 1000 V. It is what Protección Civil recommends for homes.
  • CO₂ (2 kg): ideal for sensitive electrical equipment (computer, TV, electrical panel). It leaves no residue, but it is not suitable for wood or grease fires.
  • Water with additive (6 L): good for wood and textiles, not for electricity or grease. Less versatile than ABC powder but cleaner.

Location: in a central hallway, accessible, not in the kitchen (where heat could make it fail) or in a closed cupboard. On the wall, at eye level, with a strap or bracket costing 8-12 €.

Maintenance: an extinguisher lasts 5-10 years and needs servicing every 5 years by an authorized company. Check the pressure gauge monthly: the needle in the green means it is fine; in the red, it has no pressure.

Price: 6 kg ABC powder extinguisher, 15-25 €; 5-year service, 20-30 €.

5. Fire doors and fire-resistant materials

Bedroom doors are the first barrier that delays fire if it comes from outside. A solid wooden door or one with a fire-resistant core can delay the spread of fire by 30 to 60 minutes more than a hollow door. This is no exaggeration: it is what gives you time to call 112 and for firefighters to arrive in time.

Fire-resistant materials are already included in the construction of new buildings (the DB-SI of the CTE requires it). But in homes built before 2006 they are not always present: a window with no curtains or with thick curtains without fire-retardant treatment, a hollow front door, exposed cables — these are weak points you can fix.

6. Evacuation plan

Passive safety is useless if no one knows what to do when the detector sounds. A three-step evacuation plan:

  1. Get out immediately: do not try to save belongings or check every room. Every second counts.
  2. Meet outside: at a pre-agreed point — the sidewalk in front, the streetlight on the corner — and count everyone. If someone is missing, tell 112 before going back in.
  3. Never go back in: houses burn from the inside and the ceiling can collapse in minutes. Firefighters will go in to look for you.

Write this plan down and stick it near the exits. Practice with the family: have the children run out when the detector alarm sounds, without thinking, like a game. Firefighters recommend it.

Quick investment summary

ItemPriceService lifeProtects against
Smoke detectors (pack of 4)30-50 €10 yearsFire while you sleep, nighttime toxic smoke
ABC extinguisher 6 kg15-25 €5-10 yearsFirst minutes of a real fire
Power strip with fuse10-20 €IndefiniteElectrical overload
Class F kitchen extinguisher15-25 €5-10 yearsGrease and oil fire
Electrical inspection60-120 €Check every 10 yearsFaulty installation

Total investment: 130-235 € for real protection for 10 years. Less than 20 € a year to protect your home and family from the most likely household emergency.

Common mistakes

  • Silencing the detector because of false alarms: if the kitchen sets it off, switch to a heat detector in that location. Do not remove it or cover it with film: that is what most families who suffered fatal fires did in Protección Civil data.
  • Putting the extinguisher in the cupboard under the sink: if the kitchen catches fire, you are not going to open a cupboard full of cleaning products to look for the extinguisher. Put it on the hallway wall.
  • Forgetting the meeting point: an extinguisher without an evacuation plan is like a parachute without knowing at what height to open it.
  • Not checking the extinguisher: a pressure gauge in the red is a decorative extinguisher. Check it once a month, like changing the detector batteries.

Passive safety items are not an extra: they are the foundation of any prepared home. If you do not yet have smoke detectors or an extinguisher, the home kit and the basic 72h kit include these items in their lists. For a complete evacuation plan, read the family emergency plan.

vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.titulo: Dressing in layers: the technique that prevents deadly cold (2026)
vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.resumen: It is not fashion or hiking: it is the recommendation from Health and Civil Protection against hypothermia: the three layers, which fabrics, and why cotton fails.
vestirse-por-capas-ropa-emergencia-frio.cuerpo:
The Ministry of Health's Cold Weather Plan for the 2025-2026 season records that every winter low temperatures cause hundreds of avoidable deaths in Spain. These are not mountain accidents: they are older people in apartments without enough heating, workers walking home in wet clothes, outings that run long when the temperature drops. The most repeated recommendation in official guides is always the same: dress in layers. Not for fashion — for physics.

Why layers and not one thick garment?

The human body loses heat mainly through the skin. Clothing does not generate heat: what it does is trap it. And the best thermal insulator that exists is still air. Three layers of thin fabric trap three air pockets; a single thick garment traps one. This is why Civil Protection and the Ministry of Health repeat literally: 'Bear in mind that several layers of thin clothing protect more than one thick layer, because they form insulating air pockets between them'.

In addition, layers let you adjust your temperature. If you are walking and feel hot, you take off a layer so you don't sweat. If you sweat in a single thick garment and then stop, that wet clothing becomes a body cooler. Cotton cannot handle it: moisture takes you to hypothermia faster than dry cold.

The three layers: function and material

Layer 1: the base layer (next to the skin)

Its only job is to move sweat away from the skin. If the base layer gets wet, nothing you wear over it will save you. The valid options:

  • Merino wool: natural, absorbs moisture without losing heat, smells less than synthetic. Ideal for wearing all day. A 150-200 g merino base-layer shirt costs between €25 and €50.
  • Polypropylene or technical polyester: synthetics move moisture out quickly and dry in hours. They are cheaper (€5-15) but can start to smell sooner and do not regulate temperature as well as wool.

Cotton is never used as a base layer. It absorbs sweat, holds it and stays stuck to the skin. When it gets wet — and it will get wet — it conducts cold like a sheet of water. In mountaineering jargon, cotton is said to 'kill you': it is literally the most dangerous material for cold-weather emergencies. The Ministry of Health and the WHO agree: synthetic fibers and wool are recommended.

Layer 2: insulation (the most important)

This is where real heat is generated. The mid layer traps the air your body warms. The options:

  • Fleece: the king of value for money. Light, warm, quick-drying. A mid-weight fleece costs €15-30 and works for everything: from a night with a power cut to a Sunday walk.
  • Plika (PrimaLoft, Thinsulate, etc.): synthetic insulations that imitate down but work when damp. Ideal if there is a risk of rain. In rain jackets or insulated vests. Price: €20-60.
  • Down: the best insulator by weight, but if it gets wet it loses 90% of its capacity. Good for the kit at home, not for wearing if it rains or you sweat.

For the emergency kit, a fleece is the most versatile option: it works when damp, takes up little space, costs little and covers the widest temperature range.

Layer 3: the barrier (wind and rain)

It protects you from the outside. Without this layer, the wind strips the heat from the inner layers in minutes. It is called a 'shell' in technical jargon.

  • Rain jacket or waterproof shell: with a waterproof membrane (IP ≥ 1500 mm) and sealed seams. The lightweight rain jacket (50-150 g) is so small it fits in any backpack. Price: €15-40 for functional basic models.
  • Rigid (hardshell): if prolonged heavy rain is expected (a DANA in winter, for example). More expensive (€40-80) but lasts years.

The key is for the outer layer to be breathable: if it is not, sweat inside condenses on the inside and you end up wet. Look for 'breathable' or 'breathable membrane'.

What often gets left uncovered: head, hands and feet

Ten percent of official sources forget it, but this is where frostbite and mild hypothermia begin:

  • Hat or scarf: heat is lost through the head. A wool or fleece hat costing €5-12 makes the difference between a mild night and constant shivering. A scarf protects the neck and stops wind getting under your coat.
  • Gloves: mittens are warmer than gloves (fingers share heat). A pair of wool or fleece gloves, €8-20.
  • Socks: two thin pairs work better than one thick pair (another air pocket). Merino wool or synthetic, never cotton. A pair of wool socks for emergencies costs €8-15.
  • Waterproof footwear: wet soles are the fastest entry point for cold. Waterproof boots or, at least, non-slip overshoes (€5-12) if you walk on snow or ice.

The system in practice: what to wear for each scenario

There is no single recipe for all temperatures, but these combinations cover you from a Madrid winter to a snowfall in the Sistema Central:

Approximate temperatureCombinationTotal weight (clothing)
+5 °C to 10 °CBase + rain jacket~300 g
0 °C to +5 °CBase + fleece + rain jacket~700 g
-10 °C to 0 °CBase + fleece + Plika + rain jacket~1 000 g
Below -10 °CDouble base (merino + synthetic) + thick Plika + waterproof parka + gloves + hat + double socks~1 800 g

For a backpack emergency kit, the combination of base + fleece + rain jacket covers most winter scenarios in Spain and weighs less than 1 kg in total.

Signs that something is wrong

The Ministry of Health and the Cold Weather Plan identify clear signs of hypothermia. If you detect them in yourself or another person, adding warm layers is the first step:

  • Uncontrollable shivering: the body tries to generate heat by fighting back. It is no longer uncomfortable; it is an emergency response.
  • Confusion or drowsiness: the brain loses function. The person may deny being cold.
  • Difficulty speaking: words become confused or impossible.
  • Clumsy hands: you cannot do up buttons or light a lighter.

If frostbite appears (white, yellowish, numb and firm skin) — do not rub the area and put it in warm (not hot) water. If you cannot walk on your feet, do not try to walk: you will make the injury worse.

Common mistakes

  • 'A jacket is enough for me': if it rains, if you sweat, if it is windy — it is not enough. A rain jacket on top is the difference between a night at home and a night in the emergency department.
  • Cotton as 'I always wear it': the denim shirt, the thick cotton sweater… they are normal daytime clothing. In an emergency, cotton is your enemy. Wool and synthetics keep you dry.
  • Not covering head and hands: you can have your torso covered and lose 40% of your heat through your head and extremities. A hat and gloves are not optional in extreme cold.
  • Storing warm clothing in the storage room: if the power goes out in January, you need warm clothing where you can grab it in 30 seconds, not where 'you keep the winter stuff'.

What to include in the kit

For each family member, a bag with the basics for layering:

  • Merino wool or synthetic base-layer shirt
  • Mid-weight fleece
  • Lightweight rain jacket
  • Wool or fleece hat
  • Pair of gloves (wool or fleece)
  • Two pairs of wool socks
  • Scarf or thick neckerchief

This weighs less than 2 kg per person, takes up the space of a medium bag, and covers you from a January power cut to an isolated snowfall. If you live in northern or mountain areas, add a pair of Plika (PrimaLoft) layers or a thermal vest.

A fact that is not scary: temperatures are rising

The 2025-2026 winter was, according to AEMET, the sixth warmest winter since 1961. Average temperatures were 1 °C above normal. It is not a one-off: the last eight winters have been warmer than normal. But extreme cold waves do not disappear because of the average: when they come, they come suddenly (like the Arctic air episode that Civil Protection warned about in December 2026) and temperatures can drop 15-20 °C in hours. The layer system works for that sharp drop — the one almost no one is prepared for.

This entry does not replace guidance from a healthcare professional. If you have questions about how to dress for cold due to specific medical conditions (diabetes, vascular problems, medication), consult your doctor. The complete list of materials recommended for winter emergencies is in the warmth and shelter section of the basic 72h kit.

radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.titulo: PMR446 two-way radio: legal, license-free walkie-talkies (2026)
radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.resumen: When mobile networks go down, PMR446 keeps working: license-free, under €40 per pair and legal throughout Spain. How to choose one, according to Civil Protection.
radiocomunicacion-pmr446-walkie-talkies.cuerpo:
28 April 2025 showed what preparedness guides have been repeating for years: when all mobile networks collapse at once, you are left mute. WhatsApp doesn't work, calls don't drop — they simply don't exist. And during a DANA, cell towers can be without power for days. This is where PMR446 radio communication comes in, and why more and more families are including it in their emergency kit.

What is PMR446?

PMR446 (Personal Mobile Radio 446) is a personal-use radio communication service operating in the 446 MHz UHF band (specifically 446.0 to 446.2 MHz). It has been regulated at European level by CEPT (European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations) since 1998 and is fully legal in Spain without a license. There is nothing to process, no fee to pay, no exam to take. Anyone can buy a PMR446 device and use it.

The rules are simple:

  • Maximum power: 0.5 watts (500 mW) — enough for 2-5 km in the city and up to 10 km in open country.
  • Fixed, built-in antenna — you are not allowed to replace it with a larger antenna (that would require a license).
  • 16 channels in the standard band — numbered 1 to 16, plus 8 additional channels if the device supports the digital standard (ECC Decision 05/12).
  • 180-second timeout per transmission — prevents someone from blocking the channel without realizing it.

The key is that it does not depend on any infrastructure: no towers, no carrier, no coverage. Devices communicate directly with each other (simplex mode). If you and your neighbor have PMR446 walkie-talkies, you can hear each other even if the entire network goes down.

Why is it relevant in an emergency?

PMR446 radio communication is the only means of communication between people that requires no infrastructure at all. It does not depend on towers (like a mobile phone), does not depend on the internet (like WhatsApp), and does not depend on electricity (if it runs on batteries or a rechargeable battery). That makes it the missing link between FM radio for listening (receive-only) and the mobile phone (which needs a network).

Protección Civil already knows this: the National Emergency Radio Network (REMER) has relied on amateur radio operators with radio equipment since the 1960s, and the Ministry of the Interior has published specific material on operating emergency communications equipment. In July 2026, the Government went even further: it enabled additional PMR frequencies for regional emergency services, authorizing their use automatically without prior formalities when civil protection teams move between regions. Radio communication is not a hobby: it is critical infrastructure.

What to buy: three honest tiers

You do not need to spend 500 € on firefighter radios. A pair of basic PMR446 radios is enough for family coordination. Here are real options, ordered by budget:

UseModelApprox. priceWhy
Emergency kit (1 pair)Baofeng BF-33C or Retevis RT315-25 € per pairLegal PMR446, USB-C, 16 channels, VOX. For the kit, you don't need more.
Family (4-6 units)Motorola Talkabout T6240-60 € for a pack of 4Reliable brand, display, real range of 3 km in the city. The pack of 4 covers the whole family.
Outdoor / DANAMotorola Talkabout T92 H2O20-30 € per unitIPX4 water-resistant, impact-resistant. If a DANA catches you outdoors, it withstands the rain.
Professional without a licenseKenwood TK-3701D (dPMR446)80-120 € per unitDigital + analog, encryption, rugged. For those who want to step up to professional quality without a license.

Golden rule: buy an odd number of walkie-talkies (3, 5, 7) so that no one is left without someone to talk to. And label each one with its user's name: in chaos, knowing whose device is whose saves seconds that matter.

Channels and sub-tones: the emergency configuration

PMR446 radios have 16 main channels (some models have 32 with the digital standard). Each channel can be configured with a CTCSS sub-tone (privacy code) to filter interference. For emergencies, the recommended configuration is:

  • Channel 7, sub-tone 7: this is the commonly used PMR446 channel for emergencies. Anyone on this frequency can try to make contact without congesting other channels. Use it for the emergency call and for the meeting point.
  • Channel 1, sub-tone 1: family or group communication channel. If your family has 4 walkie-talkies, assign them Channel 1 with sub-tone 1 so you do not mix with other users.
  • Channel 16, no sub-tone: open channel for listening. Useful for monitoring whether someone is talking before you transmit.

And here is the most important communication rule: always check that no one is talking before you press the button. Simultaneous transmissions produce an unintelligible squeal and block the channel. If they don't understand you, repeat. If there is noise, wait 10 seconds and try again.

Real range: what the box says vs. what happens

The box says "10 km" or "20 km". That is with perfect line of sight, at sea, with nothing between the two devices. In reality:

  • In the city (buildings, narrow streets): 0.5-2 km. Concrete walls attenuate the signal a lot.
  • In an open neighborhood or residential development: 2-4 km.
  • In open country: 5-10 km.
  • In the mountains (peak to peak): up to 15-20 km.

The practical rule: height is everything. If you are on a high floor and your neighbor is on another, you can hear each other at 3 km. If you are both in the valley, it already gets difficult at 500 meters. To improve: go up to the terrace or the highest balcony, and point the walkie-talkie vertically (the antenna is omnidirectional but works better vertically).

Typical mistakes

  • Buying walkie-talkies that are not PMR446: many cheap walkie-talkies on Amazon operate on FM or CB bands that require a license. Look explicitly for "PMR446" in the description. If it doesn't say so, don't buy it.
  • Letting the batteries run down: check the batteries every 6 months (the same reminder as for the water in the kit). If they are rechargeable, keep them charged with a power bank or solar charger.
  • Not practicing: a walkie-talkie that is never used is an expensive brick. Test it once a month with a neighbor or family member. You will see whether it works, learn to use it, and know where coverage drops in your area.
  • Listening to what is not yours: on the open channel (Channel 16 with no sub-tone) you will hear other people's conversations. Do not intervene, do not repeat what you hear. You have the right to listen, but not the right to transmit on a frequency that is not yours.
  • Confusing PMR446 with amateur radio: amateur radio requires an exam and a license (HF/VHF/UHF, 10-100 W power, regional/national range). PMR446 does not: it is plug-and-play, with no exam. They are different things.

Integration with your emergency kit

PMR446 walkie-talkies perfectly complement what you already have in the basic kit:

  • FM radio (listen) + PMR446 (talk) = complete two-way information coverage.
  • Spare batteries for the walkie-talkie in the same bag as those for the radio and headlamp.
  • Power bank to charge rechargeable walkie-talkies: a 10,000 mAh power bank charges a PMR446 walkie-talkie about 10 times.
  • Name labels: stick an adhesive label with each user's name on each walkie-talkie. During a night evacuation, knowing whose device is whose is a detail that prevents confusion.

Radio as a habit, not as a purchase

A PMR446 walkie-talkie bought and stored in a cupboard is useless. What works is the habit of using it: test one with your partner, with a neighbor, with your hiking group. You will see that they fall short in the city, that in the mountains they are another matter, and that Channel 7 with sub-tone 7 is the one that will save you if everything else fails. It is a cheap (15-40 € per pair) and legal accessory that, at the right moment, is the only means you have to say "I'm fine" to the person who matters most.

volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.titulo: Returning home after a flood: mud, damp and insurance (2026)
volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.resumen: The worst part of a DANA isn't the water: it's the day you return and smell it. To re-enter without fear, recover without going broke and document for the insurance claim.
volver-a-casa-tras-inundacion.cuerpo:
The days after a flood bring more scares than the flood itself: falls onto hidden debris, electric shocks in water that already seemed to have receded, smoke from damaged electrical installations, poisoning from generators placed in the garage. Returning is a procedure, not an emotion. This is the order, step by step.

Before entering: the checks

  • You only return when official channels authorize it —112, Civil Protection, your local council—. An open building entrance downstairs is not an authorization.
  • Inspection from outside: new cracks, a door that no longer closes as it used to, a sunken floor at the entrance, pillars. Any structural doubt: do not enter, call.
  • Electricity first: turn off the main breaker at the panel only if it is dry and accessible. If the panel is flooded or you are unsure, do not touch it: the utility company or an electrician should turn it off. A building entrance with residual water conducts much better than your common sense believes.
  • Gas: if it smells or the meter moves with everything shut off, get out and call the utility company or 112 from the street. No switches, no lighters, and do not turn on your mobile phone inside.
  • Minimum access equipment: tall boots, thick gloves, a mask against dry mud dust, and decent lighting. The 'wet indoor clothes' mindset won't cut it here.

The first 24 hours inside

  • Photos and videos before touching anything, inside and outside the house, in portrait orientation so the walls are fully included: it is your evidence for the insurance company, and from now on, every moved object will be impossible to justify. If there is no signal, the photos can wait on your phone until you get out: documenting is worth more than saving the half-fallen shelf first.
  • Floodwater is not water: it carries sewage, hydrocarbons and garage chemicals. Anything it touched that is not recoverable, out; food that was in non-hermetic containers too, even if the cardboard looks dry. Personal hygiene items (toothbrushes, baby bottles, opened cosmetics) straight into the bin: it is one of the few rules without exception.
  • Mud: remove, do not scrub. First remove layers with a shovel, ideally when it is dry; scrubbing fresh mud only spreads an impossible film. And ventilation from minute one: cross-ventilation as soon as the weather allows.
  • Do not plug in wet appliances to see if they still work. They are dried, recorded and assessed: the short circuit when you plug them back in is a story repeated in every DANA.
  • Mattresses, sofas, particleboard wardrobes, plasterboard: the non-recoverable items. They absorb dirty water and never dry out: mold guaranteed in 48 hours. The health of the house is worth more than the furniture: out the door.

Damp: the battle of the next three weeks

The house seems dry on Saturday and is soaked for the whole month, and mold is the second disaster of every flood:

  • Constant ventilation: a permanent window gap works better than opening for half an hour a day; and if you can rent or borrow dehumidifiers on the first day, they shorten weeks of misery. In homes with a basement, the basement rules: the air there does not move by itself.
  • Before replacing what was on the walls (paint, skirting boards, fitted furniture), check by touch —or with a cheap pin moisture meter— that the base material is really dry. Trapping water behind a new wall is sowing the problem for next spring.
  • The most sensitive people (asthma, allergies, babies, older adults) are the first to pay for mold. If someone starts coughing or itching and the house is still damp, discuss with a health professional not sleeping there yet: it is a health criterion, not a patience one.

Insurance: it is won on day one, not in month one

  • Report the claim to the insurance company on the same day you return, with the date, cause —flood, the exact word matters— and a stable contact phone number if your line is down. Keep a written copy: the file lives where you wrote it.
  • Evidence rules: photos from now with a full walkthrough, a list of damaged goods with model and approximate date, invoices where you have them (many are in your online store email: look for them calmly on a Sunday). And dig through your phone: photos from Christmas in your living room prove water levels and the existence of belongings better than any account.
  • Emergency repairs: yes, but documented. Boarding up a broken window or cutting off a damaged line is your duty to prevent further damage and is usually covered: keep receipts and quotes for the loss adjuster, and do not wait for them to arrive before securing the house.
  • If the home is rented, report the damage the same day and in writing to the landlord, with photos: who is responsible for what under the contract is much clearer with a date on the email.
  • And if your home falls within an area eligible for extraordinary public aid, ask at the local council about the registration and damage certificate that open the door: in every DANA, aid deadlines are missed because no one asked for a form in the first week.

The cheap lesson (and the most expensive to learn)

Every DANA leaves homes that flood the ground floor for the second time six years apart. The lesson: in a flood-prone area, what matters lives upstairs, and the electrical panel too if possible. Insurance is the patch, not the plan. Before signing a mortgage or lease, ask for the risk mapping at the local council or the river basin authority; and if you are already in one, adapt the DANA kit to your real story, not the fear of the moment.

The re-entry checks and access equipment are in the DANA/flood kit; the documentation you will need for insurance travels with the evacuation backpack and the original is kept in the home kit.
