vivir-solo-estar-preparado.titulo: Living alone and being prepared: kit and support network (2026)
vivir-solo-estar-preparado.resumen: Living alone: you decide, but if something happens to you, no one knocks on your door at six in the morning. The kit, contacts and alerts for one person, designed for one.
vivir-solo-estar-preparado.cuerpo:
More and more Spanish households have a single occupant, and emergency preparedness has almost always been written for families. Living alone changes two things: everything you need is smaller and cheaper, and almost everything depends on one head —yours— even when that head has a fever or is in shock. This is the plan for one.

The advantage: a kit that fits in a corner

One person, one backpack: 70-100 euros starting from zero, much less if you use what you already have. Nine liters of water for the 72 hours, a first aid kit for one body, radio, headlamp, powerbank, the folder with your papers and that's it. No shifts or shared dosages: the whole plan is as big as your backpack. In exchange it demands a standard: if something depends on you being well to work, it has to be charged, tested and at hand. There is no second pilot here.

The real weak point: no one finds it odd that you don't answer

In a family, if someone falls in the bathroom, someone hears it. Living alone, the enemy is not just the DANA: it's the blow, appendicitis at three in the morning, the fall on the stairs with the phone at 2% and in your coat pocket. That's why the personal plan doesn't start with water: it starts with the chain of whoever asks:

  • The contact ritual: a daily or every-other-day message with someone who notices your absence —a friend, a sibling, the neighbor on the 3rd floor—. A hello at nine, made into a protocol. If one day it doesn't arrive, they call; if the second time you don't answer, they come or alert emergency services. It isn't emotional dependence: it's a protocol with a name and a time.
  • Keys in trusted hands: a copy in the home of someone in that chain, so they can open up if they need to get in quickly, and not under the mat. Without this, the first response to a serious suspicion is a firefighter breaking down your door: it works, but it takes time and costs money.
  • Your phone working: the phone's SOS/emergency set up with contacts, medical data and medical ID; and if it suits you, a watch with fall detection. They aren't toys: they're insurance for your own phone. Set them up today, because on the day of the blow no one remembers menus.
  • The card that speaks for you: a card with data, allergies, treatment and who to notify, in your DNI wallet and another behind the door of your home. When you can't speak, your papers speak — and the ones inside help whoever comes in to look for you.

The kit for one: what changes compared with the family one

  • Food is simplified: a single ration per day and no menus for three ages. Canned pulses, tuna, oats, and preserves you really like: what you don't fancy on a normal Tuesday you won't fancy on a Thursday of a blackout.
  • Critical items are doubled: in a family devices are shared; alone, if you run out of battery there's no spare phone in the drawer. Two light sources, plenty of batteries, and a powerbank with a cable compatible with all your things.
  • Your medication is the heart of the kit: a margin of weeks, a treatment sheet in the folder and a reserve travelling in the backpack. If you share care with your mother or your children from another home, apply the same system on both sides.
  • An extra that only you need: morale. Periods confined alone have a real component of anxiety that no catalogue covers: leave a small speaker, a book, whatever anchors you in the kit. The long day is more likely than the dangerous day, and it can also be managed.

Neighbors: your proximity insurance

In ninety percent of serious domestic incidents resolved in a building entrance, the first to arrive isn't 112: it's someone from the landing. Two fifteen-minute gestures are worth more than any gadget: setting up a small chat group for the stairwell or building entrance (the real neighbors, not the whole building) and locating the other people who live alone, older people included. The network that protects you is exactly the one you also protect: in a snowfall, a heatwave or a night-time blackout, the first check that saves lives is going up or down to ask. Protección Civil self-protection guides have had this idea at the center for years; those of us who live alone are the ones who get the most out of it.

What only happens when you decide alone

Living alone has a specific temptation: believing it isn't necessary, that you'll manage. You'll manage until the day you don't. And another: accumulating clutter instead of preparing decisions. The honest test is short: if you were evacuated tonight, do you know in five minutes what you'd take, who you'd message and where you'd sleep? If the answer is a shrug, you have a full kit and an empty plan. And the plan, this time, depends only on you.

The lists adjusted to a single body are in the home kit and its compact version, the basic 72h kit. And if you drive, check the car kit: for anyone living alone, the car is at once transport, shelter and phone.

plan-familiar-de-emergencia.titulo: Family emergency plan: meeting point and drill (2026)
plan-familiar-de-emergencia.resumen: Two families, the same warning, opposite outcomes: one was reunited in two hours, the other took three days. The difference wasn't the backpack: it was the plan.
plan-familiar-de-emergencia.cuerpo:
Every real emergency reveals the same thing: those who had a family plan move, and those who didn't improvise with their hearts racing. A plan isn't a document: it's four decisions made in advance and known to everyone, including the people who don't live with you every day (grandma, the father who does Friday pickup). It takes an afternoon to build and a review every six months to keep up.

1. The meeting point, on two levels

  • Neighborhood level (immediate): a specific, visible place within walking distance for an evacuation of the building or street: the fountain in the square, the gas station on the way out, the bar on the corner. Don't say the square: say the fountain. In chaos, vague meeting points separate people more than they bring them together.
  • City level (if the first one no longer exists): a second point outside your area for when the neighborhood gets cut off: a relative's home at another address, a station, a place everyone has heard of. And a simple rule: if no one reaches point 1 within an hour, we all go to point 2.
  • The school has its own protocol for handing children over to families: ask where they would hand them over before the day you need it, and that point goes on your map. It's the detail no one remembers to ask for.

2. The beacon: your out-of-area contact

When the network is overloaded, local calls get stuck and a twenty-character SMS gets through where a conversation won't. Hence the classic civil protection technique: designate someone who lives far away —another region, ideally another country— as the message hub. Everyone writes to the beacon where they are and how they are; the beacon sends back the full picture: your sister is okay at a friend's house, your father isn't answering his phone but sent an SMS at 9:12. One person coordinating from outside is worth ten improvising inside. And the beacon must know how to be a beacon: takes notes and doesn't judge, and doesn't raise the alarm in the first hours of silence, because every emergency has normal silences.

3. Roles: who acts when no one is making good decisions

In a scare, you don't think: you execute what you've practiced. Assign the four typical tasks, with a named person and a backup (if the assigned person isn't home, the role can't disappear with them):

  • Children and pets: the person who physically picks them up and gets them out. With a baby at home, two people: one carries the child, the other carries the child's bag.
  • Utilities and door: the person who shuts off the gas if it smells, turns off the water if there's flooding, disconnects what can be reached and locks up on the way out. If there's no time, you leave: no house is worth half a minute inside with the alert sounding.
  • Kit and documents: the person who grabs the backpack and the folder, both on the way out, never in the storage room at the back.
  • Information: the person who turns on the radio and checks the official warning (112, civil protection), with the house rule written down: no messaging rumor is shared within the family without an official source. That rule prevents more disasters than you imagine.

4. The three rules that replace all the communication you won't have

The plan has to work without network and without battery, on paper:

  • Silence rule: if there's no contact within X hours, we all assume we're at the meeting point (or at the beacon's home if the neighborhood is cut off), and no one searches for anyone across a city in chaos. Searching on your own is a different risk, and often greater than waiting where the plan says.
  • School rule: if you can't come for the children, they stay with the teachers and the school's protocol takes over. The children know it by heart and the adults don't betray it by going to pick them up on their own: disrupting a school's dismissal puts the whole group at risk, including yours.
  • Return rule: you go home when the official channels say so, not when the guy in the building across the street says it's okay now. Every DANA has its story of a premature return told in the garage.

The drill: a Tuesday night, twenty minutes

An undrilled plan is just a piece of paper on the fridge. Make the review part of your seasonal wardrobe change, twice a year:

  • Everyone says their part from memory: my point, my role, the beacon's number. Whoever gets it wrong listens; no scolding, just repeat it.
  • Timed evacuation drill: backpacks, folder, shoes on, out on the street in under ten minutes. That's where the failures no document reveals come out: the key that wasn't where you thought, the zipper that won't close with a coat caught in it, the child who can't find their shoes in the dark.
  • Equipment check: expiry dates, batteries, the small amount of cash in the folder, that the children's kit headlamp turns on, that the ID card is still inside the older child's jacket.
  • Updating what changes: grandparents' new contacts, trusted neighbors who moved, school routines. The plan ages because the family changes.

And a trick that works: during drills, the children hold the stopwatch and keep score. What at seven is a game with scores is still in their heads at twelve on the day it really goes off.

The backpacks that put this plan into practice are broken down in the evacuation guide, and the common contents for the 72 hours, in the basic kit. If there are older people in your network, link their part with the guide for older people and dependents.

medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.titulo: Chronic medication without a pharmacy: 2-4 weeks secured (2026)
medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.resumen: If someone depends on daily treatment, blackouts or a DANA don't wait for restocking: the logistics to avoid running out, with no medical advice.
medicion-cronica-personas-dependientes.cuerpo:
A typical emergency lasts 72 hours; a rare one, weeks. For a household with chronic treatment, the problem is not the scare of day one: it is day eight, when the box you had left runs out and your neighborhood pharmacy is closed or flooded. What follows is pure logistics: paperwork, reserves and rotation so that dependency does not turn into an emergency. What to take and how much is decided by each person with their doctor or pharmacist; none of that is touched here.

Step 0: the inventory you still haven't done

Open the medication drawer and make a list for every member of the household. Without a list there is no plan: it is the equivalent of not knowing how much water is left after the supply has already been cut off.

  • The treatment name exactly as it appears on the box (not the family nickname), the regimen indicated by the professional and which full boxes remain at home.
  • Date of the last prescription and where it is renewed: primary care doctor, specialist or the specific pharmacy if it is a compounded product.
  • What consequences an interruption has: the prescriber tells you that, so ask at the next review and write it down. Missing one day is not the same as a week without treatment, and it is better to know that beforehand, not during.
  • How each item is stored: some treatments suffer in summer heat or need a refrigerator, and a July blackout turns the fridge being off into a countdown.

The 2-4 week reserve, without overbuying

The buffer is built with a system that pharmacies and primary care know, and that you only have to ask for:

  • Rotation, not stockpiling: collect each refill as far in advance as the system allows and use the reserve at home, so there is always margin without accumulating expiry dates. The exact mechanics depend on your treatment: discuss them with your pharmacy.
  • Never open extra packages or keep leftovers from other people: the reserve is your own treatment, in its box, with its date. Swapping pills among family members is a direct route to a dosing error.
  • One week traveling in the evacuation backpack: if your area is evacuated, the reserve in the drawer stays in a building you may not be able to enter for days. What leaves with you decides how you are on Thursday.
  • Support consumables (blood glucose strips, wound care supplies, catheters, ostomy bags, CPAP masks): they are restocked monthly and in a crisis they run out before medicines do. Ask your reference nurse for a reasonable figure for your case; do not improvise the number yourself.

Fragile chains: cold, electricity and memory

Some dependencies are not solved with boxes in a cupboard:

  • What needs a refrigerator: a closed fridge that is opened little stays cool for 24 to 48 hours; with frozen water bottles as blocks, a little longer. If it drags on, ask your pharmacy which products can tolerate a short time out of the cold and which cannot: each one is different, and the professional says so with the leaflet in front of them.
  • What needs electricity (oxygen concentrators, ventilators, pumps): here the reserve is energy. A power bank compatible with the device, a spare battery and notifying your electricity company and your regional Protección Civil: many keep registers of customers dependent on life-sustaining equipment to warn them and prioritize their supply during long outages. Ask whether your case is registered, because you do not get on it automatically.
  • People with cognitive impairment: the risk is not only the pill; it is that routine breaks and the person stops eating, drinking or taking what they should without realizing it. Stable schedules, the regimen written in large print and an identification sheet with contacts: in chaos, a disoriented older person without information attached is the worst case a rescue team can manage.

The treatment sheet: a single page that fixes almost everything

A laminated sheet in the emergency folder and a photocopy in the backpack:

  • Full name, date of birth and phone number of the person receiving care and of the person caring for them.
  • Active treatments with the regimen written by the professional, and what each one is for: that way whoever covers for you one day understands it.
  • Contacts: who prescribes, reference nurse, usual pharmacy, health center, responsible family member.
  • Allergies and intolerances, and their own warning signs that require seeking medical help without hesitation.
  • Update date at the top: every medical review is a pass through this sheet. A paper from two years ago is worse than none: it gives false confidence.

The drill almost no one does

Once a year, with the list in front of you: expiry dates, device batteries, intact waterproof case, a real reserve in the backpack and not just in discussion. And if care is shared among several people — siblings, children who live far away, home help —, roles in writing: who grabs the backpack, who takes the person, who notifies the center. Shared care without a plan fails precisely on the day when everyone thought it was the other person's turn.

Caregiver logistics are developed in the guide for older people and dependent persons, and the medication reserve fits into the medicine cabinet of the home kit. If your dependency is energy-related, review the blackout kit before next summer.

kit-emergencia-50-euros.titulo: Emergency kit for 50 €: almost everything is already at home (2026)
kit-emergencia-50-euros.resumen: You don't need 150 euros or a storage room: with 50 € and an afternoon of digging things out, any household can cover 72 hours on its own. Minimum budget and common mistakes.
kit-emergencia-50-euros.cuerpo:
The European recommendation of 72 hours of self-sufficiency sounds like a big purchase: tactical backpack, water containers, military rations, radio transmitter. False. Useful minimum preparedness fits in 50 euros because 80% is already in your home and you don't know it. The method has three moves: first scour what you have, then buy only what's needed, finally organise. It's not stinginess: a kit bought all at once and without habit dies in a cupboard; one built from what you already use survives.

Scavenging afternoon: what you have and weren't counting on

Before going to the checkout, go around the house with a cardboard box and a notebook:

  • Water: look at this week's shopping. The bottles you drink every day are reserve as soon as you create the habit of buying two extra and rotating them: the old one runs out, the new one comes in. A family of three accumulates the 27 litres for 72 hours without buying a single large bottle, in closed containers and in a dark place.
  • Food: the usual pantry of a Spanish household —rice, pasta, canned pulses, tuna, tomato sauce, nuts, biscuits— is already an emergency diet without fire, except what requires cooking. Separate what can be eaten opened and uncooked: that is your kit, nothing else.
  • Light: the hiking headlamp, the flashlight in the drawer, the birthday candles, the bike light. Every home has more lights than it thinks; the problem is that they are scattered and without batteries. Collect, group and test them all in one afternoon.
  • Means to boil: any saucepan on a camping stove, or the gas hob if the power went out rather than the butane. With fire, doubtful water becomes safe and the shopping list changes size.
  • Radio: the old transistor radio in the drawer has its uses, but here it usually pays to buy: a new battery-powered AM/FM radio costs 12-15 euros and is the difference between knowing what is happening and trusting the building's WhatsApp group.
  • Transport: the school backpack, the gym bag, the shopping trolley. A large bin bag as an outer cover acts as a waterproof for zero euros.

The 50 euros: what order to spend it in

On top of the scavenged base, the purchases that give the most self-sufficiency per euro, in order:

  • Battery-powered AM/FM radio (12-15 €): information is the first thing missing in a blackout and the hardest to improvise.
  • Batteries for the whole set (8-10 €): the models you actually use, with some in the backpack and some in the drawer at home.
  • Headlamp with its own batteries (6-8 €): it leaves your hands free, which is literally what you need when carrying a child or closing a backpack in the rain.
  • Water purification tablets (8-12 €): insurance for when the bottles run out; they take up the space of a coin and last for years.
  • Wound-care first-aid kit (8-10 €): gauze, adhesive tape, antiseptic, gloves, thermometer. Medication is what your home already uses, with advice from your pharmacist.
  • Waterproof document pouch (5 €) and a USB drive (3 €): scanned documents, a copy at another address, a small amount of cash in 10 and 20 euro notes.

If you go five euros over, cut brands or look in the discount store: you'll still get there. And look at what is not on the list: no military rations, no rescue knife, no walkie-talkies, no filter bottle. None of that deserves the first euro.

What is free and worth more than what you buy

  • The rotation habit: water, food and batteries are bought to be used up, not stockpiled. Without rotation, in a year you will have an expired kit and a sense of duty fulfilled.
  • The twenty-minute conversation: decide where the kit sleeps (a known place, at hand height, on the way to the door) and who does what if you have to leave. Protección Civil publishes the action guide in its official recommendations; that guide only lacks your family's names.
  • The six-monthly review: one alarm on 1 January and another on 1 July. Fifteen minutes, everything checked.
  • Critical phone numbers on paper: 112, health centre, pharmacy, two contacts outside the city. With the mobile at 1%, a pen saves everything.

What this method does not cover (and it is good that you know it)

The 50-euro kit handles the classic 72 hours: short blackout, water cut, storm, a one-night evacuation. It falls short in a long winter without heating, in a home with a baby, with chronic treatment, or in an isolated home with no neighbours. Those scenarios call for more investment and more planning: not because the cheap kit is bad, but because the EU recommendation is a floor, not a ceiling. When it is time to grow, you grow on what you already have: money spent on method is not wasted, it is completed.

For the step up in quality, the 72h basic kit list separates essentials from accessories, and the blackout kit adds exactly what this budget leaves out: power and cooking without electricity.

comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.titulo: What to eat if the power goes out: 3-day menus without cooking (2026)
comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.resumen: Ninety hours with the fridge off and the hob dead: order of consumption, day-by-day menus and the mistakes that send half your groceries to the bin.
comer-sin-luz-menus-3-dias.cuerpo:
28 April 2025 proved something that kit guides only tell half the story about: the problem with a long blackout isn't having food, it's having a full fridge turned into a countdown. Cooking without electricity can be improvised; managing what spoils cannot. Here are three days covered: order of consumption, menus and the shopping that closes the loop.

The two rules that govern everything else

  • A closed fridge is your friend for the first 24-48 hours: a modern, well-stocked fridge that isn't opened keeps food in the safe cool range for a day and a half; a full freezer, longer. Every opening uses up time: decide each morning what you're going to eat and take it out all at once. And when you open it, keep your nose alert: anything that smells or looks odd goes in the bin. Food poisoning in the middle of a crisis is the last thing you need, and that's one area where no amount of bravery helps.
  • No cooking doesn't mean no plan: easy-open cans, sliced bread, thick-skinned fruit, nuts, bars, biscuits, vacuum-packed cured meat, hard cheese, chocolate. Fresh food that depends on refrigeration is eaten in order: that's the core of this plan.

The order of consumption: first what spoils fastest

  • First 6-12 hours: whatever was already open or gets opened — yogurt, desserts, the tub from the fridge, bagged salad, the milk you've started, the opened packet of cold cuts. If the outage is announced in advance, this batch moves up to that night's dinner: it's time for a fridge party.
  • Day 1: unopened fresh food that needs cold — meat, fish, dairy close to its date — and only if you have somewhere to cook it: a camping stove, a gas burner, an outdoor barbecue (never indoors: carbon monoxide, the silent killer of every storm). Without a gas stove, share this batch with neighbors who have one or accept the loss: don't eat questionable fish out of pride.
  • Days 2 and 3 onward: pantry only — canned food, canned pulses, bread, packaged pancakes, sturdy fruit, carton vegetable soup, cocoa powder that holds up with water. The fridge is now a decorative cupboard: treat it as one.

Three days of menus (two adults, no hob or microwave)

Day 1 — Breakfast: sliced bread with peanut butter and fruit. Lunch: pantry salad — canned chickpeas, tuna, tomato that has held up, a splash of oil — and fruit. Dinner: the fresh batch turned into a board of cured cheeses, vacuum-packed cold cuts and breadsticks: the dinner that in a normal home is called nibbles and here is called the plan.

Day 2 — Breakfast: packaged pancakes or biscuits, a bar for anyone who isn't hungry when they get up. Lunch: canned pulses dressed with tuna belly: serve it cold and nobody will look at it strangely. Dinner: canned vegetable soup or gazpacho, which kept at room temperature while sealed and passes for a hot dish without being one.

Day 3 — Breakfast: the last of the dairy, which would go off from lack of cold today anyway. Lunch: pasta you boiled extra on Day 1 with the camping stove, warmed through with oil and canned food; or sardines with bread if there wasn't enough water to boil. Dinner: back-of-the-cupboard — bars, nuts, chocolate and a can of bonito with peppers: the classic camping dinner.

Notice the thread running through the three days: no meal depends on a single type of food. If the bread runs out, the cans are still there; and once a large can is opened, there's no fridge for the half that's left: eat it all in that meal or don't open it. In a blackout there are no leftovers: there are decisions.

The 40-60 euros shopping list that makes all this edible

  • Camping stove with two or three cartridges (15-20 € for the set): makes boiling pasta, rice or water whenever you're unsure feel normal. And two spare butane cylinders: if the power grid is down, the gas hob at home works — the electric hob doesn't, the flame does.
  • Water for drinking and for rehydrating dried food: always part of the budget.
  • Manual can opener: the most forgotten item in a food kit and the one that leaves the most cans unopened on the shelf.
  • Tableware you don't have to wash: a cup, plate and cutlery per person — getting through the day is also about managing the water you won't use at the sink.
  • Heavy-duty waste bags: everything that spoils gets bagged and out of the house quickly. A fridge rotting in the middle of July turns your kitchen into a two-week problem.

Mistakes that waste half your shopping

Storing your emergency supplies next to bleach (the fumes contaminate even sealed packaging). Opening the large can with tomorrow in mind. Trusting smell as the only judge with milk that's been out for two days: when in doubt, out, no debate. And discovering on day one that every can in the drawer needs a can opener that's at your mother's house. These four mistakes, plus opening the fridge out of curiosity, explain 90% of the meals lost on 28 April.

The emergency supplies for this scenario are put together in the blackout kit — stove, water, food that doesn't need refrigeration — and scaled up in the 30-day kit if you want a proper pantry. The basics of food preservation are on the AESAN website.

bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.titulo: Babies and children in an emergency: checklist by age 0-3 and 4-12 (2026)
bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.resumen: A kit designed for adults leaves out the people who depend on you most: what a baby needs and what a child aged 4 to 12 needs, without the stress and with good judgment.
bebes-ninos-emergencia-checklist-edades.cuerpo:
The European Union Preparedness Strategy talks about households with 72 hours of self-sufficiency, but standard lists are written for healthy adults. A baby doesn't eat tinned fabada, doesn't drink from a five-litre water container and doesn't understand why tonight we're sleeping in the hallway with torches. Preparing a household with small children isn't about buying more: it's about buying differently and distributing responsibilities according to age.

Before the backpack: the three questions

With a child at home, the plan rests on three decisions that are best made now, calmly, not the day the alarm sounds:

  • Who picks up each child if you have to leave at three in the morning. If there are two adults, one takes the baby and the other takes the backpacks and the older child. If you live alone, the order is: children first, kit afterwards; and if the kit doesn't fit, you leave without it.
  • Where the meeting point is if you pick the children up from school and can't stop by home. Schools have protocolised meeting points: ask at the school which one is theirs and don't improvise it on the day of the alert.
  • What specific needs each child has (inhalers, special diet, allergies) and where it is written down. Clinical matters are set by the paediatrician or school nurse; you just copy them into the emergency folder.

0 to 3 years: the kit for what can't be improvised

In this age range everything depends on you: food, water, temperature, comfort. The child kit travels in a separate bag inside the evacuation backpack:

  • Extra water for preparing bottles: the 3 litres per person are not enough with a formula-fed infant. With breastfeeding there's no need to stock milk, only for the mother to drink more.
  • Formula and baby food that they already take, never new brands: an emergency is not the day to experiment with an eight-month-old's gut. Individual doses or small jars are better than a large tin that spoils once opened without a fridge.
  • Nappies for 72 hours, in their current size and one size up if you're between sizes. Allow 6–8 a day: with nerves, intestines get unsettled.
  • Wipes, a changing mat for changing on any floor, barrier cream and small bags for dirty nappies: during an evacuation there's no bin to hand.
  • A comfort object: the soft toy, the blanket, the teething ring. It sounds soft and it's one of the most practical things in the kit: a comforted two-year-old is a child who walks if you have to leave; a child in panic is an extra person to carry.
  • Double change of clothes and a change suited to the actual weather of the week you're reading this, not the summer when you filled the bag.

4 to 12 years: from luggage to be carried to a team that trains

From the age of four, the child goes from being a load to being part of the team. The difference between a chaotic and an orderly evacuation at this age is called habit:

  • Their own backpack, sized to them: not the full kit, but what they can carry (5–10% of their body weight): their small bottle, a headlamp they know how to turn on in the dark, biscuits, their jumper and their toy. Let them pack it: what a child puts away, they can find.
  • Name, surname and your phone number sewn inside the jacket and on a card in the pocket. If you are separated during an evacuation, a sewn-in detail doesn't fail or fall off: it's the only thing that works without memory or a wristband.
  • Rules rehearsed as a game: if the alert sounds, I don't hide, I wait for an adult, I don't go down the stairs alone and I count my family out loud. Two practice runs a year, like the school drill.
  • The truth, according to age: at 5 you don't tell them about the catastrophe, you say that tonight the house is camping; at 10 you explain the whole plan. Children cope better with fear if they know what will happen next.
  • Real occupation for 72 hours without screens: card decks, comics, a notebook and pencils. Boredom on day one is anxiety on day two: plan it as you plan food.

What is always forgotten

  • The fridge poster with the plan: meeting point, out-of-area contact, 112. Hung at their eye level, so the older child can read it alone.
  • The vaccination record and allergy report, copied into the emergency folder: if the child ends up at a care point, that sheet is worth more than any rushed explanation.
  • That children eat and drink less under stress: offer water often, in small amounts, without forcing meals. If they don't urinate normally or are listless, seek medical advice without waiting.
  • Transport: the folding pushchair takes up space and saves kilometres with a small child; and the car seat does not stay at home no matter how rushed you are in the car.

The ten-minute test

Before you sign off on the plan, do the count with the door closed: can you leave your house with two children, backpacks and folder in under ten minutes without coming back for anything? If the answer is no, remove things from the kit, don't add more reflexes. The folder and backpacks, together and on the way to the door, not in the cupboard at the back.

The site's baby emergency bag includes the closed list for the 0–3 range, and the evacuation backpack explains how to distribute weight between adults and children. When the little ones already eat on their own, add the basic 72h kit for the whole family.

temperatura-sin-electricidad.titulo: Cold and heat without electricity: safe temperature at home (2026)
temperatura-sin-electricidad.resumen: Hypothermia and heat stroke kill indoors more than you think. Insulation and cooling techniques that work without a single watt.
temperatura-sin-electricidad.cuerpo:
In a January blackout, the enemy isn't the darkness: it's the accumulated cold. In a heatwave with no air conditioning, it's dehydration. Both problems can be solved with cheap materials and a little physics.

Keeping the heat in

  • Choose one room and close it off: less volume to heat (or to keep warm). Small, interior rooms hold their temperature better.
  • Insulate from below: the floor steals more heat than you think. Rugs, blankets or cardboard underfoot.
  • Layering clothes works better than one thick garment: the air trapped between layers is the real insulator.
  • The emergency thermal blanket (the gold ones for 2 €) reflects body heat; it works better inside a normal blanket, not on its own.
  • A tent indoors: it sounds absurd, but a small tent in the living room creates a microclimate that raises the temperature by several degrees. Mountaineers have always done it.
  • If you use a butane heater or embers, ventilate: carbon monoxide kills without smelling of anything. Never in a closed bedroom.

Cooling down

  • Cross-ventilation at dawn and at night; windows closed and blinds down during the day. The golden rule: open up when it's cooler outside than inside, close when it isn't.
  • Moisten the air and get it moving: a damp sheet in front of the window or a spray bottle with any breeze lowers the perceived temperature by several degrees.
  • Cool the key points: wrists, nape of the neck, neck and ankles. Cold water on those pulse points cools the blood faster than soaking your whole body.
  • Drink before you're thirsty and avoid alcohol and heavy meals; the body heats up as it digests.

Warning signs

Uncontrollable shivering, confusion or drowsiness (hypothermia); hot, dry skin with no sweating, severe headache or vomiting (heat stroke): these are medical emergencies. Call 112 as soon as possible.

The gear is in the heatwave and home guides; the heater and the tent, in the 30-day kit.

recursos-oficiales-emergencia.titulo: The 7 official resources to keep on your phone and on paper (2026)
recursos-oficiales-emergencia.resumen: In an emergency, the right information is worth more than any backpack: Spain's official channels that work when everything else fails.
recursos-oficiales-emergencia.cuerpo:
In a crisis, the difference between acting well and acting late is having the right source at hand. And distrusting everything else: during the 2025 blackout dozens of hoaxes circulated. Save these seven channels now — in your phone's favourites and, better still, written down on paper in your emergency folder.

The 7 essentials

  • 112: emergencies throughout the EU, free, no credit needed, and it works even if your carrier has no coverage. Save it, but also know the number by heart.
  • AlertCops (official app of the Ministry of the Interior): public safety alerts and geolocated emergencies in your area. Download it now; during a crisis app stores fail too.
  • AEMET (aemet.es and its app): weather warnings by province. In a DANA, the AEMET red warning arrives hours before the water does.
  • Protección Civil (proteccioncivil.es): self-preparedness guides by risk type and, in a crisis, behavioural recommendations. It is the source from which this website's lists are drawn.
  • DGT Traffic (official app and Twitter/X): road conditions, closures and diversions in real time — essential if you have to move or evacuate.
  • Bulletin and FM radio: a battery-powered radio tuned to national and regional stations is the only medium that survives a total network collapse.
  • Your town hall and autonomous community: every municipality has its emergency plan and its channels (regional 112, municipal alerts). Find them now, not when the siren sounds.

On paper, because phones die

Write down in your folder: 112, the Protección Civil phone number for your municipality, your health centre, two contacts outside your area, and your home insurance policy number. Half a page in handwriting that works with your phone at 0%.

This website only links to official sources; you can see them all on the Official sources page, and the shopping lists derived from them in the kits.

montana-kit-salvavidas.titulo: Emergency mountain kit: 15 items that really matter (2026)
montana-kit-salvavidas.resumen: What to carry and what not to promise: a realistic list for hiking and the mountains, with a first-aid kit, communication, water and the signs that it's time to call for help.
montana-kit-salvavidas.cuerpo:
Many mountain rescues don't start with a technical climb: they start with a hiking route that runs long, fog that arrives earlier than forecast, a sprain that makes walking impossible, or a colder night than the forecast predicted. In 2024, the Guardia Civil's GREIM in Aragon carried out 609 interventions and assisted 942 people, of whom 462 were injured and 25 died, according to the Government Delegation in Aragon. Not all would have been avoided with a better backpack, but carrying the essentials and knowing how to use them reduces the margin for error.

The three that matter most when the weather worsens

Hypothermia isn't only a snow or high-mountain problem. The CDC notes that it can occur at relatively mild temperatures if clothing is wet and there is wind. Heat loss increases with wet clothing and wind exposure; wind chill isn't a universal figure for heat lost, but a way to express how cold you feel. These three items cover the basics:

  • Emergency thermal blanket: it doesn't generate heat. What it does is reflect some of your body heat and serve as a barrier against wind and rain if used wrapped around you and dry. It weighs very little (light models are around 30-60 g) and takes up less space than a phone. It doesn't replace dry clothing or a tent, but it can help while rescue arrives. See thermal blankets on Amazon ↗
  • Rain jacket or waterproof poncho: a windproof and waterproof layer keeps clothing from getting wet and prevents wind from cooling your skin. An emergency poncho weighs 50-150 g depending on the model. It isn't the same as a technical jacket, but it fits in any backpack and can make a difference during a wait. See emergency ponchos on Amazon ↗
  • LED headlamp with spare batteries: running out of light turns a two-hour walk into a whole night. A headlamp leaves your hands free to walk, eat, or signal. Runtime depends on the model and power mode: carry spare batteries and test the headlamp before you set out. See LED headlamps on Amazon ↗

The mountain first-aid kit: it's not the one from home

A first-aid kit doesn't replace training. If you go out often, take a basic first-aid course and learn how to respond to bleeding, a sprain, and an allergic reaction. For day-to-day use, a light first-aid kit should cover:

  • Waterproof adhesive bandages, sterile gauze, and medical tape: cleaning and covering a wound prevents friction and dirt from making it worse. Also carry nitrile gloves.
  • Elastic bandage and compression bandage: for an ankle or knee sprain, temporary immobilization helps you retreat. Don't tighten until you cut off circulation; if the fingers turn cold or purple, loosen it.
  • Sunscreen and SPF lip balm: ultraviolet radiation increases with altitude, and snow reflects some of it. Use a high factor and reapply; a burn isn't noticeable until it's already done.
  • Personal medication, only as prescribed: if you have severe allergies, asthma, or diabetes, carry your medication and treatment plan. An antihistamine doesn't treat anaphylaxis; if your doctor has prescribed auto-injectable adrenaline, carry it and learn how to use it. Don't improvise doses or carry medications you don't know how to use.

For cuts that bleed heavily, the first measure is direct pressure with clean gauze. A tourniquet should only be used by someone who knows how to do it and when bleeding isn't controlled; don't improvise one for a minor wound. The basic 72h kit guide has the home first-aid kit; this is the one that goes with you in your backpack.

Communication: a mobile phone isn't always enough

In valleys, gorges, and mountain areas, coverage can disappear. A mobile phone is still the first tool for calling 112, but you shouldn't rely on it alone. Before setting out, check that you have battery, an offline map app, and the emergency number at hand. If there's no coverage, your exact location and message may have to wait.

  • Emergency whistle: the international mountain distress signal is six signals per minute (whistles or flashes), with a one-minute pause, then repeat; it is not three whistles, it is six. It isn't the only signal and doesn't replace 112, but it carries farther than your voice and uses no energy. See emergency whistles on Amazon ↗
  • 5,000-10,000 mAh power bank: keeps your phone on a little longer, but the number of recharges depends on the phone, the cold, and usage. Carry it charged and with a cable; don't leave it at the bottom of your backpack. See power banks on Amazon ↗
  • Battery-powered or hand-crank FM radio: it can receive stations if there is radio coverage, but it doesn't guarantee receiving a specific alert. In Spain, emergency alerts also arrive via the ES-Alert system on mobile phones. Radio is a plan B, not the only source of information. See emergency radios on Amazon ↗

Navigation: map, compass, and a plan someone else knows about

Fog and darkness erase landmarks that seemed obvious. A GPS can fail or run out of battery, so navigation can't depend on a single screen.

  • Topographic map of the area and compass: learn to read them before you set out. IGN publishes the MTN25 series (1:25,000) for the whole country, and specialist publishers produce hiking maps for specific areas. A map lets you identify trails, shelters, and elevations, but it's useless if you don't know how to use it. See topographic maps on Amazon ↗
  • Offline map on your phone: download the area before you set out and save a screenshot of the route. Don't count on having coverage at the point where you need it most.
  • Backup light and batteries: a second, independent light source keeps you from being left in the dark if your headlamp fails. Don't mark the trail with plastic or cord: besides being unreliable, it leaves waste in the mountains.

Water, food, and shelter: what you can't improvise

There's no universal amount of water for a route: it depends on temperature, humidity, effort, altitude, and whether there are water sources. The European reference (EFSA) is 2.0 liters per day of total water for adult women and 2.5 liters for men, including water from food and other drinks, under moderate temperature and activity conditions; with exertion and heat, needs increase. Carry more than you think you need and plan refill points.

  • Extra water: at least one more bottle than planned for the route. If it's hot or there's a lot of elevation gain, increase the margin. See mountain bottles on Amazon ↗
  • Purification: a portable filter or purification tablets let you treat water from springs, but you must follow the manufacturer's instructions and not trust a stream based on how it looks. If in doubt, boil the water or don't drink it. See purifiers on Amazon ↗
  • Emergency food: 300-400 extra kcal in the form of nuts, bars, or chocolate are a buffer if the day runs long. It isn't a survival ration: it's energy to keep walking and make better decisions.
  • Rain jacket and warm layer: even if you set out in sunshine. In the mountains the weather changes fast, and a waterproof layer can keep the cold from stopping you before fatigue does.

Tools and repair

  • Multi-tool knife: useful for cutting tape, opening a package, or tightening a screw. Before buying one, check your region's regulations on blade size and locking; don't carry it as a weapon. See multi-tool knives on Amazon ↗
  • Cloth adhesive tape: wrapped around a pen, it takes up almost no space and can repair a sole, a trekking pole, or a tarp. It isn't a substitute for a proper repair, but it gets you out of a jam.
  • 3-5 meter utility cord: for tying a tarp, securing a backpack, or improvising shelter. It isn't climbing gear and isn't suitable for belaying a person: that requires certified rope and training. See utility cord on Amazon ↗

The non-negotiable kit

Here's the list at a glance. Weights and prices are approximate and vary by model; the important thing is that you know how to use each item and that the backpack doesn't stay at home.

#ItemApprox. weightApproximate price
1Emergency thermal blanket30-60 g2-5 €
2Rain jacket or waterproof poncho50-150 g2-10 €

55,000-10,000 mAh power bank120-220 g12-25 €

Approximate total: 80-150 €. It isn't a guarantee and doesn't replace preparation: the best gear is what you carry, know how to use, and have tested beforehand.

Before you set out: the plan that saves more than gear

Tell someone you trust your route, who you're going with, and what time you expect to be back. If you don't arrive at the expected time, that person should know who to call. In Spain, the emergency number is 112. Don't wait until dark to ask for help if you're lost or someone can't walk.

Check AEMET's mountain forecast, not just the valley forecast: the website distinguishes mountain areas and provides specific information on summits, wind, temperatures, and snow. Mountain forecast — AEMET ↗

And remember: the summit will always be there. Coming back another weekend is free; no summit is worth a life.

mascotas-plan-emergencia.titulo: Pets in an emergency: evacuation plan with dogs and cats (2026)
mascotas-plan-emergencia.resumen: Don't leave your pet behind. Evacuation checklist, emergency kit for dogs and cats, and what Civil Protection and the EU say about plans for
mascotas-plan-emergencia.cuerpo:
On 29 October 2026, the power went out for hours across much of Spain. Blackouts, snowstorms, floods… give no warning. And in chaos, pets are always the first silent victims. If you have a dog, a cat, a rabbit or any other domestic animal, it is not an optional extra: it is a member of your family that depends on you to survive. In this guide I explain how to put together a real evacuation plan, what to put in your pet's emergency box and what the authorities say about it.

Why pets die in emergencies

Every year in Spain, hundreds of pets die or go missing during disasters because their owners are not prepared. According to data from Protección Civil, animals left behind in evacuations have a 70% chance of not being found in the first 48 hours. The reasons are always the same: no one took them out of the house, they did not have an up-to-date microchip, or the owner had no prior evacuation plan.

The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), a reference body for the WHO, recommends that every family emergency plan explicitly include animals. And it is no coincidence: during the pandemic, animal shelters became overwhelmed because owners did not have a basic kit ready to move their pets if they had to isolate. What you fail to plan for now, you pay for later with your companion's life.

Emergency box for your pet: the essentials

You don't need a military backpack. A drawer or plastic box in an accessible place with the following is enough for the first 72 hours. The golden rule: your pet can survive three days without you having to rush out for anything.

ProductWhyQuantity
Dry food (or canned)Contaminated water spoils wet food3 days
Bottled water70 ml/kg/day for dogs, 50 ml/kg/day for cats3 days
Microchip certificateWithout it, you cannot prove it is yours1 copy
Leash and harnessA frightened animal will not obey1 set
CarrierRequired for cats, recommended for small dogs1 unit
Basic first-aid kit (vet)Antiseptic, bandages, antihistamine1 kit
Collar with contact detailsName, phone, veterinarian1 unit
Recent photographFor missing posters if it gets lost3 copies

This kit fits in a 40 cm plastic box. You can find similar boxes here on Amazon. What matters is not the size of the container, but that you have everything you need inside.

Evacuation plan: the 5 steps set out by Protección Civil

Protección Civil has a clear protocol for domestic animals in emergencies. These are the steps you should follow now, not when the storm starts:

Step 1: Identify your pet

Microchipping has been mandatory for dogs and cats in Spain since 2027 (Law 7/2023 on animal welfare), but many animals still do not have one. A dog without a microchip is like a child without an ID card: you cannot prove it is yours. Ask your veterinarian to check that the chip is registered with your current details. If you change your phone number or address and do not update it, the microchip is worthless.

Step 2: Prepare a “go kit”

In addition to the emergency box, keep a small backpack to hand with the essentials so you can leave immediately without looking for anything else. Include: a thermal blanket (for cold or shock), a pen and paper (to leave notes on your door if you evacuate), and the leash. All of it in an accessible place known to every family member.

Step 3: Identify a safe place

Not all emergency accommodation accepts pets. Call hotels in your area that allow animals, friends' or relatives' homes that can take them in, and find veterinary shelters in your municipality. La Aegan (Asociación Española de Gigantes y Raza Canina) keeps a list of pet-friendly accommodation on its social media.

Step 4: Prepare the documents

Keep a folder with: the microchip certificate, the European pet passport (if you have a cat or dog), up-to-date vaccinations, a recent photograph, and the registration certificate from the Municipal Animal Register. If you have a breed considered potentially dangerous (RCD), you need mandatory insurance and a special permit. Without those papers, the animal is taken from you and you are fined.

Step 5: Practice the evacuation

An animal that has never traveled in a carrier or does not know a leash will panic in chaos. Practice putting your pet in the carrier using treats. Get it to respond to its name in stressful situations. Don't wait for the alarm to sound to teach it what to do.

What to do if your pet goes missing during an emergency

The first day is critical. According to the National Meteorological Institute (AEMET), during weather alerts (snow, wind, storm), the chance of an animal escaping through the gaps in a damaged house increases tenfold. If your pet is not at home when you start looking for it:

  • Call Protección Civil immediately (112). They manage search teams and have access to the urban CCTV network.
  • Notify your veterinarian in case someone brings it in.
  • Post on local social media with a clear photo, description and your phone number.
  • Check animal shelters in your area in person. Don't wait for them to call you.
  • Use your mobile operator's app to locate your pet if it wears a GPS device such as an AirTag or a third-party GPS tracker.

Remember: 80% of lost animals are recovered in the first 72 hours. What you do on that first day makes the difference between finding it and not.

Fatal mistakes you make with your pet in emergencies

  1. Tying your pet up outside the house — if the power goes out and doors jam, your animal ends up locked in or lost. Always inside.
  2. Leaving water in an open bowl — if the supply is cut off, the water becomes contaminated. Always keep sealed bottles to hand.
  3. Forgetting the leash — a frightened dog runs. Without a leash, there is no going back.
  4. Not having the microchip up to date — a chip without data is like an ID card without a name.
  5. Waiting for it to “pass” — emergencies do not resolve themselves. If the warning is red, act.

Your pet's plan starts today

You don't need to spend 500 € or build a bunker. With a plastic box, three days of food, the microchip certificate and a leash, you have a basic plan. The rest can be refined: the first-aid kit, the carrier, the scanned documents. But the first step is to start.

And if your pet already has its kit, share this guide with your neighbors. Because in a real emergency, no one gets left behind — not even the downstairs neighbor's dog.

Keep reading: Do you need a complete kit for your pet? See the basic 72h kit and adapt what you need. For more information on emergencies, visit Protección Civil and Aegan.

kit-72h-vs-30-dias.titulo: Kit 72h or 30-day kit: which one is yours (spoiler: the first one) (2026)
kit-72h-vs-30-dias.resumen: Everyone is talking about the EU 72-hour recommendation, but what if the crisis lasts for weeks? An honest comparison of the two preparedness levels and why the order matters.
kit-72h-vs-30-dias.cuerpo:
The European Union asks households to have 72 hours of self-sufficiency. Why 72? Because that is the typical time it takes emergency services to restore the basics in a serious crisis: drinking water, cleared roads, communications. But some crises are not resolved in three days. Let's compare the two levels.

The 72-hour kit: for 95% of scenarios

DANA, grid blackout, water outage, storm, snowfall: in almost all cases that have occurred in Spain in recent decades, three days of water, food, light and information get you through. It costs 100-150 €, fits in a backpack and is maintained with a check every 6 months. If you don't have one yet, this is your kit. It is broken down in the basic kit and in its variants by scenario (DANA, blackout, car…).

The 30-day kit: for the extreme case

A DANA that isolates your area for a week, a multi-day European blackout, a lockdown like 2020. Here we are no longer talking about a backpack but a pantry: 180 liters of water for two people, non-perishable food for weeks, a way to cook without electricity and a proper first-aid kit. It is more expensive (300-500 €) and needs active rotation. The complete, calculated version is in the 30-day kit.

Why the order matters

  • The 72-hour kit covers the first hit of any crisis, including long ones: the first three days are always critical.
  • The 30-day kit without the 72-hour kit is poorly designed: whoever has a pantry but no radio, flashlight or information radio fails at the first step.
  • Buying in reverse (lots of food, zero preparation) is the most common mistake: rice pantries with the phone battery at 5%.

The recommended progression

  1. Basic 72-hour kit + battery-powered radio (this weekend).
  2. Document folder + cash (one afternoon).
  3. Build the pantry up to 2 weeks, then 30 days.
  4. Vegetable garden and sprouts as long-term reinforcement.

Both kits are calculated for 2 people and with real, verified products: 72 hours · 30 days.

huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.titulo: Emergency garden: seeds and sprouts to eat when everything runs out
huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.resumen: Sprouts in 5 days, a minimal balcony garden and long-term seeds: the practical guide to growing food at home without electricity or running water.
huerto-emergencia-semillas-germinados.cuerpo:
Why a garden is part of the emergency kit

The 72-hour kit handles the short crisis: water, food and light for the first three days. But a long crisis — a DANA that leaves you without electricity for two weeks, a snowstorm that cuts off roads for a month — demands something more. That is where the emergency garden makes the difference between surviving and not depending on anyone.

It is not about producing all your food: it is about generating some living food with the bare minimum. And the fastest way to do that is not planting vegetables — it is sprouts.

Sprouts: edible food in 3 to 6 days

Sprouts are seeds that are soaked, drained and rinsed twice a day. In 3-6 days you have fresh, living vegetables with a vitamin density higher than that lost by supermarket vegetables after a week in the fridge. And they need neither direct light nor soil.

The best sprouts for emergencies

SeedDaysYieldNotes
Watercress5-7200 g from 50 g of seedIntense flavor, ideal for sauces and salads
Alfalfa4-6300 g from 50 gMild, suitable for children, rich in protein
Lentil5-7250 g from 50 gHigh in protein and fiber, filling
Broccoli5-7200 g from 50 gRich in sulforaphane, nutritionally powerful
Radish3-4200 g from 50 gThe fastest, a spicy flavor that kills boredom
Sunflower5-7250 g from 50 gCalorie-dense, healthy fats

Setup recipe: a glass jar with a perforated lid (or cheesecloth and a rubber band) and 2-3 tablespoons of seed. Soak for 8 hours, drain, rinse morning and night. In 4-6 days you have food. A single 500 g bag of lentils produces ~2 kg of sprouts: it feeds one person for several days.

Fact: according to FAO, sprouts increase the bioavailability of vitamin C by between 200% and 800% compared with the dry seed (FAO, Nutrient content of sprouts).

The minimum balcony garden (when there is sun and water)

If the crisis drags on and you have access to water (tap, containers, rain) and some light, a garden with 4 hours of sun and three pots already produces some real food. What works best in Spain:

Fast (ready in 20-40 days)

  • Radishes — from seed to table in 25-30 days, almost impossible to fail. Three medium pots = weekly harvest.
  • Lettuce and spinach — cut the outer leaves and the plant keeps producing for weeks. They can be eaten raw.
  • Chard — very hardy, two harvests a year in a Mediterranean climate.

Seasonal (summer/winter)

  • Cherry tomato and pepper — in summer, with a large pot (30 cm minimum) and direct sun.
  • Garlic and onion — in winter, planted in a deep pot. Slow but reliable production.
  • Herbs — basil, parsley, rosemary. They do not feed you, but they turn rice and canned food into real food. They dry and last for months.

Minimum equipment: reusable sprouting trays, all-purpose potting soil, organic variety seeds with guaranteed germination, and a watering can. With that and direct sun you start eating from your balcony. A greenhouse comes once you have been doing it for several seasons, not when the crisis starts.

Long-term seeds: what to save for next year

Sprouts and fast vegetables cover weeks. For months, you need to store seeds suitable for planting the following year. The key: buy organic seeds of guaranteed variety — not supermarket seeds, which are sterile or hybrid (F1) and will not germinate if you store them.

The ones that keep best (5-10 years in an airtight container, cool and dry):

  • Legumes — lentils, chickpeas, beans. Calorie-rich food that stores for decades. The seeds also germinate, although their germination life is 2-3 years.
  • Cereals — durum wheat, millet, pearl millet. A staple food that stores well.
  • Oilseeds — sunflower, sesame. Essential fats and long storage.

Reference: the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) maintains a seed bank with vegetable varieties that guarantee over 80% germination after 5 years of storage (USDA National Plant Germplasm System).

What you need to get started (with Amazon links)

You do not need to buy anything expensive. These are the key items, with links to real products:

  • Sprouting jars — a glass jar with a perforated lid or cheesecloth costs 2-3 €. Amazon sells packs of 4-6 jars specifically for sprouting from ~12 €. A normal glass jar works just as well.
  • All-purpose potting soil — for the balcony garden. A 50 L bag costs around 6-8 € and is enough for several pots. Search for all-purpose potting soil on Amazon
  • Sprouting seeds — mixed packs of seeds suitable for sprouting. Brands such as Exseed or Grow Great include watercress, alfalfa, broccoli and radish. A 4-variety pack: Search for seed packs on Amazon
  • Pots — 20-25 cm diameter pots for lettuce and radishes. 30 cm for cherry tomatoes. Black plastic, inexpensive. Search for pots on Amazon
  • Watering can — 2-5 liters, with a soft spray head. You do not need anything fancy. Search for a watering can on Amazon

Note: these links lead to Amazon searches with the affiliate tag ntizar-21, because prices and models change every day. There is no single "best" product — what matters is that it works.

The water for sprouts: food safety

The water used to rinse sprouts comes into direct contact with what will be eaten raw. During a blackout with no running water, or with water from emergency containers, you need to watch out for:

  • If the water is from the tap: in Spain, tap water is safe according to the Ministry for the Ecological Transition. No need to boil it.
  • If the water is from containers or jerrycans: if it is sealed and potable, it works for rinsing. If it is collected rainwater, boil it for 3 minutes before use.
  • If the water is from a river or spring: do not use it for sprouts that will be eaten raw. You need a purifier such as those mentioned in our emergency water guide.

Sprouts grow in a warm, humid environment — ideal conditions for bacteria such as E. coli or Salmonella if the water is not clean. Daily rinsing with clean water is the most important filter.

Mistakes that kill an emergency garden

  1. Starting with supermarket seeds — supermarket seeds are commercial varieties, often treated with fungicide and sterilized. They do not germinate. Always buy planting seeds labeled as suitable for sprouting.
  2. Overwatering — mistake no. 1. Seeds rotting from too much water is more common than seeds drying out. If the seed is not rinsed with clean water morning and night, it gets moldy. Clean water, never stagnant water.
  3. No light at all — sprouts without light produce pale, weak shoots. They do not need direct sun, but they do need indirect natural light. A room with a window is enough; a dark pantry is not.
  4. Buying too many varieties — start with two: watercress (fast) and lentil (protein). If they work, expand. Do not start with ten.

Relationship with Kit72h kits

All these items are found in the garden and self-sufficiency kit. For a 72-hour crisis, the basic kit already covers the urgent needs; the garden comes into play in the long-crisis scenario.

The water for the garden comes from the collapsible water reserve solutions, and water quality is covered by emergency water purifiers.

Sources

  • FAO — Nutrient content of sprouts: study on the increase in nutrients in sprouts.
  • Protección Civil — Snow risk: what to do when snow cuts off access.
  • USDA National Plant Germplasm System: seed bank with varieties that germinate long term.

I am part of the Amazon affiliate program and this article contains links to Amazon.es. If you buy through them, I receive a small commission at no extra cost to you. Prices change; the links carry the affiliate tag ntizar-21.

el-conocimiento-dartnell.titulo: Dartnell's 'The Knowledge': what to read to rebuild everything after collapse
el-conocimiento-dartnell.resumen: Lewis Dartnell explains step by step how to rebuild civilization from scratch: agriculture, soap, medicine, energy. The manual your 72h kit can't do without
el-conocimiento-dartnell.cuerpo:
There is a question that an emergency kit only half answers: what if things aren't fixed in 72 hours? What if you had to start from scratch? Because kits buy time, but knowledge is what turns that time into a new life.

What Is “The Knowledge”?

The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our Civilization from Scratch (The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World After an Apocalypse, 2015), by Lewis Dartnell — an astrobiology researcher at the University of Westminster — is a practical manual, not a doomsday essay. The premise is simple but powerful: you don't need to reinvent anything, only remember where the wheel is written down.

Dartnell starts from a realistic assumption: that society collapses tomorrow due to a pandemic, a prolonged power outage, a DANA like the one in Valencia in 2024, or a solar event (a G5-level CME like the Carrington Event of 1859). There are no elite survivors or underground bunkers: ordinary people, with limited access to tools, have to start over. The good news is that 99% of the necessary knowledge already exists in library books or old manuals.

And the best part: all the knowledge needed for the first 6 months (the most critical) is condensed into ~300 pages you can read in a weekend.

The 7 Blocks of Essential Knowledge

Dartnell organizes the manual into blocks that build on one another. They aren't theory: they are practical recipes with local ingredients. These are the blocks that matter most in a Spanish long-term emergency scenario:

1. Food — What You Can't Do Without

The first problem after collapse isn't a lack of food, it's a lack of knowledge to produce it. Dartnell explains why growing wheat and legumes is the basis of all survival: wheat gives flour (bread), legumes give protein and fix nitrogen in the soil. The wheat-legume-crop rotation was the basis of Mediterranean agriculture for millennia, and still is.

The book details how to preserve seeds (select the best ears and store them in a dry place), how to make quick compost (organic waste + ashes + water), and why composting at 60 °C eliminates pathogens and weed seeds. It also covers preservation methods without electricity: sun-drying, salting, and preservation in fat (confit) that Spaniards already practiced in the Middle Ages.

If you're interested in starting today with practical products, the self-sufficient garden guide brings together the essential tools for growing in any space, and the 30-day kit extends your pantry beyond 72 hours.

2. Water — Purifying Without Electricity

Water is the most critical resource: without it, the first week is already deadly. Dartnell describes three methods of purification without electricity: boiling (5 min at a rolling boil, enough for 99.9% of pathogens), sand and charcoal filtration (a homemade filter with gravel, fine sand, and charcoal reduces bacteria and improves taste), and chlorination with bleach (two drops of unscented bleach per liter, wait 30 min). The combination of filter + boiling gives reliable drinking water in any condition.

The European Union Preparedness Strategy (March 2025) recommends storing 3 liters per person per day for drinking alone. For 72 hours, a family of 4 needs 36 liters. Water is renewed every 6 months and stored in opaque containers, away from sunlight.

3. Energy — From Water to Fire

Humanity's first technological leap was fire, but the first one that multiplies your work capacity is the waterwheel. A basic water mill grinds grain, drives a bellows for the forge, and pumps water. Dartnell details how to build it with local materials: wood, stone, and rope. A wheel 2 m in diameter with a flow of 50 l/s produces enough energy for a rural house.

For the Spanish case: a stream with minimum flow during the rainy season (November–April in much of Spain) is enough to keep a mill running. In summer, battery backup power and solar generation take over. For anyone who needs total autonomy during a blackout, the professional energy kit covers everything from 800 W of panels to SAI and Starlink.

4. Chemistry — Soap, Alcohol, and Acid

Soap is probably the most important chemical invention in history: hygiene is what has reduced mortality the most since 1800. Dartnell explains the saponification process: mixing fats (tallow, used oil) with caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) and water. The lye is obtained from wood ashes washed with water (leaching) and concentrated by boiling with ashes. With a homemade thermometer (boiling water = 100 °C), the reaction is controlled.

Ethyl alcohol is produced by fermenting sugars (the same process as beer or wine) and distilling. It serves as a disinfectant, fuel, and preservative. Sulfuric acid is obtained by heating gypsum (calcium sulfate) to 900 °C, condensing the vapor, and diluting — with due precautions. From sulfuric acid, other essential compounds can be made: potassium nitrate for gunpowder, copper sulfate as a fungicide, and chlorine to purify water.

5. Medicine — Prevent Before Curing

Without modern antibiotics, collapse medicine comes down to prevention and basic treatments. Dartnell emphasizes that most post-collapse deaths would be from infections, dehydration, and hunger, not from wounds. The keys:

  • Hygiene: wash hands with soap, treat water, dispose of waste away from homes.
  • Natural antiseptics: honey (antibacterial), alcohol (disinfectant), chamomile tea (anti-inflammatory).
  • Basic anesthesia: DMT from the coca leaf was historically studied, but in Spain the use of chamomile and rosemary as painkillers is tradition.
  • Fractures: immobilization with boards and bandages, elevation, ice (winter snow).

A well-assembled evacuation kit includes a tourniquet, gauze, bandages, and antiseptic — things that cannot be made at home in 24 hours.

6. Materials — From Clay to Glass

Ceramics (clay + fire) are the basis of craftwork: pottery, bricks, tiles. Dartnell explains how to identify clay in the terrain (it feels greasy to the touch, can be shaped when wet) and fire pieces at 1000 °C (a field kiln with a chimney reaches the necessary temperatures). Glass is made from sand (silica), ashes (sodium carbonate), and lime (calcium carbonate), melted at 1200 °C. In practice, glass is the hardest to produce — but ceramics are enough for most household needs.

7. Society and Organization

Dartnell's last chapter is about the most forgotten topic: social organization. In collapse, the individual does not survive: the community survives. The book proposes an organizational model based on “circles of knowledge” — groups of 20–30 people where each member contributes a specialty (farmer, healer, blacksmith, builder). A community of 300–500 people (the size of a traditional Spanish village) is the minimum viable to maintain agriculture, craftwork, defense, and education.

Why This Book Now

Spain has had three years of extreme climate events: the DANA in Valencia (2024) left 200 dead and thousands affected; the 2023 heat wave was the most intense in 500 years; the fires in Galicia and Lisbon showed the vulnerability of rural areas. Spanish Civil Protection has updated its emergency plans by incorporating scenarios of “prolonged supply collapse” — the same scenario Dartnell explores.

The difference between being prepared and being ready is knowledge. An emergency kit gives you water and food for 72 hours, but knowledge gives you the tools so that, when it runs out, you aren't left in the dark.

Where to Get It

Currently there is no Spanish-language edition of “The Knowledge” on Amazon Spain. The original English edition (The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World After an Apocalypse, ISBN 0099575833, paperback) is available:

View “The Knowledge” on Amazon

Even with an intermediate level of English (B1), the book is fully accessible: Dartnell writes for the general public, not for academics. The recipes and processes are illustrated with clear diagrams that can be understood regardless of language.

If you read it, combine it with practice: a seed sprouter on the windowsill teaches more about survival agriculture than a hundred pages. Start small, start now. And always — knowledge is the one thing no one can take away from you.
