dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.titulo: DANA or blackout: the first 30 minutes, minute by minute (2026)
dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.resumen: The first 30 minutes decide almost everything: Civil Protection sequence minute by minute (0-10 information, 10-20 home, 20-30 plan) for DANA or blackout.
dana-apagon-primeros-30-minutos.cuerpo:
In an emergency, the first thirty minutes decide almost everything: what information you have, where you are and what resources you have left. Protección Civil boils it down to three actions — get informed, secure your home and decide — and the European Commission insists through its Union Preparedness Strategy that every household must be able to sustain itself for at least 72 hours by its own means while help arrives. This is that sequence, step by step, with the mistakes that repeat in every DANA warning and every power cut.

If you only remember one idea: the first ten minutes are for information, not action. Almost all avoidable damage in the first half hour — a car swept away in a garage, a television burned out just as the power comes back, a call to 112 to ask something the radio answers — comes from skipping that order.

Minute 0–10: get informed and communicate without crashing the network

When the power goes out or the warning arrives, the reflex is to call and post. Both things make the situation worse:

  • 112 is for emergencies involving people at risk: injured people, people trapped, fire, water rising inside an occupied home. To find out whether the warning affects you or why the power has gone out, there are much faster channels.
  • Messages before calls: WhatsApp or SMS take up far less of the network and can be sent even when voice lines are overloaded. An “I'm fine” by message is almost always enough.
  • Battery or hand-crank radio: FM is the only source that stays alive when the mobile network goes down, and it is where authorities give instructions by word of mouth. An emergency radio with hand crank and solar power costs little and depends on neither the network nor the power.
  • Look at the scope, not just the alert: a warning is not the same across the whole territory. Cross-check what you hear with AEMET's weather warnings and with information from your town hall or local Protección Civil.

If you receive an emergency message with an alarm on your mobile phone — the ES-Alert system that Spanish Protección Civil uses to warn the public by phone — it is not a hoax or a mistake: it is the same warning given by radio and by loudspeaker. And if the power cut affects only your building entrance or your street, it points to the property; if there is no power across the whole neighbourhood and you see people out in the street, it is a distribution cut and you need to wait, without making up diagnoses. In the blackout of 28 April 2025, confusion about the scope was exactly what fed the wave of hoaxes: the lessons from that day still apply to either scenario.

Everything you need to have located before it is needed — numbers, radio stations, contacts and where your documents are — is laid out in official emergency resources and in the household emergency folder.

Minute 10–20: secure the home (DANA script, blackout script)

Here the path splits.

If water is coming (DANA or flooding)

  • Get out of the basement, garage and ground floors and move up whatever can get wet: documents, footwear, paintings, keys, chargers and medication.
  • Do not go down to get the car. Thirty centimetres of water are enough to sweep away a vehicle, and the garage is the most dangerous place in the property when water gets in.
  • If water enters the home and you can do it without getting wet, cut the power at the electrical panel and do not use the lift or any connected appliance.
  • Do not cross riverbeds, fords, tunnels or flooded streets, on foot or by car: the current is much stronger than it looks and you cannot see the bottom.
  • Close shutters and windows, and put papers you cannot replace in a waterproof bag.

The scenario kit is in DANA kit; the departure plan, in evacuation kit; and what to do when the water goes down and you return home — mud, damp, insurance — in returning home after a flood.

If the power goes out (blackout)

  • Unplug sensitive equipment — television, computer, sound systems —: the surge that comes when the supply is restored is what burns out electronics. Leave one switch on with a small lamp: it will tell you when the power is back.
  • Do not open the fridge. With the door closed the cold lasts quite a while; every opening shortens it.
  • Use flashlight light, not candlelight if there are children, pets or if you are going to sleep. And if you use a gas heater, a brazier or a camping stove to get through the cold, ventilate or do not use it while sleeping: carbon monoxide has no smell and is the classic cause of household poisonings. A carbon monoxide detector is the truly cheap option.
  • Prioritise what you power: mobile and router first, then the fridge. A SAI for the home keeps the router and equipment running without you noticing, and a solar generator gives hours of light with no noise or fumes; the comparison between the two is in generator vs power station. The whole scenario laid out, in blackout kit.

If you want to go beyond the torch in the drawer, the search for rechargeable emergency flashlights ↗ and the one for high-capacity power banks ↗ show each option with its price of the day; the criteria for choosing are in best power bank for emergencies.

Minute 20–30: decide whether to stay or go

By default, stay at home if there is no structural risk, no water coming in and no one has ordered you to evacuate: it is the safest place and the one that has your resources. Going out only makes sense if there is an evacuation order, if the building is unsafe or if the water keeps rising.

If you stay:

  • Ration your mobile battery: airplane mode, minimum brightness and data only when you need it. A charged power bank is several full charges; without it, your mobile will die just when you need it most.
  • Take stock of what you have: water, ready-to-eat food, flashlight, batteries, first-aid kit and medication. If something is missing, the basic 72-hour kit and the guide to how much water you need and how to store it give you the exact count.
  • Have the family plan settled: meeting points, a contact outside the city and which number to call. That is prepared calmly, not in the 30 minutes: family emergency plan.

If you leave, take only what fits in a backpack and can be carried on foot: layers of warm clothing, water, some food, documents in a waterproof bag, charger and power bank, basic first-aid kit, usual medication, flashlight, whistle and some cash. The full list is in how to put together your 72-hour kit.

The 30 minutes in a table

StageObjectiveTypical mistake
0–10 minKnow what is happening and whom to listen toCalling 112 to ask questions or sharing the first thing that appears on social media
10–20 minSecure the home according to the scenarioGoing down to the garage for the car or leaving equipment plugged in when the power comes back
20–30 minDecide: stay or leave, and with whatImprovising the departure without documents, without water or without a meeting plan

Five mistakes that repeat in the first half hour

  1. Using 112 as an information line. Questions are resolved with the radio, mobile phone and official channels; 112 is reserved for those in danger.
  2. Going down to the garage to save the car. It is the mistake that causes the most personal injury in flash floods.
  3. Heating with a brazier or gas heater without ventilating or sleeping with it on. Carbon monoxide slips in without warning; this is explained in the carbon monoxide detector guide.
  4. Turning everything on at once when the power returns and opening the fridge every two minutes. Sensitive equipment should be unplugged beforehand and reconnected little by little.
  5. Believing and sharing any figure or hoax that circulates. In the 2025 blackout, dozens of hoaxes caused real damage; always verify before forwarding.

After the 30 minutes

The first half hour passes and the long part begins: follow only instructions from official sources (112, Protección Civil, local authorities and FM radio), do not touch fallen cables or attempt repairs yourself, and wait for the company to restore the supply. If water has come in, check before using anything again; if the outage drags on, food and cold are managed with the guides on eating without power for three days and on rotating emergency food.

And when everything returns to normal, replace what you have used: a backpack that is used on the first day and not restocked stops being useful for the next emergency. That is, literally, the last step of the 72-hour plan.

Official sources

  • Protección Civil — General recommendations by risk (Government of Spain).
  • Protección Civil — Public warning system (ES-Alert).
  • European Commission — Union Preparedness Strategy.
  • AEMET — Weather warnings.

Summary in three lines

Information first, then home, decision last: those are the three stages of the first half hour, and in that order. In a DANA, you do not go down to the garage; in a blackout, you do not turn everything on at once and the flashlight comes before the candle. Stay at home unless there is an evacuation order or real risk, and if you leave, leave prepared and with an agreed meeting plan.

comunicar-sin-red-movil.titulo: Communicating with no network: what works when mobile service goes down (2026)
comunicar-sin-red-movil.resumen: In every major emergency, mobile networks collapse within minutes: ways to communicate that don't depend on cell towers, some free and others for under 40 €.
comunicar-sin-red-movil.cuerpo:
On 28 April 2025, it became clear: when everyone tries to call at once, the network goes down. And during a DANA, antennas can be left without electricity or fiber for days. If your family plan depends on WhatsApp, you don't have a plan. Real alternatives, from free to cheap:

1. SMS and short messages

SMS uses a minimal signal that works when calls and data don't. Agree with your family: if the network is struggling, don't call — send a short SMS with your status and location.

2. The out-of-area contact

A classic Civil Protection technique: designate a person who lives far away (another region, another country) as your contact point. Local calls overload; a long-distance or other-region call sometimes gets through. Everyone calls that person, and they centralize.

3. Battery-powered FM/AM radio

It's not for talking, it's for finding out: when telecommunications collapse, broadcasting (large transmitters, their own antennas) is the last information channel still standing. A battery-powered or dynamo radio is the most underrated item in the kit.

4. PMR446 walkie-talkies

For €30–40 a pair, license-free in Spain, 2–5 km in the city (more in open country). Perfect for coordinating between houses in the same development or on a campsite. Store them with fresh batteries and don't use them as toys.

5. Messaging that works off-grid

Mesh apps (antenna-free bridges, such as Bluetooth radio links between nearby phones) exist, but they all require both people to have them installed beforehand. Install them now on the family's phones — in the middle of a crisis you can't download anything.

The family plan in one sentence

If there's no network: everyone sends an SMS to the out-of-area contact with “I'm okay / where I am / what I need”, and we meet at the agreed point if 24 hours pass without contact. Write that point on paper: under the bell tower, the motorway petrol station, your aunt's house.

The radio and power banks that support this communication are in the basic 72-hour kit and in the power outage kit.

como-montar-tu-kit-72h.titulo: How to build your 72-hour emergency kit: the complete guide (2026)
como-montar-tu-kit-72h.resumen: Since March 2025 the EU recommends 72 hours of self-sufficiency: water, food, light and a first aid kit in one backpack for €100–150, step by step and without overspending.
como-montar-tu-kit-72h.cuerpo:
How to build your 72-hour emergency kit: the complete guide (2026)

Since March 2025, the European Union Preparedness Strategy has recommended that every household have provisions for 72 hours of self-sufficiency. And it is not a desk document: with the 2024 DANAs, prolonged power outages and heatwaves that leave millions of people without supply, building a 72h kit is the cheapest and most effective self-protection measure you can take today.

You do not need to be a survivalist or spend thousands of euros. A decent basic emergency kit costs between 60 and 120 € and fits in a medium backpack. In this guide I explain exactly how to assemble it, step by step, without complications.

Step 1: choose the scenario that worries you

Before buying anything, ask yourself what type of emergency is most likely in your area. In Spain the most frequent are:

  • DANA or flooding: torrential rains that cut off supplies, leave people without power and isolate entire neighborhoods. The Mediterranean coast is especially vulnerable.
  • Prolonged blackout: cold waves that spike electricity demand and cause outages lasting hours or days.
  • Heatwave: extreme heat leaves many communities without water and hospitals become overwhelmed.
  • Wildfires: especially in summer, they can cut off access to your area and leave it without electricity supply.

The basic 72h kit covers all four scenarios. If your main risk is one specific one, you can add a specific kit such as the blackout kit, DANA kit or wildfire kit.

Step 2: water — what cannot be improvised

Water is the most critical resource and the hardest to replenish after an emergency. The rule set by the EU and Civil Protection is clear: 3 liters per person per day for drinking alone. For 72 hours, that is 9 liters per person.

For a family of four you need to store at least 36 liters of drinking water. The right strategy combines three elements:

  1. Bottled water or water in jerrycans: buy 6 liters per person to start. Store it in a cool place without direct sunlight.
  2. Purification tablets or a filter: as a plan B, if supply is cut you can purify tap or river water. Micropur tablets or filters such as LifeStraw are cheap and weigh nothing.
  3. A hydration kit: oral rehydration sachets. In heatwaves or floods, dehydration is a real risk.

Replace the water every 6 months — set a reminder on your phone when you assemble the kit. If you do not want to think about it, the Swiss 7-day reserve includes 9 liters per person with an expiration date and automatic rotation.

Step 3: food you can eat without cooking

In an emergency there may be no gas or electricity for cooking. The food in your 72h kit must be non-perishable, ready to eat and requiring no refrigeration.

The essentials include:

  • Canned goods and tins: legumes, fish in oil, vegetables. Bring a manual can opener (do not forget it).
  • Energy bars and nuts: calorie-dense, light and with no problematic expiration.
  • Freeze-dried meals: military rations that only need hot water. Ideal if weight matters to you.
  • Eat what you like: if you force yourself to eat something you cannot stand, you will reject it when you need it most. The criterion is simple: would you eat it on a normal Sunday?

For 72 hours calculate between 2,000 and 2,500 kcal per person per day. A basic 72h kit already brings together the most practical options, but if you want extra margin, the 30-day kit expands the pantry following the same logic.

Step 4: light and energy — do not underestimate darkness

When the power goes out, it is not just darkness. It is not being able to call on your mobile, not having heating, not being able to see if there is water, not being able to open the car door with the electric key. Light and energy are critical.

The minimum viable:

  • A headlamp per person: it keeps your hands free and is the most useful thing after an earthquake or flood where you have to move with your hands occupied.
  • Powerbank of at least 20,000 mAh: charges your mobile 4-6 full times. A 10,000 mAh powerbank falls short over 72 hours.
  • Battery or dynamo radio: in a general blackout, the Internet may be slow or unavailable. A radio is your link to the authorities. A dynamo one also works if the batteries run out.
  • Spare batteries: buy a pack of AA and AAA batteries and store them with the kit.

If blackouts are your main fear, add the electricity kit (60-200 €) or directly the professional energy kit with SAI, solar panels and LFP battery.

Step 5: basic first aid kit — what you need to know

You do not need a war first aid kit. With the basics you cover 90% of situations:

  • Wound care: sterile gauze, bandages, medical tape, tweezers and nitrile gloves.
  • Antiseptic: chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine to clean wounds.
  • Painkillers and antipyretics: paracetamol and ibuprofen (two different molecules, in case one does not work for you).
  • Regular medication: if someone in the household takes chronic treatment, keep at least 7 days' supply. In an emergency, the pharmacy may be closed for days.
  • Antidiarrheals: diarrhea in an emergency without access to clean water can be serious. Loperamide + oral rehydration solution.

A kit for older adults includes these same items with adapted doses, but the basic first aid kit is suitable for any adult.

Step 6: documents and money — paper before the paper runs out

In a real emergency, offices close, ATMs do not work and card payment can be impossible if power and the network go down. Prepare:

  • Stamped photocopies of DNI, NIE and passport for all family members. If you can, get them certified at your town hall.
  • Deeds and policies: insurance, mortgage, rental contract. A digital copy on a sealed USB drive.
  • Contact list: primary care doctor, pharmacy, car insurance, electricity and gas company. Written on paper: do not rely on your phone's address book.
  • Cash: small bills (5, 10 and 20 €). Without banking or e-commerce, cash is the only payment.

The advice from Spanish Civil Protection is to create an emergency folder with all of this together. If you do not want to assemble it yourself, the evacuation kit includes a specific organizer for documents.

Step 7: the backpack — not just any backpack

The container is as important as the contents. Look for a backpack with these features:

  • Minimum capacity: 30 liters. Less is not enough for 72 hours and more than one person.
  • Waterproof or with an included rain cover: if it rains, the water should not soak the contents.
  • Padded straps and a waist belt: if you have to walk with it, the belt distributes the weight and saves your back.
  • Reflective: if you have to move at night along a road, make sure you are seen.
  • Discreet color: it does not have to be black, but avoid bright colors that identify it as an emergency backpack.

You can reuse a backpack you already have. If not, a second-hand hiking one is enough: you do not need expensive gear.

Mistakes everyone makes

After analyzing hundreds of user questions, these are the most common mistakes when building a 72h kit:

Buying food you are not going to eat

The most common mistake. If nobody in your house eats canned tuna, do not buy it 'just in case'. In an emergency you will eat what you have for three days straight. Stress does not improve your palate.

Forgetting the can opener

It sounds like a joke, but it is not. Thousands of cans without a can opener are food that goes to waste. Put it in the first layer of the backpack, visible.

Storing it in the storage room

The kit has to be where everyone in the house knows about it. If only you know where it is and you end up hospitalized, the kit is useless.

Setting an expiration date and not checking it

Set a reminder every 6 months. Change the water, check the batteries and the food. A kit that expires is worse than having no kit.

Not preparing the children

Children need extra warmth (sleeping bags or thermal blankets), their favorite food (so they eat something) and a comfort object (a stuffed animal, a book). Do not underestimate the emotional factor in an emergency.

How much does it cost to build the kit?

A basic 72h kit can be built for between 60 and 120 €, depending on whether you reuse a backpack and whether you choose generic or specialized brands. Here is an indicative breakdown:

  • Water and purification: 10-15 €
  • Non-perishable food: 20-30 €
  • Flashlight + radio + powerbank: 25-40 €
  • Basic first aid kit: 15-20 €
  • Backpack: 0-30 € (free if you reuse one)
  • Documents and cash: 0 €

The basic 72h kit from Kit72h brings together all the essentials in a verified list with direct links to each product. If you prefer a more complete approach, the 30-day kit includes expanded provisions for a full month.

Keep reading

  • Basic 72h kit — the EU's 16 items
  • Evacuation kit — escaping alive
  • Family emergency plan: the steps nobody tells you about
  • How much water to store at home: Switzerland's official reserve
  • Best emergency powerbank: 2026 comparison
  • Official sources — EU, Civil Protection and more

The best time to build your 72h kit was a year ago. The second best time is today. Start with the basic kit list and keep completing it little by little. You do not have to buy everything on the same day.

coche-kit-emergencia-2026.titulo: Cars and emergencies: what is mandatory in 2026 and what is advisable
coche-kit-emergencia-2026.resumen: The connected V-16 beacon is now the only legal warning device: what else the glovebox should hold for a DANA, a snowstorm or a breakdown at night.
coche-kit-emergencia-2026.cuerpo:
The car kit is the only one you carry with you every day, and also the most heavily regulated. Since 1 January 2026 the main rule has changed — the connected V-16 beacon replaced triangles as the only legal way to signal — but the rule only covers part of the problem: signalling that you are stopped. It does not cover running out of water on a road cut off by a DANA, spending the night in the car at fourteen degrees below zero after a snowfall, or a headlight failing in the middle of a six-hour traffic jam. This article covers both halves: what the law requires and what you should add on your own.

We have ordered it the way you would actually use it: first the mandatory items, then prioritised emergency equipment, then the three most common scenarios in Spain (flooding, snow and breakdown), and finally the six-month check that keeps everything working. The full list, with links and a one-click cart, is in the car kit.

What is mandatory in Spain in 2026

The DGT is clear: since 1 January 2026 the approved connected V-16 beacon is the only legal way to signal a vehicle immobilised on the roadway. You can check that your model is certified in the DGT's official list of V-16 devices: any orange light from a DIY store will not do; it must have the approval and the connectivity (geolocation) required by the regulation.

The triangles are no longer a valid way to signal a stop: they can stay in the trunk, but they no longer fulfil the legal function. The offence for driving without a beacon is minor and carries an 80 € fine, but the real reason for the rule is flesh and blood: the DGT estimates that around 25 people die each year after being hit on the road after getting out of their vehicle, many of them while placing triangles. With the V-16 you do not get out of the car: it is switched on from inside and, in addition to the light, sends the vehicle's position to other drivers. You will find the details of the rule, the fine and how to choose one in the V-16 beacon guide.

This short list completes the mandatory on-board items:

  • Reflective vest inside the passenger compartment, within reach before you get out (and put it on before touching the trunk).
  • Documentation: vehicle registration, ITV card and insurance receipt.
  • Connected V-16 beacon with a valid battery date (many have a non-replaceable battery: if it has expired, it is useless).
ItemMandatory?Why it matters in an emergency
Approved connected V-16 beaconYes (from 1/1/2026)Signals without getting out of the car and alerts by position, not just by light
Reflective vestYes, inside the passenger compartmentThe first thing that saves you when opening the door on a road with traffic
Vehicle documentationYesAvoids problems if the car has to be moved or insured
TrianglesNo (they no longer signal)Useful as visual reinforcement, but they do not replace the V-16
First-aid kit, thermal blanket, water, flashlightNoWhat turns the car into shelter when the emergency lasts for hours

What is worth adding (by priority)

The mandatory items get you out of legal trouble; these get you out of real trouble. Ordered from most to least useful, thinking about a typical Spanish scenario: a breakdown on a motorway, a road cut off by torrential rain or a winter traffic jam.

  • Emergency thermal blanket (approx. 3-8 €): a snow traffic jam or a breakdown in February becomes endless without one; it takes up less space than a notebook. Thermal blanket.
  • LED flashlight with magnet (approx. 10-25 €): lets you change a wheel at night without anyone holding anything; the magnet attaches it to the bumper. Magnet flashlight.
  • Compact first-aid kit (approx. 15-30 €): gauze, bandages, antiseptic and gloves; the list of what it should contain and what is unnecessary is in the emergency first-aid kit. Car first-aid kit.
  • Water and something to eat (approx. 2-5 € and 10-15 €): two bottles per person and energy bars; renew every six months. Bottled water.
  • Power bank or 12 V jump starter (approx. 25-50 €): your phone is your radio, your map and your way to call 112; a dead phone cuts off all those options. 12 V car power bank.
  • Chains or textile snow socks (approx. 30-80 €) if you cross the north or the mountains in winter: check first that your car accepts the model in your size. Snow chains.
  • Tow chain or tow strap (approx. 15-30 €): gets a car out of a muddy shoulder without waiting for a tow truck.

With that, the car stops being just transport and becomes the 72-hour kit you already carry with you: several of these items are exactly the same ones we recommend for home.

Scenario 1: water — never cross a ford

It is the mistake that costs the most lives in DANA events. Moving water hides the road surface: a branch, worn asphalt or an open drain is enough. And it does not take that much water: 20 cm already makes the vehicle harder to control and 30 cm of moving water sweeps away a passenger car.

The recommendations from Protección Civil, collected by the Ministry for the Ecological Transition, are blunt: do not cross flooded sections on foot or by car, do not park in dry riverbeds or on riverbanks, and if there is a heavy rain warning do not go down into garages or basements. If water catches you while driving:

  • Do not enter: look for another route, even if it is a long detour. Turning around is always cheaper than the alternative.
  • If the water rises and the car stops, get out through the windows (not the doors, which will have the water on their side) and move to higher ground. The Red Cross sums it up in its flood guide: if you find yourself trapped, get out of the vehicle as soon as possible.
  • Call 112 and give the exact location: road, kilometre marker, municipality and direction. In an emergency 112 is the only number, and it works throughout Spain.

If you live in an exposed area, the car is also useful for evacuating in time. The full protocol, with ES-Alert warnings and document bags, is in the DANA / flood kit.

Scenario 2: cold — the snowfall that cuts off the road

In the north of the peninsula, a severe weather spell can leave a motorway cut off for hours. Spending that night in the car with the heating on is possible, but with two safety conditions: never with the engine running in a garage or enclosed space (carbon monoxide has no smell and kills within minutes) and with the exhaust pipe clear of snow so it does not become blocked. Outdoors, with the window open a finger's width, it is safe.

A thermal blanket, a hat and hot water in a thermos make those hours bearable. And before setting off in winter, check the AEMET forecast (aemet.es → Warnings): an orange or red snow warning is not decoration; it is a sign that route may have no way out.

Scenario 3: the breakdown — the five minutes that matter most

A flat tire on the M-40 at six in the evening is annoying; what comes next is what is dangerous. The protocol, in order:

  1. Pull onto the shoulder as far as you can and turn on the V-16 from inside, before getting out.
  2. Put on the vest before opening the door.
  3. Get out on the side away from traffic, with passengers off the road (behind the barrier, not in front of it).
  4. Keep things visible: the magnet flashlight on the bumper helps others brake earlier.
  5. If you have to wait, the blanket and water in the trunk decide whether the wait is twenty minutes or four hours.

In summer the script is the same but in reverse: ventilation, water and never leave anyone (not even a dog) inside a car parked in the sun.

How to maintain the kit: two checks a year

The car kit does not fail for lack of items; it fails because of expired items. The most convenient time to check it is at the clock change, twice a year:

  • Renewed water (it should be changed every six months; if it has spent the summer in the trunk, you can imagine how it tastes).
  • V-16 batteries and battery date valid.
  • First-aid kit: remove expired items and restock it.
  • Flashlight and power bank charged.
  • Chains checked and in their bag, not buried under everything else in the trunk.

Ten minutes, twice a year. It is the cheapest maintenance there is for something that can matter to you for an entire afternoon. The full, prioritised shopping list, with a one-click cart, is put together for you in the car kit, and if the car is only one piece of a larger plan, how to build your 72-hour kit shows you how to fit everything together.

carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.titulo: Emergency folder at home: documents, cash and copies ready to evacuate (2026)
carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.resumen: What goes in the emergency folder, how to copy it on paper and in the cloud, how much cash you need and what to check every six months.
carpeta-de-emergencia-documentos.cuerpo:
After every DANA, major fire or prolonged blackout in Spain, the same scene repeats: families who leave home with only the clothes on their backs and who, weeks later, cannot prove where they lived, what they had insured or what medication they needed. The emergency folder is the highest-return item in the entire 72-hour kit: a folder, a waterproof pouch, a USB drive and an afternoon of work that save weeks of paperwork. It does not replace the evacuation go-bag; it complements it: if the go-bag gets you through the first day, the folder gets you through the following month.

What goes inside: seven sections and nothing more

The typical mistake is stuffing in piles of “paperwork” and then not finding anything when you need to sign something. Organize it by sections, with dividers or labeled sleeves:

  • Identity: a photocopy of the DNI or NIE for each member of the household, including minors, plus the family book. The copy is enough to process paperwork even if you lose the original; if there is an evacuation, the original travels in the go-bag, not in the house.
  • Housing: the deed or a land registry extract if you own it, the rental contract if you rent, and the cadastral reference (it appears on the IBI receipt and on the Catastro electronic office). If you rent, add the owner’s or real estate agent’s contact details: without that phone number, any procedure gets stuck.
  • Insurance: home, car, and health or life insurance policies you have, with the policy number and claims phone number copied by hand on the first page. In a claim, a phone number to hand is worth more than a perfect policy.
  • Health: each person’s health card, a record of regular medication, known allergies, and the children’s vaccination records. If someone is on a chronic treatment, keep a recent prescription in the health sleeve.
  • Money and utilities: the IBAN of your accounts, mortgage or loan contract, and the latest electricity, water, gas and homeowners’ association fees bill with the customer or contract reference for each service: this is what lets you file a claim or reconnect after an outage without hunting for it in email.
  • Vehicle: registration certificate, vehicle inspection (ITV) card and insurer details. Useful if you need to travel, if the car is damaged, or if they ask for them at a checkpoint during the emergency.
  • Out-of-area contacts: two or three trusted phone numbers outside your city or region. If your area loses network coverage, someone outside can coordinate calls and messages.

The three levels: home, go-bag and cloud

A single format is not enough. Paper survives a phone with no battery and a blackout; the digital copy survives a flooded or smoke-filled house. The emergency folder works by being copied in three places at once:

LevelWhere it livesWhat it contains
PaperWaterproof pouch at home, always in the same placePhotocopies, policies, contracts and essential contacts
PortableEvacuation go-bag or grab-and-go documents bagOriginal identity documents, some cash and the health card
DigitalEncrypted cloud + USB drive stored outside the homeAll documents scanned, named and password-protected

Cash and cards when the power goes out

During the power outage of 28 April 2025, large areas of the country were left without card terminals and with many ATMs out of service for hours. The lesson is not “withdraw a lot of money,” but “have just enough available for two or three days, in small denominations”:

  • Discreet cash: enough for food, fuel and pharmacy for a few days, in small denominations, kept away from original documents. Do not announce it or photograph it.
  • Cards under control: write down each card number and each bank’s customer service phone number in the finance section, or keep them in your encrypted password manager. If you lose your wallet, calling the bank is the first thing to do; having the details to hand cuts the call in half.
  • Two locations for cash: some in your wallet and some in the go-bag or the car. If the emergency catches you away from home, the cash at home does not exist.
  • Sensitive files, never in the gallery: photos of documents and cards go inside a password-protected compressed file or in the phone’s encrypted notes app, not loose in the gallery.

Digital copy: do it right, once

  • Scan each document as a legible PDF, with good light and the full page: if the margin is cut off, it is no use.
  • Name files meaningfully (dni-maria.pdf, poliza-hogar.pdf), not img_4471.jpg. When you need it, you need it now.
  • Store the whole set in the cloud and on a USB drive that is not at home: work, a relative’s house or the car’s glove compartment.
  • Encrypt the package with a password that is not your phone password and write that password on paper, in a place separate from the folder. If you lose both together, the folder protects nothing.

Keep it alive: two reviews a year

An outdated folder is a false folder: it gives you the feeling of being prepared and fails just when you open it. It takes ten minutes and there are two easy dates not to forget:

  • Clock change (March and October): review policies, contracts, phone numbers, and that the minors’ documents are still valid.
  • Start of the school year: update vaccination records, medication and school or work contacts.
  • After any life change: moving house, changing bank, changing utility company or car, update the folder the same day. It is the task everyone postpones and the one you appreciate most later.

Four mistakes that cancel out the effort

  • Everything in a drawer with the clothes: if the clothes get wet, everything gets wet. A waterproof pouch costs little and solves the whole problem.
  • Originals with no copy elsewhere: a sole deed or registration certificate is no use if it is lost with the house.
  • Not digitized: arriving at a registry office or an insurer with nothing on your phone stretches any procedure by several days.
  • Never reviewed: a six-year-old folder with old phone numbers and policies is more misleading than having nothing.

Checklist for this week

  • Seven labeled sleeves or a binder with dividers.
  • Identity photocopies for everyone, including minors.
  • Housing: deed, rental contract or cadastral reference.
  • Insurance with policy number and claims phone number to hand.
  • Health: health card, medication and vaccination records.
  • Finances: IBAN, mortgage and latest bill for each utility.
  • Two contacts outside the region and cash in small denominations.
  • Everything scanned into an encrypted PDF and copied to the USB drive kept elsewhere.

The folder is only one piece: the family emergency plan decides who does what, the 72-hour kit guide assembles the rest, and the first 30 minutes guide orders what you do that same day. If you have to leave home, the evacuation go-bag already includes a waterproof folder and USB drive, and the home kit leaves room to store originals where they won’t get wet. And if you live alone, the living alone checklist gives you the same framework without depending on anyone.

botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.titulo: Emergency first-aid kit: what to actually include (and what's unnecessary) (2026)
botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.resumen: The list of what your family really needs in a health emergency, without unnecessary items. How much of each item, expiry dates and where to buy everything with
botiquin-emergencia-que-llevar.cuerpo:
An emergency first aid kit isn't about having the most items

A useful first aid kit isn't the one packed with 200 pharmacy items: it's the one that contains what your family actually uses, in sufficient quantities, within its expiry date, and within reach when an emergency hits. Most generic supermarket pharmacy kits include the basics and fall short in real emergencies — from a deep cut to an allergic reaction or a fever that won't come down.

In Spain, according to data from the Ministry of Health, more than 60% of calls to 112 are for non-urgent problems that could be resolved with a well-stocked first aid kit. In real emergencies — blackouts, floods, snowstorms — the first aid kit is the first thing people look for.

The essentials: the basics

This is what you CANNOT do without, in quantities sufficient for 72 hours:

What to includeMinimum quantityWhat it's for
Elastic bandages4 unitsImmobilize sprains, secure dressings
Adhesive dressings (various sizes)20 unitsSmall cuts, blisters, superficial wounds
Adhesive bandages20 unitsMinor wounds for children and adults
Sterile gauze (10×10)10 unitsCover medium and large wounds
Hypoallergenic paper tape1 rollSecure bandages and gauze without irritation
Nitrile gloves2 pairsProtect yourself when treating wounds (avoid cross-infection)
Antiseptic (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)2 bottlesClean wounds before covering them
Medical adhesive tape (micropore)2 rollsSecure dressings without sticking to the skin

Medication: what makes the difference

Adhesive bandages alone aren't enough. An emergency without painkillers is unnecessary suffering. According to the Spanish Society of Community Pharmacy, self-medication is the first line of action in 78% of minor cases. The essentials:

  • Paracetamol (tablets or children's syrup): fever, pain. Dose by weight; never exceed 4 g/day in adults.
  • Ibuprofen (400 mg): inflammation + pain (sprains, wound inflammation). Do not take on an empty stomach.
  • Loratadine or cetirizine (tablets): allergic reactions, hives, insect bites. One tablet a day.
  • Oral rehydration solution (sachets): diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration. Essential during DANA or floods where tap water may become contaminated.
  • Antacids (compound tablets): stress gastritis, poor diet during an emergency.
  • Antibiotic ointment (fresomicina): prevent infection in small wounds.

⚠️ Important: if anyone in the family takes long-term medication (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid), include at least 7 days of extra supply. Ask your doctor about the right amount.

What you don't need (and takes up space)

The ideal first aid kit stays lightweight. Avoid these unnecessary items:

  • Digital thermometer (it's expensive and fragile — carry an analog mercury thermometer; it costs 5 € and doesn't break)
  • Instant ice packs (they take up space and expire after 2 years — carry a small towel for cold compresses)
  • Over-the-counter antibiotics (in Spain they have NOT been sold without a prescription since 2021: it is illegal and dangerous)
  • Generic all-purpose products without a clear active ingredient
  • Complete pre-made supermarket first aid kits: they usually include the basics in insufficient quantities (2 adhesive bandages, 1 small bandage) and charge you 60% more for the pretty box

Expiry dates: check every 6 months

The Spanish Agency of Medicines (AEMPS) recommends checking expiry dates every 6 months. Expired medicines don't just lose effectiveness: in some cases (such as tetracyclines) they can produce toxins. Use a mnemonic rule: when the clocks change (March and October), check the first aid kit. Write the review date on an adhesive label inside the box.

ProductUsual expiryAlternative if it expires
Paracetamol3-5 yearsAlways keep 2 extra sachets in another box
Deworming medicines2-3 yearsReplace if the emergency coincides with parasite outbreaks
Antibiotic ointments2-3 yearsPovidone-iodine liquid (expires less quickly)
Oral rehydration solution2-3 yearsHomemade salt and sugar solution (9 g salt + 50 g sugar in 1 L of drinking water)

Kit by family profile

The first aid kit varies depending on who lives with you. Protección Civil gives these recommendations by profile:

Family with babies (0-2 years)

  • Saline solution (nasal spray): 3 extra bottles for congestion and cleaning
  • Children's paracetamol (syrup) with a dosing syringe
  • Emergency diapers (5 units) in case there is no water for changing
  • Thermal protectant for minor burns (hidroagel gel)

Older people

  • Copy of regular medication (at least 7 days of extra supply)
  • Fibrin thrombin powder for wounds that do not close (pressure ulcers)
  • Glucose meter with test strips (if they have diabetes)
  • Moisturizing lip balm (older skin cracks easily)

People with allergies

  • Specific antihistamine (if already prescribed)
  • Anti-mite treatments for covers (prevention)
  • High-protection sunscreen (some medicines increase photosensitivity)

Pets

  • Antiseptic for minor wounds (2% chlorhexidine)
  • Non-adhesive gauze to cover wounds without sticking
  • Collar to restrain an injured animal and prevent bites

Where to buy the whole kit in one go

You don't need to go to three different pharmacies. Here are the searches with everything essential:

Complete basic first aid kit (dressings, bandages, gauze, antiseptics): Search on Amazon →

Emergency medication (paracetamol, ibuprofen, loratadine): Search on Amazon →

Gloves and protective equipment: Search on Amazon →

Oral rehydration solution and electrolytes: Search on Amazon →

The first aid kit inside the 72-hour kit

The first aid kit is not standalone: it is part of the Basic 72-Hour Kit and fits perfectly into the emergency backpack. If your priority is to build the whole kit from scratch, the step-by-step guide walks you through each category.

Remember: the most important thing is not what you carry in the first aid kit, but knowing how to use it. Practice opening the bandages, applying the antiseptic, and putting on a dressing at least once a year. An emergency leaves no room for clumsiness.

How much does it cost to put together an emergency first aid kit?

A well-equipped first aid kit costs between 25 € and 45 € if you buy the components separately at a pharmacy or online. A pre-made supermarket first aid kit can cost the same and include fewer products.

Where should the first aid kit be stored?

In a dry place at room temperature (between 15 and 25 °C), accessible but out of reach of children. Not in the bathroom: humidity speeds up expiry. In the evacuation kit, it goes in the backpack in a waterproof compartment.

How many times a year should it be checked?

Twice a year: in March and October, when the clocks change. It is the ideal time to replace expired items and restock what has been used.

If you found this article useful, share it with anyone who has children or older people at home. Preparedness is a way of caring for those you love most.

apagon-lecciones-28a.titulo: Blackout: lessons from 28 April 2025 in Spain (2026)
apagon-lecciones-28a.resumen: Spain's biggest blackout in history left images of endless queues and dead mobile phones. What we learned, in a practical list.
apagon-lecciones-28a.cuerpo:
On Monday, 28 April 2025, at 12:33, the power went out across the entire Iberian Peninsula. Within minutes, metro systems, traffic lights, ATMs and card terminals stopped working; mobile networks collapsed within hours. For many, it was the first time they saw firsthand why an emergency kit is recommended. These are the lessons.

1. Information is the first thing to disappear

With no mobile phone or television, the only reliable source was a battery-powered or hand-crank radio. Those who had one knew what was happening; those who didn't relied on rumors. If you buy only one thing after reading this, make it the radio.

2. Cash was king again

Without card terminals, only businesses with manual cash registers and cash could operate. Those carrying small notes could buy; those who didn't had to wait. Keep 10-20 € notes at home for 2-3 days.

3. Your phone light isn't enough

Using your phone flashlight for hours drains the battery you need for emergencies. Use a dedicated flashlight or headlamp, with spare batteries. Candles only with extreme care — they are a common cause of fires during blackouts.

4. The elevator is not a game

People were trapped for hours. If you live in a high-rise, assume that during a blackout the stairs are the way; if you have reduced mobility, have a plan agreed with neighbors.

5. Traffic lights don't work: the road belongs to the worst driver

Cities turned into a chaos of unmarked intersections. If you drive during a blackout, treat it as an intersection where traffic from the right has priority and be extra careful.

6. The wait was long

In many areas the power returned within hours, but in others it took all night. A kit designed for 72 hours comfortably covers a national blackout; the 30-day kit covers the extreme case of something like this lasting longer.

The complete list for this scenario is in the blackout kit: radio, light, power, cooking without electricity and cash, in five sections.

almacenar-agua-comida-casa.titulo: How to store water and food at home without it spoiling (2026)
almacenar-agua-comida-casa.resumen: A poorly stored emergency pantry is money down the drain: where, how and in what order to rotate each food so it lasts until the day you need it.
almacenar-agua-comida-casa.cuerpo:
Buying the kit is the easy part. Storing it properly so it still works on the day you need it (sometimes years later) is the part almost everyone gets wrong. These rules apply equally to a bag of rice and a radio:

The three enemies: heat, light, and moisture

The ideal place is cool, dark, and dry: an interior hallway cupboard is usually better than the typical storage room next to the boiler or the terrace. Never directly on the floor (moisture, pests) or next to cleaning products (vapors can contaminate even sealed containers).

Water: the calendar rules

  • Sealed commercial containers: replace every 6–12 months. It is not that water expires: the container degrades and residual chlorine evaporates.
  • Store it away from sunlight and strong odors; plastic absorbs gasoline, bleach, or detergents.
  • If there is advance warning (storm, water outage), fill the bathtub, buckets, and pots: this is non-potable water, perfect for flushing and hygiene.
  • To store your own water long term, use only new food-grade containers with an airtight lid.

Food: first in, first out

  • Write the purchase date on each pack with a marker. Without a date, in six months you will no longer know what is old.
  • Real rotation: use the emergency pantry in your daily life and replenish it when you shop. A reserve that is never eaten gets thrown away; one that is rotated never expires.
  • Approximate shelf life when stored well: cans and jars 3–5 years (or more), rice and pasta 2–3 years, dehydrated/military food 2–5 years, powdered milk 2–3 years sealed. Bars and nuts: much less, about a year.
  • Discard bulging cans, cans rusted at the seams, or cans with deep dents: botulism, non-negotiable.

Inventory every 6 months

The same reminder as for water: check expiration dates, container condition, radio and flashlight batteries, and that the document folder is still complete. Half an hour twice a year keeps your kit alive; without it, in two years you have a storage room full of expired items.

The quantities per person and period are calculated in the 72h kit and in the 30-day kit, with real Amazon prices for each pack.

agua-cuanta-y-como.titulo: Emergency water: how much to store, how to keep it and how to purify it
agua-cuanta-y-como.resumen: 3 litres per person per day: 9 L for 72 h and 36 L for a family of 4. Jerrycans, large containers, tablets or filter: how much, where and how often to replace it.
agua-cuanta-y-como.cuerpo:
Why water is the first thing to run out

A human can go weeks without food, but only 3-5 days without water — and in summer, or if you have to exert yourself (evacuate, salvage belongings), the margin drops to 24-36 hours. In Spain, according to data from Civil Protection, 80% of emergencies affecting households are not natural disasters but supply cuts: DANA storms that contaminate water, blackouts that stop pumps, burst pipes. Water reaches the tap, but when it cuts off, it cuts off.

The European Union Preparedness Strategy (EU Strategy for Risk and Disaster Prevention, updated 2025) recommends that every household keep supplies for at least 72 hours. Water is the heaviest item and the one people most underestimate.

The 3-litre rule: broken down

3 litres per person per day just for drinking. That is the baseline set by the WHO and Civil Protection. But if you want to be realistic:

  • Summer / heat (>30 °C): increase to 4-5 L/person/day. Sweating, thirst and the need to wash your hands (basic hygiene in an emergency without running water) drive consumption up.
  • Winter / mild climate: 3 L are enough if you only consider drinking.
  • Basic hygiene (handwashing, cleaning wounds, rinsing your mouth): add 1-2 L/person/day if tap water is still available for non-drinking use.
  • Toilet cisterns and sinks: if you have advance warning (storm, DANA), fill the bathtub and sinks. That is 100-200 L of reserve for non-food use to flush the toilet and clean.
Situation1 person (72h)2 people (72h)Family of 4 (72h)
Drinking only (winter)9 L18 L36 L
Drinking + hygiene (mild weather)15 L30 L60 L
Summer / heat21 L42 L84 L

A family of 4 needs a minimum of 36-60 litres for 72 hours. That is 8-12 5 L water containers. It is more than most people plan for, and that is why in practice they run out of water on the first day.

How to store it without mistakes

Having water is not enough: you have to store it properly. Water does not expire, but the container does, and a degraded container can contaminate what it holds.

Food-grade water containers (the recommended option)

5-8 L polyethylene containers are the standard. The advantages:

  • They stack well in a cupboard or under the bed (they are not round bottles that fall over).
  • They are reusable — when you change the water every 6 months, empty, rinse and refill.
  • Price: 3-5 € per new 5 L container. 20-30 € for 5 units (which covers a family's basic need).
  • Container shelf life: food-grade plastic lasts between 2 and 5 years. If the container is cloudy, yellowing or cracked, replace it.

Commercial bottled water

Useful for a quick start: a pack of 6x1.5 L or 12x0.5 L can be bought at any supermarket and fits in the kitchen. But they are not the long-term solution: they take up more volume per litre, generate more waste, and PET plastic is less resistant over time.

Water bladders or sealed bags

Water bladders (also called "flexible bladders" or "bag-in-box" of 10-20 L) are the ideal option for large reserves. They take up less space than containers (they stack), are cheap (2-4 € each for 10 L), and you can leave them half full without the material deforming. Ideal for the garage or storage room.

What you should NEVER do

  • Reuse soft-drink or juice bottles to store water: the plastic in those bottles is not designed to hold drinking water long term, and sugar or lactic acid residues feed bacteria.
  • Store containers in the garage in the sun: UV radiation degrades the plastic and transfers flavours to the water. Always a cool, dark place.
  • Leave containers next to cleaning products: solvent vapours can pass through the plastic and contaminate the water.

Renewal: when and how

Stored water is renewed every 6 months. Set a reminder on your phone or stick a label on the cupboard with the date of the last renewal. The mnemonic rule: when the clocks change (March and October), check the containers. Pour out the old water to water plants or clean, and refill with fresh tap water.

If you use water purification tablets (see below), you can extend that window to 12 months, because the chlorine in the tablets keeps the water sterile for longer.

Making water safe to drink: three methods that work

If tap water is available but not safe to drink (a DANA contaminates the supply, for example), you have three options:

1. Boiling (the most reliable)

1 minute of boiling eliminates 99.9% of pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa). The WHO recommends it as a universal method. Drawback: you need fuel (gas, electricity) and the water cools before you can drink it. Ideal as a one-off emergency method, not for maintaining long-term reserves.

2. Water purification tablets (the kit option)

Chlorine (such as ACCUQUICK) or colloidal silver. The process is simple: one tablet per litre, wait 30 minutes, and the water is safe to drink. They take up minimal space (a 50-tablet bottle fits in your pocket), last for years, and are Civil Protection's preferred option as a complement to the emergency kit.

Buying tablets: Search for water purification tablets on Amazon →

3. Water filter (for prolonged emergencies)

Ceramic or membrane filters (such as Berkey or pump filters) remove bacteria and protozoa (but not viruses without additional chlorine). Useful if the emergency lasts more than 72 hours and you have no fuel to boil water. Price: 30-80 €. Drawback: they require maintenance (change the filter every 1000-2000 L) and do not remove heavy metals or chemicals.

Quick comparison

MethodCostTimeAdvantageLimitation
BoilingAlmost 0 €5-10 min/litreRemoves everythingNeeds fuel
Tablets (ACCUQUICK)~2 €/100 units30 min/litreLightweight, long termDoes not filter sediment
Ceramic filter30-80 €ImmediateNo energy, directMaintenance, not viruses

How much water do you need depending on your household?

Not all households consume the same. If you live with:

  • Babies: add 2 L/person/day (infant formula, bottles, cleaning). A 6-month-old baby needs ~200 mL to drink + 500 mL for formula.
  • Pets: a medium-sized dog drinks 1-2 L/day; a cat, 0.3-0.5 L/day. See the pet kit.
  • Older adults: older people have a reduced sense of thirst and can become dehydrated without realising it. Make sure they always have water within reach.

Mistakes everyone makes

1. Not having enough. "There is always tap water" — not when the supply is cut by a burst pipe. A family of 4's 36 L runs out in a day if they are only intended for drinking.

2. Storing water badly. Containers in the sun, next to bleach, or in soft-drink bottles reused for 3 years. The result is plastic-tasting water that cannot be drunk.

3. Forgetting hygiene. In an emergency without running water, washing your hands with soap and water is the number one way to prevent disease. An extra 1-2 L for hygiene is never too much.

4. Not knowing how to purify water. Having 36 litres stored is excellent. But if they become contaminated and you do not know how to purify them, the damage is done. Always keep a bottle of ACCUQUICK tablets or a filter in the kit.

How much does it all cost?

The complete water setup for 72h (family of 4) costs between 25 € and 50 €:

  • 8 x 5 L water containers (new): ~24 €
  • Bottle of 50 ACCUQUICK tablets: ~12 €
  • 1 portable water filter (optional): ~15-30 €

Buying water containers: Search for food-grade water containers on Amazon →

Buying tablets: Search for water purification tablets on Amazon →

Water in the 72h kit

Water is the backbone of any emergency kit. It is part of the Basic 72-Hour Kit, which brings together the 21 verified essentials. If your priority is to have everything ready at once, the DANA kit includes water containers and tablets as part of the setup.

Remember: storing water is not a one-off act — it is a habit. Every 6 months, check. Every clock change, verify. And do not wait for the tap to run dry to realise you have nothing.

Can you drink tap water after a DANA?

It depends. DANAs (isolated high-level depressions) usually contaminate rivers and aquifers with sediment and bacteria, but rarely affect the treatment plant. However, authorities may issue a "do not drink tap water" warning if local pipes become contaminated. Always follow Civil Protection instructions and, if in doubt, boil the water or use purification tablets.

How long does unopened bottled water last?

If it is in a sealed commercial container (factory PET bottle), the water theoretically lasts indefinitely. What degrades is the container: PET becomes brittle over time and with UV radiation. Practical recommendation: change the water every 2 years if it is in an unopened commercial bottle.

Can you purify pond or river water?

Technically yes, but it is not advisable unless strictly necessary. Purification with tablets or boiling removes pathogens, but does not remove heavy metals, pesticides or chemical contaminants. If you have no other option, boil the water (10 min) and then use tablets. As a preliminary step, filter it through clean cloth to remove visible particles.

If you found this article useful, share it with anyone who lives alone or with children. Preparedness is not paranoia: it is responsibility.
